question_text: A 2-year-old boy presents to the ED with shortness of breath in mild distress. His parents state that they were at a movie theater and eating popcorn yesterday evening when the child 'choked' on a bit of popcorn. option_b: Order urgent bronchoscopy to remove foreign body
option_c: Start needle thoracocentesis for tension pneumothorax

explanation:
• The chest x-ray shows hyperinflation of the left side and a mediastinal shift to the right, which should raise suspicion for a foreign body in the left bronchus. Hyperinflation is indicative of partial obstruction.

question_text: A 7-month-old male infant is at his pediatrician's office for his routine check-up and immunizations. He can roll over from his tummy to back but unable to roll over supine to prone. He is passing objects with his hands, and he cannot sit. His nurse mentions this to the pediatrician. This infant has development delay predominantly involving motor domain with history of maternal uncle dying between 15-20 years age, who was bed-ridden prior.

  • Early detection and diagnosis will enable early treatment.
  • Serum Creatine kinase (CK) is the primary biomarker for Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) and often used as a screening test.

question_text: A newborn female develops jaundice at 12 hours of life. Her indirect bilirubin is 21.2 mg/dL. His mother's blood type is AB+; her blood type is A+. Her direct Coombs test is negative. Her CBC shows WBC 15,200/cumm, Hb 10 g/dL, Hct 30%, MCV 98 fL, MCHC 37 g/dL, Platelets 2.75 lac/cumm. What is the next best step?
explanation:
• The patient has hereditary spherocytosis, which can be confirmed by osmotic fragility testing.
  • Osmotic Fragility Test: Spherocytes are more susceptible to lysis in hypotonic solutions. This test measures how easily red blood cells burst when placed in increasingly diluted saline solutions.
  • This patient's jaundice is not consistent with physiologic jaundice given the elevated bilirubin level within the first 24 hours of life. In this setting, with an MCHC of greater than 36 g/dL, the most likely diagnosis is hereditary spherocytosis in the newborn period.Outside the newborn period this typically presents as intermittent jaundice and palpable splenomegaly.

Option A: Neonates with G6PD deficiency can also present with non-physiologic jaundice; however, G6PD deficiency is X-linked and this patient is a female. In addition, the MCHC is normal in patients with G6PD.

Option B: Hemoglobin Electrophoresis is a laboratory technique used to separate and identify different types of hemoglobin in the blood. This test is essential for diagnosing hemoglobin disorders such as sickle cell disease, thalassemias, and hemoglobin variants.

Option C: Reduced UGT1A1 activity leads to elevated bilirubin levels, potentially causing jaundice.

KEY TAKEAWAYS: Hereditary Spherocytosis (HS) is an inherited red blood cell disorder characterized by the presence of spherical-shaped red blood cells (spherocytes) due to defects in the proteins that maintain cell membrane stability. This condition leads to hemolytic anemia as the spleen destroys the abnormal spherocytes more readily than normal red blood cells.

question_text: A preterm neonate could not be started on mother's feed due to some maternal issues. Which among the following is the best alternative to administer in such a case?

DONOR HUMAN MILK

  • Donar human milk [DHM] is the milk expressed and voluntarily donated by lactating women other than the biological mother of the recipient baby.
  • This donor human milk is pasteurized using the Holder pasteurization method [pasteurized donor human milk; PDHM] and dispensed for use of the recipient.

question_text: You are called by the newborn nursery nurse secondary to see a 1-day-old infant vomiting with every feed. The patient takes the formula well but vomits large amounts soon after his feed. The emesis is nonbilious. The only significant history is polyhydramnios during his mother's pregnancy. You obtain an abdominal radiograph and find a large, dilated stomach. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
It is a tough question, but such questions can be answered by ruling out other options easily.

  • Option A- Pyloric stenosis is an acquired condition and would NEVER present in the first few days of life, nor would it be associated with a large stomach at birth and polyhydramnios.
  • Option B- Duodenal webs and atresia would likely present with bilious vomiting.
  • Option C- Jejunoileal atresia would also likely present with bilious vomiting and abdominal distension.
  • Option D- Neonates with pyloric atresia will present with early onset of vomiting that is nonbilious, as well as a dilated stomach at birth. The mother may also have polyhydramnios during her pregnancy.

Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1st SA ed., pg. 1801

question_text: Ajay, a 3-year-old child, is the younger brother of Anuj, who is currently undergoing treatment for diphtheria in the hospital. Ajay lives in the same household and received his diphtheria vaccination 16 months ago. What is the most appropriate course of action for the care of Ajay?
option_b: Nothing, as the child is already exposed
explanation:
Explanation:

Ajay is a household contact of a diphtheria case and should receive erythromycin prophylaxis, even though he is vaccinated and asymptomatic.

  • When a confirmed case of diphtheria is identified, close contacts (like household members) are at risk of asymptomatic carriage or developing the disease.
  • Recommended Management for Asymptomatic Close Contacts (like Ajay):
    • Antibiotic Prophylaxis:
      • Oral erythromycin 40-50 mg/kg/day (max 2 g/day) for 10 days
      • OR single dose of benzathine penicillin G
    • Vaccination Review:
      • Booster only if:
      • Less than 3 doses taken previously
      • No booster in the last 5 years
      • Ajay received his last diphtheria vaccine dose 16 months ago, so he does not need a booster now.
    • Monitoring:
      • Observe for symptoms for 7 days
      • Take cultures if symptoms develop

Explanation of other options:

One booster dose (Option A): Not needed now, as Ajay received a dose within the last 5 years. Boosters are only required if the last dose was ≥5 years ago.

Nothing, as the child is already exposed (Option B): Incorrect, because vaccination does not guarantee full protection, and exposed individuals can still become carriers or symptomatic.

Erythromycin + diphtheria toxoid (Option C): Not indicated in Ajay's case, as diphtheria toxoid is only added if: Immunization is incomplete or last booster was ≥5 years ago

question_text: A 4kg post term baby is delivered at 43weeks of gestation with difficult vaginal delivery. Forceps assistance was needed while delivering the baby. On 15th day mother comes to you with complaint that child moves the right hand significantly less since birth compared to left. Child is otherwise fine, feeding well and gaining weight. What pathology you suspect in this child for the condition?
explanation:
• The child in the question has Erb's palsy.
  • Cause: excessive traction on the head, neck and arm during birth.
  • Risk factors: macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, malpresentation and instrumental deliveries. (in our case, macrosomia and instrumental delivery were present)
  • Duchenne-Erb palsy involves the upper trunks (C5, C6, and occasionally C7) and is the most common type of brachial plexus injury, accounting for approximately 90% of cases.
  • The arm is typically adducted and internally rotated at the shoulder. There is extension and pronation at the elbow and flexion of the wrist and fingers in the characteristic 'waiter's tip' posture.
  • The deltoid, infraspinatus, biceps, supinator, and brachioradialis muscles, and the extensors of the wrist and fingers may be weak or paralyzed.
  • The Moro, biceps, and radial reflexes are absent on the affected side. The grasp reflex is intact.
  • Sensation is variably affected.
  • Diaphragm paralysis occurs in 5% of cases.
  • Option C: Klumpke's palsy, involves C8-T1 with typical Claw hand deformity. Instrumental delivery is a risk factor. It is rarest of the trauma in newborn.
  • Option B: Humerus fracture will be painful and will not show waiter's tip deformity as seen in the image.
  • Option D: Pulled elbow is extended and forearm is pronated. It is generally caused after jerky lifting of the baby and not since birth. It is extremely painful.

question_text: A newborn, born to a diabetic mother, presents after 24 hours with a blood glucose (BG) < 35 mg/dl. The baby is symptomatic. What is the next best step in management?
option_a: Administer an IV bolus of Hartmann's solution
option_c: Administer IV glucose and recheck blood glucose after 20 minutes
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Neonatal hypoglycemia is defined as BG < 45 mg/dl in the first 24 hours, and < 50 mg/dl thereafter.
  • In an infant of a diabetic mother, hyperinsulinemia predisposes to severe hypoglycemia.
  • A symptomatic newborn with BG < 35 mg/dl requires urgent IV glucose therapy.
  • The recommended step is to give IV 10% dextrose (2 ml/kg bolus), followed by continuous glucose infusion, and recheck BG after 20 minutes.
  • This prevents seizures, brain injury, and other complications.

Explanation of other options:

Hartmann solution (Option A): Hartmann (Ringer's lactate) contains electrolytes but no significant glucose content, so it cannot correct hypoglycemia. Giving this delays appropriate therapy and risks neurological injury.

Recheck BG after 20 min (Option B): Simply rechecking without treatment is unsafe in a symptomatic neonate with very low glucose. Immediate correction is essential before monitoring.

Oral feeds and observe (Option D): Oral feeding may help in asymptomatic infants with borderline hypoglycemia, but in a symptomatic baby with BG < 35 mg/dl, this is inadequate and dangerous

question_text: A newborn presents with irritability and cyanosis that improves with crying. On examination, a nasogastric tube cannot be passed, and no mist is seen on laryngeal mirror testing. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient's presentations are suggestive of choanal atresia and the next best step in management is establishing an oropharyngeal airway.

Choanal atresia is the most common congenital anomaly of the nose, characterised by the blockage of the nasal passages due to the complete or partial persistence of the buccopharyngeal membrane or failure of the oronasal membrane to rupture.

Clinical features:

  • Unilateral obstruction:
    • Asymptomatic till the first respiratory infection
    • Unilateral nasal discharge
    • Persistent nasal obstruction
  • Bilateral obstruction:
    • Difficulty in mouth breathing
    • Vigorous attempts to inspire (sucking in of lips)
    • Cyanosis
    • Crying relieves cyanosis
    • Difficulty in feeding
    • Cyanotic while feeding

Management of choanal atresia:

  • Establish an oropharyngeal airway keeping the mouth open or intubate
    • An oropharyngeal airway tube or a feeding nipple with large holes is used
  • Feeding by gavage till the ability to breathe and eat without assistance is gained
  • Bilateral choanal atresia is managed by intubation and sometimes needs tracheotomy
  • Trans nasal repair is the treatment of choice and is done for neonates who are otherwise stable

question_text: A newborn developed an asymmetric Moro reflex after a complicated delivery. The poorly responsive arm hung in adduction, rotated internally at the shoulder, extended and pronated at the elbow, and flexed at the wrist. The most likely affected roots are?
explanation:
The patient described in this case has the classic signs of Erb's palsy, a paralysis of the muscles innervated by the C5-C6 roots.

  • It occurs in approximately 0.6% of all vaginal deliveries; shoulder dystocia is typically diagnosed when there is impaction of the anterior fetal shoulder behind the symphysis pubis.
  • Most such neonates are conservatively managed.

Reference: Avery's diseases of the newborn, 1st SA ed., pg. 1447

question_text: An 8-day-old infant continues to have jaundice which was first noted on the second day of life; his latest total and direct bilirubin levels are 12.5 and 0.9 mg/dL, respectively. The baby and the mother have type O positive blood, the direct and indirect Coombs tests are negative, the infant's reticulocyte count is 15%, and a smear of his blood reveals no abnormally shaped cells. He is bottle-feeding well, produces normal stools and urine, and has gained weight well. Which of the following remains in the differential diagnosis?
explanation:
This is a neonate with unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia and raised reticulocyte count & negative Coombs test.

  • Gilbert syndrome would present with a negative Coombs test, a normal (or low) hemoglobin, a normal (or slightly elevated) reticulocyte count, and prolonged hyperbilirubinemia. Thus, the likely diagnosis is option A.

Regarding other options

  • Option B- Red cell morphology would be abnormal in DIC and the patient will be quite sick. Hence ruled out.
  • Option C- Polycythemia would present with an elevated hemoglobin and would have associated clinical signs. Nothing in the question suggests polycythemia.
  • Option D- Rh isoimmunization would present with a positive Coombs test. And since both mother and baby have O+ve blood group, this is unlikely.

Reference: Avery's diseases of the newborn, 1st SA ed., pg. 1203

question_text: A 2-day-old baby boy is admitted at the neonatal intensive care unit due to high fever with a temperature of 38°C and seizures. Physical examination reveals a newborn baby with wide-set eyes, small mandible, and a cleft palate. On auscultation of the heart, there is a holosystolic ejection murmur at the fourth intercostal space in the midclavicular line. Serum chemistries show severe hypocalcemia. This syndrome is caused by mutant genes found in which of the following chromosomes?
explanation:
Clues in the question include facial dysmorphism, cleft palate, infection causing hospital admission, a likely heart disease and hypocalcemia. These findings together suggest a likely diagnosis of DiGeorge syndrome.

  • Its pathophysiology involves microdeletions of specific DNA sequences, called the DiGeorge chromosomal region (DGCR), from chromosome 22q11.2.
  • DiGeorge syndrome has characteristic features which include cardiac abnormalities, abnormal facies, thymic hypoplasia, cleft palate, and hypocalcemia.
  • It is often called the CATCH22 syndrome because of its characteristic manifestations.
  • Patients with partial DiGeorge syndrome may grow normally but patients who have complete DiGeorge syndrome have a very low immunity and increased susceptibility to infections even with common pathogens.
  • Timely diagnosis is critical since the disease is fatal without treatment.

Reference: Nelson 21st Ed, Table 98.13

question_text: A child was advised yearly vaccination with a vaccine, which is not a part of the national immunization schedule. Yearly vaccination is recommended against?
explanation:
Annual vaccination is given against Influenza Vaccine in selected high-risk groups.

  • The type of influenza vaccine currently marketed for use in India is an inactivated, quadrivalent vaccine.
  • The vaccines are highly immunogenic and safe for use above 6 months of age.
  • The vaccine is not part of the National Immunization Schedule, but recommended by IAP in selected high-risk groups like
    • Chronic cardiac, pulmonary, renal, hepatic or hematological disease
    • Asthma or wheezing in the past one year
    • Chronic diseases like Sickle Cell Anemia, DM, SLE and Morbid Obesity
    • Immunodeficiency
    • Prolonged Aspirin Use
    • Laboratory and Health-Care Workers

This syndrome is caused by mutant genes found in which of the following chromosomes?
explanation:
• The boy presents with common manifestations of DiGeorge syndrome.
  • Its pathophysiology involves microdeletions of specific DNA sequences, called the DiGeorge chromosomal region (DGCR), from chromosome 22q11.2.
  • It is often called the CATCH22 syndrome because of its characteristic manifestations.
  • DiGeorge syndrome has characteristic features which include

Cardiac abnormalities - Interrupted aortic arch, Truncus arteriosus, Tetralogy of Fallot

Abnormal facies - Hypertelorism, Anti mongoloid slant, Folded ears, abnormal philtrum, thin upper lip, Mandibular hypoplasia

Thymic hypoplasia,

Cleft palate,

Hypocalcemia.

  • Patients with partial DiGeorge syndrome may grow normally but patients who have complete DiGeorge syndrome have a very low immunity and increased susceptibility to infections even with common pathogens.
  • Timely diagnosis is critical since the disease is fatal without treatment.

explanation:

question_text: A newborn female develops jaundice at 12 hours of life. Her indirect bilirubin is 21.2 mg/dL. Her mother's blood type is AB+; her blood type is A+. Her direct Coombs test is negative. Her CBC shows WBC 15,200/cumm, Hb 10 g/dL, Hct 30%, MCV 98 fL, MCHC 37 g/dL, Platelets 2.75 lac/cumm. What is the next best step?

question_text: A 1600-g infant was born at 39 6/7 weeks gestation (via spontaneous vaginal delivery) to a 34-year-old woman with a history of chronic hypertension. In the nursery at 2 hours of age, the baby's blood glucose was 24 mg/dL before feeding. After taking 20 mL of age-appropriate formula, the blood glucose increased to 50 mg/dL. What is the most likely cause for the initial hypoglycemia in this infant?
option_c: Increased placental transport of maternal insulin in utero
explanation:
Hypoglycemia is common in small-for-gestational-age (SGA) infants, including the infant in this vignette. Of note, hypoglycemia increases with the severity of intrauterine growth restriction. The risk of hypoglycemia is greatest during the first 3 postnatal days, but fasting hypoglycemia may occur repetitively for several days after birth.

  • This early hypoglycemia usually results from insufficient hepatic and skeletal muscle glycogen content and is exacerbated by the lack of alternative energy sources (because of scant adipose tissue and decreased lactate concentrations).
  • Early enteral feeding usually can prevent hypoglycemia. Less commonly, hyperinsulinemia and/or increased sensitivity to insulin may also contribute to hypoglycemia.
  • This insulin is fetally/neonatally derived, as maternal insulin does not cross the placenta. Finally, deficient catecholamine responses to low blood sugar levels (seen in SGA infants) may also result in persistent hypoglycemia.
  • Increased gluconeogenesis would decrease, not increase, the incidence of hypoglycemia in this infant.

Reference: Cloherty and stark's manual of neonatal care, 8th ed., pg. 910

  • Smears of pustule contents typically show eosinophils. Smears from the pustules of transient neonatal pustulosis typically show neutrophils.
  • Cocci would be seen in bacterial infection and hyphae in cutaneous candidiasis.

question_text: A 2-year-old who has eczema has come for routine check-up. He is noticed to be having pallor. The remainder of his examination is normal. His mother reports that he has been eating bits of carpet from his room recently. Investigations reveal: Hb-6.6 mg/dL; WBC-10.2x10<sup>9</sup>/L; platelet count: 350x10<sup>9</sup>/L; MCV-60 fL (normal: 75-87 fL). What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
• Iron-deficiency anemia is the most likely diagnosis and iron therapy is indicated. The presence of 'pica' strongly suggests iron deficiency.
  • Iron deficiency anemia is a condition in which the body lacks enough iron to produce adequate hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. This deficiency can lead to symptoms such as fatigue, weakness, pale skin, and shortness of breath. One peculiar symptom associated with iron deficiency anemia is pica, a craving for non-nutritive substances, such as ice, clay, dirt, or paper.
  • He may well be a picky eater and survives on cow's milk and little else. In some children anemia can be due to a β-thalassemia trait. The blood parameters should be repeated after a course of treatment and if there has not been a response he should be tested for β-thalassemia trait.

Option A: Dietary advice is required but iron therapy is a must as his anemia is severe.

Option B and D: Macrocytosis is usually seen in vitamin B12 deficiency and folic acid deficiency.

KEY TAKEAWAYS: One peculiar symptom associated with iron deficiency anemia is pica, a craving for non-nutritive substances, such as ice, clay, dirt, or paper.

question_text: Outflow obstruction from the left ventricle is characterized by the following except:
option_a: It may be associated with VSD.
option_b: Subaortic stenosis is almost always recognized in infancy.
option_c: In aortic stenosis, a bicuspid aortic valve is the most common finding.
option_d: Subaortic valvular stenosis is more common in Williams' syndrome.
explanation:
• Left cardiac outflow obstruction can present in different ways. Infants presenting in the first 2-3 weeks of life usually have critical aortic valve stenosis, hypoplastic left heart syndrome or coarctation of the aorta. As the PDA duct starts to close, these babies will become very ill, in shock and heart failure. Emergency support is needed, and valvoplasty (which is not always successful) may save the baby's life - but valvotomy is the definitive treatment in this situation. Initial support should be given, and prostaglandin should be considered to keep the duct open, with correction of acidosis and treatment of the heart failure as an emergency measure.
  • Aortic stenosis normally presents and is symptomatic in teenagers with chest pain and not tolerating exercise. It is usually discovered incidentally when the murmur is found during a routine check. It is most commonly associated with bicuspid aortic valve.
  • Subaortic stenosis is rarely recognized in infancy; rather, it is usually found in children of school age and older. The systolic murmur heard at the base of the heart and on echocardiography is usually helpful in diagnosing subaortic valvular stenosis.

question_text: Which of the following is a true statement about congenital CMV infection?
option_b: Triad of SNHL, intracranial calcifications and enamel hypoplasia
option_c: Most children asymptomatic at birth can develop SNHL later in life
option_d: If mother has IgG positive for CMV, child unlikely to develop infection
explanation:
Let us evaluate the options individually

  • Option A is false. About 10% of congenital CMV are symptomatic
  • Option B is false. There is no such triad described in Congenital CMV
  • Option C is false. 60% of symptomatic & only 5% asymptomatic children at birth can develop SNHL in later life.
  • Option D is true. IgG positive mother has passed on the passive immunity to the child hence it reduces the incidence of infection in the newborn. Primary maternal infection with CMV during pregnancy is the predominant mode in developed countries, like US. In a developing country like India, most maternal infections in pregnancy with CMV are either reactivation or reinfection. Since reactivation or reinfection will have IgG present in the mother as opposed to primary infection, so the risk of fetal infection is more in primary maternal CMV infection (25-30%) compared to that in reactivation or reinfection (1-3%).

question_text: Which of the following is not a suitable method for free flow oxygen delivery to a newborn baby?
option_a: Oxygen tube kept close to the baby's nose and mouth
option_b: Oxygen mask placed over the baby's mouth and nose
option_c: Self-inflating bag attached to an oxygen mask placed over baby's mouth and nose
option_d: A reservoir bag attached to an oxygen mask kept over the baby's nose and mouth
explanation:
Explanation:

A self-inflating bag is specifically designed to provide positive pressure ventilation (PPV) and is not suitable for free-flow oxygen delivery. It delivers higher flow rates and pressures appropriate for resuscitation, unlike the gentle, continuous flow required for free-flow oxygen therapy.

Free-Flow Oxygen Delivery Methods:

  • Oxygen tube near face (blow-by)
  • Oxygen mask over face
  • Oxygen hood
  • Reservoir bag with mask

Self-inflating bag delivers positive pressure ventilation, not free-flow oxygen.

PPV Characteristics:

  • Rate: 40-60 breaths/minute
  • First breath: 30-40 cm H₂O
  • Subsequent: 15-20 cm H₂O
  • Contraindication: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia

Explanation of Other Options:

Keeping an oxygen tube close to the baby's nose and mouth (Option A): Provides free-flow oxygen by directing oxygen near the baby's face, allowing continuous oxygen supply without direct contact with the nose or mouth.

Keeping an oxygen mask over the baby's nose and mouth (Option B): Delivers free-flow oxygen efficiently, ensuring the baby inhales oxygen without requiring active ventilation from the mask.

Using a reservoir bag attached to an oxygen mask over the baby's nose and mouth (Option D): Provides high-concentration oxygen, suitable for free-flow oxygen delivery when higher oxygen levels are needed.

question_text: Which of the following is considered harmful to a newborn in the immediate postnatal period?
option_a: Cleaning the eyes with a wet, sterile swab
option_b: Giving a bath immediately after birth
option_d: Placing the baby on the mother's chest
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Newborns should not be bathed immediately after birth, as it increases the risk of hypothermia, hypoglycemia, and infections due to loss of protective vernix caseosa.
  • WHO recommends delaying the first bath for at least 24 hours (or at least 6 hours if not possible) to promote thermal regulation and early bonding.
  • Hence, giving a bath immediately is harmful in the immediate postnatal period.

Explanation of other options:

Cleaning eyes with a sterile swab (Option A): This is part of essential newborn care to prevent ophthalmia neonatorum and keep the eyes clean. It is not harmful when performed with sterile technique.

Initiating breastfeeding within 1 hour (Option C): Early initiation ensures colostrum intake, improves immunity, and reduces neonatal morbidity. Far from harmful, it is one of the most beneficial interventions.

Placing the baby on the mother’s chest (Option D): Skin-to-skin contact stabilises body temperature, promotes bonding, and stimulates breastfeeding reflexes. It is considered a cornerstone of immediate newborn care.

question_text: A 1-day-old newborn has not passed urine since birth. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
explanation:
Explanation:

If a healthy term neonate has not passed urine within the first 24 hours, the initial management is to continue breastfeeding and observe, as most will void spontaneously soon after.

  • First urine: Normally passed within 12-24 hours after delivery.
  • Early urine: May be concentrated and contain urates, causing orange/pink stains on diapers.
  • Persistent delay beyond 24 hours: Requires evaluation for possible urinary tract obstruction or congenital anomalies.

Conditions causing delayed passage of urine:

  • Posterior urethral valves (PUV)
  • Urethral atresia
  • Ureterocele
  • Urogenital sinus anomaly (females)
  • Spina bifida

Meconium passage:

  • Normal: First meconium (green-black sticky stool) should be passed within 48 hours.
  • Delayed passage seen in:
    • Hirschsprung disease
    • Meconium plug syndrome
    • Imperforate anus
    • Congenital hypothyroidism
    • Neonatal sepsis

Explanation of Other Options:

Admit to NICU (Option B): Required only if the neonate fails to pass urine beyond 24 hours or develops systemic illness/dehydration.

Start artificial feeding (Option C): Indicated only if breastfeeding is inadequate or not feasible (e.g., maternal lactation failure, poor latch).

Start intravenous fluids (Option D): Reserved for cases with signs of dehydration or underlying pathology needing urgent intervention.

Key Takeaways:

  • First urine should occur within 12-24 hours after birth.
  • Continue breastfeeding and observation is the first step in a healthy neonate with delayed urination.
  • Persistent delay (>24 hours) or systemic illness warrants further evaluation for urinary tract obstruction or congenital anomalies.
  • Meconium should pass within 48 hours; delay suggests intestinal obstruction or metabolic/septic causes.

question_text: A newborn presents with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, intrahepatic cholestasis, elevated alkaline phosphatase, and eosinophilic PAS-positive cytoplasmic granules on liver biopsy suggestive of Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. What is the most common cause of jaundice in this scenario?
explanation:
Explanation:

Neonatal hepatitis:

Neonatal hepatitis is the most common cause of conjugated jaundice in newborns and may be associated with:

  • Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia
  • Intrahepatic cholestasis
  • High alkaline phosphatase
  • PAS-positive eosinophilic granules in liver biopsy (seen in Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency subtype)

Etiology includes:

  • Viral: Hepatitis A-E, CMV, HSV, Rubella
  • Metabolic: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, galactosemia, tyrosinemia
  • Immune-mediated: Autoimmune hepatitis, neonatal lupus
  • Drug-induced: Maternal medications (anticonvulsants, antibiotics, NSAIDs)

Explanation of Other Options:

Hypoplasia of biliary tract (Option A):

  • Underdeveloped bile ducts leading to cholestasis
  • Typically shows bile duct proliferation and pale stools
  • Less common than neonatal hepatitis

Choledochal cyst (Option C):

  • Congenital dilation of bile ducts causing extrahepatic obstruction
  • Presents with jaundice and abdominal mass
  • No PAS-positive inclusions; primarily extrahepatic obstruction

Physiological jaundice (Option D):

  • Common, transient, unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia
  • Peaks at 2-4 days in term infants
  • Not conjugated, unlike in this patient

question_text: A newborn delivered at 36 weeks has breathing difficulty which improved with Fi02 30%. Chest X-ray is shown below. What is the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

A 36-week newborn with mild respiratory distress needing only 30 % FiO2 and a chest X-ray showing fluid within the interlobar fissures is most consistent with Transient Tachypnea of the Newborn (TTN).

TTN occurs more often in term or late-preterm infants and is linked to factors such as twin pregnancy, maternal asthma or hypertension, cesarean delivery without labour, precipitous birth, gestational diabetes, fetal macrosomia, and perinatal depression.

The disorder results from incomplete absorption of fetal lung fluid, which lowers lung compliance and hampers gas exchange.

Typical features include rapid breathing soon after birth (rate >60/min) sometimes with mild retractions or expiratory grunting, and any cyanosis usually resolves with low-flow oxygen (<40 %).

Chest imaging commonly reveals prominent perihilar streaking and fluid within the interlobar fissures, with occasional small pleural effusions.

Management is supportive, and most infants improve quickly without long-term problems.

Explanations for other Options:

Hyaline membrane disease (Option A): Usually affects very premature infants (<34 weeks) and causes severe respiratory distress with a reticulogranular "ground-glass" chest X-ray and air bronchograms, not a brief oxygen requirement.

Meconium aspiration syndrome (Option C): Seen mainly in term or post-term babies with meconium-stained amniotic fluid and shows patchy coarse infiltrates and areas of hyperinflation on X-ray, unlike this case.

question_text: Which of the following is true about Congenital CMV Infection?
option_a: Most Common cause of Non-Syndromic SNHL in children
option_c: Confirmation can be done by urine culture or PCR after 4 weeks of age
option_d: In developing countries, primary maternal infection can lead to congenital CMV
explanation:
Let us evaluate each option

  • Option A is true. Congenital CMV is the most common non-syndromic cause of SNHL in children. SNHL can occur in 60% of symptomatic and even 5% asymptomatic patients infected with CMV in utero.
  • Option B is false. Congenital CMV is asymptomatic in 90% cases and symptomatic in 10% cases.
  • Option C is false. Urine culture and PCR are diagnostic, but can identify congenital CMV only in the 1st 3 weeks of age.
  • Option D is false. Primary maternal infection with CMV during pregnancy is the predominant mode in developed countries, like US. In a developing country like India, most maternal infections in pregnancy with CMV are either reactivation or reinfection.
  • Also note that risk of fetal infection is more in primary maternal CMV infection (25-30%) compared to that in reactivation or reinfection (1-3%).

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 285; Cloherty & Stark’s Neonatology 8th Edition

question_text: Which of the following is used to monitor response to therapy in a patient of severe congenital CMV, who is being treated with ganciclovir?
explanation:
Fast detection methods for CMV viremia include: the antigenemia assay for detecting PP65 antigen in polymorphonuclear leukocytes from peripheral blood, polymerase chain reaction (PCR), nucleic acid sequence-based amplification (NASBA), and molecular methods such as branched-DNA signal amplification assay (b-DNA) and hybrid capture. Quantitative PP65 antigen assay performed on blood is a good test for diagnosing CMV disease and monitoring response to antiviral therapy in a high sero-endemic populations.

Reference: Cloherty & Stark’s Neonatology, 8th Edition

question_text: Not a feature of early congenital syphilis?

question_text: A 22-year-old mother presented with her 2-week-old newborn who had a large tongue and an umbilical hernia. Which investigation is most appropriate for newborn screening of congenital hypothyroidism?
option_a: A fresh blood sample and screen first for TSH levels
option_b: A fresh blood sample and screen first for T4 levels
option_c: A dried blood sample and screen first for TSH levels
option_d: A dried blood sample and screen first for T4 levels
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical manifestations indicate congenital hypothyroidism, as evidenced by the large tongue and umbilical hernia.

The screening method for congenital hypothyroidism involves using dried blood spot samples and testing for TSH levels.

  • TSH is a more sensitive and specific marker for detecting hypothyroidism in newborns
  • Elevated TSH levels indicate hypothyroidism, while low or normal TSH levels suggest normal thyroid function
  • Measuring T4 levels alone is not sufficient (Option B and C Ruled Out) for the initial screening of congenital hypothyroidism because T4 levels can be affected by various factors, including stress, illness, and medications
  • Dried blood spot testing is a simple, minimally invasive method to collect a blood sample, allowing for large-scale newborn screening programs where a small amount of blood from a heel prick is readily accessible for analysis. (Option A Ruled Out)

Key Takeaway Points:

question_text: During his 1st physical examination following birth at home with the assistance of a midwife, a 5- week-old male is suspected to have congenital hypothyroidism. His parents refused all newborn screening at the time of his birth. Which of the following may be the earliest clinical sign of congenital hypothyroidism?
explanation:
• Prolongation of physiologic jaundice, due to delayed maturation of glucuronide conjugation, is often the 1st clinical finding in an infant with congenital hypothyroidism.
  • Poor feeding, partly due to a large tongue, somnolence, and lack of interest are characteristic.

question_text: A newborn infant is found at birth to have proximal hypospadias in a short phallus with bilateral nonpalpable gonads. The karyotype is suggestive of XX and the 17-hydroxyprogesterone is elevated. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• Child is genotypic female. Phenotypically child has ambiguous genitals as the phallus is small and gonads are non-palpable. No other signs of shock or distress is mentioned. 17-OHP is elevated. These are suggestive of CAH with 21 hydroxylase deficiency.
  • Mixed gonadal dysgenesisis characterized by a unilateral streak gonad with a contralateral, often dysgenetic, testis (option b). A variant where two dysgenetic testes are present, rather than one dysgenetic testis and a streak gonad, is called partial gonadal dysgenesis. Most of patients have a 45,XO/46,XY karyotype and persistence of Müllerian structures associated with varying degrees of masculinization, including normal male genitalia.
  • Klinefelter syndrome has XXY and Turner has XO karyotype. (option c, d)

question_text: A female newborn is found to have ambiguous genitalia. Work up shows very high 17-hydroxyprogesterone and progesterone levels. Which enzyme deficiency is responsible?
explanation:
A female neonate with ambiguous genitalia is likely to have either 21 hydroxylase deficiency or 11 beta hydroxylase deficiency or 3 beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency.

  • Reason: Nelson 21st Edition Says- The most important problem caused by accumulation of steroid precursors is that in 21 hydroxylase deficiency, 17-hydroxyprogesterone is increased, which is shunted into the pathway for androgen biosynthesis, leading to high levels of androstenedione that are converted outside the adrenal gland to testosterone. This problem begins in affected fetuses by 8-10 wk of gestation and leads to abnormal genital development in females.
  • Please note that in 21 hydroxylase deficiency, there is an elevated level of 17-hydroxy progesterone, which is a screening test for this condition.
  • Hence, the likely enzyme deficiency is 21 hydroxylase deficiency.
  • Note: For better and detailed conceptual understanding, kindly listen to the video discussion of CAH by Dr Sandeep Sharma on Doctutorials App & you will never go wrong in similar questions!!!

question_text: A 4 year old boy is found to be having a large abdominal mass on routine examination. What is the next most common differential for malignant etiology in this child after nephroblastoma?
explanation:
• Most common cause of renal mass in a preschool child is Nephroblastoma. Other renal causes of an abdominal mass include polycystic kidney disease and hydronephrosis.
  • The most common malignant differential diagnosis of an abdominal mass in a preschool child is neuroblastoma, which may also present with hypertension, abdominal pain or fever.
  • Neuroblastoma is associated with periorbital ecchymosis (dark circles under the eyes), an abdominal mass which crosses the midline, and signs of bone marrow infiltration.

KEY TAKEAWAYS: Most common cause of renal mass in a preschool child is Nephroblastoma.

question_text: A newborn baby has recently been delivered. The midwife requests an urgent pediatric review of the baby because she cannot tell if the baby is male or female. The parents are asking what sex their baby is. What should you tell them?
option_a: You are unable to tell if the baby is male or female, and tell the parents it is likely to be a mixture of both sexes, i.e. ovo-testicular disorder of sex development (DSD - or hermaphroditism).
option_b: You are unable to tell right now and a detailed assessment of the baby including scans and blood tests will be needed before a specialist can tell them
option_c: You are unable to tell right now but will be able to assign a sex as soon as you get the baby's chromosomes back
option_d: You think it is likely to be a girl so tell them the baby should be named as a female on the birth certificate pending the results
explanation:
• A detailed assessment by medical, surgical and psychological specialists needs to be performed followed by a full discussion with the parents before the infant is assigned a sex.
  • Sexuality is complex, and depends on more than the baby's phenotype, chromosomes and hormone levels.
  • If there is abnormal sexual differentiation at birth, do not guess the infant's gender. A detailed assessment needs to be performed.
  • Ovo-testicular DSD is extremely rare. It is usually possible to assign the infant a sex after assessment of phenotype, sex hormones and ultrasound scans of internal structures and gonads are performed.

question_text: Parenteral nutrition is instituted for a 4-day-old infant who has a total bilirubin of 18 mg/dL and a direct bilirubin of 3.0 mg/dL. Which one of the following macronutrients in the parenteral nutrition should be restricted in this patient?
explanation:
Option B: Reason for Restriction: Infusion of lipids displaces bilirubin from albumin, increasing the risk of kernicterus.

Infusion Guidelines: Lipids should be administered at a low rate to prevent essential fatty acid deficiency while minimizing bilirubin displacement.

Why not other options:

Option A: Carbohydrate: Carbohydrates do not significantly impact bilirubin levels and are necessary for energy, so they should not be restricted.

Option C: Protein: Proteins are essential for growth and development, and while they can affect bilirubin indirectly, they are not typically restricted in this context.

Option D: Vitamin: Vitamins are necessary for various metabolic processes and are not directly related to bilirubin metabolism, so they do not need to be restricted.

Key takeaways:

In infant with elevated bilirubin levels, fat should be restricted in parenteral nutrition, as it displaces bilirubin from albumin, increasing the risk of kernicterus.

Tags: Good to know

Level: Good to know

Tag: Bilirubin metabolism

question_text: A G2P1 delivered a preterm baby at 36 weeks. The baby was admitted to the NICU and given expressed breast milk. Unfortunately, the baby did not survive. What is used to reduce pain and engorgement of the lactating breast in this case?
explanation:
Explanation:

Cabergoline is a potent dopamine D2 receptor agonist with minimal activity at D1, 5-HT, and α-adrenergic receptors. It inhibits prolactin secretion and thereby suppresses lactation, making it useful when lactation must be prevented-for instance, after fetal loss or when breastfeeding is not intended or possible.

As the drug of choice for prolactinoma, cabergoline acts specifically on pituitary lactotroph D2 receptors to reduce prolactin release. Its long half-life (approximately 65 hours) allows for lower dosing and better tolerability, which is why it has largely replaced bromocriptine.

Explanation of other options:

Pramipexole (Option A) and ropinirole are mainly used in the management of Parkinson's disease. They are D2-like receptor agonists with strong affinity for the D3 receptor subtype, though they are less effective than L-DOPA in the early stages of therapy.

Chlorpromazine (Option B), an antipsychotic, can elevate prolactin levels and is therefore inappropriate for inhibiting lactation.

Sumatriptan (Option C) is used for migraine treatment and has no influence on prolactin secretion or lactation.

Key Takeaways:

  • Cabergoline → D2 agonist → inhibits prolactin → stops lactation.
  • Long-acting, better tolerated than bromocriptine.
  • Avoid dopamine antagonists (e.g., chlorpromazine).

question_text: A 14 year old boy has fevers. He has had elbow , shoulder and hip and knee pains over the last few months. On examination, he has a temperature of 37.5°C and palpable hepatosplenomegaly. Investigations show a CRP of 30 and negative ANA. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Any arthritis that occurs in individuals < 16 years of age of unknown etiology is termed as Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis.there are 6 types of JIA.

  1. Oligoarticular
  2. Polyarticular Rheumatoid factor positive
  3. Polyarticular Rheumatoid factor negative
  4. Systemic onset
  5. Psoriatic arthritis and
  6. Enthesitis related arthritis.

Systemic onset JIA.

It is characterised by

  1. Fever
  2. Evanescent rash
  3. Hepatosplenomegaly
  4. Generalized Lymphadenopathy
  5. Serositis

They are prone for developing a life-threatening complication called Macrophage Activation Syndrome.

They will be negative for ANA and RA factor. There will be anemia, raised ESR and CRP with transaminase elevation. Ferritin may be elevated and coagulation screen may be abnormal.

Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch:58, Pg: 394

question_text:
Which of the following children are considered at-risk babies?
1. Baby with a birth weight of 2.5 kg
2. Baby on artificial feeding
3. Baby of working mother/single parent
4. Baby with weight <85% of expected weight
5. Birth order of 3 or more
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Among the given options, babies on artificial feeding and those with a working mother or single parent fall under the "at-risk" category.
  • These infants are more vulnerable to malnutrition, infection, and inadequate care, requiring closer monitoring.

Criteria for At-Risk Infants:

  • Low birth weight (<2.5 kg).
  • Twins
  • Higher birth order (≥5).
  • Artificial feeding.
  • Weight <70% of expected weight.
  • Failure to gain weight for 3 consecutive months.
  • Children with PEM or recurrent diarrhea.
  • Babies of working mothers or single parents.

These risk factors are used to identify infants who need special attention to reduce morbidity and mortality.

Key Takeaways:

  • At-risk infants include those with low birth weight, artificial feeding, PEM, frequent diarrhea, high birth order, and social risk factors.
  • Early identification allows for targeted interventions to reduce neonatal and infant mortality.

question_text: A 2700-gram, term baby, well and exclusively breastfed, was found to be icteric with a TSB of 14 mg/dl on day 5 of life. What is the management?
explanation:
Ideally decision to start phototherapy or exchange transfusion depends on American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) Charts.

Practically, the following cut-offs are often used as a ready reckoner

  • Age 24 hr- Cut-off of TSB to start PT is 10 mg/dl or more
  • Age 48 hr- Cut-off of TSB to start PT is 13 mg/dl or more
  • Age 72 hr- Cut-off of TSB to start PT is 15 mg/dl or more
  • Age 96 hr and beyond- Cut-off of TSB to start PT is 18 mg/dl or more

Reference: AIIMS Neonatal Protocols; Avery's diseases of the newborn, 1st SA ed., pg. 1152

question_text: What is the therapy of choice in asymptomatic baby born to pregnant female who gets chicken pox one day prior to delivery?
option_a: Only Acyclovir to mother and baby
option_b: VZIG to both mother and baby but no acyclovir to be given
option_c: VZIG to baby + Acyclovir to mother as well as baby
option_d: Nothing active needed since child is asymptomatic
explanation:
Mortality is particularly high in neonates born to susceptible mothers who contract varicella around the time of delivery.

  • Infants whose mothers demonstrate varicella in the period from 5 days prior to delivery to 2 days afterward are at high risk for severe varicella. These are labelled as Neonatal Varicella Syndrome.
  • These infants acquire the infection transplacentally as a result of maternal viremia, which may occur up to 48 hr prior to onset of maternal rash.
  • The infant's rash usually occurs toward the end of the 1st wk to the early part of the 2nd wk of life (although it may be as soon as 2 days).
  • Because the mother has not yet developed a significant antibody response, the infant receives a large dose of virus without the moderating effect of maternal anti-VZV antibody.
  • Newborns whose mothers develop varicella during the period of 5 days before to 2 days after delivery should receive VZIG as soon as possible after birth.
  • Because perinatally acquired varicella may be life threatening, the infant should usually be treated with acyclovir (10 mg/kg every 8 hr IV) when lesions develop.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 280

question_text: All of the following are true regarding management of chicken pox, except
option_b: Antipruritic agents like Cetirizine can be safely given
option_c: Acyclovir should be started within 24-48 hr of rash for optimum efficacy, if indicated
option_d: Acyclovir is unsafe in neonates with suspected varicella
explanation:
Management of Chicken Pox/Varicella

  • Management is symptomatic and includes antipyretics
  • Aspirin is contraindicated due to risk of Reye syndrome and ibuprofen due to risk of necrotizing fasciitis
  • Antipruritic agents and good hygiene are important.
  • The child should not attend school until no new lesions appear and all lesions have crusted.
  • Administration of oral acyclovir (20 mg/kg/ dose four times a day for 5 days) within 24 hours of onset of rash in healthy children reduces the duration of rash by one day and lesions by 25%. There may be some benefit even if started within 24-48 hours of the rash but none beyond 48 hours. However, acyclovir is generally not needed in immunocompetent children.
  • IV acyclovir (10 mg/ kg every 8 hours for 14 days) is recommended for patients with complicated varicella and illness of any severity in high-risk patients such as neonates and immunocompromised children.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 232

question_text: Which mechanism of phototherapy is chiefly responsible for reduction in serum bilirubin?
explanation:
Phototherapy (PTx) remains the mainstay of treating hyperbilirubinemia in neonates.

  • PTx is highly effective and carries an excellent safety track record of over 50 years.
  • It acts by converting insoluble bilirubin (unconjugated) into soluble isomers that can be excreted in urine and feces.
  • The most important mechanism is by Structural isomerization, where bilirubin gets converted into Lumirubin.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 174

question_text: You are planning to discharge a neonate & explain danger signs to the parents, counselling them to bring the child to hospital if the baby develops any of these signs. The danger signs will include all of the following except?
explanation:
Neonates can normally pass 6-8 stools in 24 hr and so passing >4 stools in 24 hr is not considered a danger sign.

  • Danger Signs Include
    • Temperature <35.5° C or >37.5° C
    • Fast breathing with a RR ≥ 60/min
    • Severe Chest indrawing
    • Poor feeding
    • Convulsions
    • Lethargy- Movement only when the baby is stimulated
    • Yellow palms and soles indicating severe hyperbilirubinemia

question_text: A 31-week-old neonate was delivered via LSCS. Which among the following surfactant strategies shall be useful in such a neonate?
option_d: No role of surfactant since baby is >28 weeks
explanation:
Types of surfactant administration in RDS or suspected RDS in preterm neonates

  • Prophylactic surfactant:- Surfactant is administered within 15-30min of birth, irrespective of the signs of RDS. Prophylactic surfactant therapy should be used with caution as recent evidence suggests an increased risk of BPD/ mortality compared to selective surfactant administration. It may be considered only in neonates born before 28 weeks of gestation with no/incomplete antenatal steroids or required intubation and mechanical ventilation immediately after birth.
  • Early rescue:- Surfactant is administered in an infant with features of RDS within 2 hours. Early administration of surfactant is advantageous as the presence of lung fluid helps in the uniform distribution of the surfactant. It also ensures the surfactant is administered before widespread atelectasis develops in the lungs. Early rescue surfactant therapy following a trial of CPAD is preferred over prophylactic treatment because it reduces the amount of surfactant used with comparable immediate outcomes.
  • Late rescue:- Surfactant is administered in an infant with features of RDS after 2 hours. It is usually done in outborn neonates who are transported late to referral centers.

Reference: AIIMS Neonatal Protocols 3rd Edition, Volume 2, Pages 453-454

question_text: A neonate was resuscitated successfully but found to develop hypovolemic shock. What is the next step in management?
option_a: Wait for shock to spontaneously improve
explanation:
Some neonates can develop hypovolemic shock in the post-resuscitation phase or during resuscitation owing to excessive blood loss during birth. For such neonates, volume expansion using 10 ml/kg of Normal Saline given over 5-10 minutes is the preferred initial therapy. If there is visible blood loss, consider giving O-ve PRBC transfusion. In neonates, Normal Saline is usually preferred over Ringer's Lactate.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 121; IAP 2022 Guidelines, NRP 8th Edition Guidelines

question_text: What is the cut-off to define apnea in a neonate?
explanation:
Apnea in neonates

  • Defined as Stoppage or Cessation of breathing for ≥ 20 seconds in a neonate.
  • Cessation of breathing for lesser duration is also considered apnea, if associated with bradycardia or cyanosis
  • Most common cause of apnea in preterm neonates is Apnea of Prematurity (AoP)

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 122

question_text: A child aged less than 1 yr of age is suspected to have an asthma-like illness and so was decided to start on therapy. Which of the following devices can be used in this child?
explanation:
Using Metered Dose Inhaler (MDI) with spacer to administer drugs via inhalational route has multiple advantages, like not requiring coordination with inspiration and have rapid onset of action of the drugs. However, for use below 2 to 3 years of age, we need to use MDI with spacer with a face mask.

Summary

  1. Child < 4 yr age: MDI with spacer with facemask
  2. Child 4 yr and above: MDI with spacer
  3. Child >12 yr: MDI alone is sufficient. Spacer may or may not be used.

question_text: See the picture below and tell the likely diagnosis if child has muscular dystrophy, facial weakness and characteristic facies as shown?
explanation:
Facial weakness, inverted V-shaped upper lip, and loss Facial weakness, inverted V-shaped upper lip, and loss of muscle mass in the temporal fossae are characteristic of myotonic muscular dystrophy type 1, also known as Dystrophica myotonia.

  • Posterior cataracts and endocrinopathies are also commonly seen
  • Arrhythmias and reduced GIT motility are persistent problems.
  • Myotonia is absent in neonates and infants.

question_text: Which of the following microorganism is the most common cause of aplastic crisis in Sickle Cell Anemia & Hereditary Spherocytosis?
explanation:
Human Parvovirus B19, also written as B19V, is notorious for aplastic crisis in chronic hemolytic states.

  • Individuals with chronic hemolytic anemia and increased red blood cell (RBC) turnover, including Sickle Cell Anemia & Hereditary Spherocytosis, are very sensitive to minor perturbations in erythropoiesis.
  • Infection with B19V leads to a transient arrest in RBC production and a precipitous fall in serum hemoglobin, often requiring transfusion.
  • The reticulocyte count drops to undetectable levels, reflecting the lysis of infected erythroid precursors.
  • Humoral immunity is crucial in controlling infection. Specific immunoglobulin (Ig) M appears within 1-2 days of infection and is followed by anti-B19 IgG, which leads to control of the infection, restoration of reticulocytosis, and a rise in serum hemoglobin.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 278

question_text: A  child with an underlying malignancy developed tumour lysis syndrome. Which among the following is the most likely such malignancy?
explanation:
Tumour lysis syndrome (TLS) is characterized by hyperuricemia, hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, and hypocalcemia and is caused by the destruction of a large number of rapidly proliferating neoplastic cells. Acidosis may also develop. Acute renal failure occurs frequently.

  • TLS is most often associated with the treatment of Burkitt's lymphoma, acute lymphoblastic leukemia, esp T-cell ALL and other rapidly proliferating lymphomas, but it also may be seen with chronic leukemias and, rarely, with solid tumors.
  • Manifestations occur 12-72 hours after starting chemotherapy but can rarely occur even prior to therapy.
  • This is an oncological emergency requiring hospitalization and extensive management.
  • Please note that CLL does not occur in children.

Reference: AIIMS PICU Protocols 2022, Pages 260-261; Harrison 21st Edition, Pages 573-574

question_text: All of the following are true regarding pediatric intubation, except?
option_a: Uncuffed tube is better than cuffed tube in a child aged 1 year
option_b: A 4 mm size cuffed ET tube is ideal in a 4 year old child
option_c: Depth of insertion of ET tube in a 4 year old child should be 14 cm
option_d: High cuff pressure >25 cm H20 in a cuffed ETT can cause airway necrosis
explanation:
Let us see all options individually

  • Option A is false. Only in neonates, we prefer an uncuffed tube. Beyond the neonatal period, cuffed tubes are better than uncuffed tubes. They ensure better pressure delivery in patients with poor lung compliance, prevent peritubal leakage and prevent aspirations. Thus a cuffed tube should be used in a child aged 1 year.
  • Option B is true. For an uncuffed tube, ET tube size (in mm)= (Age in yr/4) + 4. So in a 4 year old child, ideal size of uncuffed tube is 5 mm internal diameter tube. Now, we also know that size of cuffed tube to be taken is always 0.5 to 1 mm less than uncuffed tube. Hence the cuffed ET tube size to be used here will be 5 mm - 1 mm = 4 mm size Cuffed ET Tube
  • Option C is true. Depth of insertion in cm = (Age in yr/2) + 12. So it comes out to be 14 cm in a 4 year old child.
  • Option D is true. Cuff pressure in a cuffed ETT should always be kept below 20 to 25 cm H20 to prevent airway necrosis.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 765

question_text: A Child presents with absent femoral pulses with increased blood pressure in the upper limbs and dilated intercostal arteries. Best diagnosis is?
explanation:
The clinical picture is compatible with a diagnosis of Coarctation of aorta (CoA).

  • CoA refers to narrowing or constriction in the aorta.
  • The classic sign of coarctation of the aorta is a disparity in pulsation and BP in the arms and legs.
  • The femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial, and dorsalis pedis pulses are weak (or absent in up to 40% of patients), in contrast to the bounding pulses of the arms and carotid vessels. The radial and femoral pulses should always be palpated simultaneously for the presence of a radial-femoral delay. Normally, the femoral pulse occurs slightly before the radial pulse. A radio-femoral delay occurs when blood flow to the descending aorta is dependent on collaterals, in which case the femoral pulse is felt after the radial pulse.
  • In normal persons (except neonates), systolic BP in the legs obtained by the cuff method is 10-20 mm Hg higher than that in the arms. In coarctation of the aorta, BP in the legs is lower than that in the arms; frequently, it is difficult to obtain. This differential in BPs is common in patients with coarctation who are older than 1 yr, approximately 90% of whom have systolic hypertension in an upper extremity >95th percentile for age.
  • One site of collateral formation is in the intercostal arteries, which are often dilated and in untreated CoA patients beyond 8-10 years, produces the inferior rib notching sign.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 454.6

question_text:
Choose the correct statement regarding physiological jaundice in neonates
A. It is caused by inadequate hepatic conjugation capacity
B. It is caused by increased lysis of RBCs
C. Threshold for starting phototherapy is higher in pre-term babies
D. Caput succedaneum is a risk factor
explanation:
• The exaggerated physiological jaundice in neonates is a result of increased RBC lysis along with low hepatic capacity to conjugate the increased bilirubin load.
  • In pre term babies the threshold for starting the phototherapy and exchange transfusion is lower due to increased risk of neuronal damage at low bilirubin levels. (statement c)
  • Cephalhematoma is a known risk factor for jaundice due to lysis of RBC accumulated in the lesion. (statement d)

question_text: A 2-year-old child presents with a scrotal swelling since birth, which has recently become painful, red, and irreducible. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The key clinical features are: long-standing scrotal swelling, which becomes acutely painful, red, tender, and irreducible.
  • This is a surgical emergency requiring immediate intervention to prevent bowel necrosis.

Explanation of other options:

question_text: Children easily get dehydrated. What is the difference in the ECF and ICF ratio compared to that of adults?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • In neonates, extracellular fluid (ECF) volume is higher than intracellular fluid (ICF)
  • By around 3 months of age, ECF and ICF volumes become approximately equal.
  • After 3 months, ICF gradually increases and stabilizes by 1 year of age.
  • Even after stabilization, the ECF remains relatively higher in infants compared to adults when considering the ECF:ICF ratio.

Explanation of other options:

ICF is higher than ECF (Option A):

  • This is true for adults but not for neonates or infants.
  • In neonates, ECF is greater than ICF at birth and equalizes around 3 months of age.

Total body water is high (Option B):

  • While it is true that neonates have a higher total body water content (~75%) compared to adults (~60%), this does not specifically explain the ECF-to-ICF ratio difference.

ECF is equal to ICF (Option D):

  • This occurs around 3 months of age, but at birth, ECF is higher than ICF.
  • Even after 3 months, ECF remains slightly higher than ICF compared to adults.

Key Takeaways:

In neonates, ECF is higher than ICF, making them more susceptible to fluid loss and dehydration.

question_text: A 2-week-old infant presents with high conjugated (direct) bilirubin, dark-colored urine, and clay-colored stools. On examination, the infant is jaundiced but feeds normally. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Biliary atresia is the most common cause of neonatal cholestasis.
  • It presents in the first weeks of life with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, dark urine (due to bilirubinuria), and pale/clay-colored stools (due to absent bile pigments in the intestine).
  • The infant usually appears otherwise healthy and feeds well, which can delay diagnosis.
  • Early recognition is critical because untreated cases progress to cirrhosis and liver failure, and surgical correction (Kasai portoenterostomy) is needed.

Explanation of other options:

Gilbert's syndrome (Option B): Causes mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, often in adolescents or adults, not infants; urine and stool colour remain normal.

Crigler-Najjar syndrome (Option C): A disorder of unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia due to UDP-glucuronyl transferase deficiency, not associated with dark urine or pale stools.

Physiological jaundice (Option D): Common in newborns but involves unconjugated bilirubin, appears on day 2-5, and resolves by 2 weeks; stools and urine remain normal.

  • Splenic sequestration is managed with a packed red cell transfusion, as is an aplastic crisis.
  • Dactylitis is a form of VOC.
  • Chronic exchange transfusional programs to keep HbS < 30% may be necessary after an acute CNS event or in cardiomyopathy.

question_text: Which is NOT a feature of cystic fibrosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Biliary atresia is not a feature of cystic fibrosis (CF). CF can lead to liver disease and biliary cirrhosis due to thick, obstructive bile secretions, biliary atresia is a congenital absence or malformation of the bile ducts, causing severe neonatal jaundice and progressive liver damage, and occurs independently of CF.

Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR gene on chromosome 7q31.2, with the most common mutation being ΔF508, resulting in a defective CFTR protein that disrupts chloride and water transport across epithelial surfaces.

Defective chloride transport → thick mucus → obstruction

Clinical Features of Cystic Fibrosis

question_text: A 3-month-old infant presents to the pediatric OPD with complaints of persistent jaundice and pale (clay-colored) stools. On examination, hepatomegaly is noted. Laboratory investigations show conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, and liver biopsy reveals periductal proliferation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Biliary atresia presents in infancy with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, clay-colored stools, and shows periductal proliferation on liver biopsy.

  • Biliary atresia is a progressive fibro-obliterative disease of the extrahepatic biliary tree, often presenting in the first 2-6 weeks of life.
  • The key clinical features include:
    • Persistent jaundice
    • Acholic (clay-colored) stools
    • Dark urine
  • The histological hallmark is periductal fibrosis and bile duct proliferation, seen on liver biopsy.
  • Types:
    • Perinatal type (70%): No associated anomalies
    • BASM syndrome (15%): Includes Biliary atresia, Asplenia/polysplenia, Situs inversus, and other anomalies
    • Other syndromic associations (15%): Choledochal cysts, renal malformations
  • Investigations:
    • LFTs: Elevated conjugated bilirubin and cholestatic enzymes (ALP, GGT, 5'-nucleotidase)
    • Ultrasound: Absent gallbladder, "triangular cord sign"
    • HIDA scan: No tracer excretion despite phenobarbitone priming
    • Liver biopsy: Gold standard, shows periductal fibrosis and bile duct proliferation
    • Exploratory laparotomy with intraoperative cholangiogram: Confirmatory test
  • Management:
    • Kasai portoenterostomy (hepaticojejunostomy) within 8 weeks
    • Definitive treatment: Liver transplant

Explanation of other options:

Crigler-Najjar syndrome (Option A): Caused by glucuronyl transferase deficiency → results in unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. No periductal changes on biopsy.

Rotor syndrome (Option B): Caused by defects in hepatic organic anion transporters (SLCO1B1/1B3) → mild conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with normal liver histology.

Dubin-Johnson syndrome (Option C): Mutation in MRP2 gene → benign conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. The liver appears black grossly due to pigment deposition, but no bile duct proliferation.

question_text: Dystrophin protein is absent completely in which of the following diseases?
explanation:
Explanation:

Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD) is a genetic disorder caused by mutations in the dystrophin gene, resulting in the complete absence of the dytrophin protein.

Duchene muscular dystrophy

  • Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is the most common hereditary neuromuscular disease affecting all races and ethnic groups.
  • The incidence is 1 in 3,600 liveborn infant males.
  • This disease is inherited as an X-­ linked recessive trait.
  • Clinical features
    • Progressive weakness
    • Intellectual impairment
    • Hypertrophy of the calves, with proliferation of connective tissue and progressive fibrosis in muscle.
  • Becker muscular dystrophy (BMD) is a disease that is fundamentally similar to DMD, with a genetic defect at the same locus.
  • The phenotypic variation is explained by the reading frame hypothesis.
  • In more than 90% of cases, mutations that disrupt the reading frame (frameshift mutations) result in dystrophin deficiency and cause Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD).
  • In contrast, in Becker muscular dystrophy (BMD), the mutations preserve the reading frame (in-frame mutations), producing an abnormal but partially functional dystrophin protein.
    • Thus, BMD clinically it follows a milder and more protracted course.

Explanation of other options:

Myasthenia gravis (MG) (Option C): A chronic autoimmune disease of the neuromuscular junction (postsynaptic end plate) that leads to abnormal neuromuscular transmission or blockade.

Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (Option D). In LEMS, autoantibodies target voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCCs) on presynaptic nerve terminals. This leads to a reduction in acetylcholine release, which causes muscle weakness. Blockade of presynaptic calcium channels at the neuromuscular junction is characteristic of LEMS.

question_text: Vitamin K supplementation is given to neonates to prevent:
explanation:
Explanation:

Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting, and its deficiency can lead to hemorrhagic disease of the newborn (VKDB).

Hemorrhagic disease of the newborn

  • Three forms: early, late, and drug-induced.
  • Early VKDB, occurring within the first 1-14 days of life, is typically seen in breastfed infants due to insufficient vitamin K at birth (very low placental transfer), as well as limited intake in the first days and the sterile newborn gut that lacks vitamin K production.
  • Late VKDB usually develops between 2-12 weeks, mostly in breastfed infants, and can be exacerbated by malabsorption conditions like cystic fibrosis or liver disease.
  • The third form results from maternal use of medications such as warfarin that affect vitamin K function.
  • In older children and adults, vitamin K deficiency may arise from fat malabsorption disorders or the use of broad-spectrum antibiotics.
  • Prophylaxis with vitamin K supplementation is critical to preventing these conditions, especially in infants.

Prevention of Early VKDB:

  • Administer oral or parenteral vitamin K shortly after birth.

Prevention of Late VKDB:

  • A single intramuscular (IM) dose of 1 mg of vitamin K is most effective.
  • Oral vitamin K does not effectively prevent late VKDB.

VKDB due to Maternal Medications:

  • Discontinue maternal medications before delivery, if possible.
  • If discontinuation is not possible, administer vitamin K to the mother.
  • Neonate should receive IM vitamin K immediately after birth.
  • If coagulopathy persists, fresh frozen plasma (FFP) may be needed.

High-risk children (e.g., malabsorption):

  • Provide supplemental vitamin K.
  • Monitor prothrombin time (PT) periodically.

Explanation of other options:

Breast milk jaundice (Option A): Occurs due to substances in breast milk (FFA and beta glucuronidase) that decrease bilirubin conjugation or glucuronidase action. It usually requires no treatment.

Keratomalacia (Option C): Keratomalacia is an ocular disorder characterized by drying and clouding of the cornea, resulting from vitamin A deficiency.

Scurvy (Option D): Scurvy results from vitamin C deficiency.

question_text: Which amino acid does not need to be restricted in diet in MSUD?
explanation:
Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD)

  • AR inheritance
  • Defect in decarboxylation of branched chain Amino acids Valine,Leucine & Isoleucine.

Cause: Low activity of enzyme Branched Chain Alpha Ketoacid Dehydrogenase (BCKA) complex

  • Presents in neonates as poor feeding, dehydration, acidosis, cerebral depression
  • Maple syrup urine dour

Test: Raised serum levels of BAAs(Branched Amino Acids)

In Urine Adding 2,4-DNPH forms yellow-white precipitates.

  • Rx: Hemodialysis/Peritoneal dialysis

Dietary restriction of Branched chain amino acid rich foods.

  • Thiamine supplementation is effective in some cases.

Incorrect Options:

  • Leucine: Leucine is one of the branched-chain amino acids that need to be restricted in the diet of individuals with MSUD. Due to the BCKAD enzyme deficiency, leucine cannot be properly metabolized, leading to toxic accumulation in the blood and urine.
  • Isoleucine: Isoleucine, like leucine, is a branched-chain amino acid and needs to be restricted in the diet of MSUD patients due to impaired metabolism caused by the enzyme defect.
  • Valine: Valine is another branched-chain amino acid that must be restricted in the diet of MSUD patients, as it too accumulates due to the deficient BCKAD enzyme activity.

Key Takeaway:

  • Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD)involves a defect in the metabolism of branched-chain amino acids(leucine, isoleucine, and valine), requiring dietary restriction of these amino acids.
  • Methionine, being a non-branched-chain amino acid, does not need to be restricted in the diet of MSUD patients.
  • Treatment includes dietary management (restricting BCAAs) and sometimes hemodialysisor peritoneal dialysis for acute episodes, as well as thiamine supplementation, which may be effective in some cases.

Reference: Nelson textbook of paediatrics

question_text: Perinatal infection presenting with anemia, possible myocarditis, high-output cardiac failure, and ascites is most likely caused by which pathogen?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical features described - anemia, myocarditis, high-output cardiac failure, and ascites in the context of hydrops fetalis - are characteristic of Parvovirus B19 infection. This virus is the causative agent of erythema infectiosum (Fifth disease), which in perinatal transmission may result in severe complications, including nonimmune hydrops fetalis and fetal demise.

Erythema Infectiosum (Fifth Disease):

  • Causative Agent: Parvovirus B19
  • Age Group Affected: Most common in children 5-15 years (≈70% of cases).
  • Incubation Period: 4-28 days.
  • Mode of Transmission: Spread via respiratory droplets; household/close contact transmission rate is about 15-30%.
  • Clinical Features:
    • Prodromal Phase: Low-grade fever, headache, mild upper respiratory tract symptoms.
    • Rash: Classically presents with "slapped-cheek" erythema on the face, followed by a lacy reticular rash spreading to the trunk and extremities.
  • Management: Usually a self-limiting illness requiring only supportive care.
  • Complications:
    • Aplastic Crisis: Severe anemia due to suppression of erythropoiesis, particularly in children with chronic hemolytic anemia.
    • Arthropathy: Arthritis/arthralgia, especially in adults.
    • Fetal Infection: Nonimmune hydrops fetalis, intrauterine death.
    • Other Manifestations: Papular-purpuric gloves-and-socks syndrome, myocarditis.

Childhood Exanthems (First to Sixth Diseases):

Explanation of Other Options:

Treponema pallidum (Option A): Causative agent of congenital syphilis, presenting with early features such as mucocutaneous lesions, snuffles, hepatosplenomegaly, and bony changes; late signs include Hutchinson's triad (notched teeth, interstitial keratitis, deafness).

Cytomegalovirus (CMV) (Option B): Major cause of congenital infection; associated with sensorineural hearing loss, microcephaly, and chorioretinitis rather than hydrops.

Toxoplasma gondii (Option D): Leads to congenital toxoplasmosis with hydrocephalus, intracranial calcifications, and chorioretinitis.

Key Takeaways:

  • Parvovirus B19 causes Fifth disease and is linked to severe fetal outcomes, including hydrops and stillbirth.
  • It uniquely suppresses erythropoiesis → aplastic crisis in hemolytic anemia.
  • Recognizing the slapped-cheek rash helps in clinical diagnosis.

question_text: A 4-week-old child presents to the hospital with a complaint of projectile, non-bilious vomiting associated with movable, olive-shaped abdominal mass, 2.5 cms in length is seen especially after feeding. In which of the following regions, this abdominal mass can be best palpated?
explanation:
In the given scenario of projectile, non-bilious vomiting and a movable, olive-shaped abdominal mass, the most probable diagnosis is Congenital Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis (CHPS).

In CHPS, the mass is typically located in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen, just to the right of the midline, often below the liver margin.

Key takeaways:- CHPS

Definition: Thickening of the pyloric muscle, causing obstruction between the stomach and duodenum.

Epidemiology:

Age of presentation: 2 weeks to 3 months

More common in males than females

Clinical Presentation:

- Projectile Vomiting: Non-bilious, progressing to projectile after feeding

- Olive-Shaped Mass: Movable, often found in the right upper quadrant, below the liver margin

(hallmark feature)

question_text: Which of the following is false regarding neonatal cholestasis?
option_a: Kasai procedure should be done within 90 days
option_b: HIDA scan is an investigation of choice
option_c: Biliary atresia is the most common cause
option_d: Liver biopsy rules out other causes
explanation:
Explanation:

The Kasai portoenterostomy (hepaticojejunostomy) is most successful when performed within the first 60 days (8 weeks) of life. Performing the procedure after this critical window significantly reduces the success rate of achieving bile drainage and increases the likelihood of the child requiring a liver transplant.

Neonatal cholestasis is defined as an abnormal accumulation of conjugated bilirubin due to impaired bile formation or flow, with levels >1 mg/dL being suggestive. The most common cause is extrahepatic biliary atresia (EHBA).

Causes of Neonatal Cholestasis


Key Takeaways:

  • The Kasai procedure is a time-sensitive intervention with optimal outcomes when performed before 60 days of age.
  • Biliary atresia is the most common cause of persistent cholestasis in neonates.
  • The diagnostic workup combines HIDA scan (screening) and liver biopsy (confirmation).

question_text: A 6-year-old child is brought to the emergency department with continuous generalized tonic-clonic seizures lasting for the past 30 minutes. There have been no seizure-free intervals during this time. After ensuring airway, breathing, and circulation are stable, which of the following is the first-line drug that should be administered?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The child is in status epilepticus (SE) - defined as continuous seizure activity >5 minutes or recurrent seizures without regaining consciousness.
  • Immediate management focuses on ABC stabilization (Airway, Breathing, Circulation) followed by prompt anticonvulsant therapy.
  • Benzodiazepines are the first-line agents for SE as they enhance GABAergic inhibition, rapidly aborting seizure activity.
  • Among these, IV lorazepam is preferred where available, but IV or rectal diazepam and IM/IV midazolam are equally acceptable first-line agents per AHA/ILAE/AES guidelines.
  • Early treatment (within first 5-20 minutes) improves prognosis and prevents neuronal injury or progression to refractory SE

Explanation of Other Options:

Phenytoin (Option B):

  • Used in the second-line phase (20-40 min) after benzodiazepines.
  • Mechanism: blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels, stabilizing neuronal membranes.
  • Given as IV fosphenytoin (preferred due to better safety, less hypotension).
  • Not first-line due to slower onset of action (10-20 min).

Phenobarbital (Option C):

  • Considered second-line in neonates and third-line in older children.
  • Acts via GABA receptor enhancement and neuronal hyperpolarization.
  • Used when benzodiazepines and phenytoin/fosphenytoin fail.
  • Can cause respiratory depression and hypotension, requiring ICU care.

Thiopentone Sodium (Option D):

  • A barbiturate anesthetic, used only in refractory status epilepticus (40-60 min mark).
  • Induces burst suppression on EEG.
  • Requires mechanical ventilation and continuous EEG monitoring.

Key Takeaway Points:

question_text:
A 4-month-old infant is brought to the OPD with intense itching, especially at night. On examination, there are multiple excoriated papules and burrows seen over the palms, soles, and trunk.
