question_text: A 3-month-old child presents with watery eyes and photophobia. All of the following can cause these symptoms EXCEPT:
explanation:
Explanation:

Congenital Nasolacrimal Duct Obstruction (NLDO) is least likely to cause both watery eyes and photophobia.

NLDO is the most common lacrimal system disorder in infants, resulting from incomplete canalization of the nasolacrimal duct. It typically presents with persistent tearing and sometimes discharge, but photophobia is not a usual feature.

Investigation: The fluorescein dye disappearance test can confirm the presence of obstruction.

Management:

  • Conservative: Nasolacrimal massage 2-3 times daily, cleaning eyelids with warm water, and topical antibiotics if discharge is present.
  • Surgical: If symptoms persist beyond 6-10 months despite massage, lacrimal duct probing is recommended. If probing fails, options include intubation with silastic tubing, with or without balloon dilatation, or dacryocystorhinostomy.

NLDO Management:

  • Conservative: Lacrimal sac massage (2-3× daily) + topical antibiotics
  • >6-10 months: Lacrimal probing
  • Refractory: Silastic intubation ± balloon dilatation or DCR

Explanation of Other Options:

Congenital glaucoma (Option A): This condition arises from abnormal development of the anterior chamber angle, leading to impaired aqueous humor outflow. It presents with the classic triad of tearing, photophobia, and blepharospasm.

Congenital entropion (Option C): The lower lid retractors are underdeveloped, causing the lower eyelid to turn inward. The inward-turning lashes irritate the cornea, resulting in tearing, photophobia, and ocular discomfort. Management typically involves the Hotz procedure

Congenital distichiasis (Option D): This is characterized by an extra row of eyelashes arising from the meibomian glands along the eyelid margin. The additional lashes can irritate the cornea, leading to tearing and photophobia. Treatment options include diathermy or cryotherapy.

question_text: Which of the following signs is not seen in an infant with raised intracranial pressure?
explanation:
Raised intracranial pressure (ICP) in a child is a serious condition where pressure inside the skull increases, potentially due to causes like head injury, brain infection, tumor, hydrocephalus, or bleeding.

Signs of Raised ICP in infants:

  • Bulging fontanelle
  • Sun setting sign- downward gaze of eyes
  • Separation of sutures
  • Progressive macrocephaly
  • Prominent veins of scalp

KEY TAKEAWAYS: Raised intracranial pressure (ICP) in a child is a serious condition where pressure inside the skull increases, potentially due to causes like head injury, brain infection, tumor, hydrocephalus, or bleeding. Signs in children may include headache, vomiting (often in the morning), irritability, decreased alertness, bulging fontanelle (in infants), and sometimes vision changes like double vision or "sunsetting" eyes

question_text: A child is born with bilateral microtia, coloboma of the lower eyelids, absent zygomata, micrognathia, and a high but intact palate. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The description is most consistent with Treacher Collins syndrome. Persons with Treacher Collins syndrome are typically cognitively normal, but they often have conductive hearing loss. These patients have malformations involving structures arising from 1st and 2nd branchial arches.

Regarding other options

  • Goldenhar syndrome, is also associated with anomalies involving the head and neck. The phenotype includes hemifacial microsomia and anomalies of the pinna with associated deafness. Other findings include ear tags, vertebral anomalies, and Arnold- Chiari type I malformations (herniation of the cerebellum into the cervical spinal canal).
  • Pierre Robin sequence is characterized by a triad of cleft palate, micrognathia and glossoptosis.
  • Smith Lemli Opitz syndrome is associated with cleft palate, micrognathia, short nose, ptosis, high square forehead, microcephaly, hypospadias, cryptorchidism, VSD, TOF, hypotonia, mental retardation, postaxial polydactyly, 2-3 toe syndactyly, and defect in cholesterol biosynthesis.

question_text: A 6-month-old child developed hydrocephalus. On examination, he had macrocephaly, bulging fontanelles and separation of sutures. Which of the following signs will be unlikely in this child?
explanation:
Papilledema is a sign of sustained raised ICP in a patient. Since this is a 6-month-old child with open, bulging fontanelles, the intracranial pressure will be dissipated to the outside and thus, no Papilledema will be found on fundus examination.

Regarding other options

  • Positive transillumination is present due to CSF accumulation
  • Setting sun sign, also called as Sunset sign is a sign found during examination in children with hydrocephalus. Part of sclera above the eyeball becomes unduly visible, producing a fixed eyeball position in lower vertical gaze.
  • Dilated and prominent scalp veins will be a physical examination finding due to a large head in these children.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, OP Ghai 10th Edition, Pages 589-590

question_text: A 2-year-old boy presents to the Emergency Department for evaluation for easy bruising. His parents are reliable and you do not suspect nonaccidental trauma. His vital signs are within normal limits for his age. He has a family member with a blood disorder and the patient had a low birth weight. On physical examination, he has a short stature, microcephaly, hypospadias, multiple hyperpigmented skin lesions, and bilateral hypoplastic thumbs. Laboratory studies reveal pancytopenia. He was diagnosed with a syndrome and was advised HSCT. But since no matched donor was available, he was started on a drug. Which drug might have been started in this child?
explanation:
The clinical picture is suggestive of Fanconi's Anemia.

  • Fanconi anemia is an acquired pancytopenia that includes physical manifestations as well.
  • Certain features include hyperpigmentation or hypopigmentation; short stature; absent radii; hypoplastic, absent, bifid, or supernumerary thumbs; foot, hip or leg anomalies; penile or testicular abnormalities (in males); uterine, ovarian, or vaginal malformations (in females); microcephaly; renal malformations; CVS or GIT malformations.
  • Bone marrow failure with pancytopenia usually ensues.
  • Patients with Fanconi anemia are at high risk for squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck and acute myelogenous leukemia.
  • Management of these patients is multidisciplinary and should involve a haematologist.
  • HSCT is curative but if not possible, oral androgens are useful.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 367; Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 1stSA edition, pg. 2364

question_text: True regarding buffalo milk composition when compared to human milk.
explanation:

question_text: Which among the following is most dangerous type of dehydration?
explanation:
Hypernatremic dehydration(Serum Na >145 mEq/L) is the most dangerous form of dehydration because of complications of hypernatremia and of therapy.

  • Hypernatremia can cause serious neurologic damage, including central nervous system hemorrhages and thrombosis. This damage appears to be secondary to the movement of water from the brain cells into the hypertonic extracellular fluid, causing brain cell shrinkage and tearing blood vessels within the brain. In this variety, ECF remains normal but ICF decreases
  • Children with hypernatremic dehydration are often lethargic, and they may be irritable when touched. Hypernatremia may cause fever, hypertonicity, and hyperreflexia. More severe neurologic symptoms may develop if cerebral bleeding or thrombosis occurs.
  • Why slow correction is recommended in this?
  • Idiogenic osmoles are generated within the brain during the development of hypernatremia. These idiogenic osmoles increase the osmolality within the cells of the brain, providing protection against brain cell shrinkage caused by movement of water out of the cells and into the hypertonic extracellular fluid. They dissipate slowly during the correction of hypernatremia. With overly rapid lowering of the extracellular osmolality during the correction of hypernatremia, an osmotic gradient may be created that causes water movement from the extracellular space into the cells of the brain, producing cerebral edema.
  • Symptoms of the resultant cerebral edema can range from seizures to brain herniation and death.
  • To minimize the risk of cerebral edema during the correction of hypernatremic dehydration, the serum sodium concentration should not decrease by >12 mEq/L every 24 hr. The deficits in severe hypernatremic dehydration may need to be corrected over 2-4 days.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 68

question_text: A 5-year-old girl with Down syndrome (trisomy 21) presents to your office for her annual physical exam. Other than a history of a VSD repaired at the age of 7 months, she has not had any significant health problems. Mother reports her daughter is thriving in her special education kindergarten class. When you plot her height on a Down syndrome growth chart, you note that she is now at the 10th percentile for height and 75th for weight, whereas she had previously been tracking at the 25th for height and 50th for weight. What must you check before attributing her increasing BMI to diet and lack of exercise?
explanation:
• Children with Down syndrome are at increased risk for developing hypothyroidism and require regular screening.
  • This could account for decrease in height percentile with increased weight.
  • Celiac disease generally would cause poor weight gain. Cushing syndrome could cause weight gain with poor growth, but this is less common than hypothyroidism. GH deficiency also can cause these findings but is not as common as hypothyroidism.

Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 20th edition, pg-613

question_text: A male boy has a large head, large ears, large jaw and large testes. He also has features of autism and delayed development. Likely diagnosis is?
explanation:
The findings of large head, large ears, large jaw and large testes (macro-orchidism) are suggestive of Fragile X Syndrome.

  • More commonly seen in boys, it is considered to be a trinucleotide repeat disorder
  • Involves >200 CGG repeats in FMR-1 gene on Chromosome Xq27.3
  • Other features include hyperextensible joints, increased risks of ADHD, Autism, Anxiety Disorders
  • Most patients have low IQ, indicating intellectual disability and delayed development milestones during childhood.

Reference: Nelson 21st Ed, Chapter 98.5

question_text: Which of the following is not a feature associated with Down's syndrome?
explanation:
Explanation:

The correct answer is Caudal regression, which is not linked to Down's syndrome.

  • Caudal regression: Developmental anomaly involving underdevelopment of the lower spine and limbs, most often found in infants of diabetic mothers rather than in Down's syndrome.
  • Down's syndrome: Trisomy 21 disorder with multiple craniofacial, extremity, systemic, and comorbidity associations.

Down's Syndrome (Trisomy 21):

  • Cause:
    • Extra chromosome 21 due to meiotic nondisjunction.
    • Less frequent causes: Robertsonian translocation (~4%) or mosaicism (~1%).
  • Incidence:
    • 1 in 800 to 1 in 1000 live births.
  • General Features:
    • Craniofacial: Intellectual disability, flat facial profile, upward-slanting eyes, epicanthic folds, small nose, flat nasal bridge, narrow palate, small teeth, protruding tongue, brachycephaly, flat occiput, dysplastic ears.
    • Extremities: Short/broad hands, clinodactyly (5th finger), simian crease, sandal gap.
  • Comorbidities:
    • Cardiac: 40-60% with congenital defects (AVSD, VSD, PDA, ASD).
    • Gastrointestinal: Duodenal atresia, Hirschsprung disease, annular pancreas.
    • Hematological: Higher leukemia risk (ALL, AML).
    • Endocrine: Thyroid dysfunction (hypothyroidism), ↑ risk of type 1 diabetes.
    • Neurological: Early-onset Alzheimer's (APP gene on chromosome 21).
    • Musculoskeletal: Atlanto-occipital subluxation, short stature, hypotonia, growth delay, obesity.
    • Sensory: Conductive hearing loss (commonly due to serous otitis media), ophthalmic issues (cataracts, strabismus, nystagmus).
  • Diagnosis:
    • Prenatal:
      • Chorionic Villus Sampling (10-13 weeks).
      • Amniocentesis (>15 weeks).
    • Postnatal:
      • Recognition of typical features.
      • Confirmatory karyotyping for Trisomy 21.
  • Antenatal Screening:
    • First Trimester: ↑ nuchal translucency (>3 mm), ↑ β-HCG, ↓ PAPP-A.
    • Second Trimester: Triple Test (β-HCG, estriol, AFP), Quadruple Test (adds Inhibin-A).
    • Integrated Test: Combines maternal age, NT, PAPP-A, and Quadruple Test.
    • NIPS/NIPT: Cell-free fetal DNA (high sensitivity & specificity).

Explanation of other options:

Conductive hearing loss (Option A): Commonly associated due to otitis media with effusion.

Short stature (Option B): Characteristic growth delay in Down's syndrome.

Hypothyroidism (Option C): Frequently reported endocrine issue.

Key Takeaways:

  • Caudal regression is not linked to Down's syndrome; rather, it is strongly associated with infants of diabetic mothers.
  • Down's syndrome shows multisystem involvement-craniofacial dysmorphism, short stature, hypothyroidism, cardiac/GI malformations, and hearing/visual defects.

Reference:

HealthEd NZ - Antenatal Screening

UCSF Health - Prenatal Testing for Down Syndrome

question_text: A 29-day-old boy is transferred to the hospital from a peripheral center. The patient was seen for persistent vomiting and was noted by the examining physician to have projectile vomiting. A small mass is palpable in the pyloric area, and peristaltic waves are detectable. Surgical consultation is requested, IV fluids are instituted, and the patient is prepared for surgical intervention. Which of the following is a recognized risk for the development of this condition?
explanation:
Infant between 2 weeks to 3 months with projectile vomiting, visible peristalsis and palpable abdominal mass is likely to have CHPS/IHPS.

  • Risk factors for CHPS include
    1. Male gender
    2. First born child
    3. Blood groups B & O
    4. Syndromes like Apert, Edward, Zellweger, Cornelia de Lange
    5. Use of oral or systemic erythromycin, not topical.
  • Quick Review of CHPS
    • Pyloric stenosis, most commonly seen in age 2weeks to 2 months with male preponderance.
    • Clinical features include Projectile, non-bilious, immediate postprandial Infant is hungry between the feeds.
    • Diagnosis is by ultrasound abdomen that shows thickened pylorus more than 4 mm and pyloric length more than 14 mm. Target sign is suggestive of Pyloric stenosis.
    • Management is supportive initially with maintenance of electrolyte balance. Definitive treatment is Pyloromyotomy at the earliest.

Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1st SA ed., pg. 1797

question_text: A 5-year-old child being evaluated for pancytopenia was found to have abnormality as shown in the picture. He also has short stature and multiple café-au-lait macules on the body. Chromosomal breakage studies are indicative of increased fragility of chromatids. HSCT is planned but the parents are counselled about the potential for increased morbidity and mortality due to elevated risk of some specific complications. What are the likely set of complication most likely to be?
option_a: AML & Head and neck squamous cell cancers
explanation:
Pancytopenia with thumb/radial abnormalities, short stature, multiple café-au-lait macules and increased chromosomal fragility, all point to a diagnosis of Fanconi Anemia.

  • Head and neck cancer risk, like oral cancer risk is increased 4.4-fold and is accelerated by approximately 15 yr compared to non-transplanted patients.
  • These cancers are of squamous cell type and tend to be associated with HPV infection.
  • The cumulative incidence of malignancy 20 yr after transplant is 35-40% and is the major cause of morbidity and mortality in later life.
  • Please note that the risk of Acute Myeloid Leukemia, i.e., AML is also increased in patients of Fanconi Anemia.
  • As per OP Ghai 10th Edition, AML, Myelodysplasia, Oral Cancers and Liver Cancers are the likely malignancies in a patient with Fanconi Anemia.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Table 13.15

question_text: Congenital absence of seminal vesicles and vas deferens is seen in?
explanation:
More than 95% of males with cystic fibrosis are azoospermic because of failure of development of wolffian duct structures, but sexual function is generally unimpaired.

  • Many male patients with Cystic Fibrosis have an abnormality called CAVD= Congenital Absence of Vas Deferens. This contributes to azoospermia and infertility in males
  • Please note that female fertility may be reduced due to thick cervical mucus but there is no structural issues of reproductive tract in female patients with Cystic Fibrosis

question_text: The following are features of untreated phenylketonuria except?
explanation:
• By 1 year of age, microcephaly, eczematous or oily skin, hypertonicity, convulsions, dysphasia, hyperactivity with purposeless movements, and an abnormal EEG are usual.
  • In early infancy, vomiting may mimic pyloric stenosis. The skin and hair are often fair, with blue eyes.
  • Psychotic behavior with hyperactivity, destructiveness, self-injury, impulsiveness and uncontrolled behavior are noted. The general physical development is usually good. Patients with PKU who are treated early generally have an intelligence within normal range. Hyperactivity and a lower IQ than a first-degree relative have been noticed in many patients with PKU. The frequency of abnormalities associated with EEG and MRI increases with age. Demyelination is almost universal in older patients affected with both classical PKU or HPA type II.
  • Plasma phenylalanine is elevated, and phenylalanine and its metabolites appear in the urine. Phenylacetic acid accounts for the subtle mousy, musty odour of these patients.

Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 1st SA ed., pg. 637

question_text: A 35-year-old woman gives birth to a female infant who is growth restricted, microcephalic, and has a congenital heart defect. She has had 1 prior miscarriage and reports that she has a 3-year-old son with mental impairment. She also recalls being on a special diet as a child which she subsequently discontinued. Which of the following maternal conditions is most consistent with this history?
explanation:
• Intrauterine exposure of an unborn child to elevated phenylalanine concentrations due to maternal PKU can disrupt embryo-fetal development.

Phenylketonuria (PKU) is caused by mutations in the PAH gene, which codes for the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase. This enzyme is responsible for converting phenylalanine, an amino acid, into another amino acid called tyrosine.

Mechanism:

  • Deficiency of Phenylalanine Hydroxylase: In individuals with PKU, the phenylalanine hydroxylase enzyme is either deficient or inactive due to mutations in the PAH gene.
  • Phenylalanine Buildup: Without functional phenylalanine hydroxylase, phenylalanine cannot be converted to tyrosine. As a result, phenylalanine accumulates in the blood and tissues.
  • Toxic Effects: The elevated phenylalanine levels are toxic to the brain, particularly during critical periods of brain development. This causes intellectual disability, developmental delays, seizures, and other neurological issues.
  • Impaired Tyrosine Production: Since phenylalanine cannot be converted to tyrosine, the production of tyrosine (a precursor for neurotransmitters like dopamine and serotonin) is also impaired, further contributing to neurological problems.

KEY TAKEAWAYS: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is a rare genetic disorder in which the body cannot break down phenylalanine, an amino acid found in many foods, due to a deficiency in the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase. If left untreated, phenylalanine builds up in the blood, leading to intellectual disability, behavioral problems, and seizures.

Tags:

  • Topic: PHENYLKETONURIA
  • Difficulty level: GOOD TO KNOW
  • PYQ: NEET PG 2023

Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 1st SA ed., pg. 637

question_text: A 35-year-old woman gives birth to a female infant who is growth restricted, microcephalic, and has a congenital heart defect. She has had 1 prior miscarriage and reports that she has a 3-year-old son who is abnormally fair, with mental impairment. She also recalls being on a special diet as a child which she subsequently discontinued. Which of the following maternal conditions is most consistent with this history?
explanation:
Intrauterine exposure of an unborn child to elevated phenylalanine concentrations due to maternal PKU can disrupt embryo-fetal development.

  • Effects include facial dysmorphism resembling fetal alcohol syndrome, microcephaly, mental impairment, and malformations especially of the heart.
  • Hypopigmentation occurs owing to a lack of pigment formation.
  • Musty or mousy urine odour is also produced.
  • None of the other maternal conditions listed above would lead to the clinical features described in this vignette. Maternal diabetes leads to macrosomia not growth restriction.

Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 1st SA ed., pg. 637

question_text: An infant presents with hepatosplenomegaly and thrombocytopenia. Neuroimaging with CT shows periventricular calcifications. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Periventricular calcifications with hepatosplenomegaly and thrombocytopenia are hallmark features of congenital CMV infection.

  • Congenital CMV infection is the most common congenital viral infection and occurs via in utero transmission, especially during primary maternal infection.
  • The transmission risk increases with gestational age, though the severity is higher in early infection.
  • Approximately 90% of infected infants are asymptomatic, while 10% show symptomatic features, including:
    • Hepatosplenomegaly
    • Petechiae or purpura (blueberry muffin appearance)
    • Jaundice (direct hyperbilirubinemia)
    • Microcephaly
    • Intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR)
    • Chorioretinitis
    • Periventricular calcifications on CT, which are pathognomonic
    • Sensorineural hearing loss is the most common long-term complication
  • Diagnosis requires confirmation within the first 2–3 weeks of life using PCR for CMV DNA in urine or saliva.
    • IgG is not diagnostic due to maternal antibody transfer; IgM is unreliable alone.
  • Management includes:
    • Ganciclovir (IV) for symptomatic neonates, particularly those with CNS involvement.
    • Regular follow-up with hearing assessments, developmental screening, and vision monitoring.

Causes of Blueberry Muffin Rash:

Explanation of other options:

Congenital rubella syndrome (Option A): Characterized by the classic triad of sensorineural deafness, cataracts, and congenital heart defects (notably PDA). Also features salt-and-pepper retinopathy, not periventricular calcification.

Congenital herpes simplex virus infection (Option B): Manifests with vesicular skin lesions, chorioretinitis, and microcephaly/hydranencephaly. CT may show diffuse cerebral involvement, not specifically periventricular calcification.

Congenital toxoplasmosis (Option C): Presents with the triad of chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and intracerebral calcifications. Unlike CMV, calcifications in toxoplasmosis are diffuse and random, not periventricular.

Reference:

https://www.researchgate.net/figure/Causes-of-blueberry-muffin-rash_tbl1_353975855

question_text: What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Omphalocele is a congenital anterior abdominal wall defect where abdominal viscera (intestine, liver, stomach, etc.) herniate into the base of the umbilical cord.

The herniated organs are covered by a translucent sac consisting of amnion, Wharton's jelly, and peritoneum.

It results from failure of lateral body folds to fuse in the midline during embryologic development.


Explanation of Other Options:

Persistent vitellointestinal duct (Option C):

  • Results from failure of the vitelline duct (yolk stalk) to close, leaving a connection between the ileum and umbilicus.
  • Presents with fecal or bilious discharge from the umbilicus, not with organ herniation.

Bochdalek hernia (Option D):

  • A posterolateral diaphragmatic defect (most often left-sided) causing herniation of abdominal viscera into the thoracic cavity, leading to respiratory distress soon after birth.
  • Unlike omphalocele, the abdominal wall and umbilicus remain intact.

Key Takeaway Points:

  • Omphalocele → midline defect + membrane-covered sac
  • Gastroschisis → right-sided defect + no membrane
  • Omphalocele often associated with chromosomal & cardiac anomalies
  • Immediate postnatal management: cover sac with sterile saline gauze, prevent heat loss, start IV fluids, and plan surgical repair.

Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK519010/

question_text: Regarding persistent asthma in children, one of the following is true?
option_a: Eczema is a major risk factor for persistent asthma.
option_b: Low birth weight is an identifiable factor for the persistence of childhood asthma
option_c: Immunization may help reduce the likelihood of asthma development
option_d: 10% of preschool children who have recurrent cough & wheeze will have persistent asthma later on
explanation:
Early childhood risk factors for persistent asthma have been identified.

  • The risk factors have been described as major (parent asthma, eczema, inhalant allergen sensitization) and minor (allergic rhinitis, wheezing apart from colds, ≥4% peripheral blood eosinophils, food allergen sensitization) risk factors.
  • Preschool-age children who have recurrent cough and wheeze, approximately one-third, i.e. 33% of these continue to have persistent asthma into later childhood, and approximately two-thirds improve on their own through their teen years.
  • Role of immunization and birth weight have doubtful to no role in determining persistent asthma risk.

Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1st SA ed., pg. 1096

question_text: Drug most commonly used for fetal lung maturity to prevent HMD postnatally is?

Dexamethasone can also be used but is less commonly preferred compared to betamethasone for fetal lung maturity.

question_text: Which of the following is the most dreaded complication of late diagnosis of congenital hypothyroidism?
explanation:
Congenital hypothyroidism (CH) is a condition present at birth where the thyroid gland fails to produce adequate thyroid hormones, crucial for growth, metabolism, and brain development in infants.

Clinical Features

  1. Newborn Features (often subtle):
    • Prolonged jaundice (yellowing of the skin and eyes)
    • Poor feeding
    • Lethargy or decreased activity
    • Hypotonia (reduced muscle tone or "floppiness")
    • Large fontanelles (soft spots on the head, especially the posterior fontanelle)
    • Constipation
  2. Physical Signs:
    • Puffy face with a broad nose
    • Macroglossia (enlarged tongue)
    • Cold, mottled skin
    • Umbilical hernia
    • Coarse or dry skin and hair
    • Enlarged abdomen
    • Hoarse cry
  3. Growth and Developmental Features (if untreated):
    • Growth retardation
    • Delayed skeletal maturation
    • Intellectual disability (mental retardation)
    • Developmental delays in motor skills, cognition, and language

KEY TAKEAWAYS: Late diagnosis and delayed treatment can lead to impaired neurocognitive development and growth.

The risk of neurocognitive complications is significantly reduced if early diagnosis and treatment is started within first two weeks of life.

  • Difficulty level: MUST KNOW

Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21st ed., pg. 2915

question_text: A child was born with the absence of thymus gland and congenital hypoparathyroidism. This is likely to be due to maldevelopment of which of the following structures (An image was given)?

A child was born with the absence of thymus gland and congenital hypoparathyroidism. This is likely to be due to maldevelopment of which of the following structures in the labelled branchial arch structure below?
explanation:
Absence of thymus gland and hypoparathyroidism due to branchial arch defect likely suggests a diagnosis of DiGeorge Syndrome, which arises due to 3rd and sometimes 4th pharyngeal pouch hypoplasia. Option C indicates the 3rd pharyngeal pouch and is thus the likely answer here.

  • The cause of DiGeorge Syndrome is microdeletions in Chromosome 22q11.2 region
  • Can be sporadic or inherited. Inherited forms show Autosomal Dominant inheritance

Clinical features can be remembered by the mnemonic: CATCH - 22

  • C - Cardiac defects (Interrupted aortic arch syndrome > truncus arteriosus > TOF)
  • A - Abnormal facies
  • T - Thymic hypoplasia → T cell defects
  • C - Cleft palate (may/may not be present in all cases)
  • H - Hypocalcaemia - due to PTH gland hypoplasia
  • 22- Chromosome Involved

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 151

question_text: A 12-year-old child presents with short stature. On evaluation, the bone age is less than the chronological age. There are no dysmorphic features, and the child is otherwise healthy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Constitutional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP) is the most common cause of short stature in adolescents.
  • These children are healthy, have no dysmorphic features, and growth velocity is normal, but bone age is delayed compared to chronological age.
  • They usually achieve normal adult height but have a delayed pubertal growth spurt, giving the appearance of short stature during childhood.

Explanation of other options:

Achondroplasia (Option C): A genetic skeletal dysplasia with disproportionate short stature, frontal bossing, and rhizomelic limb shortening

Chondrodysplasia (Option D): Refers to abnormal cartilage/bone development, usually with skeletal deformities and dysmorphic features, absent in this case.

question_text: Levine criteria have been proposed for the diagnosis of which among the following neurological conditions?
explanation:
Levine criteria for the diagnosis of cerebral palsy include the following

Mnemonic is: POSTER

  • P: Posturing
  • O: Oropharyngeal problems
  • S: Strabismus
  • T: Tone abnormalities
  • E: Evolutional maldevelopment e.g. Persistent primitive reflexes
  • R: Reflexes are increased or brisk or exaggerated e.g. DTRs

Presence of any 4 out of 6 strongly suggests the diagnosis of cerebral palsy.

Reference: NIH Publications, Swaimann's Pediatric Neurology

question_text: A 30-hour-old full-term infant has facial and chest jaundice. He is breastfeeding well and has an otherwise normal examination. His bilirubin level is 15.5 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?

Practically, the following cut-offs are often used as a ready reckoner

question_text: A 6-year-old child is evaluated for short stature. His height is consistent with his parents' heights, and his bone age matches his chronological age. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation indicates familial short stature, which is characterized by height below the 3rd percentile for age and sex but is normal according to the child's genetic potential, as determined by parental heights.

Key features supporting this diagnosis include bone age matching chronological age and height being consistent with parental heights, suggesting genetic rather than pathological short stature.

Characteristics of Familial Short Stature:

  • Child's height is <3rd percentile of expected according to age & sex, but is normal as per his target height
  • The child has a normal puberty
  • Family history of short stature
  • Bone age = chronological age

Explanation of Other Options:

Constitutional delay (Option B): In constitutional growth delay, the child presents with delayed bone age and delayed puberty, unlike this case, where bone age matches chronological age. Most of these children tend to eventually grow to approximately the same height as their parents. Undernutrition (Option C): Undernutrition shows evidence of poor weight gain and delayed bone age, which are absent in this case. Nutritional deficiency would affect both growth and skeletal maturation, leading to a discrepancy between bone age and chronological age. Growth hormone deficiency (Option D): Growth hormone deficiency, also known as dwarfism or pituitary dwarfism, typically presents with severe growth failure, delayed bone age, and height that is significantly below parental heights.

question_text: Which is NOT seen in nutritional rickets?
explanation:
Explanation:

Spondyloepiphyseal Dysplasia (SED) is a genetic bone disorder caused by a defect in collagen, leading to short trunk dwarfism. A hallmark feature is a reduced upper segment to lower segment (US/LS) ratio. In this patient, a US/LS ratio of 0.8:1 supports the diagnosis of SED.

Measurement:

  • Upper segment (US): Total height minus lower segment
  • Lower segment (LS): Measured from pubic symphysis to the floor

US/LS Ratio Patterns:

  • Normal progression:
    • At birth: 1.7
    • At 3 years: 1.3
    • After 7 years: 1
    • Adults: 0.9
  • Short trunk dwarfism (↓ ratio): Spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia, MPS, mucolipidosis
  • Short limb dwarfism (↑ ratio): Achondroplasia, rickets, osteogenesis imperfecta, hypothyroidism
  • Proportionate short stature (normal ratio): GH deficiency, constitutional delay

US/LS = 0.8:1 indicates short trunk dwarfism → Spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia

Explanation of Other Options:

Achondroplasia (Option B): This condition causes short-limb dwarfism, leading to a decreased upper-to-lower segment (US/LS) ratio, as the limbs are disproportionately short compared to the trunk.

Growth hormone deficiency (Option C): It leads to proportionate short stature, so the US/LS ratio remains normal.

Hypothyroidism (Option D): It can cause short-limb dwarfism in children, resulting in a decreased US/LS ratio due to relatively shorter limbs.

question_text: A neonate has not passed urine in the last 24 hours since birth. Next step in management is?
explanation:
According to Cloherty & Stark, 90% neonates void urine within 24 hours and 99% do so by 48 hours.

  • Neonates without any risk factor can pass urine anytime before 48 hours of life. Until then we need to observe and feed the child.
  • If more than 48 hours have passed, the baby needs to be shifted to the ICU and evaluated for volume status & investigated.

question_text: The instrument shown is a Paladai, used for feeding preterm infants. At which of the following gestational ages is this method typically introduced as a bridge between gavage feeding and breastfeeding?
explanation:
Explanation:

The image shows a Paladai, a traditional spouted cup used as an alternative oral feeding method for preterm neonates. This method is most appropriate for infants between 32 and 34 weeks of gestation.

At this age, infants are developing their suck-swallow-breathe coordination but may not yet have the strength or endurance for full, effective breastfeeding or bottle-feeding. The Paladai allows the infant to lap or sip milk without the high energy expenditure of sucking, facilitating the transition from gavage (tube) feeds to direct oral feeds.

Explanation of Other Options:

Less than 28 weeks (Option A): Infants at this gestational age are extremely preterm with an immature gut and no suck-swallow-breathe coordination. They require parenteral nutrition via IV fluids or Total Parenteral Nutrition (TPN).

28-31 weeks (Option B): These infants still lack coordinated reflexes for safe oral feeding. The standard of care is enteral nutrition via gavage feeds (nasogastric or orogastric tube).

> 34 weeks (Option D): By this age, most preterm infants have developed sufficient suck-swallow-breathe coordination to begin direct breastfeeding or bottle-feeding.

question_text: A neonate weighing 1500 grams is delivered at 33 weeks. Which of the following would be the most appropriate method of nutrition for the baby?
explanation:
The aim of nutritional management of a preterm infant is to achieve full enteral feeding as soon as possible.

  • Feeding of LBW & preterm meconates depends on Gestational Age
    • <28 Week → IV fluids / TPN
    • 28 - 31 weeks → Tube feeds (Nasogastric/or gastric)
    • 32 - 34 weeks → Spoon feeds/Katori/ Paladai feeds
    • >34 week → Breast feeds
  • TPN is given to VLBW infants who cannot tolerate gastric tube feeds, have gastric disease, enteral feeding (by tube) is not possible or just while enteral nutrition is being established.
  • Other important indication for TPN is sick premature/LBW infants which include Infants with:
    • Significant respiratory distress required assisted ventilation.
    • Shock requiring inotropic support.
    • Seizures, renal/cardiac failure

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 153; Cloherty and stark's manual of neonatal care, 8th ed., pg. 185

question_text: Which is true about breastmilk jaundice?
option_c: Exclusive breastfeeding with bilirubin >10 mg/dL after 3-4 weeks
explanation:
Explanation:

Approximately 2-4% of term neonates who are exclusively breastfed may have total serum bilirubin (TSB) levels exceeding 10 mg/dL beyond the third or fourth week of life, a condition known as breast milk jaundice (BMJ).

It is an unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, and diagnosis is made after ruling out other causes of prolonged jaundice such as insufficient feeding, ongoing hemolysis, blood extravasation, G6PD deficiency, and hypothyroidism.

Breast milk contains high levels of β-glucuronidase, which deconjugates bilirubin that has already been conjugated by the liver and excreted into the intestine, leading to increased enterohepatic circulation and elevated serum bilirubin levels.

Most infants with BMJ remain clinically well, and dangerously high bilirubin levels are rare, so treatment is usually unnecessary. Importantly, breastfeeding should not be discontinued, as it is safe to continue feeding throughout the course of BMJ.

Breast milk jaundice Features:

  • Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (Option D ruled out)
  • Self-limiting, rarely requires phototherapy (Option B ruled out)
  • Breastfeeding continuation recommended (Option A ruled out)

Key Takeaways:

Visual Assessment of Jaundice (Adapted Kramer Rule)

question_text: A 2-month-old infant born to HIV+ mother develops recurrent diarrhea. What is the next step in management?
option_a: Stop breastfeeding and start HAART in the baby
option_b: Fresh stool sample examination for Giardia
option_c: Do HIV antibody testing by ELISA
option_d: Dried blood spot for HIV Total nucleic acid PCR
explanation:
In an HIV-exposed infant, we need to do HIV Testing, routinely at or before 6 weeks of age and testing must be done especially if the child develops symptoms at any time.

  • Testing method of choice in infants for HIV is by using Dried Blood Spots (DBS) for HIV Total Nucleic Acid (TNA) PCR.
  • Kindly note that earlier we used to perform DNA PCR, it has now been replaced by TNA PCR as per NACO updated guidelines.
  • NACO Guidelines Say..


Regarding other options

  • Breastfeeding is never stopped & HAART not started based just upon symptoms
  • Stool examination for Giardia is not needed in a 2 month old infant with recurrent diarrhea
  • HIV Antibody Testing by ELISA should not be done before 18 months of age since maternally transferred antibodies may interfere with testing.

Reference: NACO 2021 Update; OP Ghai 10th Edition, Pages 248-250

question_text: Breastfeeding should be started within how much time after birth?
explanation:
Points to remember regarding breastfeeding

  • Breastfeeding should be started as soon as possible after birth. As per WHO, UNICEF it must be started within 1 hr of birth
  • Exclusive BF till: 6 months of age. Then start complementary feed and continue to breastfeed till 18-24 months.

question_text: Indication to use prednisolone in Henoch-Schoenlein Purpura is?
explanation:
Treatment for mild and self-limited HSP is supportive, with an emphasis on ensuring adequate hydration, nutrition, and analgesia.

  • Corticosteroids are most often used to treat significant GI involvement or other life-threatening manifestations. Glucocorticoids such as oral prednisone (1-2 mg/kg/day), or in severe cases, intravenous (IV) methylprednisolone for 1-2 wk, followed by taper, reduce abdominal and joint pain but do not alter overall prognosis.
  • Corticosteroids are not routinely recommended for prevention of complications such as nephritis.
  • Corticosteroids may also be needed in any orchitis, CNS involvement and pulmonary hemorrhage

Reference: Nelson 21st Ed, Chapter 192, OP Ghai 10th Ed, Page 661

question_text:
Choose the correct statement/s about Vitamin C and Scurvy
A. It is a heat labile vitamin
B. Exclusive breastfeeding can cause scurvy in infancy
C. Therapeutic dose of vitamin C is 100-200mg/day
D. Vitamin C is predominantly stored in Liver
explanation:
• Vitamin C supplements of 100-200 mg/day orally or parenterally ensure rapid and complete cure of Scurvy. The treatment should be continued for up to 3 months for complete recovery.
  • Breastfeeding protects against vitamin C deficiency throughout infancy. In children consuming milk formula, fortification with vitamin C must be ensured.
  • Children consuming heat-treated milk should consume adequate vitamin C-rich foods in infancy. Vitamin C is easily destroyed by prolonged storage, overcooking, and processing of foods.
  • Vitamin C is not stored in the body but is taken up by all tissues; the highest levels are found in the pituitary and adrenal glands.

question_text: Which of the following is an absolute contraindication for breastfeeding?
explanation:
Explanation:
Breastfeeding is contraindicated in infants with classic galactosemia (caused by galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency).

  • Breast milk is rich in lactose, which is digested into glucose and galactose. In galactosemia, the metabolic pathway for galactose is impaired, leading to the accumulation of galactose and its toxic metabolites. This buildup results in clinical features such as poor feeding, vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly, cataracts, and the presence of reducing substances in urine.
  • For survival, these infants must be placed on a lactose-free formula, as continued exposure to galactose can be life-threatening.

Contraindications of Breastfeeding:

HIV who are on effective antiretroviral therapy (ART) and adhere to treatment should exclusively breastfeed for the first 6 months. Complementary feeding can then be introduced while continuing ART, up to 12 months of age.

Hepatitis C in mother (Option B): Breastfeeding is not contraindicated in mothers with HCV infection, as available evidence does not show transmission of the virus through breast milk.

Tuberculosis in mother (Option D): Breast milk itself is safe in mothers with drug-susceptible tuberculosis (DS-TB) once they are no longer infectious. The milk does not carry Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and only minimal, non-harmful amounts of TB medications are secreted into it. However, if the mother has active TB, direct breastfeeding should be withheld until at least 2 weeks of appropriate anti-TB therapy have been completed.

question_text: Which of the following is an absolute contraindication for breastfeeding?
option_d: Infants born to an HbsAg-positive mother
explanation:
Explanation:

Classic galactosemia in the infant is an absolute contraindication for breastfeeding.

Contraindications for Breastfeeding

Absolute Contraindications:

  • Galactosemia in infancy:
    • This metabolic disorder prevents the digestion of galactose from mother's milk, leading to toxic product buildup and potential organ damage and cataracts.
  • Lactating mother on anti-cancer agents (antineoplastic agents): Many of these agents can be secreted into breast milk and harm the baby.

Relative Contraindications:

  • Conditions like active TB without adequate treatment or a herpes infection on the breast are generally considered relative contraindications on the breast are generally considered relative contraindications.

Infections Transmitted via Breast Milk

  • Cytomegalovirus (CMV), HIV, Hepatitis B, and Hepatitis C can be transmitted through breast milk.
  • However, in India, CMV is not a contraindication, and HIV is generally not a contraindication if specific guidelines are followed.

Explanation of other options:

Alcoholic mother (Option A): This is not an absolute contraindication; breastfeeding is discouraged only if the mother is acutely intoxicated, as alcohol passes into breast milk and may affect the infant’s neurodevelopment.

Infants born to an HBsAg-positive mother (Option D): Considered not a contraindication. The baby should receive the hepatitis B vaccine and HBIG within 12 hours of birth, and breastfeeding can continue safely.

question_text: When is it recommended to introduce solid foods to an infant while continuing breastfeeding?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • According to current recommendations by World Health Organization (WHO) and American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), solid foods should be introduced to an infant while continuing breastfeeding at around 6 months of age.
  • At 6 months, infants have typically developed the necessary oral motor skills to handle solid foods, including loss of the tongue-thrust reflex, ability to sit with support, and adequate head and neck control.
  • Breast milk or formula remains the primary source of nutrition during the first year, with complementary foods gradually introduced to meet increasing nutritional demands, especially for iron and zinc.
  • Breastfeeding can go up to 2 years of age or till the time the mother wants.

question_text: A mother delivered 33 weeks old baby, via normal vaginal delivery with no complications at birth. What is the preferred method of feeding the neonate?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Such infants usually have immature suck-swallow coordination, which makes direct breastfeeding difficult.
  • However, they have adequate gut maturity, meaning enteral feeding is feasible.
  • Paladai feeding (also called cup-and-spoon feeding) is the preferred method for such neonates:
    • It allows controlled flow of milk and prevents aspiration.
    • It helps in the transition to direct breastfeeding as the infant matures.
    • It supports bonding between mother and baby while promoting breast milk feeding.

question_text: 1-month-old, His parents note that a prenatal ultrasound showed a left multicystic dysplastic kidney. Since birth, he has been breastfeeding well and makes multiple wet diapers a day. What is the most appropriate next step?
option_b: Urological consultation for an immediate nephrectomy
option_d: Renal ultrasound at 3-6 months of age
explanation:
Multicystic dysplastic kidneys (MCDK) are a common cause of flank masses in infancy. On ultrasound they present as a large cystic non uniform mass in the renal fossa. By definition, MCDK are nonfunctional. Previously, nephrectomies were commonly performed because of an association of MCDK with the development of Wilms tumor. However, the incidence of Wilms tumor in patients with MCKD is quite low and now observation and medical management is the mainstay of therapy.

  • Serial ultrasounds, commonly performed every 3-6 months during the first year of life and every 6 months thereafter, are done to monitor for involution of the mass as well as compensatory hypertrophy of the contralateral kidney.
  • Progressive involution of MCDK is seen by 5-7 years of age.

question_text: Which of the following statements is incorrect about colostrum?
option_a: Breastmilk produced in the initial 3-4 days
option_c: Contains a large number of antibodies
option_d: It contains a high amount of lactose and low amounts of protein
explanation:
Explanation:

The colostrum contains low amounts of lactose and a high amount of protein.

  • Colostrum is the initial, thick, yellow milk produced during the first 3-4 days after birth. (Options A, B ruled out)
  • Rich in antibodies (particularly secretory IgA), immune cells, and vitamins A, D, E, and K. (Option C ruled out)
  • Moderately low in fat and very low in carbohydrates (lactose).
  • This early milk provides crucial protection and immunity for the newborn.

Types of Breast Milk

Three types are produced based on the time after childbirth:

  • Colostrum: Secreted in the first 72 hours after birth.
  • Transitional milk: Secreted between day 4 and day 14 after birth
  • Mature milk: Secreted beyond day 14 and continues throughout lactation.

Explanation:

The acute onset of vomiting, diarrhea, and distress after milk ingestion indicates classical galactosemia, caused by deficiency of Galactose-1-Phosphate Uridyl Transferase (GALT).

Galactosemia:

Explanation of other options:

question_text: You examine a one-day-old girl in the nursery. She was born at 35 weeks to a G2, P2 mother via normal spontaneous vaginal delivery. There were no complications at delivery. The newborn girl had a meconium-stained bowel movement and has had three successful breastfeeding. The nurse informs you that the mother has reactive nontreponemal and treponemal test results. explanation:
Rhinitis, also called Snuffles, is a clinical finding of early congenital syphilis.

  • Early congenital syphilis can present with a variety of clinical signs and symptoms in infants.
  • Rhinitis, also known as snuffles, is a common manifestation in newborns with congenital syphilis. It is characterized by a mucopurulent or bloody discharge from the nose. Other clinical findings of early congenital syphilis can include hepatosplenomegaly, rash, lymphadenopathy, and fever.
  • Option A (Frontal bossing) and Option B (Hutchinson teeth) are characteristic physical findings associated with late congenital syphilis, which typically manifests in childhood or adolescence.
  • Option D (Sensorineural hearing loss) can occur in congenital syphilis but is more commonly associated with later stages of the disease or untreated congenital syphilis.
  • Early congenital syphilis often presents with clinical findings related to infection in multiple organ systems.

question_text: A child presents with a mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) of 105 mm. Upon administering ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF), the child consumes it eagerly and completely. Based on this assessment, under which nutritional category does the child fall?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • MUAC < 11.5 cm (115mm) is considered as Severe acute malnutrition (SAM).
  • In assessment of SAM, look for 1. Edema 2. Poor appetite 3. Complications.
  • If any of these are present- it is termed as Complicated SAM. Or else it is Uncomplicated SAM
  • As the child in the question has good appetite and there is no mention of edema or any other complication, he falls in Uncomplicated SAM.

Explanation of other options:

Complicated SAM (Option B):

  • Complicated SAM is diagnosed if there is:
    • Poor appetite (unable to complete therapeutic feeding)
    • Medical complications (e.g., infections, hypoglycemia, shock)
    • Bilateral pitting edema
  • Since the child has good appetite and no mentioned complications, this is Uncomplicated SAM.

Acute Malnutrition (Option C):

  • The term "acute malnutrition" includes both moderate acute malnutrition (MAM) and severe acute malnutrition (SAM).
  • Moderate Acute Malnutrition (MAM) is MUAC between 11.5-12.5 cm.
  • Since this child's MUAC is 10.5 cm, he falls into SAM, not just acute malnutrition.

Normal Nutrition (Option D):

  • Normal MUAC is > 12.5 cm (125 mm).
  • Since this child has MUAC of 105 mm (10.5 cm), he is severely malnourished and does not qualify as normal nutrition.

Key Takeaways:

A child with MUAC < 11.5 cm (115 mm) and good appetite with no complications is classified as Uncomplicated Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM).

question_text: What is the mid-arm circumference for severe malnutrition?
explanation:
Explanation:

Mid-Upper Arm Circumference (MUAC):

MUAC is a simple, rapid, and reliable method used to assess the nutritional status of children between 6 months and 5 years of age. A MUAC value of less than 11.5 cm in this age group indicates severe acute malnutrition (SAM).
It is important to note that MUAC is not recommended for infants below 6 months.

Procedure:

  • Ensure the child is standing upright, with the left arm free of clothing and bent at a right angle.
  • Measure the distance between the acromion (shoulder tip) and olecranon (elbow tip), and mark the midpoint.
  • Allow the arm to hang relaxed at the side, palm facing the thigh.
  • Wrap the MUAC tape around the marked midpoint. The tape should fit snugly but not tightly enough to pinch the skin.
  • Read the measurement at the zero mark of the tape and record the value.

Shakir's Tape:

Shakir's tape is a color-coded MUAC tape commonly used in field settings for screening malnutrition. The zones are interpreted as:

  • Red zone: Severe malnutrition (MUAC < 11.5 cm)
  • Yellow zone: Moderate malnutrition (MUAC 11.5-12.5 cm)
  • Green zone: Normal nutritional status (MUAC > 12.5 cm)

Reference:

question_text:
A 5-year-old has the following anthropometry values. According to WHO criteria for malnutrition, what is the diagnosis?

Explanation:

The anthropometric profile indicates chronic malnutrition (stunting).

WHO Classification Analysis:

  • Height/age: -2.5 SD → A height-for-age measurement below -2 SD (-2.5 in this instance) indicates moderate stunting, reflecting chronic malnutrition.
  • Weight/age: -3.2 SD → A weight-for-age value below -2 SD (-3.2 in this case) signifies that the child is underweight, though this parameter alone cannot differentiate between stunting and wasting.
  • Weight/height: -1.7 SD → Normal : Weight-for-height assessment, a value below -3 SD corresponds to severe acute malnutrition (SAM), while a range between -2 and -3 SD indicates moderate acute malnutrition. Weight-for-height value of -1.7 SD rules out both SAM and moderate acute malnutrition (Options A and C are ruled out).
  • The diagnosis of acute on chronic malnutrition (Option D is ruled out) is ruled out because this condition requires a weight-for-height value below -2 SD, indicating the presence of acute malnutrition superimposed on chronic malnutrition.

question_text: Chronic malnutrition is best measured by:
explanation:

Weight For Age Is <2SD

An underweight child can be wasted or stunted or both

  • Stunting

Height For Age Is <2SD

It indicates chronic malnutrition.

  • Wasting

Weight For Height Is <2SD

It indicates acute malnutrition

Explanation of other options:

Weight for Age (Option B): Weight For-Age < -2SD so Underweight.Underweight can result from both acute and chronic malnutrition, making it less specific for chronic malnutrition. A child who is underweight may be stunted (chronic) or wasted (acute) or both. It does not differentiate between short-term and long-term malnutrition.

Height-for-age is the most reliable indicator of chronic malnutrition, as it reflects the cumulative impact of long-term nutritional deficiencies and results in stunted growth over time.

question_text: What is the fluid of choice for shock in a child with severe acute malnutrition?
explanation:
Explanation:

In children with severe acute malnutrition (SAM) who develop shock, fluid management must be approached cautiously. The WHO recommends Ringer's lactate combined with 5% dextrose as the preferred solution, as it supplies both essential electrolytes and glucose, which are critical for the safe treatment of shock in these patients.

Explanation of Other Options:

Normal Saline (Option A): It contains only sodium and chloride, without any glucose. Since hypoglycemia is common in children with SAM, using normal saline alone does not correct low blood sugar. Moreover, the high chloride content may aggravate metabolic acidosis.

Ringer's Lactate (Option B): Although it offers a better electrolyte balance than normal saline, it does not provide glucose. Children with SAM have depleted glycogen stores and need glucose supplementation to prevent or treat hypoglycemia.

10% Dextrose (Option C): This solution supplies glucose but lacks essential electrolytes. Using dextrose alone may worsen existing electrolyte imbalances and does not provide sufficient volume for effective shock resuscitation.

question_text: What is the most common cause of seizures in a 2-year-old child?
explanation:
Explanation:

Febrile Seizures are the most frequent type of seizures in children aged 6 months to 5 years. They occur in the context of a significant fever (≥100.4°F) without any evidence of central nervous system (CNS) infection.

While other conditions can cause seizures in children, febrile seizures are the most common in this age group.

Definition: Seizures triggered by fever in children between 6 months and 5 years, without CNS infection.

Types of Febrile Seizures:

  • Simple Febrile Seizures:
    • Generalized tonic-clonic seizures
    • Duration <15 minutes
    • Occurs only once in 24 hours
  • Complex Febrile Seizures:
    • Focal seizures affecting a specific body part
    • Duration >15 minutes
    • Can occur multiple times in 24 hours

Management:

  • Place the child in the left lateral (recovery) position to prevent aspiration.
  • Avoid oral intake during or immediately after the seizure.

For Seizures Lasting >5 Minutes:

  • Home Management: Rectal, buccal, or nasal midazolam
  • Hospital Management: IV lorazepam or IV midazolam

Post-Seizure Care:

  • Paracetamol can reduce fever and improve comfort but does not prevent recurrence.

Prophylaxis for Recurrent Febrile Seizures:

  • Intermittent prophylaxis: Clobazam for the first 3 days of fever
  • Long-term prophylaxis (for complex febrile seizures): Valproate or other long-term anti-epileptics

Explanation of other options:

Options A,B,D can also cause seizures in children but are less common than febrile seizures.

Key Takeaways:

  • Febrile seizures = most common seizure type in young children.
  • Antipyretics do not prevent recurrence.
  • Long-term AEDs not used for simple febrile seizures.

question_text: Which statement correctly describes X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets?
option_c: It is the most common cause of rickets
explanation:
Explanation:

X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets (XLH) is caused by mutations in the PHEX gene, which encodes a phosphate-regulating endopeptidase.

Explanation of Other Options:

FGF-23 levels decreased (Option A):

XLH is characterized by elevated FGF-23, not decreased levels.

  • Mechanism:
  • PHEX mutation leads to failure in degrading FGF-23.
  • High FGF-23 causes:
    • Renal phosphate wasting → hypophosphatemia.
    • Reduced 1α-hydroxylation of vitamin D → low/inappropriately normal 1,25(OH)2D.
  • Clinical relevance:
  • Elevated FGF-23 is a biomarker for XLH, differentiating it from nutritional rickets (where FGF-23 is normal).

It is the most common cause of rickets (Option C):

  • XLH is the most common inherited form of rickets, but nutritional rickets due to vitamin D deficiency is the overall most common worldwide.
  • Clinical differentiation:
  • Vitamin D deficiency rickets:
    • Occurs in infants and children with low sunlight exposure or inadequate dietary intake.
    • Features: frontal bossing, rachitic rosary, widened wrists/ankles, delayed closure of fontanelles.
    • Biochemistry: low calcium, low phosphate, high ALP, high PTH.
  • XLH: hypophosphatemia with normal calcium, high urinary phosphate excretion, and normal PTH.

Excretion of phosphorus is decreased (Option D):

  • In XLH, renal phosphate excretion is increased due to elevated FGF-23.
  • Mechanism: FGF-23 downregulates sodium-phosphate co-transporters (NaPi-IIa and NaPi-IIc) in proximal renal tubules, preventing phosphate reabsorption.
  • Clinical implication:
    • Persistent hypophosphatemia despite normal dietary intake.
    • Phosphate supplementation is required to correct bone mineralization defects.
  • Contrast with other rickets:
    • In nutritional rickets, phosphate excretion is not elevated, hypophosphatemia is due to inadequate intake.

Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7860650/

question_text: A 10-year-old malnourished child presents with poor appetite, dry mucosa, and loss of skin turgor. What is the glucose concentration (mmol/L) in the rehydration solution specifically designed for such cases?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The clinical presentation suggests dehydration in a malnourished child, which requires treatment with ReSoMal (Rehydration Solution for Malnutrition).
  • Typical signs include poor appetite, failure to thrive, loss of skin elasticity, and dry mucous membranes.
  • ReSoMal is a specially designed rehydration fluid for malnourished children, containing 125 mmol/L of glucose. It differs from standard oral rehydration solutions by having lower sodium and higher potassium levels, tailored to the unique electrolyte requirements of these patients.
  • Its osmolality of around 300 mOsm/L ensures proper fluid absorption and balance during rehydration.

Composition of Rehydration Solutions:

Explanation of other options:

100 mmol/L (Option A): Too low to ensure effective sodium-glucose cotransport and adequate rehydration.

150 mmol/L (Option C): Higher than recommended; may cause osmotic diarrhea.

200 mmol/L (Option D): Excessively concentrated; can lead to osmotic shifts and worsening dehydration.

Key takeaways:

  • ReSoMal = low sodium, high potassium, 125 mmol/L glucose.
  • Used only in malnourished children to prevent sodium overload.

Reference:

PMC Article on ReSoMal Composition.

question_text: A patient presents with chronic small bowel diarrhea, reports a wheat allergy, and shows villous atrophy on duodenal biopsy. Serology is positive for anti-endomysial antibodies and tissue transglutaminase (TTG) IgA antibodies. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Celiac sprue (Gluten-sensitive enteropathy):

  • Etiology: T-cell mediated autoimmune disorder triggered by gluten ingestion (wheat, barley, rye).
  • Clinical Features:
    • Chronic small bowel diarrhea, growth failure, anemia
    • Abdominal distension, bloating, vomiting, anorexia, aphthous ulcers
    • Rickets, osteoporosis, short stature, muscular atrophy, peripheral neuropathy
    • Dermatitis herpetiformis may be present
  • High-risk groups:
    • Type 1 diabetes, Down syndrome, Turner syndrome, selective IgA deficiency, autoimmune thyroid or liver disease, first-degree relatives of patients
  • Diagnosis:
    • Serology: Anti-TTG IgA, anti-EMA IgA, anti-DGP antibodies
    • Total serum IgA to rule out IgA deficiency
    • Endoscopy: may show scalloped duodenal folds or normal mucosa
    • Histopathology: villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, intraepithelial lymphocytosis
  • Management:
    • Strict gluten-free diet (avoid wheat, barley, rye, oats)
    • Nutritional supplementation if deficient (iron, folate, vitamin D)

Explanation of Other Options:

Cystic fibrosis (Option A):

  • Chronic diarrhea may occur due to pancreatic insufficiency.
  • Associated with respiratory symptoms, failure to thrive, and positive sweat chloride test.
  • Does not show villous atrophy or celiac-specific antibodies.

Whipple's disease (Option B):

  • Caused by Tropheryma whipplei infection.
  • Malabsorption and diarrhea present, but biopsy shows PAS-positive macrophages.
  • No association with wheat/gluten sensitivity or anti-TTG/EMA antibodies.

Tropical sprue (Option C):

  • Occurs in tropical regions; causes malabsorption and villous atrophy.
  • No gluten/wheat association, does not produce anti-TTG or EMA antibodies.
  • Responds to antibiotics and folate supplementation, unlike celiac disease which requires a gluten-free diet

question_text: A floppy infant presents with hypotonia, hepatomegaly, and cardiomegaly on chest X-ray. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Pompe disease presents in infancy with hypotonia, hepatomegaly, and cardiomegaly, due to glycogen accumulation in lysosomes affecting cardiac and skeletal muscle.

  • Pompe disease (Glycogen Storage Disease Type II) is an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder caused by acid α-glucosidase (acid maltase) deficiency.
  • This leads to accumulation of glycogen in lysosomes, especially in the cardiac and skeletal muscles.
  • Clinical Features of Infantile Pompe Disease:
    • Hepatomegaly
    • Macroglossia
    • Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy → Cardiomegaly on X-ray
    • Feeding difficulties
    • Respiratory distress
  • Investigations:
    • Chest X-ray: Cardiomegaly
    • Elevated CK, AST, ALT
    • ECG: Short PR interval, tall QRS
    • PAS-positive vacuoles in muscle biopsy
    • Confirmatory test: Enzyme assay showing low acid α-glucosidase
  • Management:
    • Enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) - Alglucosidase alfa
    • Supportive care (nutrition, respiratory)

Explanation of other options:

Transposition of the Great Arteries (Option B): Presents with cyanosis early in life. While cardiomegaly may be seen, hypotonia and hepatomegaly are not typical features.

Tetralogy of Fallot (Option C): Causes cyanosis and a boot-shaped heart on X-ray. It does not present with generalized hypotonia or hepatomegaly.

Ebstein's anomaly (Option D): Involves downward displacement of tricuspid valve, presenting with cyanosis and right-sided heart failure. Hypotonia and hepatomegaly are not characteristic.

question_text: A 3-week-old infant presents with a cough and sore throat. The mother reports that the infant develops a paroxysm of cough followed by apnea. The total leukocyte count is >50,000 cells/μL. Which of the following drugs will you prescribe for this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

Azithromycin is the first-line treatment for pertussis in all age groups, including infants under 1 month.

  • The clinical presentation of paroxysmal cough, apnea, and marked leukocytosis (>50,000 cells/μL) in a 3-week-old infant is highly suggestive of pertussis (whooping cough), a respiratory infection caused by Bordetella pertussis.
  • The illness progresses in three stages:
    • Catarrhal stage (1-2 weeks): mild URI symptoms
    • Paroxysmal stage (2-6 weeks): paroxysmal coughing with characteristic "whoop", post-tussive vomiting, and apnea in infants
    • Convalescent stage (1-4 weeks): gradual recovery
  • Pertussis can be dangerous in infants and may lead to pulmonary hypertension, cardiogenic shock, hemorrhage, seizures, and malnutrition.
  • Azithromycin is the drug of choice across all age groups due to its safety and efficacy.
  • It eradicates the bacteria from the nasopharynx and helps reduce the risk of transmission.
  • In infants <1 month old, erythromycin and clarithromycin are contraindicated because of the risk of infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (IHPS).
  • Cotrimoxazole is also contraindicated in infants <2 months due to the risk of kernicterus.
  • Early treatment, preferably in the catarrhal stage, improves outcomes and reduces infectivity.
  • Infants with confirmed or suspected pertussis should also be isolated for at least 5 days after starting antibiotics.
  • Preventive measures include the DTaP vaccine for infants and Tdap vaccination during pregnancy (ideally between 27-36 weeks) to confer passive immunity to the newborn.

Explanation of other options:

Amoxicillin (Option B): Not effective against Bordetella pertussis; it targets gram-positive organisms, not the gram-negative coccobacilli responsible for pertussis.

Cotrimoxazole (Option C): Though it is an alternative in older children or adults allergic to macrolides, it is contraindicated in infants <2 months due to the risk of kernicterus.

Clarithromycin (Option D): Also effective against B. pertussis, but contraindicated in infants <1 month due to the risk of infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (IHPS).

Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK519008/

question_text: A 4-year-old child of a migratory family was brought to the hospital with complaints of fever, rashes, and Bitot spots. There is no vaccination card or any other information available. What should be given to the child?
option_a: Isolate, provide nutritional support, and vitamin A supplementation
option_b: Give measles vaccine and vitamin A supplementation
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The child in the question has Measles as suspected by history of fever and rashes with Bitot spots suggesting Vitamin A deficiency. Also, there is no evidence of vaccination.
  • For a child with active measles and no other complications, needs to be isolated at home with Vitamin A supplements and providing good nutrition.
  • There is no indication of hospitalization.
  • Measles vaccine is given 8-12 weeks after active measles infection.

Explanation of other options: Incorrect Choices Explanation

Give measles vaccine and vitamin A supplementation (Option B):

  • The measles vaccine is not effective during active infection and is not given immediately.
  • Vitamin A is essential, but the vaccine should be delayed until the child recovers.

Immediate hospitalization (Option C):

  • Hospitalization is only required for severe measles complications, such as:
    • Pneumonia
    • Severe dehydration
    • Encephalitis
  • This child does not show signs of severe complications, so hospitalization is unnecessary.

Only measles vaccine (Option D):

  • Vitamin A supplementation is crucial for reducing measles mortality and preventing eye complications.
  • Delaying the vaccine until after recovery is the correct approach.

Key Takeaways:

For a child with active measles and Vitamin A deficiency, the best management is isolation, nutritional support, and Vitamin A supplementation, with the measles vaccine given later (8-12 weeks post-recovery).

question_text: A 15-month-old boy has length-for-age below -2 SD. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

In this scenario, the child's length-for-age falls ≤ -2 SD below the median, indicating moderate stunting.

Stunting:
Stunting refers to a length-for-age measurement more than two standard deviations below the median according to WHO Child Growth Standards.

Causes:

  • Inadequate feeding or reluctance to feed properly
  • Poor nutrition, recurrent infections, and lack of adequate stimulation
  • Stunting is linked to delayed cognitive development, lower academic achievement, and decreased economic productivity later in life.

Explanation of other options:

Acute malnutrition (Option A): Refers to a recent, severe deficiency of energy, protein, and other essential nutrients, which may result in wasting and/or edema.

Severe wasting (Option B): Characterized by a weight-for-height measurement more than three standard deviations below the WHO Child Growth Standards median.

Moderately underweight (Option C): Defined as a weight-for-age measurement more than two standard deviations below the WHO Child Growth Standards median.

Key Takeaways:

  • Stunting = chronic undernutrition indicator.
  • WHO cut-offs: -2 to -3 SD = moderate, < -3 SD = severe.
  • Needs early intervention for growth and neurodevelopment.

Reference: World Health Organization (WHO) classification

question_text: 11 years diagnosed CKD secondary to renal hypoplasia Upon reviewing the history you found that her height is significantly below the third percentile for her age. What is the most appropriate 1st step in the management of her growth retardation?
option_a: Immediate start of growth hormone therapy
option_b: Correction of metabolic acidosis and hyponatremia if present
explanation:
This is a very useful concept-based clinical scenario, put in this Q bank to highlight a very important message for students. Read the explanation carefully.

  • For children with CKD, medical complications include growth impairment. The cause of growth impairment is multifactorial and includes malnutrition, metabolic acidosis, electrolyte imbalances (such as hyponatremia), and renal osteodystrophy.
  • A key factor is that CKD results in an apparent growth hormone-resistant state, with elevated growth hormone levels but decreased insulin-like growth factor 1 levels and abnormalities of insulin-like growth factor-binding proteins.
  • Correction of any metabolic acidosis and hyponatremia is the initial step in management of growth impairment.
  • In addition, if evidence of malnutrition is present, the addition of protein powders or supplemental renal formulas should be considered to increase caloric density.
  • Children with CKD who remain less than -2 SD for height despite optimal medical support (adequate caloric intake and effective treatment of renal osteodystrophy, anemia, and metabolic acidosis) may benefit from treatment with recombinant human growth hormone (rHuGH).
  • OP Ghai 10th Edition also says that Early recognition and management of malnutrition, mineral bone disease, metabolic acidosis and electrolyte disturbances take precedence over therapy with growth hormone.
  • A gastrostomy tube can be considered in an infant or young child if they are unlikely to take in the required volume and calories by mouth.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 519; Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 550.2; Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1st SA ed., pg. 2545

question_text: Gene mutated in Chediak-Higashi syndrome is?
explanation:
Chediak-Higashi Syndrome

  • Autosomal Recessive condition- LYST gene mutation on Chromosome 1q.
  • The gene codes for a protein involved in lysosomal intracellular transport
  • Mutations in the LYST gene produce faulty lysosomal transport

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Table 156.2

question_text: Hepatitis B subunit vaccine is derived from?
explanation:
The current subunit Hepatitis B vaccine is derived from surface antigen, i.e., HBsAg.

  • The vaccine is based upon DNA recombinant technology and uses Aluminium as an adjuvant.
  • The hepatitis B vaccine is made by taking the part of the virus that makes surface protein ("surface protein gene") and putting it into yeast cells. The yeast cells then produce many copies of the protein that are subsequently used to make the vaccine.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 198

question_text: A 6-year-old female child presented with non-blanchable, palpable petechial rash on lower limbs and buttocks, along with 3+ urinary protein and joint pains in knee and ankle. There was a preceding sore throat 2 weeks back, which was conservatively managed. What is the therapy of choice?
explanation:
The child was having a trigger factor in the form of sore throat & 2 weeks later, she presented with non-blanchable, palpable petechial rash on dependent parts, renal and joint involvement.

  • This translates to a diagnosis of Henoch-Schoenlein Purpura, HSP- Also known as IgA Vasculitis.
  • Management of HSP is Conservative- More than 90% improve in about 4 weeks.
  • Steroids, e.g., Prednisolone are indicated in severe GIT involvement

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 661

explanation:
Raised cells, raised protein in CSF but normal CSF glucose is seen in aseptic meningitis (viral meningitis).
