question_text: Not correct regarding Duchenne's muscular dystrophy is?
option_a: Normal serum CK levels in asymptomatic period
option_c: Serum CK may fall in terminal stages
explanation:
Duchenne’s muscular dystrophy

  • An X-linked recessive muscular dystrophy due to mutation in gene coding for dystrophin protein in muscle sarcolemma
  • Child grows normally till 18 months to 2 years of age
  • Starts to develop progressive myopathy, initially manifesting as frequent falls
  • Serum CK levels can be raised even in asymptomatic early stage and help to make early diagnosis
  • Gower sign is positive, Pseudohypertrophy of calf muscles is seen
  • Child is bed-ridden by 12 yr of age and death occurs by 15 yr of age
  • Serum CK levels may return to normal in late terminal stages since most muscle mass has atrophied.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Pages 614 - 616

question_text: A child brought with a 2-week history of fever, not feeding well and irritability was examined and evaluated. He had neck rigidity. His sister was already taking treatment for TB. CSF on Lumbar Puncture is likely to show which of the following findings?
explanation:
Clues in the question

  • Fever, Neck rigidity, poor feeding and irritability
  • Contact with TB patient
  • History of fever is 2 weeks in this child
  • Likely possibility is TB Meningitis

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Table 621.1

question_text: All of the following are true regarding tubercular meningitis in a child, except?
option_b: Total duration of ATT is 12 months
option_c: Basal cistern exudates are the radiological hallmark
option_d: No role of steroids in the therapy
explanation:
Let us evaluate the options sequentially

  • Option A is True: Risk factors for tubercular meningitis include young age, household contact, recent measles and protein-energy malnutrition.
  • Option B is True: As per IAP-NTEP Guidelines and OP Ghai 10th Edition, ATT comprises 2 months of Intensive therapy + 10 months of Maintenance Therapy. Total Duration of ATT is 12 months
  • Option C is True. Basal cistern exudates are the CT scan hallmark of the disease.
  • Option D is False. Intravenous Dexamethasone is followed by oral steroids for 6-8 weeks to prevent sequelae in most children.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 586 - 587.

question_text: An 11-year-old boy presents to clinic with a complaint of 1 to 2 episodes of vomiting at least 1 time per week over the past 3 months. He reports that vomiting consists of non-bloody, nonbilious food material and is preceded by several minutes of burning substernal pain. His body mass index is in the 80th percentile for age. What is the next most appropriate step in the management of this patient?
option_d: A 2-week trial of ondansetron as needed for nausea
explanation:
This patient has chronic recurrent vomiting, with at least 3 episodes of mild but frequent emesis over a 3-month period.

  • Among the most frequent causes of vomiting in the school- age child and adolescent are gastroesophageal reflux disease, which may occur after meals and is not typically associated with weight loss.
  • In a child with chronic vomiting without alarm symptoms or other concerning examination findings, the most likely diagnosis is an acid-peptic disorder such as gastroesophageal reflux disease or gastritis that should be initially treated with empiric 2 to 4-week trial of H2-receptor antagonist or proton pump inhibitor for acid suppression.
  • As per the latest studies, PPIs are superior to H2-receptor antagonists in GERD patients.
  • If there is no symptomatic improvement after a time- limited trial of these medications, it may then be appropriate to proceed with laboratory testing, imaging, or consultation with pediatric gastroenterology.
  • Ondansetron may be useful for symptomatic improvement in the setting of acute, rather than chronic, vomiting.

Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1st SA ed., pg. 1782

question_text: A 15-year-old girl presents with a painful mass involving her right fourth rib. Biopsy reveals small round blue cells. Identification of which of the following translocations by FISH would confirm the diagnosis of Ewing sarcoma?
explanation:
The t(11;22) translocation is found in more than 90% of cases of Ewing sarcoma, and results in the formation of the EWSFLI1 fusion protein. Hence, option D is the correct answer.

Regarding other options

  • Option A- Translocation t(2;13) is characteristic of alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma.
  • Option B- t(X;18) is seen in synovial sarcoma.
  • Option C- t(9;22), also known as the "Philadelphia chromosome", results in the generation of the BCR–ABL fusion protein and is found in almost all cases of chronic myelogenous leukemia and sometimes in other forms of leukemia.

Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 20th edition, pg. 2473

question_text: A 4-month-old infant presents with choking when taking his bottles, tongue fasciculation, and profound hypotonia. Which of the following would you tell the parents?
option_a: Without assisted ventilation, median age of death is at 12 years
option_b: Their child will likely be able to sit but not to walk
option_c: Tracheostomy is the only option for survival
option_d: Cough is impaired and use of an airway clearance device is recommended
explanation:
• The infant described in the vignette has spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) type I (Wernig–Hoffman disease) due to presentation as an infant with the above-described clinical features. Cough reflex is expected to be impaired and the use of a cough assist device will help to clear secretions.
  • Without assisted ventilation, children usually die within the first 2 years of life. With SMA type II, the median age of survival is 12 years without assisted ventilation. (option A)
  • In SMA type I, their child will not be able to sit or walk. (option B)
  • Noninvasive ventilation may also be presented as an option in addition to tracheostomy to prolong survival. (Option C)

KEY TAKEAWAYS: Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA) is a genetic disorder that leads to the progressive weakening of muscles due to the loss of motor neurons in the spinal cord and brainstem. It primarily affects infants and children, with symptoms such as muscle weakness, poor muscle tone, and difficulty breathing, swallowing, and moving. SMA is caused by mutations in the SMN1 gene, leading to low levels of the survival motor neuron protein essential for motor neuron health.

Tags:

  • Topic: NEUROMUSCULAR DISEASE
  • Difficulty level: GOOD TO KNOW
  • PYQ: INICET MAY 2022

Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21st ed., pg. 2997

question_text: A 12-year-old boy with type 1 diabetes mellitus, is reviewed in the outpatient clinic. In spite of maintaining good control of his diabetes, his height has remained static for 9 months. He says his appetite is alright, but he has lost interest in sports. and he can't keep up with the other boys any more. He just stays at home and watches TV, but wants to be out playing football and getting back his energy. A full blood count and C-reactive protein are normal and his HbA1C is satisfactory. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• Children with type 1 diabetes mellitus are at increased risk of thyroid disease and should be screened annually. His static height and his lethargy would support this diagnosis.
  • He is also at increased risk of coeliac disease and this should also be considered but is less likely as his appetite is good and his weight is satisfactory.
  • Eating disorders can co-exist with diabetes mellitus but he does not have the clinical features of anorexia nervosa. (Option a)
  • GH deficiency is not an autoimmune problem. Would not explain his lethargy. (Option b)
  • Blood and mucus in the stool would be expected with ulcerative colitis and anorexia and malaise and abnormal full blood count and C-reactive protein would be expected with Crohn's disease. (Option d)

question_text: Which of the following symptoms is most suggestive of a diagnosis of IgE-mediated cow's milk protein allergy rather than non-IgE mediated?
explanation:
• IgE mediated cow's milk protein allergies have a rapid onset of up to 2 hours after ingestion, whereas non-IgE mediated are more delay and may not present until up to a week after ingestion.
  • Both IgE and non-IgE mediated cow's milk protein allergy can cause pruritis, erythema, and lower respiratory tract infections including wheezing, coughing, and shortness of breath.
  • Loose stools is more characteristic of non-IgE mediated allergies.

question_text: A child presented to the clinic with complaints of malnutrition and severe dehydration. What would be the choice of IV fluid for this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

Ringer's Lactate (RL) with 5% Dextrose is commonly used as the initial IV fluid in children with severe dehydration and malnutrition. It ensures rehydration, corrects electrolyte imbalance, and supplies energy through dextrose.

Explanation of Other Options:

ORS (Option A): Oral Rehydration Solution is the first choice for mild to moderate dehydration, but in severe dehydration, especially when the child is drowsy or unable to drink, ORS is not suitable.

NS (Option B): Normal Saline is isotonic and can restore hydration, but it does not provide energy since it lacks dextrose. In malnourished children, the additional glucose is crucial.

DNS (Option D): Dextrose Normal Saline contains glucose and helps in rehydration, but it does not offer the same balanced electrolytes as Ringer's Lactate, making it less ideal in severe cases.

question_text: A child presents with the findings shown in the image below. What is the true statement regarding this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The image depicting abdominal swelling and a listless facial expression suggests Kwashiorkor.

  • Kwashiorkor is a form of protein-energy malnutrition that develops in children with insufficient protein intake.
  • It is typically characterized by edema in the limbs, a distended abdomen, and a dull or apathetic facial appearance.
  • Low levels of serum protein and albumin contribute to the development of edema in this condition.

Comparison between Kwashiorkor and Marasmus:

Explanation of Other Options:

Kwashiorkor due to calorie deficiency (Option B) is incorrect because Kwashiorkor primarily results from protein deficiency, although caloric intake may also be inadequate. The characteristic edema in Kwashiorkor is mainly due to hypoalbuminemia, not a lack of calories.

Marasmus (Options C & D) does not fit this presentation. Marasmus is characterized by severe wasting, "monkey facies," baggy pants appearance, and absence of edema. Children with marasmus appear extremely thin with prominent bones, so the pr esence of edema and a distended abdomen makes this diagnosis unlikely.

question_text: A child fed mostly rice water presents with a swollen abdomen, apathetic look, and low serum proteins. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The child's symptoms, including a distended abdomen, a dull facial expression, low serum protein and albumin levels on investigation, along with a history of predominantly consuming rice water, indicate kwashiorkor.
  • Kwashiorkor is a severe form of malnutrition caused by inadequate protein intake, especially essential amino acids. It most commonly affects children aged 1-3 years who consume diets deficient in high-quality protein sources.
  • Kwashiorkor vs Marasmus (Option B Ruled Out)
  • WELLCOME CLASSIFICATION (Protein-Calorie Malnutrition)

Explanation of other options:

Indian childhood cirrhosis (Option C): is a liver disorder mainly seen in infants and young children in India. It involves liver injury and fibrosis, causing impaired liver function. However, it does not typically present with abdominal swelling or a dull facial appearance.

Kawasaki disease (Option D): is an acute febrile illness predominantly affecting children under 5 years. It causes systemic vasculitis and presents with symptoms including high fever, non-purulent conjunctivitis, rash on the trunk, redness and swelling of palms and soles with subsequent peeling, cervical lymphadenopathy, and mucous membrane changes like strawberry tongue. (Mnemonic: CREAM features)

Key Takeaways:

  • Kwashiorkor = protein deficiency, presents with edema.
  • Marasmus = calorie deficiency, severe wasting.
  • Wellcome classification helps grade malnutrition.

question_text: A child who is exclusively fed rice water presents with a swollen abdomen and a pale, unenergetic expression, and shows signs of malnourishment with decreased serum protein and albumin levels. What is the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The presence of oedema, signs of malnutrition, and decreased serum protein and albumin levels point to the diagnosis of kwashiorkor.
  • Undernutrition is a set of conditions that result from inadequate consumption, poor nutrient absorption or excessive loss of nutrients.
  • Childhood undernutrition is an underlying cause in an estimated 45% of all deaths among under-5 children.
  • Clinical classification of undernutrition includes:
    • Marasmus
    • Kwashiorkor
    • Marasmic kwashiorkor

Explanation of other options: 

Indian childhood cirrhosis (Option C): A chronic liver disease in infants and children that presents with jaundice, pruritus, lethargy, and hepatosplenomegaly. It is related to copper accumulation in the liver.

Kawasaki disease (Option D): Characterised by vasculitis that affects medium-sized arteries, especially the coronary arteries and presents with fever, strawberry tongue, bilateral conjunctivitis, rash, and desquamation of hands and feet. This is not the given scenario.

question_text: A child presents to the pediatric OPD with the findings shown in the image below. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Based on the image findings like abdominal distension, pedal oedema, thin brittle hair, and muscle wasting, the child is likely to have Kwashiorkor.

  • Undernutrition is a set of conditions that result from inadequate consumption, poor nutrient absorption or excessive loss of nutrients.
  • Childhood undernutrition is an underlying cause in an estimated 45% of all deaths among under-5 children.
  • Clinical classification of undernutrition includes:
    • Marasmus
    • Kwashiorkor
    • Marasmic kwashiorkor

Explanation of other options:

Nephrotic syndrome (Option C): This condition is characterized by massive proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, and hyperlipidemia. While it can cause edema, poor growth, and malnutrition, the edema is typically generalized and may be present from birth, distinguishing it from kwashiorkor.

Nephritic syndrome (Option D): This syndrome presents with hematuria, hypertension, oliguria, and edema. The edema here is usually associated with renal impairment rather than protein deficiency.

question_text: What is the specific sign of kwashiorkor?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Pitting edema is the hallmark feature of kwashiorkor, caused by severe protein deficiency.
  • Low plasma albumin → decreased oncotic pressure → fluid shifts into interstitial spaces → bilateral edema, often starting in legs, feet, and sometimes face/hands.
  • Distinguishes kwashiorkor from marasmus, where edema is absent.

Explanation of Other Options:

Weight loss (Option B): Although common in malnutrition, it is not specific to kwashiorkor. In kwashiorkor, edema can mask weight loss, making it an unreliable indicator. Weight loss occurs broadly across various nutritional deficiencies.

Flag sign (Option C): This refers to alternating bands of normal and depigmented hair seen during periods of nutritional deficiency. It is not exclusive to kwashiorkor and can appear in other forms of malnutrition, such as marasmus, reflecting intermittent malnutrition.

Muscle wasting (Option D): While muscle wasting is a feature of protein-energy malnutrition, it is not unique to kwashiorkor. In this condition, it may be concealed by edema, whereas it is more obvious in marasmus.

question_text: A 6-year-old boy presents with chronic cough and foul-smelling stools. His sibling had similar complaints and died a few years ago. Sweat chloride test and CFTR gene analysis were performed. The CFTR gene codes for a protein responsible for the transport of which ion?
explanation:
Explanation:

The given clinical scenario is consistent with cystic fibrosis (CF), a genetic disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR (Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator) gene.

  • This gene encodes a chloride channel that regulates chloride ion (Cl-) transport across epithelial cell membranes in the sweat glands, pancreas, and airways.
  • Dysfunction of this channel results in thickened secretions, impaired mucociliary clearance, malabsorption, and recurrent respiratory infections.

Cystic Fibrosis:

  • Genetic Basis:
    • Gene: CFTR (Chromosome 7q31.2)
    • Common mutation: ΔF508
    • Inheritance: Autosomal recessive
  • Pathophysiology:
  • CFTR defect: Impaired chloride secretion with increased sodium absorption → dehydrated mucus.
  • Respiratory: Mucus plugging, bacterial colonization, bronchiectasis, respiratory failure.
  • Gastrointestinal: Pancreatic duct obstruction, malabsorption, steatorrhea, distal intestinal obstruction.
  • Sweat glands: Excess salt loss → contraction alkalosis.
  • Reproductive:
    • Males: Congenital bilateral absence of vas deferens → infertility.
    • Females: Thick cervical mucus impairs fertility.
  • Clinical Features:
    • Respiratory: Chronic cough, recurrent pneumonia, bronchiectasis, clubbing.
    • Gastrointestinal: Steatorrhea, malnutrition, meconium ileus.
    • Genitourinary: Infertility, delayed puberty.
    • Electrolyte imbalance: Salt-loss syndromes.
  • Diagnosis:
    • Clinical features or family history plus confirmatory evidence:
      • Sweat chloride test ≥ 60 mmol/L (on two occasions).
      • Identification of two pathogenic CFTR mutations.
      • Abnormal nasal potential difference.
    • Common microbial colonization:
      • <18 years: Staphylococcus aureus
      • 18 years: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
      • Burkholderia cepacia - rare but associated with high mortality.
    • Management:
      • Airway clearance: Chest physiotherapy, postural drainage.
      • Infection control: Antibiotics, eradication of Pseudomonas.
      • Nutrition: High-calorie diet, pancreatic enzyme replacement, fat-soluble vitamin supplements (A, D, E, K).
      • Metabolic care: Insulin for CF-related diabetes, bone health support.
      • CFTR modulators:
        • Ivacaftor, lumacaftor.
        • Trikafta (Elexacaftor-Tezacaftor-Ivacaftor): Approved for children ≥2 years, improves lung function and reduces sweat chloride levels.

Explanation of Other Options:

Na⁺ (Option A): Sodium absorption is increased secondarily, but CFTR specifically codes for chloride transport.

HCO₃- (Option B): Bicarbonate secretion is affected indirectly in CF, but it is not the primary ion transported by CFTR.

K⁺ (Option D): Potassium transport abnormalities may occur due to electrolyte imbalance, but CFTR is not a potassium channel.

Key Takeaways:

  • CFTR gene mutation causes defective chloride ion transport, leading to multisystem disease.
  • Hallmark diagnostic test: Sweat chloride ≥60 mmol/L.
  • Modern therapy includes CFTR modulators (e.g., Trikafta), which significantly improve prognosis.

question_text: A child presented with complaints of low-grade fever, neck stiffness and skin lesions. Examination revealed multiple vesicles present on palms and soles. question_text: Which of the following is correct comparing breast milk with cow's milk?
option_d: Breast milk contains more Vitamin K
explanation:
Absolute amount of calcium is less in breast milk than animal milk but since the calcium: phosphorous ratio is 2:1, the absorption is better.

Key points to note:

  • Vitamins deficient in breast milk: Vit K, Vit D, Vit B1.
  • Mineral deficient in breast milk: Fluoride.
  • Breast milk has more lactose but less fat, protein, and calcium than animal milk.
  • Breast milk is rich in whey protein (better) compared to casein of animal milk. Breast milk also has more taurine and cysteine.
  • Breast milk has more MUFA, PUFA and is especially rich in DHA, i.e. Docosahexaenoic Acid.

question_text: An 8-year-old child presented with periorbital edema and mild oliguria but no hypertension. On evaluation, he was found to have serum albumin <2.5 g/dL, serum creatinine 0.5 mg/dL, urine protein 3+, and no RBCs or RBC casts in the urine. What histopathological diagnosis will you suspect?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical features: significant proteinuria (3+), hypoalbuminemia, and edema; are characteristic of Nephrotic Syndrome. In children aged 2-8 years, the most common histopathological diagnosis is Minimal Change Disease (MCD).

  • Absence of hematuria and hypertension supports the diagnosis of idiopathic nephrotic syndrome.
  • Light microscopy typically shows minimal or no changes.
  • Electron microscopy reveals effacement of podocyte foot processes.
  • Oliguria, although more typical of nephritic syndrome, may occur in nephrotic syndrome due to worsening edema and hypoalbuminemia.

Explanation of Other Options:

  • IgA nephropathy (Option B): Presents with hematuria, often post-infectious.
  • Membranous nephropathy (Option C): More common in adults; shows thickened GBM on microscopy.
  • FSGS (Option D): Presents with steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome and may show hematuria or hypertension.

question_text: A 5-year-old child developed periorbital puffiness following an acute febrile illness. His spot urine protein sample showed protein: creatinine ratio of 3.5:1. There was no hypertension or hematuria. The child was started on oral prednisolone @ 2mg/kg/day as single morning dose. Despite 9 days of therapy, the child continues to have periorbital edema and persistently elevated protein: creatinine ratio. What next needs to be done?
option_a: Continue prednisolone in same dose for now & watch for remission
option_b: Increase dose of prednisolone to double
option_c: Start Levamisole as steroid sparing agent
explanation:
Childhood nephrotic syndrome

  • Nephrotic syndrome in a child is said to be there when there is massive proteinuria (Urine protein excretion >40 mg/m2/hr or spot urine protein creatinine ratio is >2:1) with other features like hypoalbuminemia, edema, hyperlipidemia and hypercoagulability of blood
  • A child aged 2 to 6 years and coming with only massive proteinuria and no hematuria/hypertension is treated on the lines of minimal change disease. These children need no renal biopsy routinely and are started on oral prednisolone @ 2 mg/kg/day given for 6 weeks daily, followed by 1.5 mg/kg alternate day for 6 weeks
  • If child does not respond to daily steroids for 6 weeks, he is called steroid-resistant and renal biopsy is indicated
  • Since the child in ques has received steroids at full dose only for 9 days, we shall continue the same and wait for remission. If remission doesn't come or partially comes after 6 weeks of steroid therapy, then only we will refer to a pediatric nephrologist for considering steroid resistance and doing renal biopsy.
  • Levamisole and cyclophosphamide are indicated in frequently relapsing and steroid dependent varieties and hence not the answer here.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Pages 502-503.

question_text: A 6-year-old male child presented with a boil on the leg 2 weeks ago and is now presenting with cola coloured urine, 2+ urinary protein, facial edema and has BP of 120/80 mm of Hg. There is no other symptom or rash. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A school-going-aged boy developing acute nephritic syndrome 2 weeks after a boil (pyoderma) indicates a likely diagnosis of Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis.

  • Kindly note that BP of 120/80 is Hypertension in a 6-year-old boy.

Regarding other options

  • Option A- Minimal Change Disease usually does not have gross hematuria & tends to have massive proteinuria (3+ or 4+)
  • Option B- IgA Nephropathy presents with acute nephritic syndrome within 2-6 days of preceding sore throat or pyoderma, not 2 weeks after.
  • Option D- HSP nephritis will also have palpable purpura, joint involvement with GIT manifestations and since these are not mentioned, unlikely to be the answer here.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition Pages 496-497

question_text: A 4-year-old boy presents with swelling that has increased over the past week. The swelling is most noticeable around his eyes in the mornings but is most notable in his legs in the afternoon. On examination, he has pitting edema of the bilateral lower extremities. He is also mildly hypertensive. Labs are significant for hypoalbuminemia and 3+ proteinuria. What is the most likely etiology of the child's hypoalbuminemia?
explanation:
The child's presentation is consistent with idiopathic nephrotic syndrome.

  • Nephrotic syndrome results from urinary protein losses, which lead to hypoalbuminemia.
  • The hypoalbuminemia leads to dependent edema. As such, the edema may be most noticeable around the eyes in the mornings with a shift to the lower extremities as the day progresses.
  • Hypertension may occasionally be present.
  • Typical laboratory findings include serum hypoalbuminemia, proteinuria, and hyperlipidemia.
  • Idiopathic nephrotic syndrome is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in childhood.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Pages 500-501; Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1st SA ed., pg. 2523

question_text: A 10-year-old child presented with generalized edema. On investigation, his serum cholesterol level was 238 mg/dl, urine protein was 3+ and stool microscopy revealed oval fat bodies. What is the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Nephrotic range proteinuria is defined as proteinuria >3.5 g/24 hour or a urine protein : creatinine ratio >2.

  • The triad of clinical findings associated with nephrotic syndrome arising from the large urinary losses of protein are hypoalbuminemia (≤2.5 g/dL), edema, and hyperlipidemia (cholesterol >200 mg/dL).

Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 20th ed., pg. 2521

question_text: A 4-year-old child is having first episode of nephrotic syndrome and is started on oral steroids. He develops severe abdominal pain. Which of the following complications must be considered on priority in this child and investigated?
explanation:
• Nephrotic children are in a pro-thrombotic state and if thrombosis occurs in this group it carries a significant morbidity and mortality.
  • Be particularly wary of nephrotic children who complain of chest or abdominal pain as they could be presenting with pulmonary embolism or mesenteric ischemia.

Option a, c and d are not considered on priority in this child and investigated.

KEY TAKEAWAYS: Antithrombin III: This important protein that helps to regulate blood clotting is lost in significant amounts through the urine due to glomerular damage. Low levels increase the risk of clot formation.

Protein C and Protein S: Both are critical for the regulation of clotting. Their levels may also be decreased, further promoting a prothrombotic environment.

question_text: A 12-year-old girl presents with a history of joint stiffening in the morning and feeling tired after school, with some joint pains in her lower limbs. On examination, her left knee is warm and swollen. Swelling and pain in joints is also found in 6 of her small joints of fingers. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 55, and C-reactive protein is 70 mg/l. The white cell count is normal, with a high platelet count. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
More than 5 joints involved in an adolescent girl, suggests Polyarticular JIA

  • Polyarticular-onset JIA occurs in 20% of children with JRA.
  • A group of these are rheumatoid factor IgM-positive, and they can resemble adult-onset arthritis in pattern.
  • The majority are usually female and present between 12 and 16 years of age with symmetrical small-joint involvement, flexor tenosynovitis and nodules commonly being seen.
  • Systemic features are less common in this group. Active disease in adulthood will be more common in these groups.
  • Extra-articular manifestations include lung, cardiac, aortic and vascular disease. In those patients with polyarticular JIA who are seronegative for rheumatoid factor, there is hepatosplenomegaly with fever and symmetrical arthritis.
  • Hip, neck, hand and feet joints are commonly affected, as well as the knees, wrists and ankles.
  • Soft tissue swelling is commonly seen on X-ray, while erosions can be seen in the polyarticular variety.
  • Systemic involvement is seen especially in the pauciarticular and systemic disease subtypes.

Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1stSA edition, pg. 1163

question_text: A 4-year-old male child presents to the emergency department with a history of fever for 10 days. The child also complains of loose stools, vomiting, and abdominal pain. He has bilateral redness in eyes. The child has a history of a mild episode of COVID-19 before 3 weeks. The child's labs reveal lymphocytopenia, and an elevated C-reactive protein.     • CRP
    • Procalcitonin
  • Recent evidence of COVID19:

OR

  • No other microbial cause likely

question_text: Deficiency of which of the following vitamins is associated with increased risk of thrombosis?
explanation:

  • Vitamin K deficiency leads to hemorrhagic disorders, since vitamin K is essential in the production of coagulation factors II, VII, IX, X, and proteins C and S.

  • Vitamins A is not associated with either an increased bleeding or thrombosis risk.

question_text: A neonate delivered via normal vaginal delivery is started on mother's feed. He developed vomiting, hypoglycemia, oil drop cataract, hepatomegaly and mild icterus. Urine was positive for reducing substance, but not glucose. The likely enzyme deficiency is?
explanation:
The child is presenting with a crisis, oil drop cataract and non-glucose reducing substances in urine, all after feeding. This suggests a likely diagnosis of Galactosemia.

  • Galactosemia denotes the elevated level of galactose in the blood and is found in 3 distinct inborn errors of galactose metabolism in 1 of the following enzymes: galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase, galactokinase, and uridine diphosphate galactose-4-epimerase.
  • The term galactosemia, generally designates the galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase deficiency, which produces Classic Galactosemia
  • Classic galactosemia is a serious disease with onset of symptoms typically by the 2nd half of the 1st wk of life.
  • The diagnosis should be considered in newborn or young infants with any of the following features within a few days or weeks after birth: jaundice, hepatomegaly, vomiting, hypoglycemia, seizures, lethargy, irritability, feeding difficulties, poor weight gain or failure to regain birthweight, and aminoaciduria.
  • Untreated children may show nuclear oil-drop cataracts, vitreous hemorrhage, hepatic failure, cirrhosis, ascites, splenomegaly, or intellectual disability.
  • Patients with galactosemia are at increased risk for Escherichia coli neonatal sepsis; the onset of sepsis often precedes the diagnosis of galactosemia.
  • Pseudotumor cerebri can occur and cause a bulging fontanel.
  • If untreated, death from liver and kidney failure and sepsis may follow within days. When the diagnosis is not made at birth, damage to the liver (cirrhosis) and brain (intellectual disability) becomes increasingly severe and irreversible.
  • The initial diagnosis of galactosemia is done by demonstration of a reducing substance in several urine specimens collected while the patient is on a diet containing human milk, cow's milk, or any other formula containing lactose.
  • Direct enzyme assay using erythrocytes establishes the diagnosis.
  • Complete withdrawal of lactose from the diet results in improvement of the acute symptoms.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 105.2; OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 687

question_text: A 10-year-old girl is 4 ft 10 in (147 cm) tall. Her father is 5 ft 10 in (178 cm) tall, and her mother is 5 ft 5 in (165 cm) tall. Over the past 3 years she has dropped from the 25th percentile for height to the 5th percentile. Her weight has remained stable. Radiographs show bone age is delayed. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in her management?
option_a: Send patient to the emergency department for CT evaluation of the brain
explanation:
This child has evidence of possible growth hormone deficiency. Obtaining an IGF-1 level would be the most appropriate initial choice.

  • Growth hormone deficiency is not an emergent condition but the earlier the diagnosis is made the sooner appropriate treatment can be initiated. Obtaining a growth hormone level would not be diagnostically helpful because its secretion is pulsatile.
  • Referral to a pediatric endocrinologist would be warranted if initial screening tests confirm the suspected growth hormone deficiency.

Reference: Nelson-Pediatric Symptom based diagnosis, pg. 791

question_text: During the 1-week health supervision visit, a mother who is exclusively breastfeeding asks about vitamin and iron supplementation for her healthy term infant. She explains that her previous child, who was born at 30 weeks gestation, was discharged with an oral iron supplement and vitamins. The baby has already received 1 intramuscular shot of Vitamin K at birth. Of the following, the MOST appropriate oral supplement to initiate for this infant at this visit is?
explanation:
The American Academy of Pediatrics as well as Indian Academy of Pediatrics 2021 Guidelines recommend that breastfed and partially breastfed infants be supplemented with 400 IU of vitamin D daily. Since babies are exclusively breastfed in the 1st 6 months and breast milk has low amounts of Vitamin K as well as Vitamin D, public health strategies have been devised to address their deficiencies.

Regarding other options

  • Term newborns are assumed to have adequate iron stores for the first 4 to 6 months after birth and usually do not need any supplements in the 1st few months of life.
  • The term infant has adequate calcium stores.
  • The term infant also has adequate folate stores.
  • The routine use of a standard dose of intramuscular vitamin K at birth minimizes the risk of hemorrhagic disease of the newborn, which results from vitamin K deficiency.

Reference: IAP Guidelines 2021; Cloherty and stark's manual of neonatal care, 8th ed., pg. 887

question_text: In which of the following scenarios is the child least likely to suffer from vitamin K deficiency?
option_a: A 4 day old baby of a healthy mother started on immediate breast feeding
option_b: A 2 year old who spent 21 days in NICU on total parenteral nutrition
option_c: A 1 year old with cystic fibrosis missed during early infancy
option_d: A 1 year old with prolonged history of diarrhea and multiple antibiotics therapy
explanation:
Causes of Vitamin K deficiency are:

  • Occult malabsorption of vitamin K,
    • Undiagnosed cystic fibrosis or cholestatic liver disease (e.g., biliary atresia, α1-antitrypsin deficiency).
    • Secondary to maternal intake of medications (warfarin, phenobarbital, phenytoin)
  • Result of fat malabsorption
    • Cholestatic liver disease
    • Pancreatic disease,
    • Intestinal disorders (celiac sprue, inflammatory bowel disease, short-bowel syndrome).
  • Prolonged diarrhea can cause vitamin K deficiency, especially in breastfed infants. Age.
  • Use of broad-spectrum antibiotics that eliminate the intestine's vitamin K2- producing bacteria can cause vitamin K deficiency. This scenario is especially common in the intensive care unit.
  • Patients who receive total parenteral nutrition without vitamin K supplementation.

question_text: Which vitamin is deficient in breast milk?
explanation:
Explanation:

Breast milk has low vitamin K content. Newborns are especially at risk for vitamin K deficiency, which can result in bleeding disorders like hemorrhagic disease of the newborn. Therefore, it is standard practice to give a vitamin K injection to infants soon after birth to prevent this deficiency.

Explanation of other options:

Vitamin C (Option B): Present in sufficient quantities.

question_text: A child presents with malnutrition and multiple follicular, dry papules on the elbows and knees. Improvement of the skin lesions is observed following vitamin supplementation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Phrynoderma is a follicular hyperkeratotic disorder associated with multiple vitamin deficiencies, especially vitamin A, and improves with vitamin supplementation.

  • Phrynoderma, also known as toad skin, is a condition characterized by dry, horny follicular papules distributed commonly on extensor surfaces like elbows, knees, buttocks, and thighs.
  • It is seen in malnourished individuals, particularly children, and is attributed to multiple nutritional deficiencies, especially:
    • Vitamin A
    • Vitamin C, Vitamin E,
    • B-complex vitamins, and
    • Essential fatty acids
  • The papules are due to follicular plugging and hyperkeratosis, giving the skin a rough texture.
  • The hallmark of the diagnosis is improvement of the lesions with vitamin and nutritional supplementation.

Explanation of other options:

Keratosis Pilaris (Option B): Though also present with follicular papules, it is a genetic condition unrelated to malnutrition or vitamin deficiency, and typically does not improve with vitamin supplementation.

Darier Disease (Option C): A genetic disorder of keratinization presenting with greasy, warty papules in seborrheic areas (chest, back, forehead); not related to malnutrition and does not improve with vitamins.

Lichen Planus (Option D): An autoimmune inflammatory condition with flat-topped, violaceous, itchy papules, often involving wrists and oral mucosa-does not resemble follicular papules or respond to vitamin therapy.

question_text: Classical triad of Wernicke encephalopathy of thiamine deficiency is characterized by?

Thiamine deficiency

question_text: A 4-week-old male child with normal genitalia presents to the emergency department with severe dehydration, hyperkalemia, and hyponatremia. The measurement blood levels of which of the following will be helpful?
explanation:
Let us go stepwise in this question

  • This is a male infant who presented with a salt losing crisis. Why? Because there is severe dehydration, hyponatremia and hyperkalemia suggesting mineralocorticoid deficiency.
  • Salt-wasting crisis means it is likely to be either 21 hydroxylase deficiency or 3 beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency, since both present with salt-wasting or salt-losing crisis.
  • Now, it is a male child with normal genitalia, so it cannot be 3 beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency, since it always presents with ambiguous genitalia. This means that the likely diagnosis is 21 hydroxylase deficiency.
  • Now, in 21 hydroxylase deficiency, there is an elevated level of 17-hydroxy progesterone, which is a screening test.
  • Hence, measurement of 17-hydroxy progesterone levels will help to make the diagnosis.

question_text: A child developed sudden-onset cardiac arrest. CPR was started and rhythm was checked. Since there was asystole, it was decided to give injection epinephrine to the child. However, intravenous access could not be obtained immediately. What alternative site can you inject epinephrine in such a patient?
explanation:
In pediatric cardiac arrest, if the central or peripheral venous access is not immediately achieved, intraosseous (IO) access should be secured.

  • The usual site for IO access is upper end of tibia, medial to the tibial tuberosity.
  • Other sites include distal femur, lower end of tibia above medial malleolus and anterior superior iliac spine.
  • All drugs and infusions which can be given via intravenous route, can also be administered via intraosseous route.
  • Tracheal route is not a preferred site even in emergencies. However, if even IO access is not possible, it can be considered for lipid-soluble agents like epinephrine, lidocaine, atropine and naloxone, if indicated.

question_text: An infant is brought to a hospital because her wet diaper turns black when they are exposed to air. Physical examination of infant is normal. This disorder is caused by a deficiency of?
explanation:
Dark/blackening of urine on exposure to air in an infant suggests a diagnosis of Alkaptonuria, caused by the deficiency of the enzyme, Homogentisic Acid Oxidase.

  • Alkaptonuria is a rare (approximately 1 in 250,000 live births) autosomal recessive disorder caused by a deficiency of homogentisate 1, 2- dioxygenase, also called homogentisic acid oxidase.
  • Large amounts of homogentisic acid are formed, which are excreted in urine or deposited in tissues.
  • The main clinical manifestations of alkaptonuria consist of ochronosis and arthritis in adulthood. The only sign in children is blackening of the urine on standing, caused by oxidation and polymerization of homogentisic acid. A history of gray- or black-stained diapers should suggest the diagnosis.

question_text: Which of the following vaccines should not be given to a child with severe combined immunodeficiency disorder (SCID)?
explanation:
Explanation:

MMR is contraindicated in a child with SCID.

Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) indicates a markedly weakened immune system, so live attenuated vaccines are contraindicated in these children. Live vaccines can replicate in the host and may cause serious infection when immune defenses are impaired.

General situations where live vaccines should not be administered include:

  • Primary immunodeficiency disorders
  • Conditions with significant immune suppression, such as:
    • Leukemia or lymphoma
    • Other malignancies
    • Ongoing corticosteroid therapy
    • Treatment with alkylating agents or antimetabolites
    • Therapeutic radiation
  • Pregnancy, because of potential harm to the fetus

Explanations for other Options:

IPV (Option A): IPV (Inactivated Polio Vaccine) Contains killed poliovirus, not live virus. It is Safe and recommended even in severe immunodeficiency.

Hepatitis B vaccine (Option B): A recombinant sub-unit vaccine that uses only the hepatitis B surface antigen. It Cannot cause infection and is safe for immunocompromised children.

DTaP (Option D): It Includes inactivated toxoids (diphtheria, tetanus) and acellular pertussis components. It is Entirely non-live, so it is safe to administer in SCID.

question_text: Of the following options, the best initial test for a workup for immunodeficiency is?

The initial step in the workup of a child with a suspected immunodeficiency should always include a complete blood count and differential, as this test will reveal disorders involving lymphopenia (particularly T-cell lymphopenias) and neutropenia.

  • Other hints can be found by the CBC, including small platelets associated with the Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, anemias, and evidence of eosinophilia.
  • An erythrocyte sedimentation rate is a nonspecific marker of inflammation and would not point to a specific immunodeficiency.
  • While quantitative immunoglobulins, peripheral T-cell phenotyping, and lack of antibody response to standard immunizations would all be part of an immunodeficiency investigation, these would not be considered first steps in the evaluation.

question_text: White line of Frenkel is seen in: September 2008
explanation: Ans. C: Scurvy Clinical symptoms and signs of infantile scurvy, in order of frequency are irritability, tenderness and weakness of lower extremities, a scorbutic rosary of the legs, bleeding of the gums (usually where teeth have erupted), and fever. Radiographic findings of scurvy: Dense metaphyseal line-This is due to an intensification of the zone of preparatory calcification, resulting from matrix formation failing, is has been referred to as the white line of Frenkel, but is non-specific, as it is also seen in healing rickets, and lead or phosphorus poisoning. Ground glass osteoporosis: This appears at the end of the shaft with blurring or disappearance of trabecular markings. Halo ossification centre: Also called the Wimberger's ring, it is the same effect that produces the white line of Frenkel, affecting the epiphyseal ossification center. Corner sign-Seen due to subepiphyseal infarction, or separation of the epiphysis from the metaphysis. Lateral spurs-These metaphyseal spurs project at right angles to the axis of the shaft, they may be seen due to mushrooming of epiphysis on the metaphysis, or may represent earliest calcification of periosteum elevated by a subperiosteal hemorrhage. Subperiosteal hematomas-These occur at the end of long bones, seen after about 2 weeks of onset of clinical symptoms; it is not the periosteal hemorrhage that calcifies, but the elevated periosteum, secondary to resumption of bone formation. Metaphyseal fractures-Subperiosteal comminuted fractures at the end of long bones, extending only partially through the width of the bone. Atrophy scurvy line-A radiolucent zone on the shaft side of Frenkel's white line, it has been referred to as the Trummerfeld Zone.

question_text: A child presents with generalized body aches, poor wound healing, corkscrew hairs on her arms, and white lines of Frenkel on X-ray as shown below. This clinical presentation is most consistent with which of the following micronutrient deficiencies?
explanation:
Explanation:

Vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) leads to defective collagen synthesis, resulting in fragile capillaries, bleeding, poor wound healing, corkscrew hairs, and characteristic radiological findings like white lines of Frenkel.

  • Vitamin C plays a crucial role in collagen synthesis, which is essential for maintaining the structural integrity of blood vessels, skin, bone, and connective tissues.
  • Scurvy occurs when there is prolonged deficiency of vitamin C, especially in children with inadequate dietary intake (e.g., lack of fruits and vegetables).
  • Clinical Features of Scurvy:
    • Musculoskeletal pain, particularly in legs
    • Corkscrew hairs, petechiae, ecchymoses
    • Poor wound healing, bleeding gums, anemia
    • Pseudoparalysis: refusal to move limbs due to pain
    • Frog-leg posture
    • Scorbutic rosary at the costochondral junctions
    • White lines of Frenkel (dense metaphyseal lines seen on X-ray)
    • Pelkan spurs: metaphyseal spurs
  • Radiological Signs:
    • White line of Frenkel: dense zone of provisional calcification
    • Wimberger ring: circular calcification surrounding the epiphysis
    • Scorbutic rosary: sharply defined, angular swellings at the costochondral junctions (unlike the smoother swellings in rickets)
  • Treatment:
    • Vitamin C supplementation (100-200 mg/day)
    • Symptom resolution typically begins within 1 week

Explanation of other options:

Zinc deficiency (Option A): Causes growth retardation, alopecia, delayed wound healing, hypogonadism, and dermatitis, but not corkscrew hairs or Frenkel lines.

Copper deficiency (Option C): Leads to anemia, neutropenia, and hypopigmented hair, but not the bleeding or radiologic features seen in scurvy.

Iron deficiency (Option D): Presents with pallor, fatigue, irritability, and microcytic hypochromic anemia, but not corkscrew hairs, bleeding gums, or radiologic signs of scurvy.

question_text: What is the cause of death in pediatric patients with Diabetic Ketoacidosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

In pediatric DKA, the most common cause of mortality is cerebral edema, which occurs in ~0.5-1% of cases but accounts for the majority of deaths. The exact mechanism is unclear but is thought to involve osmotic shifts during fluid therapy, ischemia, and reperfusion injury.

Other complications of DKA:

  • Cognitive impairment (from hypoperfusion or cerebral edema)
  • Venous thrombosis (due to dehydration and hypercoagulability)
  • Pancreatic enzyme elevations (secondary to metabolic stress)
  • Acute kidney injury (from severe dehydration)
  • Hypokalemia (can cause arrhythmias, but usually preventable with replacement)
  • Hypoglycemia (from overcorrection with insulin therapy)
  • Rhabdomyolysis (due to severe metabolic derangements)
  • Pulmonary edema (rare, can follow aggressive fluid resuscitation)
  • Multiple organ dysfunction syndrome (in severe cases)
  • Sepsis (can precipitate DKA but not the leading cause of death once DKA is established)

Explanation of other options:

Sepsis (Option A): Sepsis is a trigger for DKA but not the primary cause of mortality in treated pediatric DKA.

Dehydration (Option B): Severe dehydration contributes to morbidity, but with medical care it is correctable and not the leading cause of death.

Hypokalemia (Option C): Can cause fatal arrhythmias if not monitored, but cerebral edema far outweighs hypokalemia as the major cause of death in children.

Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK470282/

question_text: What alteration occurs in chloride concentration in sweat and pancreatic secretions in cystic fibrosis?
option_c: Chloride is reduced in pancreatic secretions
explanation:
Explanation:

Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR (Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator) gene, which encodes a cAMP-regulated chloride channel.

  • Diagnostic hallmark: Chloride concentration in sweat is markedly increased, typically above 60 mmol/L.
  • Pathophysiology: Dysfunction of the CFTR channel disrupts chloride transport, leading to abnormal electrolyte and fluid balance in various secretions.
  • Clinical features:
    • Persistent bacterial infections in the respiratory tract and sinuses.
    • Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency resulting in fat malabsorption.
    • Male infertility due to congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens.
  • Thus, the defining diagnostic feature is raised chloride in sweat, making Option A correct.

Explanation of Other Options:

Chloride is reduced in sweat (Option B): Incorrect, because CFTR dysfunction causes accumulation of chloride in sweat rather than reduction.

Chloride is reduced in pancreatic secretions (Option C): While pancreatic insufficiency is common, the diagnostic marker is not low chloride in pancreatic secretions but elevated chloride in sweat.

None of the above (Option D): Incorrect, since elevated sweat chloride is a well-established diagnostic criterion.

question_text: A  2-year-old boy has passed 4-6 stools daily over the last 2 days. The faces are liquid and contain no blood or mucus. While awaiting medical evaluation, which of the following oral fluids is mosteffective to prevent dehydration in this patient?
option_c: Filtered water with no added solutes
explanation:
• Humans consume approximately 2 L of fluid each day and secrete an additional 7 L of fluid from upper digestive organs (eg, salivary glands, stomach, pancreas, gallbladder). Nearly all of this fluid is reabsorbed from the gastrointestinal lumen by the small intestine epithelium. The osmotic gradient for water reabsorption is largely established by the active cotransport of sodium into the apical end of enterocytes coupled with chloride, glucose, or amino acids. Sodium is then transported out of the basolateral end of the enterocyte (sodium/potassium ATPase), which pulls water down its osmotic gradient from the gastrointestinal lumen through the tight junctions between enterocytes and into the lamina propria (and ultimately the bloodstream).
  • This young patient who recently began going to day care likely has acute infectious diarrhea of a viral etiology (eg, rotavirus, norovirus). Infections that target the small intestine cause watery diarrhea by blocking the active transport of sodium chloride into the enterocyte or by increasing chloride excretion into the gastrointestinal lumen (mediated by elevated intracellular cyclic AMP, cyclic GMP, or calcium). In this setting, oral rehydration with a hypotonic, equimolar sodium-glucose solution maximizes water and sodium reabsorption by the remaining functional enterocytes, and is the most effective oral therapy for maintaining volume and electrolyte status in children with acute infectious diarrhea.

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 1096

question_text: A newborn infant is diagnosed with a congenital anomaly which can be understood by the image illustrated below. Which of the following drugs is likely to be used in preparation for surgical correction of this anomaly?
explanation:
Image illustration is of Infants with great vessel transposition pump venous blood to the aorta and oxygenated blood back to the lungs. Therefore, they require surgical correction as soon as they are strong enough to withstand the procedure. While awaiting surgery, they are dependent on a patent ductus arteriosus to allow some oxygenated blood to flow from the left ventricle via the pulmonary artery and ductus to the aorta. The ductus can be prevented from closing by infusing the vasodilator PGE1.

question_text: A 5-year-old child is brought to the ER with complaints of 18 episodes of loose stools in the last 24 hours and vomiting twice in the last 4 hours. The child is irritable but drinking fluids. What is the optimal therapy for this child?
option_c: Intravenous fluid initially for 4 hours followed by oral fluids
explanation:
Explanation:

The best therapy for this patient is oral rehydration therapy with ORS since the child is drinking fluids.

  • Oral Rehydration Therapy (ORT) is based on the physiological principle that glucose-dependent sodium absorption in the gut remains functional during diarrhoea.
  • Thus, both glucose and sodium are transported together across the intestinal mucosa, helping to restore sodium and water lost during diarrhoea.
  • The World Health Organization (WHO) Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS) uses a 1:1 molar ratio of glucose and sodium to optimize fluid and electrolyte replacement.

Explanation of other options:

Intravenous fluids (Options A), Intravenous fluid initially for 4 hours followed by oral fluids (Option C): IV fluids are indicated only in severe dehydration, when the child cannot drink, is in shock, or has persistent vomiting.

Plain water with lithium (Option D): Plain water alone does not replace electrolytes, and lithium is not a treatment for dehydration.

question_text: In a 28-week child with suspected RDS, what of the following occurs?
explanation:
RDS occurs due to deficiency of surfactant in alveoli.

  • Surfactant lining the alveoli enhances the aeration of gas-free lungs by reducing surface tension, thereby lowering the pressure required to open alveoli.
  • Air entry into the lungs displaces fluid, decreases hydrostatic pressure in the pulmonary vasculature, and increases pulmonary blood flow.
  • In the absence of pulmonary surfactant, significantly increased alveolar surface tension leads to atelectasis, and the ability to attain an adequate FRC is impaired.
  • Alveolar atelectasis, hyaline membrane formation, and interstitial edema make the lungs less compliant in RDS, so greater pressure is required to expand the alveoli and small airways.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 122; OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 157

question_text: Upon presentation to the emergency department, a 7-year-old girl is found to have a serum glucose concentration of 700 mg/dL, pH of 7.15, bicarbonate of 13 mEq/L, and a potassium of 6.6 mEq/L. What is the first step in treatment?
explanation:
The first step in treatment of DKA is intravenous fluid resuscitation which is done prior to the administration of any insulin.

  • Although many patients have hyperkalemia on initial laboratory work due to their acidosis, they are often intracellularly depleted of potassium.
  • Administering a potassium binder would further decrease her total-body potassium and could result in cardiac arrhythmias.
  • Because insulin and correction of acidosis drives potassium intracellularly, administering insulin without supplementing the patient's potassium in IVF could also result in hypokalemia.
  • As per AIIMS PICU Protocols 2022, all patients with DKA presenting to an emergency, fluid therapy needs to be started within 1st hour of admission, using Normal Saline. In mild to moderate DKA, including those with dehydration, we give 10 ml/kg bolus over 1 hour, while in those with severe DKA or shock, we give 20 ml/kg bolus over 30 to 60 minutes.
  • Insulin should be administered after the hydration as blood glucose levels fall rapidly even without insulin. Insulin is given as IV infusion at 0.05-0.1 U/kg/hr
  • Bolus insulin or giving insulin without initial fluids is avoided.

Reference: AIIMS PICU Protocols 2022, Pages 414-415; OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 568

question_text: A 10-year-old child weighing 30 kg presents with a history of loose stools for 2 days. On examination, there is severe dehydration. Laboratory investigations are as follows. What is the initial management as per ISPAD guidelines?
option_a: Manage ABC, NS 20 mL/kg and start insulin after 1 hour
option_b: Manage ABC, NS 20 mL/kg along with insulin 0.1 IU/kg/hr
option_c: Manage ABC, NS 10 mL/kg along with insulin 0.1 IU/kg/hr
option_d: Manage ABC, NS 10 mL/kg and start insulin after 1 hour
explanation:
Explanation:

According to ISPAD guidelines, initial management of DKA includes airway-breathing-circulation (ABC), fluid resuscitation with 20 mL/kg NS, and delayed insulin initiation after 1 hour.

  • This patient has Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA), as evidenced by severe hyperglycemia (RBS 550 mg/dL), metabolic acidosis (pH 7.01), and ketonuria (urine glucose 3+ with history of dehydration).
  • As per the ISPAD 2022 guidelines, the initial management of DKA in children involves:
    • Airway, Breathing, Circulation (ABC) stabilization
    • Fluid resuscitation with 0.9% Normal Saline 20 mL/kg over 20-30 minutes to restore circulatory volume and begin correcting dehydration.
    • Insulin therapy should not be started immediately.
    • It is initiated after 1 hour of fluid therapy, typically as IV infusion of regular insulin at 0.05 - 0.1 IU/kg/hr.
    • Early insulin without adequate fluid replacement can worsen circulatory collapse and increase the risk of cerebral edema.
  • Other supportive steps:
    • Monitor vitals and GCS hourly.
    • Monitor electrolytes and glucose frequently.
    • Begin potassium replacement once urine output is adequate and insulin is started.
    • Gradually transition to subcutaneous insulin once acidosis resolves (pH > 7.3, HCO3- > 18, BOHB < 1 mmol/L) and oral intake is tolerated.

Reference:

question_text: A 3-year-old boy presents with fever and cough. A chest x-ray was done, which showed the following findings. Which of the following is the most likely underlying pathology?
explanation:
Explanation:

The given x-ray image shows right upper lobe consolidation and is consistent with a diagnosis of pneumonia, as suggested by the clinical features of fever and cough.

  • Consolidation is defined as the replacement of air in the pulmonary airspaces with fluid, protein, cells, or other materials.
  • On radiographs or CT scans, it presents as one or more relatively uniform opacities that obscure pulmonary vessels but cause little or no volume loss.
  • Unlike ground-glass opacities, which may only partially fill the airspaces, consolidation reflects more complete filling, usually indicating airspace disease.
  • The differential diagnosis takes into account the pattern, distribution, associated findings such as lymph node enlargement, hemoptysis, or fever, and patient history.
  • Substances that may cause consolidation include water (oedema), blood (haemorrhage), pus (pneumonia), cells (neoplasm), fat (lipoid pneumonia), or protein (alveolar proteinosis).
  • While most cases are due to airspace filling, it may also occur from interstitial disease encroaching into alveoli.
  • Air bronchograms are frequently seen, representing air-filled bronchi within consolidated lung, although they may be absent if bronchi are obstructed or filled with blood, pus, or tumour tissue.
  • Diagnosis typically combines clinical, laboratory, and radiographic findings.

Explanation of other options:

Right upper lobe collapse (Option A): Atelectasis refers to incomplete inflation of part or all of the lung, leading to reduced lung volume. The term 'collapse' is often used interchangeably, but should be reserved for cases of complete atelectasis. In right upper lobe atelectasis, the minor and major fissures shift, and the lobe flattens against the mediastinum, creating a triangular shadow on imaging. A juxtaphrenic peak, a sharply defined triangular opacity, may also be seen, often due to upward retraction of the pleura. Additionally, large hilar tumours can produce the 'S sign of Golden,' a reverse S-shaped configuration of the minor fissure, which is highly indicative of pulmonary carcinoma and, though initially described for the right upper lobe, may be found in atelectasis of any lobe. It is shown below.

Right upper lobe abscess (Option B): Lung abscesses typically present as fluid-filled cavities with thick walls and peripheral enhancement, often showing an air-fluid level as shown below. Because of their rounded shape, this air-fluid level appears equal in length on both posteroanterior and lateral views.

Bronchogenic carcinoma (Option D): An acquired cause of unilateral pulmonary artery obstruction, marked by the presence of a hilar mass as shown below. It is also an unlikely condition in a 3-year-old child.

question_text: Which is the ideal maintenance fluid for pediatric patients?
explanation:
Explanation:

5% Dextrose in Normal Saline (DNS) is the preferred maintenance fluid in children.

DNS is chosen because it prevents hypoglycemia by providing approximately 17 calories per 100 mL of 5% dextrose, which supplies energy for children with high metabolic demands, prevents ketone formation, and minimizes protein breakdown.

The sodium chloride component maintains extracellular fluid volume and prevents dehydration, while its isotonic nature stabilizes intravascular volume without causing harmful fluid shifts.

In contrast, hypotonic fluids such as N/2 or N/4 saline can lead to hyponatremia and hemolysis therefore, isotonic solutions with 5% dextrose are preferred for maintenance therapy in children. (Option A,C and D ruled out)

question_text: A child presents to the emergency department with a history of arrhythmia, chronic laxative use, and recurrent vomiting. Based on this presentation, which of the following electrolyte disturbances is most likely?
explanation:
Explanation:

Chronic laxative use can lead to significant electrolyte disturbances, particularly hypocalcemia. Hypocalcemia affects cardiac conduction and may result in various types of cardiac arrhythmias.

Explanation of other options: Incorrect Choices Explanation

Hyponatremia (Option A):

  • Laxative use primarily leads to hypokalemia & hypocalcemia, not hyponatremia
  • Hyponatremia is more common in conditions with excessive free water retention (e.g., SIADH, heart failure, renal failure)

Hypokalemia (Option C):

  • Laxative abuse can cause hypokalemia, but hypokalemia is more associated with muscle weakness and U waves on ECG rather than direct arrhythmias.
  • Vomiting causes hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with hypokalemia, but this is not the primary electrolyte disorder leading to arrhythmia here.

Hyperkalemia (Option D):

  • Hyperkalemia is not a typical feature of laxative abuse; rather, potassium is lost in diarrhea leading to
  • Hyperkalemia arrhythmias typically include peaked T waves, prolonged PR interval, and widened QRS-not seen in this case.

Key Takeaways:

Hypocalcemia is the most likely electrolyte abnormality in a child with laxative abuse, vomiting, and arrhythmia, due to malabsorption and calcium loss.

question_text: A child is admitted with DKA and is severely dehydrated. Their blood pressure is low and you would like to give them a fluid bolus. Their weight is 23kg. How much fluid should you prescribe in the bolus?
explanation:
Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis is summarized as:

  • Fluid Type and Rate: Start with 9% normal saline (NS) or 0.45% saline for initial rehydration.
    Avoid rapid fluid administration: Rehydrate slowly over 48 hours to prevent cerebral edema, a serious complication in pediatric DKA.
    • Typical initial rate: 10-20 mL/kg over the first 1-2 hours, then adjust based on severity and dehydration.
  • Potassium Replacement
    • Monitor Potassium Levels: Children with DKA often have depleted potassium stores.
    • Start Potassium Replacement: Once urine output is confirmed and if serum potassium is below 5.5 mEq/L.
    • Typical regimen: Add potassium chloride or potassium phosphate to IV fluids, adjusting based on serum potassium levels.
  • Insulin Therapy
    • Start Insulin: Only after initial fluid resuscitation, usually 1-2 hours after IV fluids begin.
    • Insulin Dosage: Regular IV insulin at 05-0.1 units/kg/hour.
    • Goal: Gradually decrease blood glucose to avoid rapid shifts (aim for a drop of 50-100 mg/dL per hour).
    • Transition to subcutaneous insulin: When blood glucose approaches 200-250 mg/dL and ketosis/acidosis are resolving, switch to subcutaneous insulin.
  • Monitor Blood Glucose and Electrolytes
    • Frequent Monitoring: Blood glucose hourly; electrolytes, pH, and bicarbonate every 2-4 hours.
    • Avoid hypoglycemia: When blood glucose reaches 200-250 mg/dL, add dextrose (D5 or D10) to IV fluids.
  • Correct Acidosis
    • Avoid Bicarbonate Therapy: Routine use of bicarbonate is not recommended in pediatric DKA due to the risk of worsening cerebral edema.
    • Correction with Insulin: Insulin therapy, hydration, and electrolytes usually resolve acidosis.
  • Monitor for Complications
    • Cerebral Edema: Look out for signs like headache, altered mental status, and sudden bradycardia.
      • If suspected: Decrease IV fluids, elevate the head of the bed, and consider mannitol or hypertonic saline.
    • Electrolyte Imbalances: Watch for hypokalemia, hyperkalemia, and hypoglycemia.
  • Transition to Maintenance Therapy
    • Once the child is stable, acidosis has resolved, and able to eat, transition to a subcutaneous insulin regimen.

question_text: A 7-year-old boy weighing 30 kg has been posted for surgical resection of a tumor. What is the daily maintenance fluid required for this child while he's in NPO?
explanation:
Explanation:

Based on the Holliday-Segar method, the daily maintenance fluid requirement for a 7-year-old boy who weighs 30 kg can be estimated as follows:

Calculation of maintenance fluid:

For a 30 kg child:

  1. First 10 kg: 10 × 100 mL = 1000 mL
  2. Next 10 kg (11-20 kg): 10 × 50 mL = 500 mL
  3. Remaining 10 kg (21–30 kg): 10 × 20 mL = 200 mL

Total: 1000 + 500 + 200 = 1700 mL/day

Key Takeaway Points:

  • The Holliday-Segar method assumes normal maintenance needs without ongoing losses.
  • Adjust for surgery, fever, vomiting, diarrhea, or burns.
  • Common practice for NPO children: divide total maintenance over 24 hours and adjust for perioperative requirements.

question_text: A 2-year-old boy is brought to a village hospital with loose stools for the past 3 days. His mother reports lethargy and refusal to eat. On examination, the child shows lethargy, dry mouth, sunken eyes, and delayed skin pinch recovery. How much fluid should be administered within the initial three hours if the child weighs 10 kg?
explanation:
Explanation:

The child's signs-lethargy, dry mouth, sunken eyes, and delayed skin pinch-indicate severe dehydration.

  • For severe dehydration, the initial IV fluid volume is 100 ml/kg.
  • Child's weight = 10 kg → 10 × 100 = 1000 ml.
  • IV fluid should be administered over 3 hours for children >1 year:
    • First 30 ml/kg over 30 minutes
    • Remaining 70 ml/kg over 2½ hours
  • Preferred fluid: Ringer lactate with 5% dextrose

question_text: A malnourished child, given too much food, developed hypophosphatemia & hypomagnesemia. What could be the mechanism of this?
option_b: Insulin mediated uptake of electrolytes, phosphate
option_d: Glucagon spike and cause more loss of phosphate and electrolyte
explanation:
Explanation:

Insulin mediated uptake of electrolytes, phosphate is the mechanism responsible for the development of hypophosphatemia & hypomagnesemia in the child.This sudden intracellular shift leads to hypophosphatemia, hypokalemia, and hypomagnesemia-the hallmark of refeeding syndrome.

Refeeding syndrome is a serious metabolic complication seen when severely malnourished individuals are given nutrition too rapidly, including via total parenteral nutrition. The sudden carbohydrate intake triggers a surge in insulin, shifting the body from a catabolic to an anabolic state.

Elevated insulin stimulates glycogen and protein synthesis and activates the sodium-potassium ATPase pump, driving potassium into cells. Magnesium and phosphate also move intracellularly, leading to hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and marked hypophosphatemia-the key biochemical feature of this condition. Insulin additionally reduces renal phosphate reabsorption, worsening the deficit. Hyperglycemia may develop as the pancreas struggles to match the abrupt rise in blood glucose.

Risk factors include prolonged starvation, chronic alcoholism, delayed nutritional support, anorexia nervosa, or massive weight loss in obesity. If unrecognized, these electrolyte imbalances can cause life-threatening complications such as arrhythmias, myocardial infarction, respiratory failure, liver dysfunction, seizures, confusion, coma, or death. Prevention relies on correcting fluid and electrolyte disturbances beforehand, giving thiamine, and advancing calorie intake slowly and carefully.

Explanations for other Options:

Catecholamine spike increases electrolyte uptake (Option A): Catecholamines may cause transient shifts of potassium but are not the primary trigger for the profound phosphate and magnesium drop seen in refeeding.

Urinary loss of phosphates (Option C): Renal wasting can lower phosphate, but in refeeding syndrome the major mechanism is intracellular shift, not kidney loss.

(Option D): Glucagon predominates during fasting, not during refeeding; it does not explain the post-feeding hypophosphatemia.

question_text: A child with severe hypovolemic shock was administered fluids, followed by starting on IV epinephrine infusion. Currently, the child is on maximal dose of IV epinephrine @ 2 microgram/kg/min. Patient is normotensive but continues to have shock with low cardiac output on echocardiography. A trial of vasodilators didn't work. What next agent to be considered?
explanation:
Therapy with Type III PDE Inhibitors like Milrinone is considered when the shock patient is normotensive with low cardiac output and high vascular resistance despite use of epinephrine and vasodilators.

  • However, these agents have a short half-life and should be discontinued as soon as patient develops tachyarrhythmia, hypotension or diminished systemic vascular resistance
  • Dose of Milrinone is 0.3 to 0.7 micrograms/kg/min as IV Infusion.
