question_text: A 5-year-old child presents with loose stools, irritability, and hasty drinking. On examination: sunken eyes and delayed skin pinch. What is the appropriate management?
option_a: Administer the first dose of IV antibiotic and immediately refer to a higher center
option_b: Give oral fluids and ask the mother to continue the same and visit again the next day
option_c: Give zinc supplementation and oral rehydration solution only and ask mother to come back if some danger signs develop
option_d: Consider severe dehydration, start intravenous (IV) fluids, IV antibiotics, and refer to a higher centre
explanation:
Explanation:

The child has severe dehydration, indicated by:

  • Irritability
  • Hasty drinking (thirsty, drinks eagerly)
  • Sunken eyes
  • Delayed skin pinch

Management of severe dehydration:

  • Immediate intravenous fluid therapy:
    • Bolus: Isotonic saline (0.9% NaCl) or Ringer's lactate, 20 mL/kg over 15-30 min.
    • Maintenance & deficit correction: Based on weight and ongoing losses.
  • Address underlying causes:
    • IV antibiotics if bacterial infection suspected (e.g., dysentery, septicemia).
  • Close monitoring:
    • Vital signs (HR, BP, O2 saturation)
    • Mental status
    • Urine output
  • Referral:
    • Transfer to a higher-level care facility for advanced monitoring and treatment.

Explanation of Other Options:

Administer the first dose of IV antibiotic and immediately refer to a higher centre (Option A): While antibiotic therapy may be indicated in some cases of diarrhea, the priority in this scenario is to address the dehydration and provide appropriate fluid replacement. Referral to a higher center is necessary for the management of severe dehydration.

Give oral fluids and ask the mother to continue the same and visit again the next day (Option B): Given the signs of dehydration mentioned, providing oral fluids alone may not be adequate to correct the dehydration rapidly. Prompt intervention with IV fluids is required in severe dehydration cases.

Give zinc supplementation and oral rehydration solution only and ask the mother to come back if some danger signs develop (Option C): Zinc supplementation and oral rehydration solution are essential components of managing diarrheal illnesses, but in cases of severe dehydration, intravenous fluid therapy is necessary.

Key Takeaway Points:

question_text: A 6-year-old child is brought by parents with complaints of bedwetting at night. Which of the following is the treatment of choice?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The treatment of choice for primary nocturnal enuresis is behaviour therapy, especially enuresis alarm training, bladder training exercises, and restricting fluids before bedtime.
  • These methods aim to condition the child to wake up in response to bladder fullness and have the highest long-term success rates.
  • Desmopressin may provide rapid symptom relief but has a high relapse rate when stopped, hence it is reserved for refractory cases or when quick control is needed (e.g., school trips). (Option C ruled out)

Explanation of other options:

Anticholinergics (Option B): Useful in children with daytime wetting or reduced bladder capacity, but not the first-line choice for nocturnal enuresis.

Imipramine (Option D): Tricyclic antidepressant, less effective, risk of cardiotoxicity, used only when other treatments fail.

question_text: A 25-day-old infant is brought to the Emergency Department. In the triage the patient was having tachycardia upto 190 beats per minute, and hypotension with a BP of 58/39 mmHg. The patient's skin is mottled and the capillary refill is 5 seconds with weak pulses in all extremities. The patient's abdomen is distended and the liver edge is palpable below the costal margin. You ordered a 20 mL/kg NS bolus. Reassessment following the bolus reveals that the patient has developed rales and is now arousable only to stimulus. The next step in the management of this patient would be?
option_b: Repeat fluid bolus with restriction 10 mL/kg
explanation:
This patient is exhibiting feature of decompensated cardiogenic shock.

  • When considering the treatment of this patient, fluid bolus worsened this patient's clinical status, so no role of further fluid boluses. Hence options A and B are ruled out.
  • The next step in management is to improve systemic perfusion through improved cardiac output. This may be achieved with catecholamines.
  • In neonatal shock, IV Dopamine infusion is always the 1st agent to be started if it is a fluid-refractory shock. IV Epinephrine is considered only if Dopamine resistant.
  • Please note that in older children, IV Epinephrine infusion is preferred in cold shock and IV Norepinephrine infusion in warm shock.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 88; Manual of Pediatric Emergencies & Critical Care, Suchitra Ranjit, 2nd ed., pg. 192

question_text: A 7 years-old boy has history of regular bed-wetting, twice a week, since many years. With thorough investigations, an organic cause was ruled out. The boy was mentally distressed due to bed-wetting. What should be the initial therapy?
option_b: Bladder training with reward for daytime control
option_d: Bell and pad based classical conditioning
explanation:
The child is suffering from nocturnal enuresis and the 1st line therapy is always non-pharmacological, comprising motivation & use of alarm devices.

Management of nocturnal enuresis

  • Active treatment started after ruling out organic causes and beyond 6 years of age.
  • Fluid restriction in the evening is advised to most children
  • 1st line therapy is always non-pharmacological, comprising motivation & use of alarm devices.
  • Motivational therapy alone is successful in only 25% patients, using rewards for dry nights. However, bladder training exercises have not been found to be useful.
  • Another 1st line therapy is use of alarms, also known as bell and pad-based classical conditioning. These special devices are useful 7 years of age onwards and is effective in 2/3rd Whenever the child gets wet, the sensors in the device make the alarm ring, waking the child. This slowly conditions the child to awaken when bladder is full and void urine.
  • The combination of motivational and alarm therapy is successful in upto 60-70% of patients.
  • Pharmacotherapy using oral desmopressin is used if 1st line measures fail. But have a risk of relapse and side effects.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Pages 527-528

question_text: Most important mechanism of nephrotic syndrome is?
explanation:
As per Nelson 21st Ed, the current understanding of Nephrotic Syndrome has significantly evolved.

  • Earlier, we used to follow the underfill hypothesis, which stated that hypoalbuminemia produces fall in oncotic pressure and causes edema.
  • Now, we know that although hypoalbuminemia is an initiating cause, the actual cause for most clinical edema is primary Na+/H2O retention, the so called Overfill Hypothesis.
  • The overfill hypothesis postulates that nephrotic syndrome is associated with primary sodium retention, with subsequent volume expansion and leakage of excess fluid into the interstitium.
  • There is accumulating evidence that the epithelial sodium channel in the distal tubule may play a key role in sodium reabsorption in nephrotic syndrome.
  • The clinical weaknesses of this hypothesis are evidenced by the numerous nephrotic patients who present with an obvious clinical picture of intravascular volume depletion: low blood pressure, tachycardia, and elevated hemoconcentration.
  • Furthermore, amiloride, an epithelial sodium channel blocker, used alone is not sufficient to induce adequate diuresis.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 545

question_text: A 7-year-old boy, recently treated with chemotherapy, presents with abdominal pain, vomiting, oliguria, and periorbital puffiness. Investigations reveal hyperuricemia, elevated creatinine, and hyperkalemia. What is the next best step in management?
explanation:
Explanation:

The presentation is consistent with tumor lysis syndrome (TLS), characterized by metabolic derangements following chemotherapy.

  • The most crucial initial step in management is vigorous hydration, which helps prevent uric acid crystal deposition and supports renal clearance.

Tumor Lysis Syndrome (TLS):

  • Caused by rapid tumor cell breakdown releasing intracellular metabolites.
  • Typical biochemical abnormalities:
    • Hyperkalemia
    • Hyperphosphatemia
    • Hypocalcemia
    • Hyperuricemia
  • Can lead to acute kidney injury and multiorgan dysfunction.
  • Most common in hematologic malignancies (e.g., Burkitt lymphoma, ALL).

Clinical Features:

  • Abdominal symptoms: pain, distension.
  • Urinary symptoms: dysuria, oliguria, hematuria, flank pain.
  • Hypocalcemia manifestations: vomiting, anorexia, cramps, tetany, seizures, altered sensorium.
  • Usually occurs 12-48 hours post-chemotherapy, though can occur spontaneously in high tumor burden malignancies.

Prevention and Monitoring:

  • Pre-treatment labs: uric acid, electrolytes, calcium, phosphorus, creatinine.
  • Adequate hydration prior to chemotherapy.

Explanation of Other Options:

Probenecid (Option B): A uricosuric agent that enhances uric acid excretion but increases risk of uric acid nephropathy and stones; contraindicated in TLS.

Allopurinol (Option C): A xanthine oxidase inhibitor used prophylactically to prevent uric acid accumulation but not the immediate management in established TLS.

Rasburicase (Option D): A urate oxidase enzyme that degrades uric acid; useful in high-risk or established TLS but hydration is the first-line step.

Key Takeaways:

  • TLS is an oncologic emergency with severe metabolic consequences.
  • Hydration is the first and most important management step.
  • Allopurinol and rasburicase are adjuncts for prevention or treatment after stabilization.

Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK518985/

question_text: A 2.5-year-old child presents with high grade fever, barking cough and stridor while crying. Child accepts fluids normally. On examination respiratory rate is 34/ min and temperature of 102°F. Next best step of management?
option_c: Nasal wash for influenza and RSV
explanation:
The diagnosis in this case is mild croup, because child has fever, stridor and barking cough. As per Table given in OP Ghai 10th Ed, stridor only on cough or crying is mild croup while stridor at rest indicates moderate to severe croup.

  • Effectiveness of Oral Corticosteroids: Oral corticosteroids are effective in viral croup as they reduce laryngeal mucosa edema through their anti-inflammatory action. They are beneficial even in mild croup, reducing hospitalization, duration of hospitalization, and the need for additional interventions like epinephrine.
  • Indications for Nebulized Epinephrine: Nebulized epinephrine is indicated for moderate to severe croup, including cases with moderate to severe stridor at rest, possible need for intubation, respiratory distress, and hypoxia. It is not typically used for mild croup.
  • Antibiotics are not Indicated: Antibiotics are not typically indicated in croup as it is primarily caused by viral infections.

Management Summary For Croup

  • Mild Croup: Manage with humidified air or oxygen and encourage fluid intake, and if needed, oral dexamethasone.
  • Moderate to Severe Croup: Administer nebulized epinephrine,
  • Hospitalization: Consider hospitalization for cases with worsening symptoms, difficulty breathing, dehydration, severe stridor at rest, hypoxia, cyanosis, depressed mental status, poor oral intake, or when reliable observation is necessary.
  • Additional Information: Nonprescription cough and cold medications should not be used in children younger than 4 years of age. Heliox (a helium-oxygen mixture) may be considered in severe croup cases when intubation is being considered, although evidence is inconclusive.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Ed, Table 15.3; Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 20th edition, pg-2034

question_text: A 7-year-old boy presented with proximal muscle weakness and low IQ. Gower's sign is present. Which of the following protein (shown in the given figure) will be absent in this case scenario?
explanation:
Option B: The probable diagnosis is Duchenne muscular dystrophy(DMD). The dystrophin gene is one of the largest in the body and mutations can occur at many different sites in it. Duchenne muscular dystrophy is a serious form of dystrophy in which the dystrophin protein is absent from muscle. It is X-linked recessive disorder and usually fatal by the age of 30. Most common cause of death is respiratory failure. Patients with DMD will show malignant hyperthermia after anasthesia. Partial mutation of dystrophin gene leads to Beckers muscular dystrophy. Diagnostic test is Multiplex ligation probe dependent amplification(MLPDA).

Option A: Actin: Actin is a fundamental protein in muscle contraction and is present in all muscle cells.

Option C: Sarcoglycans: Sarcoglycans are part of the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex; they may be reduced but are not absent in Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Mutation in gene for sarcoglycan produces limb girdle muscle dystrophy.

Option D: Laminin: Laminin is a component of the extracellular matrix and is not absent in muscle diseases like Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

Key takeaways:

Tags: Fmge jan 2023

Absence of dystrophin is characteristic of Duchenne muscular dystrophy, which presents with proximal muscle weakness and Gower's sign.

Reference: Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology, 26th Edition, Page no. 252

question_text: A 7-day-old female newborn had an abnormal result on newborn screening revealing an absence of T-cell receptor excision circles (TREC), which raises concern regarding severe combined immunodeficiency. Of the following, the MOST appropriate next test to confirm the diagnosis is

explanation:
• Severe combined immunodeficiency represents a group of genetic primary immunodeficiencies defined by dysfunction of humoral and cell mediated immunity.
  • The definitive test for quantifying lymphocyte subsets is flow cytometry.
  • Left untreated, children with severe combined immunodeficiency die early in life owing to infection, but the condition is curable with allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant.

question_text: Which of the following is true regarding the mechanism of breast milk jaundice?
option_d: Difficulty in excretion of conjugated bilirubin
explanation:
Explanation:

Breast milk jaundice typically presents as unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia in otherwise healthy, term infants, appearing after the first week of life (late onset).The condition is thought to be caused by beta-glucuronidase in breast milk, which deconjugates bilirubin in the intestine, increasing enterohepatic circulation and slowing bilirubin excretion.

Explanations for other Options:

Late onset (Option B): Breast-milk jaundice does usually present after day 5-7, so it can be described as "later" than physiologic jaundice. However, the mechanism, specifically involves unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, not just timing.

Beta glucronidase enzyme involved (Option C): β-glucuronidase in breast milk indeed contributes by deconjugating bilirubin in the gut, but the primary mechanism is still the resulting unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. This is a contributing enzyme rather than the core biochemical abnormality.

Difficulty in excretion of conjugated bilirubin(Option D): This describes disorders with direct (conjugated) hyperbilirubinemia, such as biliary atresia or neonatal hepatitis, and is not the mechanism in breast-milk jaundice.

question_text: The parents of a 2-month-old girl are concerned that their child may be at risk for autism because her 18-month-old cousin was recently diagnosed with autism. Which of the following most accurately describes an early sign of autism?
option_a: Absence of social smile by 6 months of age
option_b: Not using single words by 10 months of age
option_c: Not using 2-word phrases by 18 months of age
option_d: Lack of make-believe play by 12 months of age
explanation:
• Absence of a social smile and/or limited eye contact by 6 months of age may be an early sign of autism.
  • Additional early signs of autism include
    • Absence of babbling, pointing or other gestures by 12 months
    • Not using single words by 16 months or 2-word phrases by 24 months
    • Stereotypic use of language; lack of make-believe play by 18 months.

question_text: An early marker of Mineral and Bone Disorder in CKD Patient is?
explanation:
Chronic kidney disease is characterized by systemic disorders of calcium, phosphorus, PTH, and vitamin D metabolism that can not only lead to bone disorders (renal osteodystrophy) but also vascular and soft tissue calcification. Previously called Renal Osteodystrophy, it is now called as CKD-MBD.

  • Efforts have focused on the role of the hormone fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23) and its cofactor, Klotho, in CKD-MBD.
  • An elevated FGF23 results in increased urinary phosphate excretion and suppression of 1-αhydroxylase activity, leading to reduced 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol (1,25(OH)2D) values and increased PTH secretion.
  • Elevated FGF23 is the first sign of altered osteocyte function in pediatric and adult CKD, is seen as early as CKD stage 2 (GFR 60-90 mL/min/1.73 m2), and occurs despite normal calcium, phosphorus, PTH, and 1,25OH2 D levels.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 550.2

question_text: A Child is having macrocephaly, large hands and feet, low IQ, is tall for age, has hypertelorism, seizures and premature tooth eruption. The testicular size is normal and the child is often clumsy in his activities. Name the most likely genetic abnormality?
explanation:
The clinical picture is fitting into a diagnosis of Sotos Syndrome, previously called as Cerebral Gigantism. Key features

  • Microdeletions in 5q35 region in NSD-1 gene
  • Overgrowth, macrocephaly, prominent forehead, prominence of extraaxial fluid spaces on brain imaging, large hands and feet, hypotonia, clumsiness, mental disabilities are common
  • As opposed to Fragile X syndrome, large testes are not seen.
  • Premature tooth eruption seen in many patients

Reference: Nelson 21st Ed, Table 98.13

question_text: Wolf Hirschhorn syndrome involves which among the following genetic abnormalities?
explanation:
Wolf Hirschhorn syndrome.

  • Also known as 4p- (deletion of4pl6), this syndrome is characterized by microcephaly and unusual development of the nose and orbits that produces an appearance suggesting an ancient Greek warrior's helmet.
  • Other anomalies commonly seen include cleft lip and palate and cardiac and renal defects.
  • Seizure disorders are common, and the majority of patients have severe intellectual disability.

Reference: CDT Pediatrics 2020/Page 1097

question_text: A 7-month-old infant presents with diarrhea and mucocutaneous lesions since weaning. The symptoms have been present since weaning was started. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient's presentation with diarrhea and mucocutaneous lesions, which started since weaning is suggestive of a zinc deficiency disorder called as acrodermatitis enteropathica.

This rare autosomal recessive condition occurs due to impaired zinc absorption from a defective ZIP4 protein, typically becoming apparent when breast milk (naturally rich in bioavailable zinc) is replaced with solid foods.

Acrodermatitis Enteropathica:

  • Autosomal recessive disorder.
  • Severe zinc deficiency due to impaired intestinal absorption (ZIP4 protein defect).
  • Early infancy onset: Vesiculobullous, dry, scaly skin lesions (periorificial, buttocks, acral areas).
  • Associated with alopecia, eye changes, chronic diarrhea, growth retardation, and stomatitis.
  • Laboratory Findings:
    • Low serum zinc (<50 µg/dL).
    • Low alkaline phosphatase (zinc-dependent enzyme
  • Treatment: 2-3 mg/kg/day oral zinc therapy.

Explanation of Other Options:

Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (Option A):

  • Triad: eczema, recurrent infections, thrombocytopenia.
  • X-linked recessive immunodeficiency.
  • Not triggered by weaning and no characteristic periorificial lesions.

Pediatric epidermolysis bullosa (Option C):

  • Group of genetic skin fragility disorders present at birth.
  • Blisters occur at sites of mechanical trauma, not periorificially.
  • Not associated with diarrhea or alopecia.

Atopic dermatitis (Option D):

  • Chronic eczematous skin disease of infancy.
  • Usually flexural or extensor involvement, pruritic.
  • No diarrhea, no mucosal lesions, not weaning-related.

Key Takeaway Points:

question_text: A 13-year-old boy, above the 99th centile for height, with gynecomastia and small testes. He has antisocial behavioral, more in school and is very aggressive. Most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• Klinefelter syndrome patients have XXY chromosomes.
  • They are tall, slim and have disproportionally long legs.
  • The testes tend to be small for age.
  • The phallus tends to be smaller than average, and cryptorchidism is more common than in the general population.
  • Approximately 80% of adults have gynecomastia; they have sparser facial hair. The most common testicular lesions are spermatogenic arrest and Sertoli cell predominance. The sperm have a high incidence of sex chromosomal aneuploidy. Azoospermia and infertility are usual.
  • Behavioral or psychiatric disorders may be apparent long before defects in sexual development. These children tend to have learning disabilities and deficits in 'executive function' (concept formation, problem solving, task switching, and planning), and the condition should be considered in boys with psychosocial, learning, or school adjustment problems. Affected children may be anxious, immature, or excessively shy and tend to have difficulty in social interactions throughout life.

question_text: What type of chromosomal abnormality is associated with acute promyelocytic leukemia?
explanation:
• Childhood acute leukemias can be divided into myelocytic and lymphocytic.
  • Acute myelocytic leukemias (AML) involve greater than 20% of myeloid blasts in either of these.
  • Myeloid lines include erythrocytes, granulocytes, monocytes, and megakaryocytes.
  • Acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL) involves the B and T cell lymphocyte lineage.
  • There are different chromosomal rearrangements that can occur, including translocations, deletions, and inversions.
  • Chromosomal translocation (15;17) has a specific association with acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL). This translocation involves the alpha retinoic acid receptor gene on chromosome 17, which is why the specific treatment for APL is all-trans retinoic acid.

Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 20th edition, pg. 2442

question_text: Which chromosomal abnormality is indicated by the karyotyping given below?
explanation:
Explanation:

The karyotype examination indicates Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome) with the following features:

  • Total chromosome number: 47
  • Sex chromosomes: XY (male)
  • Additional chromosome: +18 (extra copy of chromosome 18)

The identification of three copies of chromosome 18 establishes the diagnosis of Edwards syndrome (Trisomy 18).

Karyotype interpretation:

  • A normal male karyotype is written as 46,XY.
  • The presence of an additional chromosome is indicated by a "+" sign.
  • In trisomy, the total chromosome count becomes 47.

Edwards syndrome (Trisomy 18):

  • Karyotype: 47,XY,+18or 47,XX,+18.
  • Caused by the presence of three copies of chromosome 18.
  • Associated with multiple congenital anomalies.

Common viable trisomies:

  • Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome)
  • Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome)
  • Trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome)

Explanation of other options:

Trisomy 13 (Option B): Would appear as 47, XY, +13 (Patau syndrome), not +18.

Trisomy 21 (Option C): Represents Down syndrome, karyotype 47, XY, +21.

Trisomy 11 (Option D): Not a recognized viable trisomy in humans.

Key Takeaways:

  • Edwards syndrome = Trisomy 18.
  • Common viable trisomies: 21 (Down), 18 (Edwards), 13 (Patau).

question_text: Look at the image and tell the associated genetic abnormality?
explanation:

question_text: A child with Trisomy 21 developed Transient Leukemia. Such patients are likely to show which additional genetic abnormalities?
explanation:
Upto 10% of Down Syndrome patients can develop Transient leukemia, previously called as Transient Myeloproliferative Disorder.

  • Those developing Transient Leukemia in such patients are often found to have GATA-1 mutations in the transcription factors, producing proliferation of blast cells.
  • 20-30% of these patients tend to develop AML-M7 leukemia by 3 years of age.

question_text: Anticipation phenomenon occurs in which of the following?
explanation:
Anticipation is a pattern of inheritance in which symptoms became manifest at earlier ages and with increasing severity as traits are passed to subsequent generations.

  • The genetic defect in myotonic muscular dystrophy is on chromosome 19 at the 19q13 locus.
  • It consists of an expansion of the DM gene that encodes a serine– threonine kinase (DMPK), with numerous repeats of the CTG codon.
  • Myotonic dystrophy often exhibits a pattern of anticipation in which each successive generation has a tendency to be more severely involved than the previous generation.
  • Anticipation Phenomenon is also seen in Fragile X Syndrome

Reference: CDT Pediatrics 2020/page 1087; Nelson 21st Ed/Chapter 627

question_text: Steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome is defined as failure to achieve remission after how many weeks when on a daily corticosteroid therapy regimen.
explanation:
Explanation:

Steroid resistance in nephrotic syndrome is diagnosed when there is no remission despite 6 weeks of treatment with daily corticosteroids.

Steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome

  • Steroid resistance in nephrotic syndrome is diagnosed when there is no remission despite 6 weeks of treatment with prednisolone (2 mg/kg/day). Can be of 2 types:
    • Primary (initial) steroid resistance, where there is no response to steroids from the beginning
    • Secondary (late) steroid resistance, which develops during relapse treatment.
  • All steroid-resistant patients should undergo a kidney biopsy.
  • Common findings include:
    • FSGS (Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis) or
    • MCD (Minimal Change Disease)
    • Rarely, membranous nephropathy may be seen in older children

Genetic Causes of Steroid Resistance:

  • Genetic mutations in genes like NPHS2 (podocin), NPHS1 (nephrin), PLCE1, and others.
  • Next-generation sequencing can help identify these mutations, which are linked to progressive kidney damage and a lower risk of recurrence after kidney transplantation.

Management:

  • The treatment focuses on inducing remission of proteinuria while minimizing medication side effects.
  • Drug of choice is Calcineurin inhibitors.
  • Tacrolimus is generally more efficacious and preferred.
  • Cyclosporine is relatively safer if there is severe hypokalemia or seizures.
  • Combination of choice: Calcineurin inhibitors + ACE inhibitors (e.g., Enalapril) or ARBs (e.g., Losartan) + low dose steroids.
  • Low dose steroids (1 to 1.5 mg/kg alternate day or double the maintenance dose) are added for a few weeks for synergistic action and better response, provided there is no steroid toxicity.
  • CNIs are slow-acting, and steroids can help improve outcomes initially.

question_text: A Child is having short stature, triangular face, frontal bossing, micrognathia and clinodactyly. Name The Likely Syndrome?
explanation:
Russell Silver Syndrome, also called as Silver Russell Syndrome is a type of syndrome arising due to complex genetic mechanisms

  • 50% of Silver-Russell patients have hypomethylationof H19 and IGF2
  • 10% cases arise to maternal uniparental disomy involving chromosome 7
  • Rare mechanisms are implicated in the other forms.
  • Features include triangular facies, IUGR, short stature, clinodactyly, small jaw, frontal bossing, GERD and severely reduced subcutaneous fat.

Reference: Nelson 21st Ed, IAP Textbook of Pediatrics 5th Ed

question_text: A child had typical clinical characteristics of Down Syndrome and was evaluated for genetic abnormalities. All of the following are the mechanisms of Down Syndrome except?
option_c: Trisomy due to meiotic non-disjunction of chromosomes
explanation:
Mechanisms of Down Syndrome

  • In approximately 95% of the cases of Down syndrome, there are 3 copies of chromosome 21. The origin of the supernumerary chromosome 21 is maternal in 97% of the cases as a result of errors in meiosis. The majority of these occur in maternal meiosis I (90%).
  • Approximately 1% of persons with trisomy 21 are mosaics, with some cells having 46 chromosomes
  • Another 4% have a translocation that involves chromosome 21. The majority of translocations in Down syndrome are fusions at the centromere between chromosomes 13, 14, 15, 21, and 22, known as robertsonian translocations. The translocations can be de novo or inherited.
  • Very rarely is Down syndrome diagnosed in a patient with only a part of the long arm of chromosome 21 in triplicate (partial trisomy ).
  • Isochromosomes and ring chromosomes are other rarer causes of trisomy 21.
  • Deletions do not produce Down Syndrome

Reference: Nelson 21st Ed, Chapter 98.2

    • Mandibular hypoplasia

question_text: A 12-years old boy presents with a deafness and recurrent hematuria, with investigations suggestive of chronic kidney disease. There is a family history of death of maternal uncle due to similar illness. Kidney biopsy showed a normal appearance on light microscopy, but an abnormal electron microscopy. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Deafness + Recurrent Hematuria in a male child with positive family history suggests a diagnosis of Alport Syndrome.

  • Alport syndrome (AS), or hereditary nephritis, is a genetically heterogeneous disease caused by mutations in the genes coding for type IV collagen, a major component of basement membranes.
  • Approximately 85% of patients have X-linked inheritance caused by a mutation in the COL4A5 gene encoding the α5 chain of type IV collagen.
  • Recurrent gross or microscopic hematuria with increased risk of bilateral SNHL is seen.
  • Ocular abnormalities, which occur in 30-40% of patients with X-linked AS, include anterior lenticonus (extrusion of the central portion of the lens into the anterior chamber), macular flecks, and corneal erosions.
  • Genetic testing is clinically available for X-linked AS and COL4A5 mutations. Prenatal diagnosis is available for families with members who have X-linked AS and who carry an identified mutation.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 537.2

question_text: Hypoplastic ribs, scalp defects, cleft palate, rocker bottom feet, hypotelorism and holoprosencephaly is characteristic of?
explanation:
Features of Patau syndrome (Trisomy 13) as per Nelson:

  • Scalp defects (e.g., cutis aplasia)
  • Microphthalmia, corneal abnormalities
  • Cleft lip and palate in 60%-80% of cases
  • Microcephaly
  • Microphthalmia
  • Sloping forehead
  • Holoprosencephaly (arhinencephaly)
  • Capillary hemangiomas
  • Deafness
  • Cong heart disease
  • Missing ribs
  • Polydactyly
  • Hypoplastic and Hyperconvex nails

Point to note: Rocker-bottom feet are more commonly seen in Edward Syndrome, but have also been described sometimes in Patau Syndrome. However, Cleft palate , Scalp defects & Cleft lip/palate are very specific for Patau Syndrome.

question_text: Most common cardiac lesion in down's syndrome is?
explanation:
Affected individuals with Down Syndrome are more prone to congenital heart defects (50%) such as atrioventricular septal defects, ventricular septal defects, isolated secundum atrial septal defects, patent ductus arteriosus, and tetralogy of Fallot. MC congenital heart disease in down syndrome is endocardial cushion defect, also called as complete AV septal defect or atrioventricular canal defect.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 98.2 And Chapter 453.5

question_text: Which of the following is most commonly associated with Tetralogy of Fallot?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most common association with Tetralogy of Fallot is for Down's syndrome.

Tetralogy of Fallot is also associated with Alagille syndrome and DiGeorge syndrome.

Down's syndrome

  • Due to Trisomy 21, the result of meiotic nondisjunction in either maternal or paternal gamete.
  • The overexpression of genes located on chromosome 21 contributes to the clinical features.

Down syndrome associations:

  • Congenital Heart Disease:
    • 40% of children have congenital heart defects, primarily endocardial cushion defects (40-60% of cases)
    • Commonly associated with AVSD, Ventricular Septal Defect, Atrial Septal Defect, Patent Ductus Arteriosus, and Tetralogy Of Fallot.
  • Gastrointestinal Malformations: 12% have atresias, especially duodenal atresia. There is an increased risk of annular pancreas and Hirschsprung disease.
  • Ophthalmic Problems: Increased risk of cataracts, nystagmus, strabismus, and visual acuity issues. Regular eye evaluations are advised from infancy onward.
  • Hearing Defects: 40-60% experience conductive hearing loss, often due to serous otitis media in the first year. Routine hearing assessments are recommended before 6 months of age and annually.
  • Thyroid Dysfunction: Hypothyroidism occurs in 13-54% of patients.
  • Atlanto-occipital Subluxation: Incidence ranges from 10-30%. A lateral neck radiograph is recommended.
  • Physical Growth: Linear growth is typically slower, and children may become obese with age. Muscle tone often improves, but regular monitoring of height and weight is necessary.
  • Malignancies: Increased risk of lymphoproliferative disorders, such as acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, acute myeloid leukaemia, myelodysplasia, and transient lymphoproliferative syndrome.
  • Early-Onset Alzheimer's Disease: The APP gene, located on chromosome 21, plays a significant role in amyloid plaque formation, a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease.

Explanation of other options:

Klinefelter syndrome (Option A): Commonly associated with mitral valve prolapse, ASD, partial atrioventricular canal defect, and patent ductus arteriosus.

Edwards syndrome (Option B): Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18) is associated with ventricular septal defect (VSD), patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), and polyvalvular dysplasia.

In Turner's syndrome (Option D): The cardiac abnormalities seen are coarctation of the Aorta and a bicuspid aortic valve. TOF is not a part of this condition.

question_text: What is the diagnosis of the patient having the following type of karyotype, as shown in the image?
explanation:
Explanation:

Down Syndrome (Trisomy 21) is caused by the presence of an extra copy of chromosome 21, resulting in a total of 47 chromosomes.

Key Points:

  • Down Syndrome Features:
    • Intellectual disability (mild-to-moderate).
    • Characteristic facial features: flat facies, upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, small nose.
    • Hypotonia, single transverse palmar crease, clinodactyly.
    • Congenital heart disease (AV canal, VSD, ASD).
    • Increased risk of hypothyroidism, leukemia, and early-onset Alzheimer disease.
  • Inheritance:
    • Most cases are nondisjunction (trisomy 21); rare cases due to translocation or mosaicism.

Key features of Karyotyping:

  • A karyotype is a visual representation of an individual's chromosomes, arranged in pairs by size and position of the centromere.
  • In a normal human karyotype, 46 chromosomes are arranged in 23 pairs (22 pairs of autosomes and 1 pair of sex chromosomes).
  • The chromosomes are photographed during metaphase, when they are most condensed and visible.
  • They are then arranged in descending order of size, with the sex chromosomes placed last.

Explanation of Other Options:

Turner Syndrome (Option A) :

  • Karyotype: 45, XO
  • Features: short stature, ovarian dysgenesis, webbed neck, shield chest.
  • Only affects females.

Klinefelter Syndrome (Option C):

  • Karyotype: 47, XXY (extra X chromosome in males).
  • Features: tall stature, small testes, gynecomastia, infertility.

Edward Syndrome (Option D):

  • Karyotype: 47, XX+18 or 47, XY+18
  • Features: severe intellectual disability, clenched fists with overlapping fingers, micrognathia, rocker-bottom feet, congenital heart defects.

question_text: Down syndrome children have decreased risk of developing the following as compared to general population?
explanation:
Explanation:

Neuroblastoma is the correct answer. While Down Syndrome is typically associated with an increased risk of many medical conditions, it shows a protective or negative association with certain solid tumors.

According to Nelson Pediatrics, conditions which are less prevalent in Down syndrome than in the general population include:

  • Solid pediatric tumors (e.g., Neuroblastoma and Wilms Tumor).
  • Epithelial tumors in adults.
  • Ischemic heart disease (atherosclerosis is rare).

Explanation of Other Options:

  • Alzheimer disease (Option A): Individuals with Down syndrome have a markedly increased risk of early-onset Alzheimer's disease, likely due to the overexpression of the Amyloid Precursor Protein (APP) gene located on chromosome 21.
  • Leukemia (Option C): There is a significantly increased risk of leukemia in Down syndrome, particularly Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) and Acute Megakaryoblastic Leukemia (AMKL).
  • Celiac disease (Option D): There is a known increased association between Down syndrome and autoimmune conditions, including Celiac disease and hypothyroidism.

question_text: A mother brings her 3-year-old son with Down syndrome to the clinic because his gums have been bleeding for 2 weeks. She reports that he has been less energetic than usual and also has bone pains. Examination reveals that the child has an oral temperature of 100°F, pallor, splenomegaly, gingival bleeding, and bruises on the lower extremities. Which of the following is most likely?
explanation:
Presence of Constitutional Symptoms, Pallor suggesting anemia, Splenomegaly and bleeding manifestations suggesting thrombocytopenia with bone pains suggests a likely Leukemia. Fever can be due to neutropenia or as a constitutional symptom.

  • Aplastic anemia is less likely to have splenomegaly, bone pains and will not usually be associated with Down Syndrome.
  • A high susceptibility to leukemia is associated with certain heritable diseases (Klinefelter syndrome, Bloom syndrome, Fanconi syndrome, ataxia telangiectasia, neurofibromatosis) and chromosomal disorders such as Down syndrome.
  • Children with Down syndrome have a 10- to 15-fold increased risk for developing leukemia and should have routine screening performed at well-child checks. Siblings of an acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) patient have a two- to fourfold increased risk for ALL, and the monozygotic twin of a child who develops ALL in the first year of life has a more than 70% chance of also developing ALL. A few cases of ALL are associated with p53 gene aberrations. Overall, these genetic links account for a small number of total ALL cases.
  • Other options won't have pancytopenia and bone pains.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Pages 621-622; Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 1stSA edition, pg. 2443

question_text: Identify the incorrect match for an abnormality and the corresponding common syndrome where it is commonly seen?

Such questions are frequently asked in recent times. This question's explanation also covers an extra-edge rare but important syndrome, which students can add to their existing notes. Let us evaluate the options individually.

question_text: All of the following can be diagnosed on Karyotyping except?

  • Karyotyping is useful to diagnose aneuploidies (aberrant number of chromosomes) or missing arms in chromosomes.
  • Thus, Karyotyping can identify Down, Edward, Patau, Turner & Klinefelter Syndromes.
  • Noonan Syndrome occurs commonly due to gene mutations in PTPN-11 gene and sometimes other genes involved in the RAS-MAPK pathway. Thus karyotype will often miss most such cases.

question_text: In which trimester is the Quadruple Test done for Antenatal Screening of Down Syndrome?

question_text: A 10-year-old boy presents with pain and swelling at the great toe, serum uric acid of 9.4 mg/dL, spasticity, dystonia, and self-biting of lips. Which enzyme is most likely deficient?
explanation:
Explanation:

The triad of hyperuricemia, neurological dysfunction (spasticity, dystonia), and self-injurious behavior is diagnostic of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome.

  • Caused by deficiency of hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyl transferase (HGPRT) enzyme.
  • Inherited in an X-linked recessive
  • Leads to excess uric acid and impaired purine salvage pathway.

Explanation of other options:

Cystathionine beta-synthase (Option A): Deficiency causes homocystinuria with lens dislocation, thromboembolism, and skeletal anomalies-not hyperuricemia or self-mutilation.

Dihydrothymidine oxidase (Option B): Deficiency involves pyrimidine metabolism disorders, not associated with uric acid elevation.

Xanthine oxidase (Option D): Deficiency leads to xanthinuria with low uric acid, not elevated levels.

Key Takeaways:

  • HGPRT deficiency = Lesch-Nyhan syndrome.
  • Classical features: hyperuricemia, neurological dysfunction, and self-injurious behavior.

question_text: Which among the following is the most common cause of bronchiolitis obliterans in children?
explanation:
Bronchiolitis obliterans (BO) is an uncommon form of obstructive lung disease that occurs as a result of a severe insult to the small airways and ultimately leads to fibrosis and obliteration of the bronchioles.

  • Epidemiology studies suggest that BO occurs frequently in children of Asian and South American descent.
  • In children, the leading cause of BO is infectious, with adenovirus being the most common offending agent.
  • BO also occurs in patients with lung or bone marrow transplants (BMTs) and in those with autoimmune disorders.
  • Other causes include toxic inhalation injury or aspiration, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, drug toxicity, and Stevens-Johnson syndrome, SJS.

Reference: Rudolph's Pediatrics 23rd Ed/Chapter 508

question_text: A child presented with mucosal bleeds, superficial petechiae and purpurae, but no muscle bleeds or joint bleeds. He was evaluated and his platelet count was found to be normal. His PT and aPTT were also within normal limits. However, the ristocetin assay was abnormal while there was normal platelet aggregation in response to ADP. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Let us go stepwise. The child has features of platelet-related bleeds and thus coagulation defects are ruled out.

  • Now since platelet count is normal, it can't be thrombocytopenia including ITP.
  • This means that the patient has a likely platelet functional disorder.
  • Rare qualitative disorders of platelet function include the autosomal recessive disorders Glanzmann's thrombasthenia (absence of the platelet Gp IIb/IIIa receptor) and Bernard-Soulier syndrome (absence of the platelet Gp Ib-IX-V receptor).
  • Both are inherited in an autosomal recessive fashion and present with bleeding symptoms in childhood.
  • Now in Bernard-Soulier Syndrome, platelets aggregate normally in response to agonists like ADP, collagen and epinephrine. However, the platelets fail to aggregate in the presence of Ristocetin. This is also called an abnormal Ristocetin test or response.
  • Kindly note that in Glanzmann Thrombasthenia, the response to ristocetin is normal, but platelet aggregation is abnormal or deficient in response to agonists like ADP, collagen and epinephrine.

Reference: Harrison 21st Edition, Pages 908-909; Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 511.11

question_text: The following statements are true with regard to Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome except:

option_b: It is associated with microthrombocytopenia, eczema and immunodeficiency

option_d: Low levels of IgM and increased levels of IgA, IgD and IgE can found
explanation:
• This is inherited as an X-linked recessive disease and defect in WASP gene.
  • It is usually characterized by immune dysregulation (immune deficiency, eczema or autoimmunity) and microthrombocytopenia.
  • They have triad of eczema, recurrent infections and (option b)
  • The platelets are small, and it can present with minor bruising as well as life-threatening GIT or intracranial bleeding.
  • WAS is associated with low levels of IgM and increased levels of IgA, IgD and IgE, due to dysfunctional B cells. (option c, d)
  • Using prophylactic antibiotics and immunoglobulin for infection is the conventional therapy. Splenectomy is usually effective in increasing platelet numbers and reducing bleeding complications, but also increases the risk of infection. Stem cell transplantation is curative and gene therapy may help in the future.
  • Major complications associated with WAS include autoimmune phenomena, including hematological cytopenia, small- and large-vessel vasculitis, lymphoproliferative disease, and lymphoma.

question_text: A child presented with petechiae, purpura and platelet count of 10,000. Bone marrow aspirate shows increased megakaryocytes. What is the treatment to be given?
explanation:
Explanation:

First-line treatment for severe thrombocytopenia with bleeding or very low counts is intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) or high-dose corticosteroids to rapidly raise the platelet count.

Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) is the most likely diagnosis in a child with petechiae, purpura, severe thrombocytopenia (platelets ~10,000/µL), and bone marrow showing increased megakaryocytes, which indicates peripheral platelet destruction rather than marrow failure.

Explanations for other Options:

Bone marrow transplant (BMT)(Option A): Reserved for marrow failure syndromes (e.g., aplastic anemia, leukemia) or certain congenital disorders, not for typical ITP where the marrow is functioning.

Methotrexate (MTX) (Option B): An antimetabolite used in cancer therapy and some autoimmune diseases; it has no role in the acute management of ITP.

Aspirin (Option D):It is Contraindicated because it inhibits platelet function and would worsen bleeding risk.

question_text: Which of the following is a known risk factor for language delay?
explanation:
Isolated language delay

  • The cause of language delay is multifactorial. It can be due to biologic factors, such as hearing loss or cognitive difficulties, autism, or environmental causes.
  • Children whose first-degree relatives have a history of language, speech, or reading delays are at greater risk for language disorders.
  • Other known risk factors include premature birth, male gender, and low socioeconomic status.
  • There is no evidence to support a relationship between speech delays and birth order, history of otitis media, or multilingual environments.

Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 20th edition, pg-193

question_text: All of the following are phagocytic disorders except?
explanation:
Ataxia Telangiectasia is considered to be a type of Combined B and T cell defect.

All others are examples of phagocytic disorders. For details, kindly refer to the detailed classification flow-chart discussed in the Doctutorials Pediatrics Video Lectures.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition

question_text: False about thumb sucking among the following is
option_a: In adolescence, it is a sign of insecurity
option_b: Needs treatment after 6 years of age
explanation:
• Thumb sucking is normal in infancy and toddlerhood, i.e., upto 4-5 years.
  • It is a behavioral problem, which may be self-soothing, i.e., a source of pleasure.
  • Persistent thumb sucking in adolescence is more common in girls and may be sign of insecurity. Persistent thumb sucking in older children can cause dental malalignment.
  • Treatment is not required till the age of 4-5 years. After that behavioral therapy in the form of positive reinforcement (giving reward for not sucking the thumb) is treatment of choice. Negative reinforcement (application of noxious agents to thumb) is second line of treatment.

question_text: At what age does autism spectrum disorder usually become evident?
explanation:
• Autism spectrum disorder usually presents at this age because this is when language and social skills rapidly develop.
  • 12-24 months: Concerns may emerge at this stage but problems are less obvious and overdiagnosis is a problem.
  • Screening tools may be applied as early as 18 months of age.

question_text: A term baby with a birth weight of 3 kg was on exclusive breastfeeds. On day 5 of life, the child was found to be having a weight of 2.4 kg. There was no history of apnea, vomiting or hypothermia. What could be the likely cause of weight loss in this child?
explanation:
Let us see objectively here. The baby had a normal birthweight and was on exclusive breastfeeds.

  • We know that every normal term neonate on breastfeeds can lose between 7-10% of birth weight in the 1st week of life. This is a physiological phenomenon.
  • However, the weight loss in this case is 600 g in the 1st This translates to (600/3000) X 100= 20% weight loss
  • Any weight loss >10% in term and more than 15% in preterm babies is pathological.
  • Most common cause of pathological weight loss in the early neonatal period is Dehydration, owing to inadequate breast feeds.
  • Ensuring adequate breastfeeds can easily take care of this condition.
  • Regarding other options, Remember that CCF due to PDA will cause weight gain in neonates due to Na/H20 retention, not weight loss.
  • Metabolic disorder is unlikely since there is no symptoms suggestive of the same.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Ed, Page 11, Nelson 21st Edition

question_text: A neonate with hypoglycemia is being managed using IV Dextrose infusion. He needs a bolus or hiking in Dextrose rate every time tapering is tried and more than 7 days have passed with the child being on IV dextrose infusion. What shall be done next?
explanation:
Recurrent/ resistant Hypoglycemia

  • This condition should be considered when the infant fails to maintain normal BGL despite a GIR of 12 mg /kg/min or when stabilization is not achieved by 7 days of therapy.
  • High levels of glucose infusion may be needed in these infants to achieve euglycemia.
  • Hyperinsulinism must be excluded because it is the most common cause of persistent hypoglycemia.
  • Hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia can be congenital [due to mutations affecting the regulation of insulin secretion from the pancreas] or acquired [neonates with maternal diabetes, birth asphyxia, polycythemia, Rh incompatibility, and severe intrauterine growth restriction, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome. etc.]
  • Many patients may have underlying metabolic disorders or hypocortisolism
  • Hydrocortisone is often considered in such cases.

Reference: AIIMS Protocols In Neonatology, 3rd Edition, Volume 2, Page 305

question_text: Which of the following condition you do not expect risk of developing cerebral palsy?
option_a: A 2 year old child, born at 32 weeks gestation
option_b: A 4 year old child, born at term and had birth asphyxia due following obstructed labor
option_c: A 14 year old child had significant head injury at 13 years of age
option_d: A 12 year old child, who developed kernicterus at 10th day of life
explanation:
Cerebral palsy (CP) is a group of permanent neurological disorders affecting movement, posture, and muscle tone, resulting from brain damage that occurs before, during, or shortly after birth.

Risk factors of developing cerebral palsy

  • Prenatal insult
  • Preterm birth
  • Birth asphyxia
  • CNS infections
  • Toxin exposure like bilirubin (Kernicterus)
  • CNS hemorrhage
  • Metabolic disorders

KEY TAKEAWAYS: Cerebral palsy is a non-progressive motor disorder that affects a growing brain. Hence, insult after brain growth is nearly complete, does not cause Cerebral palsy.

Tags:

  • Topic: CEREBRAL PALSY
  • Difficulty level: GOOD TO KNOW
  • PYQ: NEET PG 2021

Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21st ed., pg. 3168

question_text: Which among the following is not included in the triad of necrotizing enterocolitis?
explanation:
Hypokalemia never constitute the triad of necrotising entercolitis, following is an explanation for the same :-

Pneumatosis intestinalis
