question_text: Gold standard investigation for Whooping cough?
explanation:
Gold standard test for Pertussis is Isolation of organism by nasopharyngeal swab culture.

  • The specimen is obtained with deep nasopharyngeal aspiration or with the use of a flexible swab, preferably a Dacron or calcium alginate–tipped swab, held in the posterior nasopharynx for 15-30 sec (or until cough occurs).
  • The preferred isolation media are Regan-Lowe charcoal agar with 10% horse blood and 5-40 μg/mL cephalexin, and Stainer-Scholte media with cyclodextrin resins. Cultures are incubated at 35-37°C in a humid environment and examined daily for 7 days for slow-growing, tiny, glistening colonies.
  • As per CDT 2020: “The preferred method of diagnosis in most centers is identification of B pertussis by PCR from nasopharyngeal specimens.”
  • Please note that initially many patients present with a lymphocytic leukocytosis with a low ESR.

Reference: Nelson 21st Ed, CDT Pediatrics 2020, 1280; OP Ghai 10th Edition, Pages 265-266

question_text: Which procedure is being performed in this 2-year-old child who presented with low urine output and serum potassium 7.2 despite medical management?
explanation:
Age is a defining factor in dialysis modality selection: 85% of infants and children from birth to 5 yr of age initiate maintenance dialysis treatment using peritoneal dialysis, whereas 50% of children ≥ 13 yr of age initiate maintenance dialysis treatment with hemodialysis.

  • Peritoneal dialysis utilizes the patient's peritoneal membrane to transport fluid and solutes. Excess body water is removed by an osmotic gradient created by the relatively high dextrose concentration in the dialysis fluid; wastes are removed by diffusion from the peritoneal capillaries into the dialysis fluid.
  • Access to the peritoneal cavity is achieved by a surgically inserted, tunneled catheter.
  • Peritoneal dialysis may be provided either as continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD) or as an automated therapy using a cycler (APD), which allows exchanges of peritoneal fluid to be performed automatically during sleep by a cycler machine. APD is the PD modality of choice in countries without cost restraints.
  • Because peritoneal dialysis is not as efficient as hemodialysis, it must be performed at least 6 times per week.
  • Contraindications to peritoneal dialysis use include anatomic abnormalities (e.g., significant surgical adhesions, omphalocele, gastroschisis, or bladder exstrophy), peritoneal injury (including injury secondary to previous severe peritoneal infections), or lack of an appropriate caregiver.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 550.3

question_text: Patient with juvenile rheumatoid arthritis hemoglobin of 10.5 g/dL. Iron studies show normal transferrin saturation and an elevated ferritin. You suspect anemia of chronic disease. Which of the following is likely to have contributed to his anemia?
option_c: Enhanced release of iron from macrophages
explanation:
• Anemia of chronic disease is multifactorial and likely due to impaired iron mobilization and decreased intestinal absorption of iron.
  • Cause: Chronic inflammation leads to reduced iron availability, impaired erythropoiesis (red blood cell production), and decreased red blood cell lifespan.
  • Mechanism: Inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-6) increase hepcidin production, which traps iron in cells and limits its availability for red blood cell production.
  • As in this vignette, the anemia is usually mild to moderate, normocytic, and normochromic. Serum iron levels are low, but transferrin saturation is normal and serum ferritin is typically elevated due to the inflammatory state. Additionally, in anemia of chronic inflammation, production of hepcidin, a peptide hormone synthesized by the liver, is increased.
  • Hepcidin acts as a negative regulator of iron release by acting to decrease ferroportin expression.

Option A and C: As ferroportin is required for both intestinal transport of iron and macrophage release of iron, the decrease in ferroportin leads to decreased iron absorption and decreased release of iron from macrophage stores.

Option D: Humans do not have a mechanism of active iron excretion.

KEY TAKEAWAYS: Anemia of Chronic Disease (ACD), also known as Anemia of Inflammation, is a type of anemia commonly seen in chronic infections, autoimmune diseases, cancer, and chronic kidney disease.

Blood Tests: Show low hemoglobin, normal or low iron, high ferritin (indicating stored iron), and normal to low transferrin saturation.

question_text: The presentation of a child with severe combined immune deficiency can be as all of the following except?
explanation:
Severe Combined Immunodeficiency has a heterogeneous clinical and immunological phenotype, and in many cases the abnormalities are unknown. It can arise from a number of defined molecular defects.

  • Patients can present with failure to thrive, diarrhoea and recurrent opportunistic infections, which can be very severe.
  • Recurrent thrush and skin rashes from viral infections also occur.
  • Interstitial pneumonitis due to opportunistic infections is commonly seen. Pneumocystis carinii, respiratory syncytial virus, cytomegalovirus, adenovirus, influenza and parainfluenza are all responsible for respiratory infections.
  • If BCG is given at birth to these children, they may develop BCG infection. This may have severe consequences, with widespread disease in the lungs, liver, spleen and GIT.
  • Bacterial and fungal pneumonias have also been described, and prognosis is poor if effective measures are not taken early.
  • A bone marrow transplant is the only curative procedure in these cases, and early referral should be made to avoid Enzyme replacement therapy and gene therapy can be used in other types of SCID.

question_text: Which of the following is associated with congenital absence of vas deferens and seminal vesicles?
explanation:
Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens (CBAVD) and seminal vesicles is strongly associated with Cystic Fibrosis.

Other options:

(A): Tuberous Sclerosis: Seizures, intellectual disability, ash leaf spots, renal angiomyolipomas not affect the vas deferens or seminal vesicles.

(C): Kallman Syndrome: Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, anosmia, delayed puberty not structural defects like CBAVD.

(D):Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome: 46,XY with female phenotype, undescended testes, absent uterus.but it does not involve the absence of the vas deferens.

Key Takeaway:Cystic Fibrosis

Cause: Mutation in CFTR gene (autosomal recessive).

Key Features: Thick mucus, chronic respiratory infections, malabsorption, infertility in males.

Diagnosis: Sweat test (elevated chloride), genetic testing.

Treatment: Airway clearance, CFTR modulators (ivacaftor), lung transplant (severe cases).

Reference: Nelson textbook of paediatrics

question_text: What is the Most common clinical manifestation of mumps?
explanation:
Epididymo-orchitis is the next most common manifestation of mumps (after parotid gland swelling), developing in 15-30% of cases in postpubertal males, with bilateral involvement in 10 - 30% of those cases

question_text: A 33 year old lady presents with bilateral swelling and discomfort around her face. This caused her pain when she is chewing. It started 2 days ago and she also has mild fever and headache. She mentioned she had been in contact with someone with a similar illness 2 weeks ago. On examination, she has bilateral parotid enlargement which are tender.Which of the following is a likely cause?
explanation:
Fever, parotid swelling and pain during chewing indicates parotitis. Bilateral parotitis is usually due to viral infection by Mumps virus.

There are many causes of parotid swellings. Viruses include mumps, coxsackie A virus, parainfluenzae virus, CMV and varicella zoster virus.

Hypothyroidism can do so, but not hypoparathyroidism.

The incubation period for mumps is usually 18 to 21 days. Mumps is caused by a paramyxovirus, and are spread from person to person by saliva droplets or direct contact with articles that have been contaminated with infected saliva. The parotid glands (the salivary glands between the ear and the jaw) are usually involved.

Unvaccinated children between the ages of 2 and 12 are most commonly infected, but the infection can occur in other age groups. Orchitis (swelling of the testes) occurs in 10-20% of infected males, but sterility only rarely ensues; a viral meningitis occurs in about 5% of those infected.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 207, Pg: 1615-1618

question_text: A mother with no prenatal care gives birth to a term infant with findings of IUGR, microcephaly and hepatosplenomegaly. His hemogram shows thrombocytopenia. BERA test reveals sensorineural hearing loss. Ophthalmic examination shows chorioretinitis. The most important diagnostic study for evaluation in this newborn is
explanation:
• The newborn in the question shows characteristics of congenital CMV infection.
  • In addition to those findings mentioned above, these patients can have petechiae and purpura, ventriculomegaly, periventricular calcifications, cerebral atrophy, cortical dysplasia, and chorioretinitis.
  • The most important diagnostic study in the evaluation of newborn CMV disease is viral culture, preferably done before 3 weeks of life to help exclude the possibility of perinatal CMV acquisition.
  • Viral PCR is a useful adjunct to culture techniques but does not replace viral culture.
  • Tissue biopsy, while sometimes used for diagnosis, is not standard and is more commonly used in the lung and liver than in the brain.
  • CMV antibody titers are generally not helpful in diagnosis.

question_text: A full-term baby girl is born small for gestational age. She has absence of bilateral red reflexes in eyes cataracts, multiple petechial spots on skin, and a continuous machine-like murmur on auscultation. Which of the following statements about the diagnosis of the baby is accurate?
option_a: This infant needs an audiology evaluation because sensorineural hearing loss is a common association
option_b: This infant needs a renal ultrasound because she is likely to have renal abnormalities
option_c: The infant's condition is likely to have occurred because of a maternal illness during the third trimester
option_d: Intravenous antiviral therapy should be initiated and viral cultures should be obtained
explanation:
• This infant has the classic features of congenital rubella syndrome including low birth weight, heart defect (patent ductus arteriosus), and congenital cataracts.
  • Other clinical findings associated with congenital rubella syndrome include purpura, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, retinopathy, glaucoma, pulmonary artery stenosis, meningoencephalitis, thrombocytopenia, and hemolytic anemia.

    • Sensorineural hearing loss
    • Neurodevelopmental abnormalities
    • Growth retardation
    • Endocrine disease (diabetes mellitus, thyroid dysfunction)
  • Maternal infection may or may not be clinically apparent, and infection during the first month of pregnancy is most likely to result in fetal infection with the involvement of multiple organs.
  • No treatment is available for CRS. All the management is supportive.

  • Nerve deafness is most common finding of CRS
  • Salt and Pepper retinopathy is characteristic ophthalmic finding

question_text: A 3-year-old boy presents with recurrent urinary tract infections. His mother reports frequent urination, weak urinary stream, and dribbling of urine. On examination, a palpable bladder is noted. What is the most sensitive investigation that can be employed to determine the underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical features-frequent urination, weak stream, dribbling, palpable bladder, and recurrent UTIs-suggest urinary tract obstruction, most commonly due to vesicoureteral reflux (VUR).

Micturating cystourethrography (MCU) is the most sensitive investigation for diagnosing VUR. It involves filling the bladder with contrast and taking X-rays during urination to visualize the bladder, urethra, and retrograde urine flow. MCU also helps detect posterior urethral valves and neurogenic bladder.

Explanation of Other Options:

Ultrasonogram (Option A): Useful as an initial screening tool to assess kidney size, shape, and detect hydronephrosis, but it is not the most sensitive for identifying urinary flow problems or vesicoureteral reflux, as it cannot show retrograde urine flow.

Urine routine examination (Option C): Helpful for detecting active urinary tract infections and monitoring treatment response, but it cannot reveal the anatomical or functional cause of recurrent UTIs.

DMSA scan (Option D): Primarily used to detect renal scarring from prior infections. While it assesses kidney damage, it does not evaluate bladder or urethral function during voiding and cannot identify the underlying cause of obstruction or reflux.

question_text: A child is a known case of VSD with surgery planned after 3 months. He had 1 episode of severe bronchiolitis last year requiring hospitalization. Now, there is another outbreak of RSV infection in the community. What prophylactic agent you will consider in this child?
explanation:
Administration of palivizumab (15 mg/kg IM once a month), a neutralizing humanized murine monoclonal antibody against F-protein of RSV, is recommended for protecting high-risk children against serious complications from RSV disease.

  • Immunoprophylaxis reduces the frequency and total days of hospitalization for RSV infections in high-risk infants in about half of cases.
  • Ribavirin is therapeutic, not prophylactic.

Reference: Nelson 21st Ed/Chapter 418

question_text: A 5-year-old boy presents with hematemesis and splenomegaly. History reveals exchange transfusion in the neonatal period. What is the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Portal vein thrombosis (PVT) is the most common cause of portal hypertension in children.

Etiology in children:

  • Umbilical vein catheterization or exchange transfusion in the neonatal period is a significant risk factor.
  • Other causes: neonatal sepsis, abdominal infections, hypercoagulable states.

Pathophysiology:

  • Thrombosis of the portal vein → obstructed portal blood flow → portal hypertension → splenomegaly and variceal bleeding.

Explanation of Other Options:

Splenic vein thrombosis (Option A):

  • Usually causes isolated gastric varices and splenomegaly.
  • Less likely here, as hematemesis + history of neonatal exchange transfusion suggests portal vein involvement, not isolated splenic vein.

Budd-Chiari syndrome (Option C):

  • Caused by hepatic vein obstruction, leading to hepatomegaly, ascites, and sometimes jaundice.
  • Hematemesis is less prominent; splenomegaly may be mild.

Liver cirrhosis (Option D):

  • Causes portal hypertension and splenomegaly, but rare in a 5-year-old without chronic liver disease.
  • Liver function abnormalities are usually present.

question_text: A 10-year-old child presents with recurrent infections. On examination, the child's height is below the expected range for age, with a Z-score less than - 2 SD. The history reveals improper feeding practices by the parents. What is the most appropriate term to describe this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The features described are consistent with stunting, a form of chronic malnutrition defined by low height-for-age.

The diagnosis is confirmed when the Z-score is below -2 SD as per the WHO growth standards. Contributing factors in this case include a history of inappropriate feeding practices and recurrent infections, both reflecting prolonged nutritional deficiency.

Explanation of Other Options:

Wasting (Option B): This refers to low weight-for-height and reflects acute malnutrition. Since the child shows reduced height-for-age rather than weight loss, wasting is not the correct diagnosis. It usually presents with rapid-onset muscle loss and a thin appearance.

Malnutrition (Option C): A broad term that covers all forms of nutritional deficiencies. Although the child is malnourished, the findings specifically point to stunting, which highlights the chronic and long-term impact on growth.

Kwashiorkor (Option D): This condition is marked by edema, hair depigmentation, and dermatosis, commonly arising from protein deficiency with adequate calorie intake. These features are absent here, and the predominant finding is stunted growth, making Kwashiorkor an unlikely diagnosis.

question_text: A baby is born with macrocephaly/hydrocephalus, intraparenchymal calcification, SNHL and chorioretinitis. The mother is suffering from which teratogenic infection?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • These features of hydrocephalus, SNHL and chorioretinitis with intracranial calcifications are seen in congenital toxoplasmosis.
  • All other infections will show microcephaly.

Explanation of other options: Incorrect Choices Explanation

CMV (Option B): Congenital Cytomegalovirus (CMV) Infection - Key Features:

  • Microcephaly: A hallmark finding in congenital CMV; macrocephaly is not typical.
  • Periventricular calcifications: Characteristic of CMV; helps distinguish it from toxoplasmosis, which shows diffuse or basal ganglia calcifications.
  • Sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL): One of the most common long-term complications; although not exclusive to CMV, it is a major non-genetic cause of SNHL in infants.

These features help differentiate CMV from other TORCH infections in neonates.

Varicella (Option C): Congenital Varicella Syndrome - Key Features:

  • Limb hypoplasia
  • Cicatricial (scarring) skin lesions
  • Microcephaly
  • Cortical atrophy
  • Hydrocephalus and intracranial calcifications are not features of congenital varicella syndrome.
  • Neurological deficits may be present, but the classic findings listed above help distinguish it from other TORCH infections like toxoplasmosis or CMV.

Rubella (Option D):

  • Congenital rubella presents with the classic triad:
    • PDA (Patent Ductus Arteriosus)
    • Cataracts
    • SNHL
  • Microcephaly is seen, but intracranial calcifications and hydrocephalus are not features of rubella.

Key Takeaways:

Congenital toxoplasmosis is characterized by hydrocephalus, intracranial calcifications, SNHL, and chorioretinitis. Other TORCH infections usually cause microcephaly instead of macrocephaly/hydrocephalus.

question_text: An infant had refractory hypocalcemia in first few weeks of life and was diagnosed with congenital hypoparathyroidism. The child was referred to a pediatric cardiologist for further evaluation and also evaluated for a microdeletion defect. Which other clinical manifestation will often be present in such a child?
explanation:
An interesting question, similar to what many of you may encounter in clinical practice too. Let us go stepwise. Information given:

  • Infant with refractory hypocalcemia due to congenital hypoparathyroidism
  • Some cardiac disease
  • A microdeletion defect.
  • Now, the microdeletion defect with hypoparathyroidism and cardiac disease is DiGeorge Syndrome. It occurs due to microdeletions in 22q11.2.
  • Most of these patients have thymic aplasia due to 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouch hypoplasia.
  • Thymic aplasia causes reduced T-lymphocytes and cellular type of primary immunodeficiency. Such patients predisposed to recurrent viral and fungal infections. Thus D is the likely manifestation to be found in such patients.

Reference: Nelson 21st Ed, Chapter 151

question_text:
A neonate born at term is noted to have a faint petechial rash, macrocephaly and marked hepatosplenomegaly. Growth parameters are at the fifth percentile for gestational age. No other significant findings are noted on physical examination. The maternal history is unremarkable. Prenatal laboratory studies for hepatitis B virus, syphilis, and human immunodeficiency virus are negative, and the mother is rubella immune. A computed tomography brain scan of the neonate is performed.

Of the following, the MOST likely etiology of this infant's illness is?
explanation:
The CT scan shows diffuse cerebral calcification. This, along with macrocephaly, rash and hepatosplenomegaly indicates a likely diagnosis of congenital toxoplasmosis.

  • Most newborns with congenital toxoplasmosis are asymptomatic at birth, Symptoms presenting in newborns with toxoplasmosis can include temperature instability, rash (maculopapular or petechial), hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, generalized lymphadenopathy, pneumonitis, microcephaly, meningoencephalitis, seizures, and chorioretinitis.
  • The classic triad of chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and diffuse intracranial calcifications is rarely seen in congenital toxoplasmosis.
  • Pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine in combination with folinic acid is recommended as first-line therapy for toxoplasmosis.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 284-285; Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1st SA edition page 1724

question_text: A pregnant woman is diagnosed with HIV infection at 34 weeks of gestation. Her viral load was 1200 copies/mL, and she was then started on ART. She delivers a 2.5 kg term baby at 38 weeks. What is the most appropriate postnatal prophylaxis for the newborn?
option_a: Both nevirapine and zidovudine for 12 weeks, along with exclusive breast milk feeding
option_b: Nevirapine for 6 weeks with exclusive breastfeeding
option_c: No breastfeeding and initiate exclusive formula feeding
explanation:
Explanation:

The most appropriate postnatal prophylaxis for a newborn born to a retropositive mother with a viral load of 1200 copies/mL is administration of both nevirapine and zidovudine for 12 weeks, along with exclusive breastmilk feeding.

  • Despite advances in HIV treatment, infants remain at risk of infection during pregnancy, delivery, or breastfeeding, with nearly half of new child infections linked to breastfeeding.
  • To address this, the WHO emphasises universal testing and treatment for pregnant women, retesting HIV-negative women during pregnancy and breastfeeding, and enhanced prophylaxis for infants whose mothers did not receive effective ART early.
  • Infants considered high risk include:
    • Those born to mothers diagnosed at delivery or postpartum
    • Infected during pregnancy or breastfeeding
    • Starting ART late or on ART for less than 4 weeks
    • Failing to achieve viral suppression (viral load copies > 1000/ ml)
  • These infants should receive dual prophylaxis with zidovudine and nevirapine for six weeks, which can be extended to 12 weeks in breastfeeding cases. (Options B, C, and D ruled out)
  • WHO infant feeding guidelines stress continued breastfeeding with ART, as the benefits outweigh risks, with prophylaxis beyond 4-6 weeks adding little benefit if the mother's viral load is suppressed.
  • The 2021 guidelines recommend viral load testing for all pregnant women with HIV at 34-36 weeks or at delivery at the latest, if not already done.

question_text: Which among the following are components of Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC)?
option_a: Skin to skin contact, prevent infections, early discharge
option_b: Breastfeeding, Skin to skin contact, Early discharge

question_text: A 2-month-old infant, born to an HIV-positive mother, presents with recurrent diarrhea. What is the next best step?
option_a: Test stool for giardia and give antibiotics
option_b: Dried spot sample for HIV DNA PCR
explanation:
Explanation:

The most appropriate next step in this infant with recurrent diarrhea, born to an HIV-positive mother, is to perform a dried spot sample for HIV DNA PCR, which is a reliable test for early diagnosis of HIV in infants.

  • Maternal Antibodies: Infants born to HIV-positive mothers will initially test positive due to maternal antibody transfer. These antibodies typically disappear by 6-18 months, though they may persist up to 24 months.
  • Diagnosis of HIV in Infants:

  • Testing Protocols:
    • Rapid HIV tests: Useful for immediate results, but must be confirmed with PCR.
    • Breastfed infants: Testing is done 12 weeks after breastfeeding ends to rule out infection acquired through lactation.
    • High-risk infants: Viral testing within 12-24 hours, then repeat at 2-3 weeks, 4-8 weeks, and 4-6 months if required.
  • Definitive Diagnosis:
    • For non-breastfed infants, HIV can be excluded with:
      • Two negative virologic tests at ≥1 month and ≥4 months
      • Two negative antibody tests at ≥6 months

Explanation of Other Options:

Test stool for giardia and give antibiotics (Option A): May help if diarrhea is infectious, but does not address the key concern of ruling out HIV in a high-risk infant.

Antibody test for HIV (Option C): Not suitable for infants <18 months, as maternal antibodies can interfere with interpretation.

Aerobic culture (Option D): Identifies bacterial infections, but does not rule out HIV, which is the main concern here.

Key Takeaways:

  • HIV DNA PCR is the gold standard for early infant diagnosis.
  • Maternal antibodies persist up to 18-24 months, making antibody tests unreliable in early infancy.
  • Stepwise testing protocol is crucial for accurate confirmation or exclusion of HIV.

question_text: A child presents with recurrent sinusitis and repeated lung infections. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in the CFTR gene. Which test is considered the gold standard to confirm the diagnosis of cystic fibrosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Cystic fibrosis is caused by a CFTR gene mutation leading to defective chloride transport across epithelial cells.
  • The sweat chloride test is the gold standard diagnostic test, with chloride levels ≥60 mmol/L being diagnostic.
  • It directly measures abnormal electrolyte transport and is the most reliable confirmatory tool despite genetic testing.

Explanation of other options:

Lung biopsy (Option B): Rarely used; invasive and not diagnostic for CF. Used mainly for histopathology in other lung diseases.

Chest X-ray (Option C): May show bronchiectasis or hyperinflation, but findings are nonspecific and cannot confirm CF.

Nasal swab culture (Option D): Identifies infections like Pseudomonas, but is not confirmatory for CF diagnosis.

question_text: An adolescent 16 year old boy has been having multiple attacks of rhinosinusitis since birth. At the age of 10 years, he had productive cough with hemoptysis and HRCT revealed cystic spaces with honeycombing which required antibiotics & chest physiotherapy. There was no situs inversus. The treating doctor advised a semen analysis to check for sperm counts. What syndrome the doctor is thinking about?
explanation:
The patient has recurrent rhinosinusitis, history suggesting bronchiectasis, but there is no situs inversus. Since semen analysis has been advised to check for azoospermia, the doctor is likely thinking about Young Syndrome.

  • Young's Syndrome is a rare condition that encompasses a combination of syndromes such as bronchiectasis, rhinosinusitis and reduced male fertility.
  • In individuals with this syndrome the functioning of the lungs is usually normal but the mucus is abnormally viscous.
  • The reduced fertility (obstructive azoospermia) is due to functional obstruction of sperm transport down the genital tract at the epididymis, where the sperm is found in viscous, lipid-rich fluid.
  • Possible causes include genetics, helminthic infections and exposure to mercury during childhood, but the cause is unknown.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 417; Nelson 21st Edition

question_text: Identify the condition shown in the image below.
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical image clearly demonstrates bladder exstrophy, where the bladder mucosa is exposed on the anterior abdominal wall due to abnormal embryonic development.

  • Etiology:
    • Caused by disruption of normal developmental processes during pregnancy.
    • Precise inciting factors remain undefined.
  • Pathology & Pathophysiology:
    • Failure of the cloacal membrane to develop normally.
    • Early rupture → epispadias (incomplete urethral formation).
    • Later rupture → bladder exstrophy.
  • Types:
    • Spectrum ranging from isolated epispadias to more complex forms of bladder exstrophy.
  • Clinical Features:
    • Males:
      • Shortened penis due to separation of the pubic symphysis.
      • Wide spacing of penile crura.
      • Poorly developed erectile tissue (corpora cavernosa).
    • Females:
      • Short and anteriorly placed vagina.
      • Bifid clitoris (split into two halves).
  • Complications:
    • Abnormal urinary function.
    • High susceptibility to urinary tract infections.
    • Long-term risk of adenocarcinoma of the bladder.
  • Surgical Management:
    • Immediate step: Cover the exposed bladder mucosa with a moist sterile wrap until surgery.
    • Definitive staged surgical repair:
      • Closing and repositioning the bladder inside the abdomen.
      • Urethral reconstruction.
      • Repair of the abdominal wall defect.
      • Genital reconstruction to ensure function and cosmetic outcome.

Explanation of Other Options:

Omphalocele (Option B):

  • Herniation of abdominal viscera into the base of the umbilical cord due to failure of normal return of the bowel.
  • Covered by a three-layered sac (peritoneum, Wharton's jelly, and amnion).
  • Centrally located at the umbilicus.
  • Frequently associated with chromosomal anomalies and syndromes (e.g., Beckwith-Wiedemann).
  • Long-term prognosis is generally poor due to associated anomalies.

Gastroschisis (Option D):

  • Protrusion of bowel contents through a paraumbilical defect, usually to the right of the umbilicus.
  • No protective covering membrane (bowel is exposed directly to amniotic fluid).
  • Typically not associated with chromosomal anomalies.
  • Can be associated with bowel atresia or malrotation.
  • Carries a better long-term prognosis compared to omphalocele.

Persistent vitellointestinal duct (Option C):

  • Persistence of the vitelline duct results in communication between the intestine and the umbilicus.
  • Presents with fecal discharge through the umbilicus.
  • Occasionally associated with ileal prolapse through the duct.
  • Represents a distinct entity compared to abdominal wall defects like omphalocele and gastroschisis.

Reference:

NCBI Bookshelf - Bladder Exstrophy

question_text: A 6-month-old infant presents with chronic cough, failure to thrive, and recurrent respiratory infections. On examination, there are crepitations in both lungs. A sweat chloride test is ordered. Which of the following conditions is being evaluated using this test?
explanation:
Explanation of answer:

Sweat chloride levels are elevated in cystic fibrosis, making it a key diagnostic test for this autosomal recessive disorder.

  • Cystic fibrosis (CF) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR gene located on chromosome 7q32.
  • The CFTR protein functions as a chloride channel in epithelial cells.
  • A defect in this channel leads to abnormal ion transport, causing thickened secretions in the lungs, pancreas, and other organs.
  • The sweat chloride test is the gold standard diagnostic tool for CF.
  • It is performed using pilocarpine iontophoresis, which stimulates sweat production.
  • The sweat is collected and analyzed for chloride content.
  • Interpretation:
    • Chloride >60 mmol/L in children and adults is diagnostic of CF.
    • 30-59 mmol/L is borderline and requires further testing.
    • <30 mmol/L is generally considered normal.
  • This elevation occurs due to defective chloride reabsorption in sweat ducts. On the other hand, chloride levels are decreased in pancreatic secretions in CF.
  • Additional diagnostic tools include:
    • Genetic testing for common mutations like F508del.
    • Nasal potential difference (NPD) measurement to assess CFTR function.
    • Fecal elastase to evaluate pancreatic function.
    • Chest imaging to assess pulmonary involvement.
    • Serum electrolytes may show hyponatremic, hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis due to salt loss (known as contraction alkalosis).
    • Transepithelial Intestinal and Rectal Biopsies: These can be used to directly evaluate CFTR function, though they are generally reserved for research or challenging cases.

Explanation of other options:

Phenylketonuria (Option A): Caused by a deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase. Diagnosed by plasma phenylalanine measurement, not sweat chloride.

Gaucher's disease (Option C): A lysosomal storage disorder due to β-glucocerebrosidase deficiency. Diagnosis is made by enzyme assays and genetic testing, not sweat chloride levels.

Osteogenesis imperfecta (Option D): A disorder of type I collagen synthesis, diagnosed by genetic testing or collagen studies, not sweat chloride analysis.

Reference:

https://www.researchgate.net/publication/5507809_Cystic_fibrosis_in_adults_Diagnostic_and_therapeutic_aspects

https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/cystic-fibrosis

question_text: A child presents with anemia, mental retardation, bone pains, and hepatosplenomegaly. Bone marrow biopsy shows a characteristic "crumpled tissue paper" appearance of macrophages. What is the most likely enzyme deficiency in this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

Gaucher disease, caused by glucocerebrosidase deficiency, leads to accumulation of glucocerebroside in macrophages, giving the classic "crumpled tissue paper" appearance on bone marrow biopsy.

  • Gaucher disease is the most common lysosomal storage disorder, inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern.
  • It is caused by deficiency of the enzyme glucocerebrosidase (β-glucosidase), leading to accumulation of glucocerebroside in macrophages.
  • Key Features of Gaucher Disease:
    • Hepatosplenomegaly (due to infiltration by Gaucher cells)
    • Pancytopenia or anemia
    • Bone pain, osteopenia, avascular necrosis
    • Neurological involvement in some types (especially Type 2 and Type 3
    • Characteristic Gaucher cells: lipid-laden macrophages with "crumpled tissue paper" cytoplasm in bone marrow biopsy
  • Types of Gaucher Disease:
    • Type 1 (non-neuronopathic): Most common, affects spleen, liver, bone
    • Type 2 (acute neuronopathic): Infantile onset, severe neurological symptoms
    • Type 3 (chronic neuronopathic): Slower neurological progression
  • Treatment:
    • Enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) with recombinant glucocerebrosidase
    • Substrate reduction therapy (SRT) in select cases

Explanation of other options:

Hexosaminidase-A (Option A): Deficiency causes Tay-Sachs disease, characterized by progressive neurodegeneration, cherry-red macula, and no hepatosplenomegaly or "crumpled tissue paper" cells.

Iduronate 2-sulphatase (Option B): Deficiency causes Hunter syndrome (MPS II), a mucopolysaccharidosis presenting with coarse facial features, developmental delay, and hepatosplenomegaly, but not the marrow findings seen in Gaucher disease.

Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (Option C): Deficiency causes G6PD deficiency, a hemolytic anemia triggered by oxidative stress (e.g., infections, fava beans), with no bone involvement or Gaucher cells.

question_text: An 8-year-old boy presented with dark-coloured urine, oliguria, hypertension, and facial puffiness for 3 days. The urine test is positive for albumin. He had a history of throat infection 2 weeks back. On microscopic examination, enlarged, pale glomeruli and epithelial humps are seen. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

A child presenting with dark urine, proteinuria, oliguria, hypertension, and edema, along with a history of a throat infection two weeks earlier, is suggestive of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

Explanation of other options:

Post-staphylococcal glomerulonephritis (Option A): While Staphylococcus aureus infections can also cause glomerulonephritis, they are less commonly associated with the classic immune complex deposits seen in PSGN.

Nephrotic syndrome (Option C): Children with nephrotic syndrome presents with the clinical findings of hypoalbuminemia, oedema, proteinuria and hyperlipidemia. But doesn't cause cola coloured urine.

IgA nephropathy (Option D): Also known as Berger nephropathy, is a chronic glomerular disease in children characterised by an increased concentration of IgA in the mesangial glomerular deposits with no systemic disease. It presents with gross hematuria within 1-2 days of a previous upper respiratory or GI infection and not after weeks; hence, it is not the diagnosis here.

question_text: A 12-year male with sickle cell disease presents with fever for 2 days and vague complaints of arthralgias. He has a history of multiple sickle cell crises and subsequent admissions. For which of the following infections is this patient at higher risk?
explanation:
Patients with splenic dysfunction, whether congenital or acquired, are at higher risk for infections with encapsulated organisms such as S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, H. influenza type b, and Salmonella spp.

  • Sickle cell anemia patients tend to develop Autosplenectomy & splenic function is reduced. This creates an environment for increased risk of infections by the capsulated organisms.
  • Empiric antibiotic coverage for these organisms should include coverage for these when treating a child with splenic dysfunction and fever. In addition, these patients should follow recommendations for vaccination for S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, and H. influenza type b, including polysaccharide 23-valent pneumococcal vaccine and early meningococcal vaccine as well as appropriate boosters.
  • The other organisms listed are not encapsulated and pose no higher risk in patients with splenic dysfunction than in the general population.

Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1st SA edition., pg. 2337

question_text: A 2-year-old male child was admitted with recurrent bloody stools, atopic dermatitis like rash and petechiae. On CBC, his TLC was normal and platelet count 20000/mm3. What is the next best step to establish the diagnosis?
explanation:
This is a male child presenting with a triad of

  1. Atopic dermatitis-like rash
  2. Recurrent bloody stools indicating recurrent infections
  3. Petechiae due to thrombocytopenia.
  • This is the classic triad seen in patients with Wiskott Aldrich Syndrome.
  • The disease occurs due to mutations in WASp gene mutations, present on Chromosome 11p22.23
  • Hence, patient needs to be screened for WASp gene expression.

Regarding other options

  • Anti platelet antibody should be checked in isolated thrombocytopenia where you suspect ITP.
  • Bone marrow aspiration will be needed in bicytopenia or pancytopenia.
  • LFT and RFT have no role in the evaluation of such a case.

Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 21st edition, Chapter 152, Page 1117

question_text: A Child has sickle cell disease. He is at increased risk of developing infection with which of the following bacteria?
explanation:
Patients with sickle cell anemia are particularly susceptible to infections caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae. This increased vulnerability is primarily due to the functional asplenia (or absence of spleen function) that often develops in these patients. The spleen typically plays a key role in filtering bacteria, especially encapsulated organisms like S. pneumoniae.

Other organisms to which sickle cell patients are more susceptible include:

  • Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib)
  • Neisseria meningitidis
  • Salmonella species(often linked to osteomyelitis in these patients)
  • Parvovirus B19(which can cause aplastic crisis)

KEY TAKEAWAYS: Children with sickle cell are more susceptible to infection with encapsulated bacteria like salmonella, Pneumococcus, Meningococcus, E.coli etc. due to splenic atrophy.

Tags:

  • Topic: SICKLE CELL ANEMIA
  • Difficulty level: MUST KNOW
  • PYQ: INICET MAY 2022

Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 21st ed, page number: 2142

question_text: A 5-year-old child first presented with facial puffiness that progressed to generalized edema. Urine examination showed marked proteinuria. Light microscopy appeared normal, but  likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The described case is consistent with Minimal Change Disease (MCD), the leading cause of nephrotic syndrome in children.

  • It is characterized by edema that often begins around the eyes and later becomes generalized, significant proteinuria, normal findings on light microscopy, and the classic feature of podocyte foot process effacement seen on electron microscopy.

Minimal Change Disease (MCD)

Definition:

  • Responsible for about 70-90% of nephrotic syndrome in children and 10-15% of adult cases.
  • Most often occurs as a primary renal disorder, but may also be linked to Hodgkin's lymphoma, allergic conditions, NSAIDs, lithium therapy, or certain infections.
  • It is most common in boys, with onset usually between 2-6 years of age.

Clinical Features:

  • Early sign: Periorbital puffiness that later progresses to generalized edema (legs, ascites, pleural effusion, hydrocele).
  • Proteinuria: Heavy, often around 10 g/day, causing severe hypoalbuminemia and bland urine sediment.
  • Less frequent findings:
    • Hypertension (30% in children, ~50% in adults)
    • Microscopic hematuria (20-30%)
    • Atopy (eczema, asthma, allergic rhinitis) in about 30-40% of cases
    • Reduced kidney function in 25-40% of patients

Pathology:

  • Light Microscopy: Normal glomeruli.
  • Immunofluorescence: Typically negative, though small IgM deposits may occasionally be seen in the mesangium.
  • Electron Microscopy: Uniform effacement of podocyte foot processes (hallmark feature).

Laboratory Findings:

  • Urine: 3+ to 4+ proteinuria
  • Serum albumin: Markedly low, often <1 g/dL
  • Renal function (BUN/Creatinine): Normal unless complicated by hypovolemia or acute kidney injury
  • Complement levels (C3): Normal

Management:

  • First-line: Corticosteroids (Prednisolone)
    • Initial dose: 60 mg/m²/day (or 2 mg/kg/day, max 60 mg) for 6 weeks
    • Then: 40 mg/m² (or 1.5 mg/kg, max 40 mg) every other day for 6 weeks
  • Prolonging treatment beyond 12 weeks increases adverse effects without improving outcomes.
  • Relapsing or steroid-resistant cases: May require cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil, or mycophenolate mofetil.
  • Over 90% of children respond to steroids, making the prognosis favorable.

Explanation of Other Options:

Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (Option A): This condition demonstrates focal and segmental sclerosis on light microscopy. Since the light microscopy in this case was normal, FSGS can be excluded. Additionally, FSGS generally follows a more progressive course and often shows poor response to initial therapy.

Membranous Glomerulonephritis (Option C): More commonly seen in adults, this disorder is characterized by subepithelial immune deposits on electron microscopy and diffuse thickening of the glomerular basement membrane on light microscopy, which are not present here.

Post-streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (Option D): Usually presents with hematuria, low complement (C3) levels, and other features of acute nephritic syndrome rather than isolated nephrotic syndrome. On electron microscopy, the classic finding is subepithelial "hump-like" deposits, which differ from the podocyte foot process effacement seen in this case.

question_text: A 7-year-old girl presents with cramping abdominal pain, palpable rash on legs, buttocks, and forearms, along with proteinuria and microscopic hematuria. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The combination of cramping abdominal pain, rashes located on the back of the legs, buttocks, and the extensor surfaces of the forearms, along with laboratory evidence of proteinuria and microscopic hematuria, points toward Henoch-Schonlein purpura (HSP) as the most probable diagnosis.

Henoch-Schönlein Purpura (IgA Vasculitis):

It is the most common vasculitis in children and is generally mild in nature.

  • Age: Peak occurrence is between 3 and 18 years, though it can present in children younger than 3 years or older than 10 years. In adults, it is rarer and tends to be more severe and chronic.
  • Gender: Males are affected more frequently than females (M:F ratio 1.5:1).
  • Investigation of Choice (IOC): Biopsy

Tetrad of Symptoms:

  • Skin Involvement (90-100%):
    • Rash: Palpable purpura usually appears on gravity-dependent regions such as the lower limbs and buttocks, and is bilaterally symmetrical.
    • Subcutaneous edema may also be present.
  • Renal Involvement:
    • Glomerulonephritis can present with hematuria, proteinuria ± edema ± hypertension (HTN).
  • Joint Involvement:
    • Arthritis or arthralgia: Non-deforming, primarily affecting large joints like knees and ankles, typically resolving within 2 weeks.
  • Gastrointestinal (GIT) Manifestations:
    • Symptoms include colicky abdominal pain.
    • Melena, intussusception, and vomiting may also occur.

Explanation of other options:

Systemic lupus erythematosus (Option A): usually manifests with a broader range of symptoms, such as fatigue, joint pain, and skin rashes, and is less frequently seen in children. Laboratory tests in SLE show positive antinuclear antibodies and anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies, which are absent in HSP.

Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) (Option C): commonly presents with edema, high blood pressure, and reduced urine output following an upper respiratory or skin infection caused by group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus. Urinalysis often reveals hematuria, proteinuria, and red blood cell casts. HSP, in contrast, is generally not preceded by infections and does not involve hypertension or oliguria.

Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) (Option D): is characterized by the classic triad of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney failure. Although HSP can involve the kidneys, it usually presents with isolated proteinuria and microscopic hematuria, without the additional features seen in HUS.

question_text: A 12-month-old male child is brought to your office for a well-child examination and immunizations. You have been following the child since delivery and are aware that he has acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS) and a Markedly reduced CD4 count (~10%). Which of the following vaccinations should he not receive?
explanation:
• All the vaccines mentioned, except varicella, are killed or synthetic vaccines.
  • Live virus vaccines are contraindicated in the case of AIDS with a markedly reduced T-cell count. The IPV is the inactivated version of the live polio vaccine, oral polio vaccine (OPV).
  • Live attenuated vaccine includes
    • Oral polio vaccine
    • Measles, Mumps, Rubella
    • Influenza
    • BCG
    • Rotavirus
    • Epidemic typhus
    • JE
    • Oral typhoid
    • Yellow fever
    • Plague

Both killed and live available

LATEST UPDATE ON LIVE VACCINE & HIV POSITIVES

In all Asymptomatic AIDS patients, ALL LIVE VACCINES can be given EXCEPT OPV

Tags:

  • Topic: IMMUNIZATION
  • Difficulty level: MUST KNOW
  • PYQ: FMGE JUNE 2022; INICET NOV 2022; MAY 2022; NOV 2021;JULY 2021: NEET PG 2021;2023

question_text:
Choose the correct statements about Hand Foot and mouth Disease
i. Humans are the only carriers
ii. Self-resolving in 10-14 days
iii. Lab confirmation is needed for specific treatment
iv. GBS is a known complication
explanation:
• Management is supportive, directed toward the relief of pain, lowering of fever, and adequate oral hydration because of the self-limiting nature of HFMD. Admission and intravenous fluids might be required if the child is unable to taking orally, dehydrated, clinically ill, or in case of CNS or cardiac complications.
  • Pain and fever can be managed with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and acetaminophen but preferably avoided in children with dehydration.
  • Prognosis of HFMD is excellent. Most of the cases recover within few weeks without residual sequelae. Acute illness lasts for 10-14 days. Some may develop serious complications.
  • CNS complications (more common with Enterovirus 71 than Coxsackievirus): Rhombencephalitis (brainstem encephalitis), acute flaccid paralysis, aseptic meningitis, Guillain-Barré syndrome, acute cerebellar ataxia, and benign intracranial hypertension.

Tags:

  • Topic: OTHER VIRAL INFECTIONS
  • Difficulty level: MAY KNOW
  • PYQ: FMGE AUG 2020, INICET NOV 2022

Reference: Treatment guideline for HMFD, IAP 2022

question_text: A child with fever presents with the following appearance, as shown. What complication can happen of this child also has an underlying chronic hematological disorder?
explanation:
Presence of fever along with bilateral erythematous flushing or papules on the cheek, producing slapped cheek appearance, suggests the likely diagnosis of Erythema Infectiosum, also known as Fifth Disease.

  • Complications include arthropathy, ITP, aseptic meningitis.
  • Individuals with chronic hemolytic anemia and increased red blood cell (RBC) turnover are very sensitive to minor perturbations in erythropoiesis. Infection with B19V leads to a transient arrest in RBC production and a precipitous fall in serum hemoglobin, often requiring transfusion. The reticulocyte count drops to undetectable levels, reflecting the lysis of infected erythroid precursors.
  • This can cause either pure red cell aplasia or sometimes transient aplastic crisis
  • These hematological complications are more common in Sickle Cell Anemia and Hereditary Spherocytosis when they get Parvovirus B19 infection.
  • Arthralgias are more common in adults, while complications like Pure Red Cell Aplasia (PRCA) and Transient Aplastic Crisis are more common in children and adolescents.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Pages 234-235; Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 278

question_text: A 7-year-old child from a malaria-endemic region presents with fever, seizures, altered sensorium, and coma. On examination, no focal neurological deficits are noted. A peripheral blood smear confirms the presence of Plasmodium falciparum.  What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The presentation of fever, seizures, altered consciousness, and coma in a child from a malaria-endemic area, with a blood smear positive for Plasmodium falciparum, is highly indicative of cerebral malaria.

  • Cerebral malaria represents the most severe neurological manifestation of falciparum infection.
  • It typically presents with fever, headache, body aches, convulsions, and, in advanced stages, confusion, delirium, and coma.
  • The absence of focal neurological deficits favors this diagnosis, distinguishing it from other causes of meningoencephalitis.

Explanation of Other Options:

Tuberculous meningitis (Option A): Usually evolves gradually over weeks, often with focal neurological findings. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) typically reveals lymphocytic pleocytosis, low glucose, and elevated protein.

Viral meningitis (Option B): More commonly presents with fever, headache, and meningeal irritation such as neck stiffness. Marked alterations in consciousness or recurrent seizures are less typical. CSF generally shows lymphocytic predominance with normal glucose and protein.

Fungal meningitis (Option D): Rare in children and generally associated with immunosuppression. It progresses slowly, with headache, fever, and neck stiffness preceding mental status changes and seizures.

question_text: A 5-year-old boy, presents to the OPD as shown in the image. Which of the following is the causative agent?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation of fever, painful oral ulcers, and vesicular rash on hands and feet is classic for Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease (HFMD).

Coxsackie virus, particularly type A16, is the causative agent of this condition.


Explanation of Other Options:

Pox virus (Option A):

  • Causes varicella or smallpox, both presenting with pustular or umbilicated lesions.
  • Rash typically spreads centrifugally (from trunk to limbs) and is not limited to palms/soles/oral mucosa.
  • Does not present with the oral ulcers typical of HFMD.

HHV 7 virus (Option C):

  • Causes Roseola infantum (Exanthem subitum / Sixth disease).
  • Features: High-grade fever for 3-5 days followed by a maculopapular rash beginning on the trunk → spreading to neck and limbs.
  • No oral lesions or vesicular eruptions on hands/feet.

HIV virus (Option D):

  • Causes immunodeficiency leading to opportunistic infections and non-specific skin rashes.
  • Oral ulcers may occur but are aphthous or candidal, not associated with characteristic HFMD vesicular rash on hands and feet.

question_text: A 3 month old child has recurrent candidiasis and chest infections. She is currently undergoing immune work-up and is found to have low CD4 count. Which vaccine should always be avoided in this child?
explanation:
Low CD4 count suggesting possible immunodeficiency.

Live vaccines are generally avoided due to the risk of causing disease in immunocompromised children.

Measles is a live attenuated vaccine.

Other options:-

Option A and B - DPT and IPV are inactivated vaccines, which are safe in immunocompromised children.

Option D - Tetanus toxoid (TT) is also a killed vaccine and can be safely given in immunocompromised children.

Key Takeaway:-

Ref:-Nelson textbook of paediatric

question_text: A 5-year-old child develops fever with rash. Rash is polymorphous, itchy and starts on trunk and disappears after few days. Most probable diagnosis is?
explanation:
Clues here

  • Fever with Itchy rash
  • Starts from trunk
  • Polymorphous nature of the rash

All these findings are suggestive of Chicken pox/Varicella infection.

Regarding other options

  • Measles presents with a non-itchy maculopapular rash which first starts on the face, behind the ears and then goes to the trunk
  • Fifth Disease presents with bilateral slapped cheek appearance
  • RMSF presents with non-itchy rash & the child has toxicity, petechiae and transaminitis commonly associated.

Reference: OP Ghai 9th Ed, Pg 210-11, Nelson 21st Ed

question_text: Identify the incorrect match for pediatric infection and characteristic feature on clinical examination?
option_a: Petechiae at junction of soft and hard palate- Pertussis
option_d: Dew drops on rose petal appearance- Varicella
explanation:
Petechiae at the junction of soft and hard palate are often seen in patients of Epstein Barr Virus- EBV Infection.

  • Also note that Nagayama spots are seen in 6th disease, caused by HHV-6.
  • Forchheimer Spots are seen in soft palate region in patients of Rubella, also called German Measles.
  • Dew drops on rose petal appearance has been described for skin vesicular lesions seen in Varicella or Chicken Pox.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Pages 232-234

question_text: A child develops fever with rash. The pediatrician noticed Koplik Spots in the mouth. Likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Fever with rash can occur in multiple conditions, but the presence of Koplik spots in the mouth indicate a likely diagnosis of Measles.

Measles Clinical Picture

  • Fever + 3 C’s (Cough/Coryza/Conjunctivitis)
  • Koplik Spots in oral cavity (1st appear opposite lower 2nd molar toothQ)
  • Rash: Maculopapular, non-itchy, Initially on the Face, especially as erythematous macules behind the ears, along the hairline or on the posterior aspects of cheekà Then Spreads To The Trunk and limbs over the next 2-3 days. The rash fades in the same sequence, leaving a brawny discolouration.
  • Measles is also called as Rubeola

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 231

question_text: The mother of a 15-year-old adolescent girl recently diagnosed with infectious mononucleosis calls for more information. She reports that her daughter, although tired, seems comfortable and is recovering nicely. She remembers that her 20-year-old son had mononucleosis when he was 10 years old, and he received an oral medicine. She requests the same medication for her daughter. Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?
option_a: Explain that medications are not routinely used in EBV infection.
option_b: Call the pharmacy and order oral prednisone 50 mg daily for 5 days (1 mg/kg/d).
option_c: Call the pharmacy and order oral acyclovir 250 mg four times per day (20 mg/kg/d).
option_d: Have her come to the clinic for a single dose of 50-mg intravenous methylprednisolone (1 mg/kg)
explanation:
Supportive care alone usually is required for a patient with acute EBV infection.

  • Steroids have been used historically; current literature suggests their use only in impending airway compromise due to tonsillar hypertrophy or other life-threatening complications.
  • Acyclovir suppresses viral shedding acutely but has no long-term benefit and is not routinely recommended. Acyclovir has a role only in HSV and sometimes, VZV infections.
  • Amoxicillin and ampicillin are ineffective antiviral medications and induce a rash in some EBV-infected patients.

Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1st SA edition., pg. 1586

question_text: A 2-year-old male child presented with high grade fever since 3 days, followed by the onset of non-pruritic, maculopapular rash. The rash first appeared on the trunk and spread to face but spared the palms and soles. On examination, there was no lymphadenopathy but aphthous ulcer-like lesions were found on the uvula and the uvulo-palatoglossal junction, as shown in the picture. What is the most likely etiological agent?
explanation:
Clues in the question

  • Fever with rash, rash appearing on trunk initially and then spreads to the face
  • Nagayama spots on uvula and uvulo-palatoglossal junction as shown in the image.
  • All this points to a diagnosis of Roseola Infantum, also known as Exanthem Subitum or Sixth Disease
  • Causative Agent is Human Herpes Virus-6, followed by Human Herpes Virus-7
  • Peak age is 6 months to 3 years
  • Rash appears within 12-24 hr of subsiding of fever
  • Treatment is mostly supportive.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 234

question_text: Which among the following is true regarding Mumps?
option_a: Patient is not infectious prior to clinical parotid enlargement
option_c: Salivary gland involvement includes only parotid glands
option_d: Mumps orchitis frequently leads to infertility
explanation:
Let us evaluate each option individually

  • Option A is false. The child is infectious and virus can be isolated from saliva as long as 6 days before to 9 days after the appearance of salivary gland enlargement.
  • Option B is true. As per Nelson 21st Edition, The meningoencephalitis in mumps patient may occur before, along with, or following the parotitis. It most commonly manifests 5 days after the parotitis.
  • Option C is false. Although parotid gland is most commonly involved, mumps virus can also involve submandibular salivary gland and may be sometimes involved in the absence of parotid gland involvement.
  • Option D is false. Orchitis is unilateral in 70% cases and bilateral in 30% cases. As per Nelson 21st Edition, Atrophy of the testes may occur, but sterility is rare even with bilateral involvement.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 235; Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 275

question_text: A 12-year-old child is suffering from myoclonic jerks throughout the day since 1 month. Teacher reports irritability and loss of concentration. Parents give no significant history other than fever with rash that the child had at 1 year of age which resolved spontaneously. There is also associated EEG abnormalities. What investigation will lead you to the diagnosis?
option_b: Anti measles IgG antibody in CSF
option_d: MRI Brain for mesial temporal sclerosis
explanation:
Analyse carefully. History of fever with rash at 1 yr of age, now child presenting a decade later with myoclonic jerks, changes in memory and irritability, plus EEG abnormalities. Looks like the primary infection was Measles and now child is presenting with SSPE.

Earlier, brain biopsy with EEG was needed for diagnosis. Currently, detection of IgG Anti-Measles Antibody in CSF is used to make the diagnosis in a child with compatible clinical symptoms.

Additional points to note:

  • Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) is a chronic complication of measles with a delayed onset and an outcome that is nearly always fatal.
  • Clinical manifestations of SSPE begin insidiously 7-13 years after primary measles infection. Subtle changes in behaviour or school performance appear, including irritability, reduced attention span, and temper outbursts. This initial phase (stage I) may at times be missed because of brevity or mildness of the symptoms. Fever, headache, and other signs of encephalitis are absent.
  • The hallmark of the 2nd stage is massive myoclonus, which coincides with extension of the inflammatory process site to deeper structures in the brain, including the basal ganglia. Involuntary movements and repetitive myoclonic jerks begin in single muscle groups but give way to massive spasms and jerks involving both axial and appendicular muscles. Consciousness is maintained.
  • In the 3rd stage, involuntary movements disappear and are replaced by choreoathetosis, immobility, dystonia, and lead pipe rigidity that result from destruction of deeper centers in the basal ganglia. The sensorium deteriorates into dementia, stupor, and then coma.
  • The 4th stage is characterized by loss of critical centers that support breathing, heart rate, and blood pressure. Death soon ensues.
  • EEG shows Radermacker complexes & prognosis is poor
  • Intrathecal IFN-Alpha is used, along with Carbamazepine to control the myoclonic jerks in these patients.

Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 20th ed., pg. 1545

question_text: Period of infectivity in measles?
option_a: 4 days before to 5 days after onset of rash
option_c: 5 days before to 2 days after resolution of fever
option_d: 2 days before to 3 days after resolution of rash
explanation:
Important period of infectivity to remember

  • Measles period of infectivity: 4 days before to 5 days after the onset of rash
  • Rubella communicable period: 5 days before to 6 days after the onset of rash
  • Chicken pox infectivity: From 24 to 48 hours before the onset of rash Till all lesions have crusted
  • Mumps period of isolation: Till the parotid swelling subsides

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Ed, Pages 230-236

question_text: A child presented with febrile illness, followed by altered perception of objects and occasional hallucinations. He was labelled as "Alice in Wonderland" Syndrome. This is seen with which among the following viral infections?
explanation:
According to Nelson 21st Edition, Perceptual distortions of sizes, shapes, and spatial relationships, known as the Alice in Wonderland syndrome (metamorphopsia), may be a presenting symptom in EBV infections.

  • Alice in Wonderland Syndrome, Also called Todd’s Syndrome or Dysmetropia. It is a rare neurological disorder characterized by distortions of visual perception, the body image, and the experience of time.
  • People may see things smaller than they are, feel their body alter in size or experience any of the syndrome's numerous other symptoms.
  • Can also be seen in migraine and other CNS conditions like tumours and psychoactive drugs.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 281

question_text: A 5-year-old boy presents with low grade fever, headache and nasal congestion. He has a flushed face and has developed lacy reticular rash on the trunk and external surface of his arms and legs. He also has strawberry-like tongue. Palms and soles are spared. His mother has been ill with low grade fever and joint stiffness and pain. Which of the following is most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• Scarlet fever is an upper respiratory tract infection associated with a characteristic rash, which is caused by an infection with pyrogenic exotoxin (erythrogenic toxin)–producing GAS in individuals who do not have antitoxin antibodies.
  • The rash appears within 24-48 hour after onset of symptoms, although it may appear with the first signs of illness. It often begins around the neck and spreads over the trunk and extremities.
  • The rash is a diffuse, finely papular, erythematous eruption producing bright red discoloration of the skin, which blanches on pressure. It is often accentuated in the creases of the elbows, axillae, and groin. The skin has a goose-pimple appearance and feels rough. The cheeks are often erythematous with pallor around the mouth. After 3-4 days, the rash begins to fade and is followed by desquamation, initially on the face, progressing downward, and often resembling a mild sunburn. Occasionally, sheet-like desquamation may occur around the free margins of the fingernails, the palms, and the soles.
  • The pharynx is red, the tonsils are enlarged and often covered with a white, grayish, or yellow exudate that may be blood-tinged. There may be petechiae or “doughnut” lesions on the soft palate and posterior pharynx and the uvula may be red and swollen.
  • In addition, the tongue is usually coated and the papillae are swollen. After desquamation, the reddened papillae are prominent, giving the tongue a strawberry appearance.
  • Typical scarlet fever is not difficult to diagnose; the milder form with equivocal pharyngeal findings can be confused with viral exanthems, Kawasaki disease, and drug eruptions. Staphylococcal infections are occasionally associated with a scarlatiniform rash.
  • A history of recent exposure to a GAS infection is helpful, as evidenced here by sick mother with joint pain and fever. Identification of GAS in the pharynx confirms the diagnosis.

Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 20th edition, pg-1328

question_text: The X-linked lymphoproliferative (XLP) syndrome is classically associated with overwhelming infection by which of the following agents?
explanation:
• XLP disease, also referred to as Duncan disease after the original kindred in which it was described, is an X-linked recessive trait characterized by an inadequate immune response to infection with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV).
  • There is a marked impairment in production of antibodies to the EBV nuclear antigen, whereas titers of antibodies to the viral capsid antigen have ranged from absent to greatly elevated. XLP has an unfavourable prognosis.

Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1st SA edition., pg. 1018

question_text: A female child has recurrent candidiasis and respiratory infections since she was 3 months old. Now immunodeficiency workup is being considered. Which vaccine is contraindicated?
explanation:
• In immunodeficient individuals, esp B and T cell deficiencies, all live vaccines are contraindicated. Among the options Measles vaccine is a live vaccine and hence contraindicated.
  • Killed or Inactivated vaccines, subunit vaccines are safe in such children.
  • Live viral (but not live bacterial) vaccines may be given in neutrophil and/or phagocyte defects.
  • Kindly note that DPaT is an acellular type of DPT vaccine and is safe to give in an immunocompromised child.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 215

question_text: Which among the following is a correct match for vaccine and corresponding adverse event?
option_a: MMR Vaccine before 9 months of age- Autism
option_b: Reconstituted Measles Vaccine for more than 4 hours- Toxic Shock Syndrome
explanation:
Let us evaluate options sequentially

  • Option A is incorrect. There is no correlation between MMR vaccine and Autism
  • Option B is correct. Live vaccines like BCG & Measles/MR once reconstituted, should be utilized within 4 hr and any remaining vaccine thereafter should be discarded. If used >4 hr of reconstitution, It increases the risk of Toxic Shock Syndrome, caused by Staphylococcus aureus.
  • Option C is incorrect. Pertussis component in Whole cell DPT vaccine is responsible for encephalopathy in some patients, but not Pneumococcal Conjugate Vaccine.
  • Option D is incorrect. BCG Vaccine can sometimes cause Axillary Lymphadenitis, not Varicella Vaccine.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Pages 216-220

question_text: Most common cause of aseptic meningitis in children?
explanation:
Mumps is the most common cause of aseptic meningitis in children, according to OP Ghai 9th Ed, page 213.

  • Almost 1-10% children developing mumps tend to develop aseptic meningitis. Some children tend to develop full-blown meningoencephalitis.
  • Other neural manifestations of mumps include auditory nerve damage with deafness, cerebellar ataxia, facial neuritis, transverse myelitis and Guillain-Barre syndrome.

Reference: OP Ghai 9th Edition, Page 213

question_text: A 5-year-old male child has history of frequent falls, difficulty in walking and in getting up from sitting position. His muscle biopsy findings are shown. What is true regarding this condition?
option_d: Early diagnosis and therapy shows excellent prognosis
explanation:
The child has features of proximal muscle dysfunction in view of the mentioned symptoms & Gower Sign positivity.

  • The slide shows dystrophic/atrophic muscle fibres with increased connective tissue network. These are typical findings of Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
  • It has no viral prodrome and is a genetically transmitted X-linked recessive condition.
  • Although new molecular agents have been introduced, in general it has poor prognosis with death usually occurring before the 3rd decade of life.

question_text: All of the following are true statements for encephalitis except?
option_a: Herpes simplex encephalitis has a reasonably good prognosis
option_b: Varicella zoster virus encephalitis is predominantly 'cerebellar'
option_c: Mumps encephalitis can cause unilateral nerve deafness
option_d: Herpes simplex encephalitis predominantly affects the temporal lobe
explanation:
• Herpes encephalitis has a very poor prognosis in its full-blown form. Death is common and in survivors, severe neurological sequelae are common.
  • Temporal lobes are selectively affected and an EEG would reveal bitemporal spikes. MRI or CT scans would show density in bilateral temporal lobes.
  • Post-infectious encephalitis in varicella infection is cerebellar and presents with ataxia, nystagmus and poor co-ordination.
  • It is self-correcting and has a good prognosis.

question_text: Two weeks after a viral syndrome, a 2-year-old develops bruising and generalized petechiae that is more prominent over the legs. He has neither hepatosplenomegaly nor lymph node enlargement. Laboratory testing reveals a normal hemoglobin, hematocrit, and white blood cell count and differential. The platelet count is 15,000/mm3. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• Immune (or idiopathic) thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) is common in children. In most cases, a preceding viral infection can be documented.
  • The platelet count frequently is less than 20,000/mm3, but other laboratory test results are normal, including the bone marrow aspiration (which may show an increase in megakaryocytes).
  • These patients have no hepatosplenomegaly or generalized lymphadenopathy.
  • Treatment consists of observation or possibly intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), intravenous anti-D (in Rh-positive patients), immunosuppressives, or steroids. The history must be reviewed for other possible causes of thrombocytopenia, including recent MMR vaccination, drug ingestion, and human immunodeficiency virus.

Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 1stSA edition, pg. 2402

question_text: A 5-year-old boy presented with a low fever and a modestly itchy skin rash. On physical examination the exanthema consisted of erythematous maculo-papular rash that started on the trunk and the limb roots, with an appearance of goose bumps of the skin. Hyperemic and hypertrophic tonsils and modest hepatomegaly were also present. The day after the exanthema spread to the face and to the latero-cervical and retro-auricular regions. After two days the lesions took on a purpuric color and blanching as shown. The Child is vaccinated for age. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
• Measles and rubella could be excluded not only for the different appearance but mainly because the child had received specific vaccines.
  • In scarlet fever, the rash begins after one to five days from a feverish onset and starts at the limb roots, then spreads over the entire body surface, typically sparing the perioral region (the Filatov mask). The tongue is white and patinated with red margins, then peels and takes on a raspberry appearance.
  • In our case, the clinical picture was very different due to the onset of the exanthema (although identical in morphology and distribution) at the same time as the onset of fever. Additionally, the fever was low fever, there were good general conditions and an absence of lymphadenomegaly and tonsillar exudate.
  • Typically, the exanthema involves the face with an intense red color. It is mainly on the cheeks with a 'slapped cheek' appearance and spares the perioral area that remains pale.
  • Subsequently, the erythema spreads to the trunk and limbs. Maculo-papular lesions are often itchy and tend to merge into larger patches (megalo-erythema), pale in the center creating a reticulated or cockade appearance.

question_text: A 5-year-old boy presents with low grade fever, headache and nasal congestion. He has a flushed face and has developed lacy reticular rash on the trunk and external surface of his arms and legs. Palms and soles are spared. His mother has been ill with low grade fever and joint stiffness and pain. Which of the following is most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• Scarlet fever is an upper respiratory tract infection associated with a characteristic rash, which is caused by an infection with pyrogenic exotoxin (erythrogenic toxin)-producing GAS in individuals who do not have antitoxin antibodies.
  • The rash appears within 24-48 hour after onset of symptoms, although it may appear with the first signs of illness. It often begins around the neck and spreads over the trunk and extremities. The rash is a diffuse, finely papular, erythematous eruption producing bright red discoloration of the skin, which blanches on pressure.
  • It is often accentuated in the creases of the elbows, axillae, and groin called as Pastia line. The skin has a goose-pimple appearance and feels rough. The cheeks are often erythematous with pallor around the mouth.
  • After 3-4 days, the rash begins to fade and is followed by desquamation, initially on the face, progressing downward, and often resembling a mild sunburn. Occasionally, sheet-like desquamation may occur around the free margins of the fingernails, the palms, and the soles.
  • The pharynx is red, the tonsils are enlarged and often covered with a white, grayish, or yellow exudate that may be blood-tinged. There may be petechiae or 'doughnut' lesions on the soft palate and posterior pharynx and the uvula may be red and swollen.
  • In addition, the tongue is usually coated and the papillae are swollen. After desquamation, the reddened papillae are prominent, giving the tongue a strawberry appearance.
  • Typical scarlet fever is not difficult to diagnose; the milder form with equivocal pharyngeal findings can be confused with viral exanthems, Kawasaki disease, and drug eruptions. Staphylococcal infections are occasionally associated with a scarlatiniform rash.
  • A history of recent exposure to a GAS infection is helpful, as evidenced here by sick mother with joint pain and fever. Identification of GAS in the pharynx confirms the diagnosis.

Mnemonic for Day of appearance of rash in a febrile patient is

  • Very Sick Person Must Take Double Tablets
  • Very - Varicella (day 1)
  • Sick - Scarlet fever (day 2)
  • Person - Pox-small pox (day 3)
  • Must - Measles (day 4)
  • Take - Typhus (day 5)
  • Double - Dengue (day 6)
  • Tablets - Typhoid (day 7)

question_text: A 1-year-old male patient presents with lethargy and intermittent fussiness started approximately 10 hours before. The patient has had decreased intake, but normal stool and urine output, no fevers. About one week ago everyone in the home had a viral gastritis that resolved after 48 hours. On your exam, vitals are stable, the patient is sleepy yet arousable on exam, his abdomen is soft and non-tender. Other systems are normal. As you turn to leave exam room the patient started to cry and you noticed that he bent his knees and raised his legs to his abdomen. What is the treatment of choice for this patient's condition?
explanation:
• This patient's probable diagnosis is intussusception. Most commonly occurring at the terminal ilium/colonic junction where the terminal ileum telescopes inside the large intestine.
  • This diagnosis most commonly occurs from the age 3 months to 6 years.
  • The most classic signs/symptoms are intermittent colicky abdominal pain, knee to chest positioning to relieve pain and current jelly stools. Although current jelly stools are a classic sign; it is important to note that this is a very late finding noted by necrosis from the mesenteric lining from the intussuscepted bowel and may not always be seen.

  • Another non-specific finding is a lethargic and intermittently fussy patient as noted by our patient in the vignette. Often there is a history of a recent viral illness as seen in our patient.
  • Air contrast enema is the correct answer choice. With the air contrast enema intussusception can both be diagnosed and treated.

question_text: Which of the following viral infection increases risk of developing lymphoma?
explanation:
Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV)-associated lymphoma is a type of lymphoid malignancy linked to EBV infection, a virus that primarily targets B cells. EBV can contribute to lymphomagenesis by promoting cell proliferation, survival, and evading immune responses. EBV-associated lymphomas occur more frequently in immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV, organ transplant recipients, or elderly patients

Types of EBV-Associated Lymphomas

  • Burkitt Lymphoma (BL): Often seen in endemic areas (such as in African populations), and predominantly affecting children, Burkitt lymphoma presents as a highly aggressive B-cell lymphoma with a characteristic "starry-sky" appearance on histology.
  • Hodgkin Lymphoma (HL): Specifically the mixed cellularity and lymphocyte-depleted subtypes are commonly associated with EBV. EBV infection contributes to the Reed-Sternberg cell formation seen in HL.
  • Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma (DLBCL): Particularly prevalent in immunocompromised hosts, EBV-positive DLBCL is an aggressive lymphoma that may present extranodally.
  • Primary CNS Lymphoma: Strongly linked with EBV in immunocompromised patients, especially in the context of HIV/AIDS. It typically presents with neurological symptoms.
  • Peripheral T-Cell and NK/T-Cell Lymphomas: In particular, NK/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type, has a strong association with EBV and is more common in East Asia and Latin America.

KEY TAKEAWAYS: Latent EBV Infection: EBV establishes a latent infection in B cells, expressing latency genes (like LMP1, LMP2) that help evade immune detection and promote cell proliferation. Latency patterns vary across lymphoma types and influence their aggressiveness.
