question_text: A 5-year-old boy presents with low-grade fever, headache, and mild upper respiratory tract symptoms for four days. On examination, a bright red rash is seen on the cheeks, which later spread to the trunk and limbs. The causative agent of this condition is a single-stranded DNA virus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical picture is suggestive of Erythema infectiosum (Fifth disease), which is caused by Parvovirus B19, a single-stranded DNA virus belonging to the Parvoviridae family.

It is characterized by an initial phase of low-grade fever, headache, and mild upper respiratory tract symptoms, followed by the classic "slapped cheek" rash on the face.

The rash later extends to the trunk and limbs, forming a lacy or reticulated pattern.

The age of onset (around 5 years) and the typical progression of findings are characteristic of this self-limiting childhood illness.

Erythema Infectiosum (Fifth Disease):

Explanation of other options:

Hand, foot, and mouth disease (Option A): This illness is caused by Coxsackievirus A or Enterovirus 71, both of which are single-stranded RNA virusesbelonging to the Picornaviridae family. It is characterized by vesicular eruptions on the hands, feet, and oral mucosa. The distribution and morphology of the rash differ significantly from those of erythema infectiosum, and the causative agent is not a DNA virus.

Measles (Option B): A single-stranded RNA virus from the Paramyxoviridae family causes measles. It presents with high-grade fever, cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis, followed by a maculopapular rash that starts behind the ears and spreads downward. The presence of Koplik spots-tiny white lesions on the buccal mucosa-one day before the rash is a distinctive diagnostic feature.

Rubella (Option D): Caused by a single-stranded RNA virus of the Togaviridae family, rubella manifests with a fine pink-red maculopapular rash that spreads in a descending pattern. Forchheimer spots-transient petechiae on the soft palate—are seen in about 20% of cases. Unlike erythema infectiosum, rubella does not produce a “slapped cheek” rash, and its viral type also differs.

question_text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a 5-year-old girl presenting with fever, cough, conjunctival redness, runny nose, and a characteristic rash, as shown in the image?
explanation:
Explanation:

The combination of fever, cough, conjunctivitis, runny nose, and the presence of Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa, as seen in the image, is indicative of measles.

Measles

  • Measles (rubeola) is a highly contagious childhood viral illness caused by the measles virus, an RNA virus belonging to the Paramyxoviridae
  • Transmission: The virus spreads through droplet aerosols, either via the respiratory tract or conjunctiva.
  • Pathogenesis: Initial infection leads to primary viremia, affecting the reticuloendothelial system. This is followed by secondary viremia, which causes systemic symptoms.
  • Incubation Period: Typically 8-12 days.
  • Period of Infectivity: Children are contagious from 3 days before until 4 days after the appearance of the rash.

Clinical Features:

  • Common in preschool-aged children.
  • Prodromal phase: Fever, runny nose, conjunctivitis, and a dry cough.
  • Koplik spots: Small, gray-white lesions on the buccal mucosa opposite the lower second molars, appearing 2-3 days after symptom onset; pathognomonic for measles.

Rash:

  • A maculopapular erythematous rash appears around day 4.
  • Begins on the hairline, behind the ears, and posterior cheeks, then spreads to the rest of the body over 2-3 days.

Management:

  • Primarily supportive and symptomatic.
  • Measures include antipyretics, good hygiene, adequate hydration and nutrition, and maintaining a humidified environment.

Explanation of Other Options:

Mumps (Option A): Usually presents with swelling of the parotid glands and lacks the typical progression of respiratory symptoms followed by rash seen here. Since there is no parotid involvement, mumps is unlikely.

Chickenpox (Option C): Characterized by vesicular lesions at different stages and does not present with prodromal respiratory symptoms or Koplik spots. The rash is intensely pruritic and appears in successive crops, unlike the presentation in this case.

Erythema infectiosum (Option D): Features a "slapped cheek" appearance with a lacy rash on the trunk, without the prodromal respiratory symptoms or Koplik spots. The absence of this classic facial rash pattern makes this diagnosis unlikely.

question_text: A child presents with fever and a rash that begins on the face, particularly behind the ears, cheeks, and buccal mucosa, and then spreads to the rest of the body. On examination, characteristic Koplik's spots are seen on the buccal mucosa.
explanation:
Explanation:

Koplik's spots along with a descending maculopapular rash and prodromal symptoms confirm the diagnosis of measles.

  • Measles (rubeola) is a highly contagious viral illness caused by an RNA virus of the Paramyxoviridae family.
  • It typically affects children, especially those who are unvaccinated.
  • The classic clinical course involves:
    • Prodrome (3-4 days): High fever, cough, coryza (runny nose), and conjunctivitis-collectively known as the 3 C's.
    • Koplik's spots: These are pathognomonic and appear on the 2nd or 3rd day of illness. They are tiny bluish-white spots with a red halo, typically found on the buccal mucosa opposite the lower molars.
    • Rash (exanthem): Appears on the 4th day of illness, starting behind the ears and spreading to the face, trunk, and limbs in a cephalocaudal pattern. The rash is erythematous, maculopapular, and often confluent.
    • Course: The rash fades in the order it appeared, leaving behind brownish discoloration and fine desquamation.
  • Measles is transmitted via droplet nuclei from respiratory secretions and is contagious from 3 days before to 4 days after the onset of rash.
  • Management is mainly supportive, with antipyretics, hydration, and vitamin A supplementation.

Explanation of other options:

Rubella (Option B): Rubella also causes a maculopapular rash that begins on the face and spreads, but it is milder, non-confluent, and often associated with postauricular and occipital lymphadenopathy. Forchheimer spots (rose-colored spots on the soft palate) may be seen, not Koplik's spots.

Varicella (Option C): Caused by the varicella-zoster virus, it presents with a pruritic rash appearing in crops at different stages (macules → papules → vesicles → crusts), typically starting on the trunk. Koplik's spots are not seen in varicella.

Mumps (Option D): Caused by a paramyxovirus, mumps presents with parotitis, fever, and sometimes orchitis or meningitis. A rash is uncommon, and Koplik's spots are absent.

question_text: An 8-year-old boy presents with progressive difficulty in walking and rising from a squatting position. A muscle biopsy was performed, and the image is shown below. Which of the following statements is correct regarding this condition?
option_c: It is a mitochondrial storage disorder
option_d: Early treatment has an excellent prognosis
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation and biopsy findings showing fatty replacement of muscle fibers are characteristic of Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD). This X-linked recessive disorder results in progressive proximal muscle weakness, with death usually occurring in the late teens to early 20s (third decade) due to respiratory or cardiac complications.

  • Inheritance pattern: X-linked recessive
  • Type of mutation: Frameshift mutations → disrupted reading frame
  • Dystrophin protein: Deficient, truncated, unstable (<3% of normal)
  • Age of onset: Before 5 years
  • Early symptoms: Hip girdle weakness, delayed walking, Gowers' sign, frequent falls, lordotic posture
  • Progression: Rapid, severe, early onset
  • Loss of ambulation: Typically by 10-14 years
  • Muscle involvement: Proximal muscle weakness, calf pseudohypertrophy
  • Cardiac involvement: Common, worsens after ambulation loss
  • Cognitive impairment: 20-30% (IQ <70), possible autism-like behavior, epilepsy
  • Respiratory involvement: Sleep apnea, recurrent infections, respiratory failure
  • Investigations:
    • Genetic testing (deletion/duplication analysis; NGS if negative)
    • Muscle biopsy (endomysial connective tissue proliferation, dystrophin abnormalities)
  • Steroid therapy: Prednisone (0.75 mg/kg/day) or Deflazacort (0.9 mg/kg/day) → slows muscle decline, prolongs ambulation
  • Life expectancy: Late teens to 20s

Gowers sign

Explanation of Other Options:

Previous history of viral prodrome (Option B): Viral prodrome (fever, malaise) is not a feature of DMD and does not contribute to its etiology.

It is a mitochondrial storage disorder (Option C): DMD arises from dystrophin gene mutations, not mitochondrial storage defects.

Early treatment has an excellent prognosis (Option D): Although steroids slow progression, the long-term prognosis remains poor, with death typically in the 3rd decade.

question_text: A 3-year-old was diagnosed with croup. Which of the following is the most common causative organism?
explanation:
Explanation:

Croup, also known as laryngotracheobronchitis, is an acute viral infection affecting the glottic and subglottic regions of the upper airway, leading to inflammation, edema, and characteristic clinical features such as barking cough, inspiratory stridor, and hoarseness.

It predominantly affects children between 3 months and 5 years, with peak incidence in the second year of life.

The most common causative agents are parainfluenza viruses (types 1, 2, and 3), responsible for approximately 75% of cases, followed by other viruses including influenza A and B, adenovirus, respiratory syncytial virus, and measles. Among the options provided, influenza virus is the most appropriate choice.


Explanation of Other Options:

Hemophilus influenza (Option A): H. influenza type B can cause epiglottitis, not croup.

Streptococcus pneumoniae (Option B): S. pneumoniae is a bacterial pathogen, not commonly associated with viral laryngotracheobronchitis.

Diphtheria (Option D): Diphtheria causes membranous pharyngitis with airway obstruction, not typical viral croup.

Key Takeaways:

question_text: Which of the following infections carries the lowest risk of perinatal transmission?
explanation:
Explanation:

Rubella infection, though capable of causing severe intrauterine transmission during pregnancy (especially in the first trimester), is associated with the least risk of perinatal transmission when compared with HSV, CMV, and Hepatitis B. Other infections such as HSV, CMV, and Hepatitis B carry a much higher likelihood of perinatal transmission and result in significant neonatal morbidity.

Congenital Rubella Syndrome (CRS):

  • Causative Agent: Rubella virus
  • Mode of Transmission: Vertical transmission from mother to fetus during pregnancy; highest risk during the first trimester
  • Critical Risk Period: First trimester → carries the greatest fetal risk
  • Classical Triad:
    • Sensorineural deafness
    • Cataracts
    • Congenital heart disease (commonly PDA)
  • Other Clinical Features:
    • Salt and pepper retinopathy (speckled retina)
      • Blueberry muffin lesions (bluish-red dermal nodules)
      • Microcephaly
      • Micrognathia
      • Developmental delay
      • Thrombocytopenic purpura
      • Jaundice
      • Hepatosplenomegaly
  • Diagnosis: Clinical features + lab confirmation (rubella-specific IgM, rubella RNA detection)
  • Management: No specific antiviral therapy; prevention through MMR vaccination prior to pregnancy
  • Complications: Developmental delay, cognitive impairment, seizures, ocular defects (e.g., cataracts), and cardiac anomalies (e.g., PDA)

Explanation of Other Options:

Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) (Option A): Can be transmitted antenatally, intrapartum, or perinatally; associated with severe neonatal disease (skin lesions, keratoconjunctivitis, encephalitis, disseminated infection).

Cytomegalovirus (CMV) (Option B): Most common congenital infection with perinatal spread; causes hepatosplenomegaly, petechiae, microcephaly, chorioretinitis, and later hearing loss.

Hepatitis B (Option D): High risk of perinatal transmission, especially in HBeAg-positive mothers; infants often progress to chronic infection leading to long-term hepatic complications.

Key Takeaways:

  • Rubella → least risk of perinatal transmission.
  • HSV, CMV, and Hepatitis B → high perinatal transmission risk with severe neonatal outcomes.
  • Prevention of CRS → MMR vaccination before pregnancy.

question_text: A 5 years old presents with a swollen joint. Her knee joint has been swollen for several days. There is some mild tenderness but she continues to walk, with a slight limp. Her mother reports that 3 weeks ago she had a bout of gastroenteritis associated with a fever. There were two episodes of bloody diarrhoea and she vomited once. Her symptoms resolved without treatment. On examination she is afebrile. Her right knee is swollen with only mild tenderness on passive movements of the joint. What is the most likely cause?
explanation:
Reactive arthritis is a type of inflammatory arthritis that develops in response to an infection in another part of the body, commonly in the urinary tract, gastrointestinal tract, or respiratory system. It typically occurs after infections caused by bacteria like Chlamydia, Salmonella, Shigella, or Campylobacter.

Key Features:

  1. Joint Symptoms: It often affects the knees, ankles, and feet, causing pain, swelling, and stiffness. It is usually asymmetric, meaning it may only affect one side of the body.
  2. Enthesitis: Inflammation at the sites where tendons and ligaments attach to bones, especially in the heels, can be a hallmark.
  3. Conjunctivitis and Urethritis: Many patients also experience eye inflammation (conjunctivitis) and urinary symptoms (urethritis), which are part of the condition's classic triad (Reiter's syndrome).
  4. Skin Manifestations: Skin rashes, including keratoderma blennorrhagicum (scaly lesions on the soles of the feet and palms), can occur.

Option B: Septic arthritis has acute history of fever and limited joint movement with other signs of joint inflammation.

Option C: HUS has characteristic presentation with the triad of acute renal failure, microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia.

Option D: Rickets has no pain or swelling.

KEY TAKEAWAYS: This is the most common cause of acute hip pain in children. It occurs in children aged 2-12 years of age. It often follows or is accompanied by a viral infection. Presentation is with sudden onset of pain in the hip or a limp. There is no pain at rest, but there is decreased range of movement, particularly external rotation.

question_text: Which among the following intrauterine infection produces hydrocephalus in the baby?
explanation:
Most of the congenital infections have either small sized head or normal sized head.only one infection has large sized head(hydrocephalus) that is toxoplasmosis.

Other options:

(A): Rubella: there is microcephaly in CRS(Congenital Rubella Syndrome)

(B): HSV: There may be microcephaly in Congenital HSV infection.

(C): CMV: There is microcephaly in Congenital CMV infection.

Key takeaways:

Congenital Toxoplasmosis occurs when Toxoplasma gondii is transmitted from mother to fetus.

Classic triad of Congenital toxoplasmosis

I) Hydrocephalus

ii) Diffuse intracranial calcification

iii) Focal chorioretinitis

Diagnosis: Serology, PCR, and imaging (ultrasound, CT, MRI).

Treatment: Pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine with folinic acid; corticosteroids for severe cases. Prevention: Pregnant women should avoid cat litter, undercooked meat, and unwashed produce.

question_text: A 3-month-old baby comes with complaints of deafness, cataract, and patent ductus arteriosus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The classical triad of deafness, cataract, and patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) strongly suggests congenital rubella syndrome.

  • Congenital Rubella Syndrome (CRS) occurs when rubella infection is acquired by the mother during early pregnancy, particularly within the first trimester.
  • The virus causes widespread fetal damage through viremia, which is most intense from 10 to 17 days after maternal infection.
  • The risk of congenital defects is highest in the first 12 weeks and significantly decreases after 20 weeks gestation.
  • The characteristic clinical features of CRS include:
    • Sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) - the most common feature
    • Ocular defects - particularly cataracts (most common), glaucoma, and "salt and pepper" retinopathy
    • Cardiac anomalies - classically patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), followed by pulmonary artery stenosis and ventricular septal defect
    • Other features: microcephaly, intellectual disability, growth retardation, hepatitis, bone lesions, and increased risk of autoimmune conditions like diabetes and thyroid disorders.
  • Diagnosis is confirmed with Rubella-specific IgM, PCR for viral RNA, or viral culture.
  • Management is supportive, with no specific antiviral treatment.
  • Prevention is crucial and is achieved through vaccination (MMR/MMRV - live attenuated RA 27/3 strain), which is highly effective (95% after one dose, 99% after two doses).
  • Pregnant women exposed to rubella may be offered immunoglobulin, but it does not reliably prevent fetal infection.

Explanation of other options:

Congenital herpes simplex virus infection (Option A): Typically presents with skin vesicles, chorioretinitis, keratoconjunctivitis, and neurological complications like microcephaly or hydranencephaly. PDA and cataracts are not hallmark features.

Congenital toxoplasmosis (Option B): The classic triad includes chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and intracranial calcifications, not PDA or cataracts.

Congenital cytomegalovirus infection (Option C): Commonly presents with microcephaly, periventricular calcifications, chorioretinitis, and sensorineural hearing loss, but PDA and cataracts are not typical.

question_text: Which congenital infection is least teratogenic to the fetus/ neonate?
explanation:
HSV Antenatal transmission: In utero infection with HSV has been documented but is uncommon.

Transmission

  • in utero => 5.5%
  • peripartum/during childbirth -> 80% - leads to prematurity PROM
  • post birth -> 14.5%

Explanation of Incorrect Answers:

  • CMV (Cytomegalovirus):
    • CMV is the most common cause of congenital viral infection and has significant teratogenic effects. It can lead to neurological impairments, hearing loss, and growth restriction. CMV is the leading cause of congenital disabilities due to prenatal infection.
  • Rubella:
    • Rubella infection in the first trimester can lead to severe teratogenic effects, including congenital heart defects, cataracts, deafness, and growth retardation. Rubella is highly teratogenic and causes significant birth defects if contracted during pregnancy.
  • Chickenpox (Varicella):
    • Varicella infection in pregnancy, especially during the first and second trimesters, can lead to congenital varicella syndrome, causing limb abnormalities, cataracts, skin scarring, and neurological issues. Neonatal varicella can also cause serious complications.

Key Takeaway:

  • HSV-2 is the least teratogenic among the congenital infections, with lower risk of severe birth defects compared to CMV, Rubella, and Chickenpox.
  • CMV and Rubella are particularly known for their serious teratogenic effects, especially when contracted during the first trimester of pregnancy.
  • Chickenpox can also have serious congenital consequences, especially if the mother contracts the infection in the early stages of pregnancy.

Reference: Nelson textbook of paediatrics

question_text: An infant presents with recurrent chest infections and tachypnea. Identify the likely clinical condition.
explanation:
Explanation:

CCAM presents in infancy with recurrent respiratory infections and tachypnea due to malformed cystic lung tissue.

  • Congenital Cystic Adenomatoid Malformation (CCAM), now known as Congenital Pulmonary Airway Malformation (CPAM), is a rare developmental malformation where hamartomatous lung tissue forms cysts, typically limited to a single lobe.
  • These cysts impair normal lung function, leading to symptoms such as tachypnea, recurrent chest infections, and respiratory distress, even in early infancy.
  • On chest X-ray: Multicystic mass, often with mediastinal shift.
  • Diagnosed prenatally or postnatally with imaging (X-ray/CT).
  • Management: Surgical resection-often done before 1 year due to risk of malignant transformation (e.g., pleuropulmonary blastoma).
  • Pathogenesis: Embryological injury before the 35th day of gestation disrupts bronchopulmonary development.

Explanation of other options:

Right-sided Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia (Option B): Presents with severe respiratory distress immediately after birth, not recurrent infections. Bowel loops in the chest may shift mediastinum. Not typically associated with chronic recurrent chest infections in infancy.

Congenital Lobar Emphysema (Option C): Causes overinflation of a pulmonary lobe, leading to compression of adjacent structures and acute respiratory distress, usually at birth or within a few days. Recurrent infections are not a hallmark feature.

Cystic Fibrosis (Option D): Can cause chronic lung infections, but usually presents with failure to thrive, steatorrhea, clubbing, and positive sweat chloride test. Onset is typically later and more systemic in presentation.

Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6709284/

question_text: A 4-month-old infant is brought to the pediatric emergency with a 3-day history of cough, rhinorrhea, and increasing difficulty in breathing. On examination, the child has nasal flaring, chest retractions, and expiratory wheeze. Oxygen saturation is 88% on room air. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism responsible for this illness?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) is the most common etiologic agent of acute bronchiolitis in infants - responsible for ~70-80% of cases.
  • Affects mainly infants aged 1-6 months, but can occur up to 2 years of age.
  • RSV infection peaks during winter and early spring
  • It spreads via respiratory droplets and direct contact; incubation period is typically 4-6 days.
  • RSV causes inflammation, edema, and necrosis of small airway epithelial cells, leading to bronchiolar obstruction, air trapping, and hyperinflation-classic features of bronchiolitis.

Explanation of Other Options:

Rhinovirus (Option C):

  • Major cause of common cold and upper respiratory infections, not typical bronchiolitis.
  • Can exacerbate asthma in older children.

Key Takeaway Points:

question_text: What is the best management approach for a patient presenting with fatigue, hemoglobin below 9 g/dL, and sickle-shaped red blood cells on peripheral smear?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The patient's symptoms of fatigue, low hemoglobin, and the presence of sickle-shaped red blood cells on peripheral smear suggest sickle cell disease.
  • Blood transfusions are commonly used in patients with symptomatic anemia or acute complications. The goal is to raise hemoglobin levels and reduce the proportion of sickle-shaped cells in circulation.
  • Sickle Cell Anemia:
    An autosomal recessive disorder caused by a substitution of valine for glutamic acid at position 6 of the beta-globin chain. This mutation alters red blood cell shape and function, producing rigid, sickle-shaped cells that can cause multiple complications.
  • Pathophysiology:
    Sickled red cells obstruct microcirculation, leading to ischemic damage and progressive splenic dysfunction. This increases susceptibility to infections, particularly from encapsulated bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Neisseria meningitidis.
  • Management:
  • Hydroxyurea: Reduces cell count and increases fetal hemoglobin (HbF), mitigating clinical manifestations.
  • For sickling crises:
    • IV analgesia with opioids
    • IV fluids
    • Fresh blood transfusion (note: packed red cells are avoided as they may worsen hemoconcentration)
  • Voxelotor: Prevents HbS polymerization.
  • Monoclonal antibodies (Crizanlizumab): Reduce the frequency of vaso-occlusive crises.

Explanation of other options:

IV antibiotics (Option A): Needed during infection but not primary here.

Deferoxamine (Option C): Used for iron overload, not first-line therapy.

Wait and watch (Option D): Not appropriate for symptomatic anemia.

Key Takeaways:

  • Blood transfusion = cornerstone of acute management.
  • Hydroxyurea reduces crisis frequency.
  • Packed RBCs are avoided; fresh whole blood preferred.

question_text: Which of the following is true about Congenital CMV?
option_b: Triad of SNHL, periventricular brain calcification and enamel hypoplasia is mostly seen
option_c: Most asymptomatic children tend to develop hearing loss in later life
option_d: If pregnant mother is IgG positive, the chances of fetal or neonatal infection are low
explanation:
Incorrect Option Explanations:

  1. Approximately 20-30% infections are asymptomatic This is incorrect because approximately 85-90% of congenital CMV infections are asymptomatic at birth. Only a small proportion of infants exhibit clinical symptoms.
  2. Triad of SNHL, periventricular brain calcification, and enamel hypoplasia is mostly seen The classic triad for symptomatic congenital CMV includes sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL), periventricular calcifications, and microcephaly, but enamel hypoplasia is not a commonly recognized feature of congenital CMV.
  3. Most asymptomatic children tend to develop hearing loss in later life This is partially true, but not entirely accurate. While 10-15% of asymptomatic children with congenital CMV may develop sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) later in life, the majority remain unaffected.

Key Takeaway:

question_text:
A male infant presents with abdominal distention, a history of recurrent urinary tract infections, and urinary retention on examination. Imaging reveals bilateral hydronephrosis.
What is the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Posterior urethral valves (PUV) are congenital mucosal folds in the posterior urethra that obstruct urinary flow - a condition seen only in male infants.

The combination of:

  • Urinary retention
  • Recurrent UTIs
  • Abdominal distension (palpable bladder)
  • Bilateral hydronephrosis on imaging

is classically diagnostic of PUV.

Posterior urethral valves:

Explanation of Other Options:

Vesicoureteric reflux (Option A):

VUR refers to the backward flow of urine from the bladder into the ureters and kidneys due to an incompetent vesicoureteral junction. Although it can lead to recurrent urinary tract infections, its hallmark feature is retrograde urine flow, not urinary retention or abdominal distension, which are absent in this case.

Horseshoe kidney (Option C):

This is a congenital fusion anomaly in which the lower poles of the kidneys are joined. While it may occasionally result in hydronephrosis, it usually does not present with urinary retention or recurrent UTIs as seen in this scenario.

Pelviureteric junction obstruction (Option D):

PUJ obstruction causes impaired drainage of urine between the renal pelvis and ureter, often leading to unilateral hydronephrosis. The typical presentation is an asymptomatic flank mass, upper abdominal discomfort, or occasional UTIs - not the bilateral hydronephrosis and urinary retention described here

question_text: A 10-year-old boy is brought by his family because of frequent episodes of drooping of the right or left side of his mouth that last 1-3 min each. He is completely awake and alert during the episodes but has difficulty talking. He said to you that I am embarrassed by them because "Spit drips out of the drooping side of my mouth." He had one nocturnal seizure 6 months ago, and no work up has been done. He has unremarkable history and physical exam. He is otherwise a healthy boy who does quite well in school. EEG shows centrotemporal spikes. What are you going to tell the family?
option_a: The seizure and the mouth drooping are unrelated.
option_b: He needs to have a video EEG to capture an episode.
option_c: He has a form of epilepsy that he is likely to outgrow.
explanation:
Clues in the question include

  • Partial seizures with intact awareness
  • Age 2-12 years and male gender
  • Normal mental status otherwise
  • EEG showing centro-temporal spikes
  • All of this fits into a diagnosis of Benign Childhood Epilepsy with Centro-Temporal Spikes (BECTS), also called as Benign Rolandic Epilepsy.
  • Patients are usually otherwise normal, and the most common seizure occurs shortly after going to sleep, with focal motor activity affecting the face and tongue, resulting in dysarthria or drooling.
  • There is no loss of consciousness (simple partial seizure).
  • EEG shows Centro-temporal spike, often with a surface dipole in which the spike is surface-negative in the Centro-temporal region, and surface-positive over the frontal region.
  • It has a favourable prognosis, and seizures usually remit around puberty. However, atypical forms of BECTS are also recognized.
  • Carbamazepine & Oxcarbazepine are 1st-line drugs in Rolandic Epilepsy.

Reference: Swaimann's Pediatric Neurology, Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 611

question_text: A 7-year-old boy has non-blanching rashes on the legs and buttocks. He also complains of joint pains, abdominal pain, vomiting, and blood in the stool. Lab investigations revealed a normal platelet count, and urine analysis shows hematuria +++ and proteinuria +. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical scenario of purpura in legs and buttocks, arthritic pain, abdominal pain and normal platelet level are characteristic of Henoch-Schönlein Purpura (HSP).

Henoch-Schönlein Purpura (HSP)

Aetiology

  • The exact cause is unknown.
  • Immune-mediated vasculitis, often following an upper respiratory infection.
  • Genetic predisposition, with HLA-B34 and DRB1, was observed in some cases.
  • Most common in Males.

Pathophysiology

  • Inflammation of small blood vessels affecting skin, joints, intestines, and kidneys.
  • Triggered by immune system response to infections.
  • Leakage of fluid and blood cells into tissues.
  • Immune complex deposition, particularly IgA, in affected vessel.

Clinical Features

  • Palpable Purpura: Raised, purplish-red rash, mainly on lower limbs and buttocks.
  • Joint Involvement: Joint swelling, commonly in knees and ankles.
  • Abdominal Pain: Often severe, may include vomiting, diarrhoea, gastrointestinal bleeding, or intussusception
  • Renal Involvement: Less common, presents as Chronic renal failure.

Diagnosis

  • Clinical Criteria:
    • Palpable purpura plus at least one of:
      • Diffuse abdominal pain
      • Arthritis or arthralgia
      • Biopsy-proven IgA deposition
      • Renal involvement (hematuria &/ proteinuria)
  • Laboratory involvement:
    • Elevated ESR or CRP indicates inflammation.
    • Platelet Counts are normal.

Complications

  • Intussusception
  • Chronic Renal Failure due to Long-term kidney damage, in severe cases.
  • Neurological Complications: Rare; may include seizures, headaches, or peripheral neuropathy.

Treatment

  • Mild Cases: Rest, hydration, and pain relievers.
  • Moderate to Severe Cases: Corticosteroids (e.g., prednisone) to reduce inflammation.
  • Severe or Resistant Cases: Additional immunosuppressive medications may be required.

Explanation of other options:

Systemic lupus erythematosus (Option A): Malar rash is virtually pathognomonic in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). It involves the cheek, bridge of the nose, and lower eyelids but characteristically spares the nasolabial folds.

Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (Option C): In Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) children present with a sudden appearance of bruises and mucosal bleeding, like epistaxis, oral oozing and prolonged bleeds with superficial trauma. The platelet levels are low in this condition, unlike the given scenario.

Polyarteritis arteritis nodosa (Option D) rare in childhood, is characterised by the presence of either a biopsy showing small and mid-size artery necrotising vasculitis or angiographic abnormalities.

question_text: The following are true with regard to Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome except?
option_a: It is inherited as an autosomal dominant disorder
option_b: It is associated with micro thrombocytopenia, eczema and immunodeficiency
option_c: Intrinsic abnormalities of B-cell function are a common feature
option_d: Low levels of IgM and increased levels of IgA, IgD and IgE can be found
explanation:
Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome

  • This is inherited as an X-linked recessive disease and is a rare condition.
  • It is usually characterized by immune dysregulation (immune deficiency, eczema or autoimmunity) and micro thrombocytopenia. Patients with WAS are compromised immunologically, and are susceptible to pyogenic, viral and opportunistic infections. They also develop eczema, a spectrum of autoimmune phenomena and lymphoproliferative disease.
  • The platelets are small, and it can present with minor bruising as well as life-threatening GIT or intracranial bleeding. The T cells are progressively reduced in number and function during childhood, which leads to both restricted defects in proliferative responses of WASp T cells and impaired delayed-type hypersensitivity (DTH) responses.
  • Deficient antibody responses to polysaccharide (PS) antigens in particular, and low or absent levels of iso-haemagglutinins, suggest that there are also intrinsic abnormalities of B-cell function. WAS is associated with low levels of IgM and increased levels of IgA, IgD and IgE. Gene mutations are expected with classic WAS.
  • Using prophylactic antibiotics and immunoglobulin for infection is the conventional therapy. Splenectomy is usually effective in increasing platelet numbers and reducing bleeding complications, but also increases the risk of infection. Stem cell transplantation is curative and gene therapy may help in the future.
  • Major complications associated with WAS include autoimmune phenomena, including hematological cytopenias, small and large vessel vasculitis, lymphoproliferative disease, and lymphoma.

Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1st SA ed., pg. 1027

question_text: A baby was born to a HIV+ mother, who was not taking antiretroviral therapy. The baby was started on exclusive breastfeeds. What should be the initial prophylaxis to start in the baby according to the latest guidelines?
option_c: Oral Nevirapine + Oral Zidovudine for 6 weeks
option_d: Oral Nevirapine + Oral Zidovudine for 12 weeks
explanation:
Guidelines for HIV according to NACO 2021 & WHO Updated Guidelines

  • Any baby born to HIV+ mother is labelled as HIV-exposed infant, regardless of the infection status
  • All HIV-exposed infants are preferably started on exclusive breast feeds (EBF). If EBF is not possible or available, exclusive replacement feeding (ERF) can be considered, provided the family has resources and are motivated enough to continue the same.
  • All HIV-exposed infants are categorised into low-risk and high-risk as follows:


  • All HIV-exposed infants need to be started on Anti-Retroviral (ARV) Prophylaxis
  • In low-risk infants, we start oral nevirapine daily for 6 weeks
  • In high-risk infants, we start combination therapy using oral nevirapine + oral zidovudine.
  • While using combination therapy, the duration for ARV Prophylaxis depends on the mode of feeding. For EBF, it is 12 weeks, while for ERF, it is 6 weeks.

Reference: NACO 2021 Update, Table 3.1.7, Page 180; OP Ghai 10th Edition, Pages 248-250

question_text: An infant visits a pediatric presenting with symptoms of abdominal distension, anorexia, and lassitude. He was diagnosed with Hirsch sprung disease. What is the cause of Hirsch sprung disease?
option_a: Congenital absence of ganglion cells in both myenteric plexus and submucosal plexus of a segment of distant colon
option_d: Paralysis of colonic smooth muscles due to trauma during parturition
explanation:
Option A: Some children have a genetically determined condition of abnormal colonic motility known as Hirschsprung disease or aganglionic megacolon, which is characterized by abdominal Distension, anorexia, and lassitude. Distension of segment proximal to aganglionic segment is seen. The disease is typically diagnosed in infancy, and affects as many as 1 in 5000 live births.

It is due to a congenital absence of the ganglion cells in both the myenteric and submucous plexuses of a segment of the distal colon, as a result of failure of the normal cranial-to-caudal migration of neural crest cells during development.

Option B: (Congenital absence of colon): This would lead to severe gastrointestinal issues but is not the specific cause of Hirschsprung disease.

Option C: (Hyperactivity of colon smooth muscles): This would not explain the symptoms; Hirschsprung disease involves an absence of ganglion cells, leading to decreased motility.

Option D: (Paralysis of colonic smooth muscles due to trauma during parturition): Trauma can affect nerves, but Hirschsprung disease specifically results from a congenital lack of ganglion cells.

Key takeaways:

Hirschsprung disease is caused by the congenital absence of ganglion cells in the myenteric and submucosal plexuses of the distal colon, leading to symptoms like abdominal distension and anorexia.

Level: Must know

Tag: GI motility

Reference: Ganong's review of medical physiology, 26th edition, Page 1144

question_text: Ideal time of surgery in CDH?
explanation:
The ideal time to repair the diaphragmatic defect is under debate.

  • As per Nelson 21st Ed, most experts wait at least 48 hr after stabilization and resolution of the pulmonary hypertension.
  • If the newborn is receiving ECMO, an ability to be weaned from this support should be a consideration before surgical repair.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 345.1

question_text: An infant with a history of recurrent pneumonia is diagnosed with TEF at 8 months of age. Which of the following statements is correct?
option_a: The infant most likely has an H-type TEF
option_b: The infant most likely has proximal esophageal atresia with distal fistula
option_c: The infant likely has a previously undetected, associated finding of imperforate anus
option_d: The infant is unlikely to have gastroesophageal reflux
explanation:
The key to making the diagnosis is age and features in this question.

  • This infant likely has an H-type TEF, found later in infancy with recurrent pneumonias and/or feeding difficulty.
  • Patients with esophageal atresia and distal fistula present in the first hours of life because of their inability to swallow oropharyngeal secretions.
  • Infants with imperforate anus also present as neonates.
  • All patients with TEF are at high risk for gastroesophageal reflux.

Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1st SA ed., pg. 1783

question_text: A 3-day-old male neonate who has not yet passed meconium developed abdominal distension. There is no history of fever. On rectal examination, forceful expulsion of stool was observed. A barium enema is performed; the findings are shown in the image below. Which of the following is the gold standard for the diagnosis of the above condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical scenario, along with barium imaging showing a narrow aganglionic segment, a transition zone, and proximal bowel dilation, is suggestive of Hirschsprung disease. The gold-standard diagnostic test for confirmation is a rectal suction biopsy.

Hirschsprung Disease

  • It is the most common congenital motility disorder and is characterised by the absence of ganglionic cells in the distal intestine.
  • Pathophysiology:
    • The absence of ganglionic cells (aganglionosis) in the distal segment of the intestine leads to tonic contraction and functional obstruction of the affected bowel segment.

Clinical Presentation:

  • Neonates: Delayed passage of meconium, constipation, obstruction
  • Later presentation: Chronic constipation, failure to thrive, enterocolitis

Classification:

  • Short Segment (75%): Limited to the segment distal to the splenic flexure.
  • Long Segment (20%): Extends proximal to the splenic flexure.
  • Total Colonic Aganglionosis (5%): The entire colon is affected. 

Diagnosis:

  • X-ray
    • Reveals bowel distension and air-fluid levels.
  • Barium enema
    • Classic findings are based on the presence of an abrupt narrow transition zone between the normal dilated proximal colon and a smaller-­ caliber obstructed distal aganglionic segment.
  • Anorectal manometry
    • Evaluates rectoanal inhibitory reflex
    • High sensitivity and specificity (>90%), but not considered the definitive test for young infants; technically difficult to perform to perform.
    • Absence of rectoanal inhibitory reflex suggests Hirschsprung disease.
  • Rectal suction biopsy: The Gold Standard Test for confirming Hirschsprung disease.
    • Procedure: A biopsy must be taken 2 cm above the dentate line and must include adequate
    • Staining:
      • Acetylcholinesterase: Identifies hypertrophied nerve bundles and the absence of ganglion cells.
      • Calretinin: Used as an alternative when acetylcholinesterase staining is inadequate.

Management:

  • Primarily Surgical: Resection of the aganglionic bowel and pull-through of normal bowel.
  • Medical Management: Stabilization and treatment of enterocolitis prior to surgery.
  • Surgical Approach: Trend toward less invasive techniques, including laparoscopic and single-stage procedures.

question_text: A baby presents with abdominal pain. On examination, a mass is palpable in the left lumbar region. A barium enema is performed, and the image shown below is obtained. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The presence of abdominal pain, a palpable abdominal mass, and the characteristic "claw sign" on barium enema is diagnostic of Intussusception.

  • Intussusception is the telescoping of a proximal bowel segment (intussusceptum) into a distal segment (intussuscipiens).
  • It is the most frequent cause of intestinal obstruction in infants between 5 months and 6 years.
  • Types: Ileocolic (most common), colocolic, and ileoileal.

Clinical Features:

  • Triad:
    • Severe intermittent abdominal pain
    • "Red currant jelly" stools (blood + mucus)
    • Palpable abdominal mass
  • Radiology:
    • Barium enema → Coiled spring sign / Claw sign
    • Ultrasound → Target sign / Doughnut sign

Management:

  • Spontaneous resolution occurs in some infants.
  • Hydrostatic reduction (saline/barium enema under fluoroscopy or USG guidance) is preferred.
  • Surgical reduction is indicated if:
    • There is shock, perforation, necrosis
    • Hydrostatic reduction fails
    • Recurrence is frequent

Explanation of Other Options:

Volvulus (Option B): Presents with abdominal pain, distension, and constipation. Imaging shows the coffee-bean sign or omega sign, not the claw sign.

Duodenal atresia (Option C): Presents in neonates with bilious vomiting soon after birth. Imaging shows the double bubble sign, not claw sign.

Intestinal obstruction (Option D): Presents with pain, distension, constipation. X-ray shows multiple air-fluid levels; barium studies are avoided in acute obstruction.

Key Takeaways:

  • Intussusception is the most common cause of intestinal obstruction in infants 5 months-6 years.
  • Classic triad: Abdominal pain + currant jelly stools + palpable mass.
  • Radiological signs: Claw sign (barium enema), Target sign (USG).

question_text: A new born baby presents with abdominal distention, vomiting & absence of bowel movement for 3 days. The barium study is shown below. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• Hirschsprung disease is aganglionosis of bowel. It presents in newborn with delayed passage of meconium, abdominal distention and absence of bowel movement on auscultation.
  • The barium enema has segments of dilated bowel followed by transition zone followed by constricted zone of aganglionic bowel. (typical in the above image)

Option A: Volvulus is rotation of bowel on its axis and presents acutely with bilious vomiting and abdominal distention. The barium study shows coffee bean sign.


Option B: Intussusception is bowel in bowel presenting with abdominal pain, vomiting and red-currant jelly stools. It is rare in neonates.

Option C: Celiac disease is not presented in neonates. It is seen after 6 months of age with failure to thrive, diarrhea/constipation and signs of vitamin deficiency due to malabsorption.

  • Difficulty level: GOOD TO KNOW
  • PYQ: NEET PG 2021

Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21st ed, pg no: 1962

question_text: All of the following are common complications in survivors of CDH, except?
explanation:
Hepatic fibrosis is not mentioned as a complication in CDH survivors.

Among other options:

  • Option B- Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is reported in >50% of children with CDH. GERD is more common in children whose diaphragmatic defect involves the esophageal hiatus.
  • Option C- Recurrent diaphragmatic hernia is reported in 5-20% in most series.
  • Option D- Intestinal obstruction is reported in up to 20% of children and may result from a midgut volvulus, adhesions, or a recurrent hernia that became incarcerated. Children with patch repairs are at highest risk.
  • Children with CDH typically have delayed growth in the 1st 2 yr of life.
  • Neurocognitive defects are common and may result from the disease or the interventions.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 345.1

question_text: A >48-hour neonate has still not passed meconium after birth. What is the investigation of choice?
explanation:
A water-soluble contrast enema is the investigation of choice in delayed passage of meconium since it is both diagnostic and therapeutic.

  • It can diagnose Hirschsprung disease, meconium ileus, atresias
  • Can also remove meconium plug in meconium plug syndrome and have therapeutic action.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 358

question_text: A 24-day old baby is presented to you with complaints of non-bilious projectile vomiting. Child is not gaining weight and cachexic on examination. Which of the following condition is highly likely?
explanation:
• Pyloric stenosis, most commonly seen in age 2weeks to 2 months with male preponderance.
  • Clinical features include Projectile, non-bilious, immediate post-prandial vomiting. Infant is hungry between the feeds.
  • Diagnosis is by ultrasound abdomen that shows thickened pylorus more than 4 mm and pyloric length more than 16mm. Target sign is suggestive of Pyloric stenosis.

  • Management is supportive initially with maintenance of electrolyte balance. Definitive treatment is Pyloromyotomy at the earliest.

Option B: Duodenal atresia has bilious vomiting.

Option C: Hirschsprung disease has a history of delayed passage of stool and gaseous abdominal distention.

Option D: Necrotizing enterocolitis will present earlier in 1-2 weeks with passage of bloody stool, feed intolerance, abdominal distention in background of prematurity or history of formula feeding.

question_text: A young child has recently moved house and has been complaining of abdominal pain, which parents have put down to the child been upset about the move. He is now developed with seizures and renal failure. You suspect a poisoning. What is the most likely cause?
explanation:
• Lead poisoning is more common in younger children due to the tendency for pica. In a child that has recently moved to an older home which may have lead paint this should be considered.
  • Gastrointestinal symptoms of lead poisoning include anorexia, abdominal pain, vomiting, and constipation, often occurring and recurring over a period of weeks.
  • Central nervous system symptoms are related to worsening cerebral edema and increased intracranial pressure. Headaches, change in mentation, lethargy, papilledema, seizures, and coma
  • At high levels (>100 μg/dL), renal tubular dysfunction is observed.

question_text: A child has been diagnosed as Idiopathic hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. Most common association will be?
explanation:
Hyperbilirubinemia is the most common clinical association of pyloric stenosis, also known as icteropyloric syndrome. Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia is more common than conjugated and usually resolves with surgical correction. It may be associated with a decreased level of glucuronyl transferase as seen in approximately 5% of affected infants; mutations in the bilirubin uridine diphosphate glucuronosyltransferase gene (UGT1A1) have also been implicated. If conjugated hyperbilirubinemia is a part of the presentation, other etiologies need to be investigated.

Other coexistent clinical diagnoses have been described, including eosinophilic gastroenteritis, hiatal hernia, peptic ulcer, congenital nephrotic syndrome, congenital heart disease, and congenital hypothyroidism.

Reference: Nelson 21st Ed/Chapter 355

question_text: A neonate presented with complaints of bilious vomiting with minimal abdominal distension. His X-ray abdomen was done and is shown below. What is the likely diagnosis?

question_text: A 3-day old neonate comes to you with not passed stool since birth. You suspect Hirschsprung disease. What is the gold standard diagnosis for the same?

  • Patients with aganglionosis demonstrate a large number of hypertrophied nerve bundles that stain positively for acetylcholinesterase with an absence of ganglion cells.

question_text: A neonate was diagnosed as a case of trachea-esophageal fistula with esophageal atresia and was posted for surgery next week. As an intern working in the department, you notice certain pre-operative monitoring and management being done. All of the following are allowed to be performed in a pre-operative case of TEF except?
explanation:
Pre-operative management principles in TEF with EA:

  • Ensure a patent airway
  • Pre-operative proximal pouch decompression to prevent aspiration of secretions
  • Use of antibiotics to prevent consequent pneumonia
  • Prone positioning minimizes movement of gastric secretions into a distal fistula
  • Esophageal suctioning minimizes aspiration from a blind pouch.
  • Endotracheal intubation with mechanical ventilation is to be avoided if possible because it can worsen distention of the stomach.

question_text: Which of the following is the most common variety of TEF?

question_text: A young child with congenital hydrocephalus was treated with a successful ventriculoperitoneal [VP] shunt. Four months' postsurgical repair, the child presented with fever, nuchal rigidity and irritability. You suspect meningitis. What is the next best step?

question_text: A healthy 6-month-old boy is found incidentally to have a duplicated collecting system with no dilation. He has been asymptomatic and has been growing well. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
explanation:
• About 25% of anomalies recognized prenatally are congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract. These disorders are varied and may be caused by malformations in the renal parenchyma, disruption in renal migration, or abnormalities in the developing collecting system.
  • Duplication of the collecting system is the most frequently seen congenital urinary tract anomaly and may occur as either complete duplication or partial duplication, which is more common.
  • Duplication is likely the result of ureteric bud duplication. Two distinct pelvicalyceal systems and either one ureter or two ureters that converge proximal to the bladder are present in children with partial duplication.
  • Children with complete duplication also have two distinct pelvicaliceal systems but with two ureters. One ureter typically inserts in the trigone area of the bladder, while the second may insert there or elsewhere in the genitourinary system. In girls, it may enter at the bladder neck, urethrovaginal septum, vagina, cervix, uterus, Gartner duct, or a urethral diverticulum. In boys, it may insert into the posterior urethra, prostatic utricle, seminal vesicle, ejaculatory duct, or vas deferens.
  • For patients, like this boy, who are asymptomatic and do not have dilatation or urinary tract infection, treatment is not indicated and the patient may be observed.

question_text: A child was diagnosed with TOF. He underwent a successful surgical complete repair. After how much time of surgery can the prophylaxis of infective endocarditis be stopped?

explanation:
According to the latest guidelines, lifelong IE prophylaxis is not needed in most patients. The prophylaxis is recommended in uncorrected disorders esp cyanotic diseases like TOF and then for 6 months after successful surgical repair. After that, IE prophylaxis can be safely stopped.

Extra-Edge: Conditions where antibiotic prophylaxis is needed against IE

  • Prosthetic cardiac valves
  • Past history of IE
  • Uncorrected cyanotic heart disease, palliative shunts and conduits
  • During 1st 6 months following complete surgical repair of CHDs
  • Repaired CHDs with residual defects at or adjacent to the site of repair
  • Cardiac transplantation recipients with cardiac valvulopathy

question_text: Which of the following is called Christmas disease?

Hemophilia B, also known as factor IX deficiency or Christmas disease, is the second most common type of hemophilia. question_text: You are teaching a group of medical students the differential diagnosis of edema in children. You take them to the bedside of a patient who has edema associated with hypoproteinemia secondary to proteinuria. Of the following, the feature you are MOST likely to observe in this patient is?
option_b: Edema that improves throughout the day
explanation:
Nephrotic syndrome usually presents with edema that is periorbital and more prominent early in the morning and with minimal systemic symptoms.

  • Edema is the most easily identified clinical feature associated with hypoproteinemia.
  • Impaired cardiac function leads to worsening peripheral edema as the day progresses and is associated with exertion and increased activity.
  • Pitting edema is not pathognomonic for any specific underlying etiology.

question_text: A 9-yr old boy passes hard infrequent stools for the last 2 years. Also, sometimes he soils his under wear. On examination, you found an anal fissure and his rectum is full of hard stools. All other examination is normal. Your most likely diagnosis is functional constipation. What is the most effective initial treatment?
option_a: Combination of Polyethylene glycol solution & enema
option_d: High fiber diet and follow up after 3 months
explanation:
The child has now presented with severe constipation with rectal impaction.

  • The 1st step in treatment of severe constipation is disimpaction which requires administration of Polyethylene glycol solution (movicol) (or mineral oil) ± rectal enema
  • As per OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 301, any child with constipation who has hard stools felt on per rectal examination or has abdominal fecoliths or retentive encopresis should undergo immediate disimpaction as the first step in management.

question_text: A 3 1/2 years old child presents to you with a 24-hour history of a limp and pain in her left thigh. There is no history of trauma. Her temperature is 38.9° C and her pulse is 150 beats/min. On examination the left thigh is swollen and held flexed and abducted. She holds it as still as possible and cries if it is moved. The upper leg is slightly red and is warmer to touch than the right leg. She has no other medical history and her mother has given some paracetamol, which had no effect on the pain. What is the likely cause of the clinical condition?
explanation:
• The child has very acute history and flexed and abducted position of the thigh at rest suggest septic arthritis. Ultrasound (and diagnostic aspiration), blood tests for culture and tests for inflammatory markers should be performed and intravenous antibiotics started.
  • Septic arthritis, also known as infectious arthritis, is a joint infection typically caused by bacteria (often Staphylococcus aureus) but can also be caused by viruses or fungi.
  • The infection leads to inflammation within the joint, causing symptoms like sudden, severe joint pain, swelling, warmth, redness, and restricted movement, often accompanied by fever. It most commonly affects large joints like the knee, hip, shoulder, or elbow.

Option B: Reactive arthritis has no fever and usually has a history of infective illness in recent past.

Option C: There is no history of trauma for diagnosing fracture.

Option D: JIA has chronic illness more than 6 weeks of fever and pain.

KEY TAKEAWAYS: Septic arthritis, also known as infectious arthritis is a joint infection typically caused by bacteria (often Staphylococcus aureus), causing symptoms like sudden, severe joint pain, swelling, warmth, redness, and restricted movement, often accompanied by fever.

question_text: What is the amount of milk given to a term baby in the first 24 hours after delivery?
explanation:
Explanation:

On the first day of life, a term newborn usually receives about 60 ml of milk per kilogram of body weight.

  • This volume is tailored to match the limited stomach capacity of the infant and to support a gradual adaptation of the gastrointestinal system, allowing feeding tolerance to improve as digestion matures.

question_text: An infant presented with progressive jaundice and pale coloured stools. Liver biopsy revealed bile plugs and bile ductular proliferation. Likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The clinical picture is suggestive of neonatal cholestasis. The most common cause of neonatal cholestasis is Extra hepatic biliary atresia (EHBA).

  • Biliary atresia is characterized by bile ductular proliferation, the presence of bile plugs, and portal or perilobular edema and fibrosis, with the basic hepatic lobular architecture intact.
  • In neonatal hepatitis, there is severe, diffuse hepatocellular disease, with distortion of lobular architecture, marked infiltration with inflammatory cells, and focal hepatocellular necrosis; the bile ductules show little alteration.
  • Giant cell transformation is found in infants with either condition and has no diagnostic specificity.

question_text: Identify the enzyme deficient in Von-Gierke Disease?
explanation:
Glucose-6-Phosphatase deficiency produces GSD-1, also called as Von-Gierke's Disease. Deficiency of the enzyme leads to inadequate hepatic conversion of glucose-6-phosphate to glucose through normal glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, resulting in fasting hypoglycemia and accumulation of normal structure glycogen in the liver.

question_text: A 12-year-old boy seen in your clinic has a history of Wilson disease. Which of the following tissues may accumulate excessive copper if the disease is left inadequately treated?
explanation:
Wilson disease is a metal metabolism disorder characterized by excessive copper deposition in the liver, brain, kidneys, and eyes.

  • Features include hepatic failure or cirrhosis, hemolytic anemia, KF rings in the eyes, sunflower cataracts, neuropsychiatric manifestations and parkinsonism-like features
  • In CNS, the excess copper gets deposited into basal ganglia.
  • Patients with Wilson disease may suffer from arthralgias and osteoarthritis but do not typically develop copper deposition in the bones, pancreas, ovaries, or salivary glands.
  • Also note that pancreas and ovaries show deposition with iron in hemochromatosis, but these are not much affected by copper deposits in Wilson Disease.
  • Infants with neonatal iron storage disease typically have excessive iron deposition in the liver, heart, pancreas, and salivary glands.

Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1st SA ed., pg. 1939

question_text: Which of the following statements about vitamin A toxicity is false?
option_b: It can cause fissures at the corner of the mouth, pruritis and alopecia
option_c: An infant with preference for carrots and butternut squash can develop toxicity
option_d: Symptoms subsides with withdrawal of source
explanation:
• Signs of subacute or chronic toxicity can include
    • Headache, vomiting, anorexia
    • dry, itchy desquamating skin
    • fissuring at the corners of the mouth
    • alopecia and/ or coarsening of the hair
    • swelling of the bones
    • enlargement of the liver and spleen
    • diplopia, increased intracranial pressure, irritability, stupor
    • desquamation of the palms and the soles of the feet.
  • Radiographs may show hyperostosis affecting several long bones, especially in the middle of the shafts.
  • Symptoms may subside rapidly on withdrawal of the vitamin, but the rate of improvement depends on the amount of vitamin A that has built up in tissues.
  • In young children, toxicity is associated with vomiting and bulging fontanels.
  • Acute hypervitaminosis A, such as after consumption of a single large (30-60 mg dose) of vitamin A may include nausea, vomiting, and drowsiness; less-common symptoms include diplopia, papilledema, cranial nerve palsies, and other symptoms suggesting pseudotumor cerebri.
  • A syndrome of severe congenital malformations may occur in infants of mothers who have consumed therapeutic doses (0.5-1.5 mg/kg) of oral 13-cis-retinoic acid (e.g., Accutane), generally taken for the treatment of acne or cancer, during the 1st trimester of pregnancy.
  • Excessive intake of carotenoids is not associated with toxicity but can cause yellow coloration of the skin that disappears when intake is reduced; this disorder (carotenemia) is especially likely to occur in children with liver disease, diabetes mellitus, or hypothyroidism and in those who do not have enzymes that metabolize carotenoids.

question_text: A 19-year-old mother notices that her 3-week-old neonate has increasing jaundice. On physical examination, the infant now exhibits generalized jaundice, hepatomegaly, and acholic stool. Laboratory studies show total serum bilirubin of 10.1 mg/dL (0.1-1.0 mg/dL), direct bilirubin of 10 mg/dL (0.0-0.3 mg/dL), AST of 123 U/L (8-20 U/L), ALT of 140 U/L (8-20 U/L), glucose of 77 mg/dL (70-110mg/dL), and creatinine of 0.4 mg/dL (0.6-1.2 mg/dL). USG revealed non-visualization of the gall bladder. The infant developed progressively worsening jaundice and dies of liver failure at 9 months of age. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
option_c: Genetic defect in secretion of bile into canaliculi
explanation:
Severe persistent conjugated hyperbilirubinemia in neonate lasting >3 weeks is caused by biliary obstruction.

question_text: A 14-month-old boy whose parents presents to your office for a health supervision visit. The boy is at the third percentile for weight and for height. He is pale and his liver is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin. His parents bring with them laboratory results. explanation:
The absence of hemoglobin A (α2 ß2) on hemoglobin electrophoresis with only hemoglobin A2 (α2 δ2) and F (α2 γ2) present is diagnostic of ß-thalassemia major.

  • Thalassemia major is managed with chronic red blood cell transfusions, and the resultant iron overload is the most common complication of its therapy.
  • Iron overload causes endocrinopathies, hepatic dysfunction, and cardiomyopathies.
  • Complications of iron overload and death and can be prevented through aggressive chelation.

question_text: A 4-year-old child is presented with abdominal lump. Bone scan is being done to rule out which of the following condition?
explanation:
Among the given options, Neuroblastoma frequently produces bony metastasis.

  • Bony metastases in Neuroblastoma often occurs to orbital bones, producing proptosis and/or Raccoon Eyes/Panda Eyes. Vertebral spread is also reported.
  • As per Nelson 21st Edition, Metastatic spread in Neuroblastoma, which is more common in children >1 yr old at diagnosis, occurs through local invasion or distant hematogenous or lymphatic routes.
  • The most common sites of metastasis overall in Neuroblastoma are the regional or distant lymph nodes, long bones and skull, bone marrow, liver, and skin.
  • Kindly note that bone scan is needed in Neuroblastoma as well as Clear cell sarcoma variant of Wilms tumour in children.

question_text: "I am a pediatric malignancy. I often afflict young children & can produce lung, lymph node and liver metastases. FNAC & Blind Biopsy is not recommended in me. I respond well to chemotherapy with Vincristine, Actinomycin-D and Doxorubicin. Who am I?"
explanation:
Clues to the diagnosis of Wilms Tumour here.

  • Clue 1- Pediatric malignancy in young children. Wilms tumour occurs in children aged 2-3 years.
  • Clue 2- Metastases to lung, lymph nodes and liver is seen in Wilms tumour
  • Clue 3- Blind biopsy is avoided since it can upstage the disease, as per Nelson 21st Imaging studies include plain abdominal radiography, abdominal ultrasonography (US), and CT of the abdomen to define the intrarenal origin of the mass and differentiate it from adrenal masses (e.g., neuroblastoma) and other masses in the abdomen
  • Clue 4- Responds to chemotherapy with Vincristine, Actinomycin-D and Doxorubicin- Seen in Wilms Tumour. After radical nephrectomy, most patients receive chemotherapy using the said agents.

question_text: A 2-month-old, is evaluated for jaundice and failure to thrive. He undergoes a percutaneous liver biopsy that shows a paucity of bile ducts. Which of the following would not be considered an appropriate investigation in the course of disease evaluation?
explanation:
• The finding of bile duct paucity on liver biopsy, in the setting of poor growth, is characteristic of Alagille syndrome, a multisystem, inherited disorder with highly variable clinical features. A paucity of bile ducts is considered the most important and constant feature of this disease.

    • Abnormal faces like broad forehead, wide eyes, long nose, underdeveloped jaw

    • Echocardiogram for cardiac defects
    • AP and lateral chest radiographs for butterfly vertebrae
    • Ophthalmologic examination for anterior chamber involvement
    • Renal ultrasound and renal function testing to identify renal complications

question_text: A 10-year-old child with severe acute liver failure is being cared for in the intensive care unit. Which of the following laboratory findings best reflects worsening liver function in this patient?
explanation:
• Rising total bilirubin in the setting of acute liver failure with loss of hepatic function is an ominous sign that is likely multifactorial in nature.

Aminotransferases levels may remain stable or trend downward even as bilirubin rises as liver failure and hepatocellular dealt progress.So, up trending AST/ALT do not necessarily reflect loss of hepatic function.

question_text: Dubin Johnson syndrome and Rotor Syndrome can be distinguished on the basis of all of the following except?

question_text: A preterm infant born at 28 weeks develops signs of respiratory distress syndrome. Which statement accurately describes the changes in surface tension and lung compliance in this condition?
option_c: Both surface tension and compliance decreased
option_d: Both surface tension and compliance increased
explanation:
Explanation:

Surface tension increased and compliance decreased; this statement is accurate regarding surface tension and compliance in a preterm baby with respiratory distress syndrome (RDS).

Elastic tissue recoil and surface tension are the two opposing forces to lung compliance, and are not opposing forces to each other.

Two primary factors influence lung compliance:

  • Elastic forces of the lung tissue:
    • These forces are primarily determined by the presence of elastin and collagen fibres within the lung parenchyma (the functional tissue of the lungs).
    • In a deflated lung, these fibres are contracted and kinked. As the lung expands during inspiration, these fibres stretch and unkink, generating an elastic force that opposes further expansion.
  • Surface tension:
    • A thin layer of fluid lines the inside of the alveoli. At the air-fluid interface within the alveoli, surface tension arises from the stronger attraction between water molecules compared to the attraction between water molecules and air molecules.
    • This surface tension creates an inward pull, attempting to minimise the surface area of the fluid lining the alveoli. Consequently, this inward pull contributes to the elastic recoil of the lungs, making them tend to collapse.

Reference: Pulmonary Compliance - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf

question_text: A preterm neonate develops respiratory distress soon after birth. The pediatrician suspects neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) due to inadequate surfactant secretion. Which type of pulmonary cell is primarily responsible for surfactant production in the lungs?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Type 2 pneumocytes are cuboidal cells located in the alveoli.
  • They synthesize and secrete pulmonary surfactant, composed mainly of dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine (DPPC), phospholipids, and surfactant proteins (SP-A, SP-B, SP-C, SP-D).
  • Surfactant reduces alveolar surface tension, prevents alveolar collapse (atelectasis), and enhances lung compliance.
  • Surfactant secretion begins around 20-24 weeks gestation and becomes adequate after 34-36 weeks, which explains why preterm neonates are at high risk of RDS.

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

Type 1 pneumocyte (Option A): Flat squamous cells covering ~95% of alveolar surface; specialized for gas exchange, not surfactant secretion.

Alveolar macrophage (Option B): Immune phagocytic cells that clear pathogens and debris; no role in surfactant production.

Dust cells (Option C): Another name for alveolar macrophages → immune defense role only, not surfactant secretion.

Key Takeaway points:

Clinical Correlation:

  • Neonatal RDS: Caused by surfactant deficiency → alveolar collapse, hypoxemia, "ground-glass" appearance on CXR. Treated with exogenous surfactant & maternal steroids (Betamethasone) if preterm delivery anticipated.
  • ARDS (Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome): Secondary surfactant dysfunction due to alveolar damage (sepsis, trauma, aspiration, etc.).

question_text: Which of the following cells are deficient is a premature infant with RDS?
explanation:
• Hyaline membrane disease
  • Also called as respiratory distress syndrome (RDS)
  • Major cause of this disease is Deficiency of pulmonary surfactant produced by type II alveolar cells
  • Commonly seen in.

    • Maternal diabetes (Gestational diabetes mellitus)

Surfactant lipids

Major surfactant lipids is:

question_text: In preterm baby with respiratory distress syndrome which of the following lipid would be deficient?

question_text: A 5-month-old boy is admitted to the hospital for evaluation because of repeated episodes of sleep apnea. During a ventilatory response test, his ventilation did not increase when PaCO2 was increased, but decreased during hyperoxia. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this infant's apnea?
explanation:
The central chemoreceptors respond to changes in [H+] in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which are brought about by changes in arterial PCO2. The failure of CO2 to increase ventilation indicates that the central chemoreceptors are not functioning properly.

The peripheral chemoreceptors are stimulated by hypoxia, hypercapnia, and acidemia, and thus are functioning appropriately because ventilation decreased when PO2 was increased (hyperoxia).

Obstructive sleep apnea is caused by upper airway obstruction due to hypotonic pharyngeal or genioglossus muscles or too much fat around the pharynx, but not because of obstruction of the tracheobronchial tree by bronchospasm.

Diaphragmatic fatigue can cause hypoventilation, but is not associated with apneic episodes, perhaps because of the increased contribution of the accessory muscles of respiration.

The reflex effect of stimulation of the irritant receptors by mechanical or chemical irritation of the airways is bronchoconstriction and cough.

Reference: Ganong, pp 672-678, 693-694. Levitzky, pp 196-198, 201-210.

question_text: A preterm infant admitted to the NICU shows reticulo-granular opacities on X-ray with white out appearance. The child had chest retractions, tachypnea, and nasal flaring. A diagnosis of Hyaline membrane disease was made. The following phospholipid is used as a test for diagnosis of fetal lung maturity.
explanation:
The given clinical scenario is highly suggestive of Hyaline membrane disease or Respiratory distress syndrome which is due to defective production of surfactant.

The active component of surfactant is phosphatidylcholine(lecithin)

  • Choline + PA→ phosphatidylcholine (PC) (lecithin)
  • Ethanolamine + PA→ phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) (cephalin)
    • It is a component of cell membrane and plays a role in blood coagulation
  • Serine + PA → phosphatidylserine (PS) (option c)
    • It plays a role in programmed cell death
  • Inositol + PA → phosphatidylinositol (PI)(option d)
    • It plays a role as a secondary messenger

Reference: Harper's illustrated biochemistry 32nd edition and LIPPINCOTT illustrated reviews 6th edition biochemistry page 204-6.

question_text: A newborn infant has severe respiratory distress and is noted to have pseudoepicanthus, flattened ears and nose, and bilateral club feet. There is no family history of renal failure. Abdominal ultrasonography reveals bilaterally enlarged echogenic kidneys with poor corticomedullary differentiation; there are no cysts or hydronephrosis. Of the following, the MOST likely cause of this neonate's condition is-
explanation:
• Potter syndrome/Potter sequence/oligohydramnios sequence is the characteristic phenotypic features in the neonate caused by oligohydramnios.
  • The characteristic features include pulmonary hypoplasia (respiratory distress in the newborn), abnormal facial appearance (pseudoepicanthus, flattened ears and nose, recessed chin), and limb abnormalities (club feet and hip dislocation).

  • Potter syndrome type 1 occurs in association with ARPKD.
  • On ultrasonography, patients with ARPKD have enlarged echogenic kidneys without obvious renal cysts whereas ADPKD is associated with macrocysts. (Option A)

KEY TAKEAWAYS: Potter syndrome/Potter sequence/oligohydramnios sequence is the characteristic phenotypic features in the neonate caused by oligohydramnios

  • Difficulty level: MAY KNOW

Reference: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics, 1st SA Edition, Page Number-1969.

question_text: A 13-year-old adolescent presents for follow-up 3 months after a diagnosis of acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis. Laboratory testing at this visit reveals microscopic hematuria and a persistently low C3. Based on these findings, what diagnosis should you consider at this time?
explanation:
• This patient was diagnosed with acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (APSGN) likely based on clinical presentation, because biopsy is no longer routine for diagnosis. However, at this visit, his C3 remains low. In APSGN, it is expected that the C3 levels will normalize in 2 to 3 months. Because this patient continues to have depressed C3, he was likely misdiagnosed initially. Persistent hypocomplementemia is suggestive of membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis.

Option C: Recurrent painless gross hematuria, frequently associated with an upper respiratory tract infection, is typical of IgA nephropathy. These patients often develop chronic renal disease over decades.

Option B: The classic triad associated with IgA vasculitis (HSP) is purpuric rash, arthritis, and abdominal pain.

  • Difficulty level: GOOD TO KNOW
  • PYQ: FMGE JAN 2023; DEC 2021

question_text: A full-term baby with weight 3.5kg born to a primi mother with minimal antenatal care develops respiratory distress within 1 hour of birth. Child cried immediately after birth. On examination the baby looks an appropriate size for his gestational age, he is not dysmorphic. His lips and tongue appear slightly blue. He is making an intermittent grunting expiratory sound, and his respiratory rate is 70 breaths/min. Air entry is reduced on the left side of his chest, with no increase in resonance on percussion. CVS examination WNL(with in normal limit). His abdomen appears slightly concave. His chest radiograph is shown. Most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• The child in the question has all the findings suggestive of congenital diaphragmatic hernia.
  • The X ray is suggestive of air filled loops in chest, i.e., intestinal loops. There is mediastinal shift to the right. As bowels loops are shifted in chest, abdomen is scaphoid. Due to compression of the intestines in the lung, lungs are immature and hence develops respiratory distress.
  • Immediate surgical exploration and reduction of loops into the abdomen is the definitive management.
  • The child had developed distress immediately after birth, with no history of illness in mother, so sepsis or pneumonia is less likely. (option c)
  • Transient tachypnea of newborn is the most common cause of respiratory distress in full term babies. But, the X ray findings and clinical findings are not matching. (option a)
  • There are no risk factors for pneumothorax, as child had cried spontaneously. (option b) Also, scaphoid abdomen is not seen in pneumothorax. X ray does not show any signs of pneumothorax.

  • Difficulty level: MUST KNOW

question_text: A 14-year old boy develops severe breathlessness during a game of football. On examination, there is absent breath sounds on the right, hyper-resonance on percussion and the trachea is deviated to the left. RR 28, O2 saturation 90%, HR 110, BP 110/90, Temp 36.5°C. How would you immediately manage this patient?
option_b: Insertion of a large bore cannula in the 2nd intercostal space, mid clavicular line on the right.
option_d: Urgent chest x-ray to confirm diagnosis
explanation:
• This is a primary spontaneous tension pneumothorax in a teenager. It is an emergency and can lead to cardiac arrest.
  • It needs immediate management of a large bore cannula inserted in the 2nd ICS mid-clavicular line, followed by the insertion of a chest drain in the right axilla (5th Intercostal space, mid axillary line), then with high flow oxygen 15L via a non-rebreathe mask, which will then be titrated.
  • Getting an X-ray to prove your diagnosis is not appropriate as your patient will deteriorate rapidly.
