question_text: After encouraging coughing, what is the next step in the management of a choking infant?
explanation:
CHOKING IN INFANTS:

  • In this age group a combination of back blows and chest thrusts is the recommended practice. To begin with five back blows are performed, checking after each one to see if the foreign body has been expelled.
  • Place infant on forearm- face down with head pointing towards the ground. With the hand of the rescuer supporting the jaw (keeping it open). With the free hand five back blows are given.
  • If this does not improve the situation the infant is turned over(still head down) and placed along the rescuer's arm. Then 5 chest thrusts are performed. Two fingers are placed at the lower edge of the sternum (below nipple line). If the infant is too large then they can be placed on the lap of the rescuer.

CHOKING IN CHILDREN:

  • If the child is coughing this should be encouraged. Back blows are the first step with the child supported in a leaning forward position. This should be attempted as 5 back blows with hand placement between shoulder blades, checking after each blow to see if the foreign body has been expelled.
  • If this fails the Heimlich manoeuvre should be performed. This is repeated 5 times unless the object is expelled.
  • Place the child on a flat surface (supine). Assess airway for evidence of visible object causing obstruction. Open the airway and given 5 inflation breaths. Then continue the BLS algorithm as per the Basic Life Support
  • Each time breaths are attempted look in the mouth for evidence of foreign body and remove it if visible. If effective breathing commences, place in the recovery position and monitor.

KEY TAKEAWAYS:

question_text: You are formulating a differential diagnosis for a newborn infant with respiratory distress. Which of the following is MOST closely associated with the development of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (hyaline membrane disease)?
explanation:
• Prematurity is the strongest predisposing factor to surfactant deficiency disease or respiratory distress syndrome (RDS).
  • While low birth weight infants are also at risk, the risk is more related to the gestational age of the infant.
  • Maternal diabetes does predispose newborns to RDS by causing delayed surfactant release compared to infants of comparable gestational age, but is not as strong of a risk as prematurity itself.
  • Cesarean delivery predisposes more to a condition known as transient tachypnea of the newborn, related to excessive fluid retention within the lungs.
  • Meconium in the amniotic fluid may cause respiratory disease if aspirated into the infant's lungs but the pathophysiology of the disease differs from RDS.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 157; Avery's diseases of the newborn, 1st SA ed., pg. 653

question_text: Retinopathy of prematurity is commonly predisposed by?
explanation:
As per Nelson 21st Ed, the most important factor involved in retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) is low gestational age.

  • Nelson says The risk factors associated with ROP are not fully known, but prematurity and the associated retinal immaturity at birth represent the major factors.
  • Oxygenation, respiratory distress, apnea, bradycardia, heart disease, infection, hypercarbia, acidosis, anemia, and the need for transfusion are thought by some to be contributory factors.
  • Generally, the lower the gestational age, the lower the birthweight, and the sicker the infant, the greater the risk for ROP.
  • Hyperoxia, co-morbidities and mechanical ventilation are other co-factors, but less important than prematurity alone.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 648

question_text: A newborn presented with chest retractions, dyspnea, and lethargy. The pediatrician diagnosed the baby with respiratory distress syndrome. This occurs due to a deficiency of:
explanation:
Explanation:

Lecithin (phosphatidylcholine) is the key surfactant component deficient in neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.

  • Neonatal Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS), also known as Hyaline Membrane Disease (HMD), is a condition most commonly seen in premature infants born before 34-35 weeks gestation due to a deficiency of pulmonary surfactant.
  • Surfactant is synthesized by type II pneumocytes and reduces surface tension in the alveoli, preventing their collapse during expiration.
  • The primary phospholipid component of surfactant is phosphatidylcholine, commonly known as lecithin, especially in its active form-dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC).
  • Surfactant production starts around 20 weeks of gestation but becomes functionally adequate only after 34-35 weeks.
  • In premature infants, low levels of lecithin lead to alveolar collapse, impaired gas exchange, tissue hypoxia, and formation of a proteinaceous hyaline membrane lining the alveoli.
  • Clinical presentation includes:
    • Tachypnea
    • Chest wall retractions
    • Grunting respiration
    • Cyanosis
    • Decreased air entry
  • Classic X-ray features:
    • Ground-glass opacities due to alveolar atelectasis
    • Air bronchograms
    • Reticulogranular pattern
  • Management involves:
    • NICU admission
    • Supportive care (e.g., IV fluids, oxygen)
    • Surfactant replacement therapy if needed
    • Respiratory support (CPAP or mechanical ventilation)

Explanation of other options:

Dipalmitoyl inositol (Option A): A phospholipid involved in cellular signaling, not a surfactant component, and not relevant to RDS pathophysiology.

Sphingomyelin (Option C): Present in cell membranes and used in the L/S ratio to assess lung maturity, but it does not directly contribute to surfactant function or alveolar stability.

Dipalmitoylphosphatidylethanolamine (Option D): Although it is a membrane phospholipid, it lacks the surface tension-reducing ability of dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (lecithin), which is essential for preventing alveolar collapse.

question_text: The newborn infant of a 28-year-old primigravida has severe respiratory distress due to pulmonary hypoplasia and is noted to have pseudo epicanthus, flattened ears and nose, and bilateral club feet. There is no family history of renal failure. Abdominal ultrasonography reveals bilaterally enlarged echogenic kidneys with poor corticomedullary differentiation; there are no cysts or hydronephrosis. The liver, spleen, pancreas, and gallbladder are reported to be normal. Of the following, the MOST likely cause of this neonate's condition is-
explanation:
The child has pulmonary hypoplasia producing severe respiratory distress, abnormal facies & bilateral clubfeet, with structural renal anomalies. All this suggests a diagnosis of Potter's Syndrome.

  • Potter syndrome/Potter sequence/oligohydramnios sequence is the characteristic phenotypic feature in the neonate caused by oligohydramnios.
  • The characteristic features include pulmonary hypoplasia (respiratory distress in the newborn), facial appearance (pseudo epicanthus, flattened ears and nose, recessed chin), and limb abnormalities (club feet and hip dislocation).
  • Types of Potter syndrome
    • Type I: Associated with ARPKD
    • Type II: Associated with renal agenesis or hereditary renal dysplasia
    • Type III: Associated with ADPKD
    • Type IV: Associated with obstructive uropathy and hydronephrosis
  • Potter syndrome type 1 occurs in association with ARPKD.
  • On ultrasonography, patients with ARPKD have enlarged echogenic kidneys without obvious renal cysts whereas ADPKD is associated with macrocysts.

Reference: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics, 1st South Asian Edition, Page Number-1969.

question_text: An expectant mother comes for a routine visit. She states that she was told that her unborn child may have posterior urethral valves. Which of the following statements is true about the condition?
option_a: It occurs with equal frequency in males and females
option_b: The unborn child will need a CT scan immediately after birth
option_c: No postnatal evaluation or follow-up is required if the neonate has a normal respiratory function at birth
option_d: The risk of end-stage renal disease or chronic renal insufficiency is relatively high, needing follow-up
explanation:
Let us evaluate each option

  • Option A is False. Posterior urethral valves occur in boys, not girls.
  • Option B is False. Antenatally diagnosed PUV needs post-natal USG and MCU, not CT Scan for diagnosis.
  • Option C is False. Postnatal evaluation and follow-up is needed in PUV irrespective of respiratory functions.
  • Option D is True. Nelson 21st Edition Says- Of those who survive the neonatal period, approximately 30% eventually require kidney transplantation and 15% have renal insufficiency. In some series, kidney transplantation in children with PUVs has a lower success rate than does transplantation in children with normal bladders, presumably because of the adverse influence of altered bladder function on graft function and survival.
  • The risk of end-stage renal disease or chronic renal insufficiency is 25% to 30%.
  • Postnatal evaluation includes VCUG or postnatal USG.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 555; Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1st SA ed., pg. 2545

question_text: A male child presents with arthralgia and abdominal pain. On examination, there is palpable purpura over the lower limbs. The child has a preceding history of an upper respiratory tract infection. Which of the following is the treatment of choice for this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The constellation of arthralgia, abdominal pain, palpable purpura on lower limbs, and a prior upper respiratory tract infection is typical of Henoch-Schonlein Purpura (HSP). In moderate to severe disease, glucocorticoids are the treatment of choice as they reduce inflammation and provide symptomatic relief.

  • Etiology
    • Exact cause unknown.
    • Immune-mediated small vessel vasculitis, often post upper respiratory tract infection.
    • Associated with genetic predisposition (HLA-B34, DRB1).
    • More common in boys.
  • Pathophysiology
    • IgA-mediated immune complex deposition in small vessels.
    • Inflammation of skin, joints, kidneys, and intestines.
    • Leakage of blood and plasma into tissues.
  • Clinical Features
    • Palpable purpura: Purplish-red rash, mainly on buttocks and legs.
    • Joint involvement: Swelling and pain in knees/ankles.
    • Abdominal pain: May include vomiting, diarrhea, GI bleeding, or intussusception.
    • Renal involvement: May present as hematuria, proteinuria, or chronic renal failure.
  • Diagnosis
    • Clinical criteria: Purpura plus at least one of:
      • Diffuse abdominal pain
      • Arthritis/arthralgia
      • Biopsy showing IgA deposition
      • Renal involvement
    • Laboratory: ESR/CRP elevated; platelet counts normal.
  • Complications
    • Intussusception
    • Chronic renal disease (long-term damage).
    • Rare: Neurological manifestations (headaches, seizures).
  • Treatment
    • Mild cases: Rest, hydration, analgesics.
    • Moderate-Severe cases: Glucocorticoids (e.g., prednisone).
    • Refractory cases: Immunosuppressive agents may be considered.
  • Prognosis
    • Most recover completely.
    • Prognosis depends on extent of renal involvement.

Explanation of Other Options:

Azathioprine (Option A): Immunosuppressant mainly used in autoimmune disorders like SLE. Reserved for severe renal involvement in HSP, not first-line.

Methotrexate (Option B): Commonly used in rheumatoid arthritis and autoimmune diseases but not indicated for HSP.

Cyclosporine (Option C): Used in transplant immunosuppression and some nephrotic syndromes. Not a routine first-line therapy for HSP.

question_text: A neonate born at 32 weeks develops RR of 70/min and expiratory grunting, soon after birth. The next step will be?
explanation:
Any preterm neonate <34 weeks presenting with respiratory distress soon after birth, is likely having RDS.

  • CPAP is usually sufficient in mild to moderate RDS and is mostly the initial therapy to be started in a patient with RDS.
  • CPAP is often given via nostrils and the pressures range from 5-7 cm H2O
  • CPAP minimizes lung injury, improves oxygenation and reduces progressive alveolar collapse
  • If distress worsens or in extreme preterm neonates, Surfactant Replacement Therapy (SRT) should be administered and is generally considered the best therapy.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 157; Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 122

question_text: A preterm neonate at 28 weeks developed severe HMD, for which nasal CPAP followed by surfactant was administered using MIST technique. However, due to persistent apneic episodes and pH on ABG below 7.20, the child was intubated and started on mechanical ventilation. Which among the following is the acceptable PaO2 levels to be targeted during mechanical ventilation in this child, ensuring adequate oxygenation and minimal free radical injury?
explanation:
The goal of mechanical ventilation in HMD is to improve oxygenation and ventilation without causing pulmonary injury or oxygen toxicity. According to Nelson 21st Ed, acceptable ranges of ABG values vary significantly among institutions but generally recommended target values are as follows:

  • PaO2 50-70 mm Hg
  • PaCO2 45-65 mm Hg (and higher after the 1st few days when risk of IVH is less)
  • pH 7.20-7.35

Also note that ventilation is done in HMD, rates are kept high, ≥ 60/min while the tidal volume is kept low, about 4-6 ml/kg.

Extra Edge Point- The SpO2 to be targeted in preterm neonates receiving oxygen or ventilation is 91-95% as per most references.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 122; AIIMS Protocols In Neonatology 3rd Edition, Volume 1

question_text:
Which are components of Downe's score?
1.Respiratory rate
2.Feeding
3.Grunting
4.Cyanosis
explanation:
Explanation:

Downe's Score is used to assess and quantify respiratory distress in term neonates. It evaluates parameters such as respiratory rate, grunting, and cyanosis. The scoring is typically performed every 30 minutes and documented on a chart to monitor the severity and progression of respiratory distress.

Downe's Score assesses respiratory distress in term neonates:

Interpretation:

  • Maximum score: 10
  • Severe distress: ≥7
  • Frequency: Assess every 30 minutes

Feeding is NOT a component of Downe's score. (Option A,C and D ruled out)

Key Takeaways:

question_text: A neonate with respiratory distress is being monitored using the Silverman Anderson scoring method. The child has a respiratory rate of 60/min, there is no cyanosis on 30% oxygen, some lag in inspiration on upper chest, there are minimal retractions in lower chest that are just visible, there are no xiphoid retractions or nasal flaring and intermittent grunting can be heard with stethoscope. What is the total score?
explanation:
Silverman Anderson Score


  • Silverman Anderson Score does not include assessment of skin colour, breath sounds or tachypnea but correlates well with mortality.
  • Here, the total score in this question is 3.

Reference: AIIMS Neonatal Protocols 3rd Edition Volume 1, Pages 160-162

question_text: What is the amount of oxygen given to a term infant with respiratory distress during resuscitation?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The amount of oxygen administered to a term infant with respiratory distress during resuscitation is guided by the severity of distress and the infant's oxygen saturation levels.
  • According to the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), resuscitation should begin with 21%-30% oxygen in both term and late preterm infants (≥35 weeks), with subsequent adjustments made based on oxygen saturation monitoring.
  • The target is to maintain SpO2 between 90%-95%.

Explanation of Other Options:

50% (Option B), 70% (Option C), and 100% (Option D): These higher oxygen concentrations are not recommended as initial oxygen therapy during resuscitation of term infants because:

  • Higher oxygen concentrations can lead to oxidative stress.
  • They may cause tissue damage.
  • Current evidence supports starting with room air (21% oxygen) and titrating up as needed.

question_text: A three-year-old boy presents to the clinic with poor head control and increased difficulty walking and climbing stairs for the past few months. Upon further investigation, the child's maternal uncle had similar symptoms at the same age and passed away in his late twenties. On physical exam, you notice his calf muscles are enlarged. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• Duchenne muscular dystrophy is a X-linked recessive disorder caused by a mutation in the dystrophin gene.
  • Children are not usually symptomatic at birth and usually achieve their baby milestones. Poor head control may be the first sign in infancy. Most boys are unable to walk by 12 years of age.
  • Patients often present with difficulty running and climbing stairs. Due to proximal muscle weakness, these patients need to use their hands to push from the floor and then their thighs in order to stand (Gower’s sign).
  • Creatinine kinase (CK) levels are elevated from birth onwards and are elevated even before symptoms are apparent.
  • Individuals also have calf enlargement or pseudohypertrophy since it is fat deposition and proliferation of collagen that enlarges the calf.
  • They also have elevated CK levels, calf hypertrophy, and are more prone to cardiac and respiratory failure later in life.
  • Diagnosis is made by muscle biopsy.

Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1st SA edition, pg. 2967

question_text: In children with GBS, all are true EXCEPT:
option_b: Plasmapheresis is not preferred in refractory cases
option_d: Albuminocytological dissociation in CSF is characteristic
explanation:
Explanation:

Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) is an acute immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy characterized by rapidly progressive, symmetrical, ascending flaccid paralysis, often preceded by an infection.

In children, the diagnosis of GBS is guided by the Brighton Criteria, summarized by the mnemonic FAME:

Areflexia of the affected limbs is a mandatory diagnostic criterion, as weakness without areflexia is uncommon in classical presentations.

Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination typically shows albuminocytologic dissociation, defined as elevated protein (100-1000 mg/dL) with a normal white blood cell count, which may be normal if sampled within the first 48 hours but usually peaks by 7 days.

Management of GBS in children involves intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) as the first-line therapy, which is highly effective in hastening recovery. Plasmapheresis is equally effective and is indicated in patients who are refractory to initial therapy. (Option C ruled out)

Supportive care, including frequent monitoring of vital capacity and negative inspiratory force, is crucial to identify impending respiratory failure, which occurs in approximately 30% of pediatric cases.

Aggressive rehabilitation is essential for functional recovery.

Investigations in GBS

question_text: A 7-year-old boy with a history of renal dysplasia and chronic kidney disease is seen for a health supervision visit. He has a history of increased thirst and polyuria. His current medications include sodium bicarbonate, ferrous sulfate, calcium carbonate, and calcitriol. His weight is at the fifth percentile, and his height is at the third percentile. He has a heart rate of 89 beats/min, a respiratory rate of 16 breaths/min, and a blood pressure of 90/60 mm Hg. The rest of the examination findings are unremarkable. Of the following, the MOST appropriate dietary restriction for this child is?
explanation:
Dietary restriction of phosphorus in chronic kidney disease controls hyperphosphatemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism. Nelson Says CKD patients of all ages should typically follow a low-phosphorus diet with the goal of maintaining age-appropriate serum phosphorus values. Some patients are also often given phosphate-binders with meals as a part of the management and prevention of CKD-MBD.

  • Protein restriction is not recommended in infants and children who have chronic kidney disease.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 550.2; Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1st SA ed., pg. 2545

question_text: A 3-month-old child has a respiratory rate of 56/min with no danger signs as per IMNCI. There is no chest indrawing. The child falls in which category?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • In our question, the child has RR > 40, hence, fast breathing. This falls in PNEUMONIA.
  • There are no chest indrawing or other danger signs, hence NOT SEVERE PNEUMONIA.

Explanation of other options:

Cold and Cough (Option B):

  • A child with cough and normal respiratory rate (i.e., RR < 50/min in a 3-month-old) is categorized under cold and cough.
  • Since this child has fast breathing (RR = 56/min), pneumonia is the correct classification.

Severe Pneumonia (Option C):

  • Severe pneumonia is diagnosed if there is:
    • Chest indrawing
    • Any general danger sign (e.g., inability to drink, lethargy, convulsions, stridor, severe malnutrition)
  • Since this child does not have chest indrawing or other danger signs, it is pneumonia, not severe pneumonia.

Allergy (Option D):

  • Allergic reactions may cause cough and respiratory symptoms, but they do not typically cause fast breathing alone as seen in pneumonia.
  • There is no mention of wheezing, skin rash, or other signs of allergy, making allergy an unlikely diagnosis.

Key Takeaways:

A 3-month-old with RR = 56/min and no chest indrawing or danger signs is classified as pneumonia under IMNCI guidelines.

question_text: The image shows a laryngoscopic view of the most common cause of stridor in children. Based on the findings, identify the condition.
explanation:
Explanation:

The laryngoscopic image shows floppy, omega-shaped epiglottis which is characteristic of laryngomalacia.

Laryngomalacia

  • M/c congenital laryngeal anomaly in children; characterized by floppy tissues above the vocal cords that collapse during inspiration, causing stridor.
  • Accounts for 45% to 75% of stridor cases in infants.
  • Appear within the first 2 weeks of life and can worsen for up to six months, with gradual improvement often occurring thereafter.
  • Factors deciding severity and clinical course
    • Gastroesophageal reflux disease
    • Laryngopharyngeal reflux disease
    • Neurological conditions

Investigations

  • Diagnosis is made mainly by clinical symptoms.
  • Outpatient flexible laryngoscopy is done to confirm the diagnosis but is not suitable for a baby as well as when dysphagia is suspected.
    • Laryngoscopy sows the omega sign: The inward curling of the epiglottis to become omega-shaped.
  • Airway films and chest radiographs are done when the work of breathing is moderate to severe.
  • A contrast swallow study or Flexible endoscopic evaluation of swallowing (FEES) is considered when dysphagia is suspected.
  • Complete bronchoscopy is done for those with moderate to severe obstruction.

Treatment

  • Expectant observation for most infants as the spontaneous resolution of symptoms as the child grows is seen.
  • Laryngoesophageal reflux and GERD are treated with proton pump inhibitors or histamine receptor antagonists, considering the possible iron deficiency anaemia.
  • Supraglottoplasty is done in case of severe disease that causes progressive respiratory distress, cyanosis, failure to thrive, or cor pulmonale.
  • Earlier intervention is needed in children with cardiac disease, neurologic disease, pulmonary disorders, or craniofacial anomalies

Explanation of other options:

Laryngeal papilloma (Option B): Laryngeal papilloma is an overgrowth of the epithelium caused by HPV and not by floppy tissues above the vocal cords as seen in the given image.

Chronic epiglottitis (Option C): Chronic epiglottitis is diagnosed clinically, and laryngoscopy is not usually done. It is an inflammatory condition and may cause stridor but it is not the most common cause.

Laryngocoele (Option D): An abnormal dilation of the saccule of the larynx, but not the most common cause of stridor in children.

question_text: On examination, what is a 'Harrison Groove' indicative of?
explanation:
• A Harrison groove (or sulcus) is a horizontal depression along the lower border of the chest at diaphragm insertion site.
  • It represents chronic tachypnoea and may be present in certain congenital heart defects or respiratory conditions.

Tags:

  • Topic: MISCELLANEOUS
  • Difficulty level: GOOD TO KNOW

Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 21st ed., pg. 375

question_text: Which among the following is the most common cause of pneumonia in an HIV+ child?
explanation:
Pneumocystis jirovecii is the most common cause of pneumonia in children with HIV.

  • Hypoxemia in a sick child with resp distress is the hallmark
  • CXR reveals diffuse ILD-like changes without hilar lymphadenopathy
  • Sputum, Respiratory Secretions or BAL fluid can be used for identification of the organism.
  • DOC is IV Cotrimoxazole, given for 21 days
  • Steroids are added if PaO2 < 70 mm Hg or A-a O2 gradient is > 30 mm Hg.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 420

question_text: A neonate is born with intestines protruding from the abdominal wall without any protective covering. What is the next best step in management?
option_a: Cover with a silo and wait
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The description is classic for gastroschisis, a congenital defect in which intestines protrude freely through a defect in the abdominal wall (usually to the right of the umbilicus) without a protective sac.
  • Because primary closure may cause increased intra-abdominal pressure and respiratory compromise, the immediate step is to place the exposed bowel in a silo bag to protect it, allow gradual reduction, and prevent fluid and heat loss.
  • Once the intestines are reduced gradually, definitive closure of the abdominal wall is performed.

Explanation of other options:

Cover with gauze (Option B): Sterile saline gauze may be used temporarily during transfer, but the definitive next step is silo placement.

Immediate repair in OT (Option C): Not preferred initially, as abrupt reduction risks abdominal compartment syndrome and cardiorespiratory compromise.

Wait and watch (Option D): Contraindicated; untreated gastroschisis leads to sepsis, dehydration, and death.

question_text: Parents complain that their child is always tired, gets fatigued more if climbs stairs and also develops episodes of breathlessness in supine position. What is the investigation to perform for likely etiology?
explanation:
Incorrect Option Explanation:

  • Spirometry: While spirometry can be helpful in assessing respiratory conditions(like asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease), the symptoms described are more suggestive of a cardiac issue rather than a primary lung condition. Spirometry would not be the first investigation to address a potential heart issue.
  • Chest X-ray: A chest X-ray could provide information about the lungs, heart size, or fluid buildupbut is not as detailed or specific as echocardiography when assessing the heart's structure and function.
  • MRI Thorax: MRI thorax is a more specialized and detailed imaging modality used in certain cardiac conditions, but echocardiography is typically the first-line and most accessible investigation for suspected cardiac issues, especially in children.

Key Takeaway:


Reference: Nelson textbook of paediatric

question_text: A 12-year-old healthy boy has noticed some muscle weakness. He has experienced increasing difficulty lifting his backpack and walking long distances. He has no trouble with schoolwork, and he continues to play the piano and video games without tiring. His 38-year-old maternal uncle recently became wheelchair bound for unclear reasons. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• This patient does not have muscle weakness that precludes extended use of distal muscles (hands) or limits his manual dexterity. The child's presentation at age 12 years and a 38-year-old wheelchair-bound maternal uncle suggests a diagnosis of Becker muscular dystrophy.

Option A: Duchene muscular dystrophy has earlier onset and more severe muscle weakness.

Option B: Myasthenia gravis has muscle weakness progressively over the day. The muscle function improves with rest.

Option D: Guillain Barre syndrome has progressive ascending peripheral neuropathy. Starts as a glove and stocking pattern. Later involves respiratory muscles.

KEY TAKEAWAYS: Becker's muscular dystrophy (BMD) is a genetic disorder characterized by progressive muscle weakness and wasting, primarily affecting the muscles of the hips, pelvis, thighs, and shoulders. Caused by mutations in the DMD gene, BMD is similar to Duchenne muscular dystrophy but is typically milder and progresses more slowly. Symptoms often appear in adolescence or early adulthood and may include difficulty walking, muscle cramps, and heart issues like cardiomyopathy

Tags:

  • Topic: MUSCULAR DYSTROPHY
  • Difficulty level: GOOD TO KNOW

Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1st SA edition, pg. 2977

question_text: A 6-year-old boy with nasal discharge is brought to the pediatric clinic. He has a history of allergic rhinitis that is controlled with cetirizine in the spring and fall. He was in his usual state of health until 2 weeks ago when he developed fever and malaise. His maximum temperature was 38.4°C, and the fever lasted for 2 days. He has had a runny nose since the onset of this illness, which worsened after about 1 week as the discharge changed in color from clear to white and became thicker. He has a temperature of 98°F, heart rate of 80 beats/min, respiratory rate of 22 breaths/min, and blood pressure of 106/70 mm Hg. He has audible nasal congestion, white discharge in the right nare, and swelling of the nasal turbinates in the left nare. Of the following, the feature in this patient that would MOST support a diagnosis of acute bacterial sinusitis is?
explanation:
A diagnosis of acute bacterial sinusitis would be most supported by the symptom duration of 2 weeks.

  • As per OP Ghai 10th Edition, Persistent fever, facial pain or heaviness, nasal obstruction or discharge, cough, dental pain, ear fullness and earache beyond 7-10 days after an upper respiratory tract infection suggests the diagnosis of infective rhinosinusitis
  • According to the "Clinical Practice Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Acute Bacterial Sinusitis in Children Aged 1 to 18 Years" published by the American Academy of Pediatrics in 2013, the persistence of nasal discharge for 10 or more days without improvement meets criteria for acute bacterial sinusitis.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 386; Clinical Practice Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Acute Bacterial Sinusitis in Children Aged 1 to 18 Years, AAP, 2013

question_text: A 10-month-old boy presents with second lobar pneumonia over the last 3 months. The level of all immunoglobulins is low, and the tonsils are hypoplastic as are the adenoids. Peripheral blood B lymphocytes are absent. Most likely immune pathology?
explanation:
• This affects males, with a repeated history of bacterial infection. It usually occurs after 6 months of age and before 2 years of age.
  • The most frequent sites of infection are otitis, sinusitis and pneumonia, (Respiratory system) and the most common organisms are Hemophilus influenzae and Streptococcus pneumoniae. (encapsulated).
  • All isotypes of immunoglobulins are absent or very low. Circulating mature B cells are absent, as are specific antibodies. T cells are normal. Arrest occurs at maturation of Pre-B cells.
  • The treatment is lifelong immunoglobulin replacement every 6-8 weeks and maintenance of IgG. Infections should be treated, and physiotherapy should be given for bronchiectasis.

SPOTTERS- All Ig Low, Absent B cells, Normal T cells

Tags:

  • Topic: IMMUNE DISORDERS
  • Difficulty level: GOOD TO KNOW

Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1st SA ed., pg. 1012

question_text: An infant has paroxysms of nocturnal cough with fever. The child also has chest retractions, gasping and cyanosis. TLC is 50000 with lymphocytosis. Management?
explanation:
Let’s first make the diagnosis and then discuss the management.

  • Presence of paroxysmal cough, esp nocturnal, with fever and lymphocytic leukocytosis suggests likely Pertussis, also called Whooping Cough.
  • OP Ghai clearly says that the whoop during cough may not be present in the infants, who present with apneic or cyanotic spells.
  • Extreme leukocytosis of 50000 or more cells/mm3 is also more common in infants with Pertussis.
  • Macrolides like Azithromycin & Erythromycin are the drugs of choice. They reduce period of communicability and respiratory tract carriage but do not shorten the course of illness.
  • Erythromycin is used for chemoprophylaxis of close contacts, especially those <2 years of age.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Pages 265-266

question_text: The following are common viral causes of pneumonia in children except?
explanation:
Common causes of Viral pneumonia in pediatric patients are

  • Adenovirus
  • Rhinovirus
  • Influenza (flu)
  • Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and
  • Parainfluenza virus.

Reference: Feigin & Cherry's Textbook of Pediatric Infectious Diseases, 6th ed.

question_text: A mother brings her 9-month-old child to hospital for fever and cough. The child is having RR of 48/min but no chest retractions or other signs. What is the next step in management?
option_b: Send back home after starting oral antibiotics
explanation:
The child has no fast breathing or chest indrawing, hence unlikely to be pneumonia.

  • More likely this is a simple viral respiratory infection. Hence no need for antibiotics
  • Symptomatic relief and oral Paracetamol for fever can be considered
  • Also note the categorization of fast breathing in children

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 815

question_text: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the office with a few petechiae and bruising on the face, chest, back, and lower extremities, which her mother noticed early this morning. The mother states that her daughter has been healthy except for a viral upper respiratory illness 2 weeks ago. Laboratory assessment reveals a platelet count of 25,000/microlitre without any splenomegaly. Which of the following statements regarding the likely diagnosis is correct?
option_a: Hemarthroses commonly occur in this disorder
option_b: Spontaneous recovery within several weeks is excepted
option_c: Platelet transfusion should be urgently performed
option_d: Prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time are prolonged
explanation:
The diagnosis fits into a diagnosis of acute-onset ITP.

Points to note:

  • Onset of petechia 2 weeks following a viral illness
  • Platelet count showing thrombocytopenia
  • No splenomegaly.

Since there is no mucosal or life-threatening bleeding, only observation is sufficient. There is no role of platelet transfusions in acute ITP. As per OP Ghai 10th Edition, many children with ITP are stable with a platelet count of 20-30000/Microliter and have no symptoms or mild bruising and petechiae. Expectant wait and watch policy can be used if there is no active bleeding.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 372, ASH Guidelines 2019

question_text: A child presented with a history of fever for 2 days, dyspnea, drooling and inspiratory stridor. Lateral x-ray neck findings are shown below. Which is the most common causative organism in India for this condition in children?
explanation:
Explanation:

The lateral neck X-ray demonstrates the characteristic thumb sign, caused by a swollen, rounded epiglottis. This finding, along with the child's symptoms of fever, drooling, dyspnea, and inspiratory stridor, is suggestive of epiglottitis, which in India is most commonly caused by Haemophilus influenzae type B (Hib).

Acute epiglottitis

Life-threatening infection that causes profound swelling of the upper airways, which can lead to asphyxia and respiratory arrest.

Causative Agent

  • Pre-vaccine Era: Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib)
  • Post-vaccine Era:
    • Streptococcus pneumoniae (M/c), Streptococcus pyogenes, non-typeable influenzae and Staphylococcus aureus (Option B, C ruled out)
    • Hib cases have decreased by 99% due to widespread vaccination

Clinical Features

  • Characterized by an acute rapidly progressive and potentially fulminating course of high fever, sore throat, dyspnea, and rapidly progressing respiratory obstruction.
  • The degree of respiratory distress at presentation is variable.
  • The initial lack of respiratory distress can deceive the unwary clinician; respiratory distress can also be the first manifestation.
  • Often, the otherwise healthy child suddenly develops a sore throat and fever.
  • Within a matter of hours, the patient appears toxic, swallowing is difficult, and breathing is labored.
  • Drooling is usually present, and the neck is hyperextended in an attempt to maintain the airway.
  • The child may assume the tripod position, sitting upright and leaning forward with the chin up and mouth open while bracing on the arms.
  • A brief period of air hunger with restlessness may be followed by rapidly increasing cyanosis and coma.
  • Stridor is a late finding and suggests near-­ complete airway obstruction.
  • Complete obstruction of the airway and death can ensue unless adequate treatment is provided.

Diagnosis

  • Laryngoscopy
    • Large, cherry-red, swollen epiglottis
  • Lateral neck X-ray
    • Thumb sign

Treatment

  • Immediate Treatment:
    • Secure the airway with endotracheal or nasotracheal intubation or, less often, with tracheostomy.
    • Intubation is generally for 2-3 days.
    • Intubation decreases mortality from 6% to <1% in epiglottitis cases.
    • Culture Collection: Blood, epiglottic surface and CSF in certain cases after the airway is stabilized.
  • Antibiotics: Ceftriaxone, cefepime or meropenem given parenterally for 10 days.

Explanation of other options:

RSV (Option D): It is the most common cause of bronchiolitis and viral pneumonia in infants and young children, typically presenting with cough, wheezing, tachypnea, and sometimes respiratory distress and cyanosis. Unlike epiglottitis, RSV does not cause the thumb sign on lateral neck X-ray nor drooling or severe inspiratory stridor.

question_text: A newborn presents with respiratory distress and frothing from mouth on Day 1 of life. The baby is cyanosed. What could be the most likely cause?
explanation:
Respiratory distress with frothing from mouth is suggestive of Tracheo-esophageal fistula with esophageal atresia in a newborn. Excess frothing is due to failure to swallow his own salivary secretions. Cyanosis may occur due to aspiration pneumonia.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 175

question_text: Which among the following is the single most important factor predicting survival and prognosis in a patient with CDH?
explanation:
Although CDH is characterized by a structural diaphragmatic defect, a major limiting factor for survival is the associated pulmonary hypoplasia .

  • Pulmonary hypoplasia is characterized by a reduction in pulmonary mass and the number of bronchial divisions, respiratory bronchioles, and alveoli.
  • The pathology of pulmonary hypoplasia and CDH includes abnormal septa in the terminal saccules, thickened alveoli, and thickened pulmonary arterioles.
  • Biochemical abnormalities include relative surfactant deficiencies, increased glycogen in the alveoli, and decreased levels of phosphatidylcholine, total DNA, and total lung protein, all of which contribute to limited gas exchange.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 122.10

question_text: A child with nephrotic syndrome on high dose steroids comes in contact with an active case of chicken pox in neighborhood. He is not vaccinated to varicella. Which of the following treatment is advised for this child?
option_d: Observe and treat only if symptomatic
explanation:
• Following close contact with varicella infection, give immunocompromised children on immunosuppressive agents varicella-zoster immune globulin if available; immunize healthy household contacts with live vaccines to minimize the risk of transfer of infection to the immunosuppressed child, but avoid direct exposure of the child to gastrointestinal or respiratory secretions of vaccinated contacts for 3-6 weeks after vaccination.
  • Live vaccines are contraindicated for this child. (Option A)
  • IV acyclovir is recommended by some literature. (Option C)

KEY TAKEAWAYS: Live vaccines are contraindicated in patients with nephrotic syndrome.

Tags:

  • Topic: NEPHROTIC SYNDROME
  • Difficulty level: MUST KNOW
  • PYQ: NEET PG 2022; 2021; FMGE JAN 2023; DEC 2020

Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 21st ed., pg. 2753

question_text: A term baby is born to a 30-year-old woman who had little prenatal care. Immediately after birth he has cyanosis and respiratory distress. Chest auscultation in the delivery room reveals right-sided heart sounds and absent left-sided breath sounds. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
option_a: Assess the abdomen to evaluate for possible congenital diaphragmatic hernia.
option_c: Perform a needle thoracostomy for possible pneumothorax.
option_d: Prepare the infant for extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO)
explanation:
Evaluation of neonates born with respiratory distress and unilateral breath sounds includes an abdominal examination.

  • With asymmetrical breath sounds, pneumothorax and congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) are considered. This infant's scaphoid abdomen and the presence of bowel sounds in the chest suggest CDH
  • Blind needle thoracostomy without a CXR being done prior, is avoided because intestinal perforation may occur.
  • The patient is stabilized and the need for ECMO is ascertained after the infant's initial therapy response is evaluated. Many cases of CDH are diagnosed by prenatal ultrasound.
  • Infants with CDH do not respond to typical steps of neonatal resuscitation, and often have worsening respiratory status upon bag-mask ventilation (BMV), ultimately requiring intubation.
  • The diagnosis of CDH can be made by locating on plain imaging the nasogastric feeding tube in the chest where the stomach has been displaced from the abdomen.

Reference: Avery's diseases of the newborn, 1st SA ed., pg. 772

question_text: An infant presented with progressive respiratory distress and mediastinal shift to the right. CXR showed the following finding. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This child fits into the description of congenital lobar emphysema.

  • Clinical manifestations usually become apparent in the neonatal period but are delayed for as long as 5-6 yr in 5% of patients.
  • Clinical signs range from mild tachypnea and wheeze to severe dyspnea with cyanosis.
  • CLE can affect one or more lobes; it affects the upper and middle lobes, and the left upper lobe is the most common site.
  • The affected lobe is essentially non-functional because of the overdistention, and atelectasis of the ipsilateral normal lung can ensue.
  • With further distention, the mediastinum is shifted to the contralateral side, with impaired function seen as well.
  • A radiolucent lobe and a mediastinal shift are often revealed by radiographic examination.

Reference: Nelson 21st Ed/Chapter 420

question_text: An infant presented to pediatric emergency with breathing difficulty, high respiratory rates and scaphoid abdomen with SpO2 of 90% on room air.. What should be avoided?
explanation:
The clinical presentation with scaphoid abdomen is consistent with a diagnosis of Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia

  • CDH is an absolute contraindication to Bag And Mask Ventilation.
  • Prolonged mask ventilation in the delivery room, which enlarges the stomach and small bowel and thus makes oxygenation more difficult, must be avoided and a naso- or orogastric tube placed immediately for decompression. If distress is severe, intubation can be done.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 345.1

question_text: A Case on infant with breathing difficulty, high RR and scaphoid abdomen is seen in emergency. What should be avoided?
explanation:
Scaphoid abdomen/boat shaped abdomen a suspicious feature of CDH(Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia).

Bag and Mask Ventilation is absolutely contraindicated in CDH cases.

In CDH cases The intestines are herniating into the thoracic cavity through the diaphragm. If bag and mask ventilation is performed, some air will enter the lungs, while some will pass into the abdomen through the esophagus. The air entering the abdomen will increase intra-abdominal pressure, potentially worsening the diaphragmatic hernia.

Intubation: All infants with known DH Should be intubated immediately after diagnosis. Bag-and-mask ventilation is contraindicated

Incorrect Options Explanation:

  • Free Flow Oxygen:
    • Explanation: Free flow oxygen is generally not harmful in CDH. However, it's not the most effective treatment to manage respiratory distress caused by CDH, and oxygen supplementation should be used cautiously in the acute setting.
    • Why it's not the best choice: While oxygen should be administered to all infants in respiratory distress, intubation is more crucial for proper ventilation in CDH cases.
  • PPV (Positive Pressure Ventilation):
    • Explanation: PPV can be useful if intubation is not immediately available. It may provide temporary ventilation support until intubation can be performed. However, this is a more cautious approach and should be followed by intubation.
    • Why it's not the best choice: While PPV can be used if intubation is delayed, it does not replace intubation and should not be relied on as the sole means of ventilation in CDH.
  • Endotracheal Intubation:
    • Explanation: Endotracheal intubation is the gold standard for airway management in cases of CDH. It secures the airway and allows for proper ventilation, reducing the risk of complications like air entering the abdomen or increased intra-abdominal pressure.
    • Why it's not the best choice: Intubation is actually the most important intervention for CDH, so this option is not correct in this context. It should be performed immediately in CDH cases.

Key Takeaway:

  • Bag and Mask Ventilation (BVM) should always be avoided in Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia (CDH) because it can lead to air entering the abdomen, worsening the hernia and compressing the lungs.
  • Endotracheal intubation is essential for securing the airway and preventing complications in CDH.
  • Positive-Pressure Ventilation (PPV) may be used temporarily, but it should be followed by intubation for definitive management.

Reference: Nelson textbook of paediatrics

question_text: A term infant is delivered vaginally to a 22-year-old mother. Immediately after birth he is noted to have a scaphoid abdomen, cyanosis, and respiratory distress. Heart sounds are heard on the right side of the chest, and the breath sounds seem to be diminished on the left side. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in his resuscitation?
explanation:
The case describes diaphragmatic hernia.

  • Because of herniated bowel in the chest, these children often have pulmonary hypoplasia. Bag-and-mask ventilation will cause accumulation of bowel gas (which is located in the chest) and further respiratory compromise.
  • Therefore, endotracheal intubation is the best course of action.

Reference: Avery's diseases of the newborn, 1st SA ed., pg. 772

question_text: A 15-day old child presented with respiratory distress was brought to emergency with bag and mask ventilation. Now the child is intubated. Chest X-ray shows right-sided deviation of mediastinum with scaphoid abdomen. His Pulse rate has increased. What is the next step?
explanation:
• Mediastinal deviation, scaphoid abdomen with respiratory distress suggests the diagnosis of congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH).
  • The resuscitation of a CDH patient consists of a) Stabilization by intubation & mechanical ventilation with 100% O2 b) Nasogastric suction.
  • This child has already been intubated, now nasogastric suction should be done to aspirate swallowed air and to prevent distension of the herniated bowel which would further compress the lung

Reference: Avery's diseases of the newborn, 1st SA ed., pg. 772

question_text: A newborn presents with respiratory distress. A CT scan reveals bowel loops herniated into the left hemithorax/mediastinum. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The CT scan reveals herniation from the left posterolateral region, which is characteristic of a Bochdalek hernia-the most common type of congenital diaphragmatic hernia in children.

Key clinical features include:

  • Respiratory distress soon after birth
  • Bowel sounds in the chest
  • Scaphoid (sunken) abdomen due to displacement of abdominal contents into the thoracic cavity

Early surgical correction is essential in all cases to relieve pulmonary compression and prevent further complications.

Explanation of other options:

Morgagni Hernia (Option B): Morgagni hernia accounts for only 2-3% of congenital diaphragmatic hernias.

  • Location: Right anterior, typically through a retrosternal defect
  • Clinical Presentation: Often asymptomatic or may present later in life with gastrointestinal symptoms rather than respiratory distress.

Hiatal Hernia (Option C): In this condition, the gastroesophageal junction herniates through the diaphragm, typically seen in a hiatal hernia.

  • Clinical Presentation: Primarily presents with gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) symptoms such as heartburn and regurgitation, rather than respiratory distress.
  • Imaging Findings: No bowel loops are visualized in the chest cavity on imaging studies.

Traumatic Diaphragmatic Hernia (Option D):

  • Traumatic diaphragmatic hernia occurs due to blunt or penetrating trauma to the abdomen or lower chest.
  • A clear history of trauma is essential for diagnosis.
  • It is most commonly left-sided because the liver offers protection on the right.
  • Unlike congenital hernias, it presents postnatally following injury.

Key Takeaways:

Bochdalek hernia is the most common congenital diaphragmatic hernia, characterized by bowel loops in the left mediastinum, respiratory distress at birth, and a scaphoid abdomen.

question_text: What is the most likely diagnosis for a neonate presenting with frothing from the mouth and respiratory distress, with the X-ray provided below?
explanation:
Explanation:

The neonate's symptoms are suggestive of esophageal atresia with tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF). This diagnosis is supported by the hallmark signs of frothing at the mouth, respiratory distress, and the classic X-ray finding of a coiled tube in the upper esophagus.

  • TEF arises from abnormal embryonic development of the trachea and esophagus.
  • Clinically, it typically presents with frothing and bubbling at the mouth and nose, coughing, cyanosis, and worsening respiratory distress during feeding.
  • The condition is frequently associated with VACTERL anomalies.

Clinical Features:
A neonate with frothing at the mouth, respiratory distress, and difficulty feeding raises suspicion for TEF. The diagnosis is often confirmed by a chest X-ray showing a coiled nasogastric tube in the upper esophagus.

Pathophysiology:
TEF occurs due to abnormal embryonic development of the trachea and esophagus, leading to an incomplete separation between the two structures.

Etiology:

  • Embryologic defect: Faulty partitioning of the trachea and esophagus during early development.
  • Genetic syndromes: Can be associated with Feingold syndrome, CHARGE syndrome, or anophthalmia-esophageal-genital syndrome.
  • Other factors: Advanced maternal age, maternal obesity, smoking, low socioeconomic status, or unknown causes may contribute.

Types of TEF:

  • Type A: Esophageal atresia without a fistula.
  • Type B: Esophageal atresia with a proximal fistula.
  • Type C: Esophageal atresia with a distal fistula (most common).
  • Type D: Esophageal atresia with both proximal and distal fistulas.
  • Type E (H-type): Fistula without esophageal atresia.

Presentation:

  • Frothing or bubbling from the mouth and nose.
  • Coughing, choking, and cyanosis, especially during feeding.
  • Respiratory distress that worsens with attempts to feed.
  • Recurrent pneumonia may occur with distal fistulas or H-type fistulas.

Diagnosis:

  • Chest X-ray: Coiled nasogastric tube in the upper esophagus; may show a gasless or gas-filled abdomen depending on fistula type.
  • Contrast esophagogram can be used if the diagnosis is unclear.

Management:

  • Immediate care: Secure airway, prevent aspiration, and start antibiotics if necessary.
  • Surgical intervention: Ligation of the fistula and primary end-to-end esophageal anastomosis is standard.
  • Alternative options: Delayed repair, gastrostomy feeding, or use of gastric/jejunal/colonic segments in cases of long-gap atresia (>3-4 cm).

Complications:

  • Respiratory: Aspiration pneumonia.
  • Esophageal: Feeding difficulties, strictures, poor growth.
  • Associated anomalies: Often occurs with VACTERL association (vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheal, esophageal, renal, limb anomalies).

Prognosis:

  • Early diagnosis and surgical management have improved survival.
  • Long-term outcomes may include feeding difficulties, esophageal narrowing, and respiratory complications.

Explanation of Other Options:

Transient Tachypnea of the Newborn (Option A): This condition usually causes mild respiratory distress that improves within 1-3 days after birth. Chest X-ray typically shows normally inflated or slightly overinflated lungs with streaky perihilar markings and a shaggy cardiac silhouette, while the peripheral lung fields remain clear. It is generally self-limiting and resolves without intervention.

Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia (Option B): X-ray in this condition shows bowel loops or cyst-like structures within the thoracic cavity, often on the left side, with displacement of the mediastinum to the opposite side and a gasless abdomen. It occurs due to a defect in the diaphragm, allowing abdominal organs to herniate into the chest.

Respiratory Distress Syndrome (Option D): Primarily seen in premature infants, this condition develops within the first 24 hours of life. X-ray typically reveals underinflated lungs with a fine granular pattern throughout and prominent air bronchograms. It results from a deficiency of pulmonary surfactant, which is more common in preterm newborns.

question_text: Which of the following is the most common type of congenital diaphragmatic hernia?
explanation:
Explanation:

Bochdalek hernia, a posterolateral diaphragmatic defect, is the most common type of congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH), typically occurring on the left side.

  • Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) is a developmental defect of the diaphragm that allows abdominal contents to herniate into the thoracic cavity, impairing lung development (pulmonary hypoplasia).
  • Bochdalek Hernia - Key Features:
    • Location: Posterolateral diaphragm (usually left-sided)
    • Cause: Failure of pleuroperitoneal membrane closure during embryogenesis
    • Clinical Presentation:
      • Respiratory distress in the neonatal period
      • Scaphoid abdomen (due to displaced abdominal contents)
      • Decreased breath sounds on the affected side
      • Mediastinal shift on imaging
    • Diagnosis: Antenatal ultrasound or postnatal chest X-ray
    • Management: Initial stabilization with ventilation, followed by surgical repair

Explanation of other options:

Hiatal Hernia (Option A): Involves stomach herniation through the esophageal hiatus. Typically acquired in adults, not a common form of congenital diaphragmatic hernia.

Morgagni Hernia (Option B): Anterior diaphragmatic defect through the foramen of Morgagni. It is less common and often asymptomatic or incidentally found.

Umbilical Hernia (Option D): Protrusion of abdominal contents through the umbilical ring, common in infants, but not a type of diaphragmatic hernia.

question_text: A 28 wk premature neonate developed respiratory distress soon after birth. Likely cause is deficiency of?
explanation:
Surfactant deficiency (decreased production and secretion) is the primary cause of RDS.

  • In the absence of pulmonary surfactant, significantly increased alveolar surface tension leads to atelectasis, and the ability to attain an adequate FRC is impaired.
  • The major constituents of surfactant are dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine (lecithin), phosphatidylglycerol, apoproteins (surfactant proteins SP-A, SP-B, SP-C, and SP-D), and cholesterol.
  • Lecithin is the most important constituent of surfactant responsible for lowering of surface tension.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 122; OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 157

question_text: A 7-year-old girl is admitted to the hospital in respiratory distress due to pneumonia. This is her third admission in the past 6 months. At this time, you are suspecting cystic fibrosis (CF) and order a sputum culture. Which organism would be most consistent with a diagnosis of cystic fibrosis?
explanation:
This girl has recurrent pulmonary infections.

  • The presence of P aeruginosa on a sputum sample strongly suggests the diagnosis of CF.
  • Patients with CF have a high prevalence of colonization with P aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus, and Burkholderia cepacia.
  • The innate defenses of the airway epithelium cells of CF patients may be compromised, making them unable to fight these organisms.

Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1st SA ed., pg. 1414

question_text:
Which of the following statements matches the diagnosis of acute respiratory distress in a child?
1) Within 7 days of known insult
2) Respiratory failure not fully explained by cardiac failure or LV dysfunction
3) New Chest Infiltrates
4) PaO2/FiO2: 100-200 mm Hg
explanation:
The criteria listed match the definition of Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS), which includes:

Within 7 days of a known insult: ARDS typically develops within 7 days of the inciting event (e.g., pneumonia, trauma, aspiration).

Respiratory failure not fully explained by cardiac failure or LV dysfunction: This indicates that ARDS is primarily a pulmonary issue, not due to heart failure.

New chest infiltrates: Chest X-ray or CT shows new, bilateral infiltrates indicative of ARDS.

PaO2/FiO2: 100-200 mm Hg: This range falls within the classification of moderate ARDS, based on the PaO2/FiO2 ratio.

Thus, all the given points are correct and align with the diagnostic criteria for ARDS in children.

 

Key takeaways:-Paediatric ARDS guideline

question_text: Most common cause of death in diphtheria?
explanation:
Although the commonest complication in Diphtheria is respiratory failure due to occlusion of the airways by the membrane, most common cause of death is usually toxin-mediated cardiomyopathy and myocarditis.

  • Toxic cardiomyopathy occurs in 10–25% of patients with respiratory diphtheria and is responsible for 50–60% of deaths. Subtle signs of myocarditis can be detected in most patients, especially the elderly, but the risk for significant complications correlates directly with the extent and severity of exudative local oropharyngeal disease, as well as delay in administration of antitoxin.
  • The first evidence of cardiac toxicity characteristically occurs during the 2nd and 3rd wk of illness as the pharyngeal disease improves but can appear acutely as early as the 1st wk of illness, a poor prognostic sign, or insidiously as late as the 6th wk.
  • Tachycardia disproportionate to fever is common and may be evidence of cardiac toxicity or autonomic nervous system dysfunction.
  • Neurological complications are also toxin-mediated and may include palatal palsy in 2nd week of illness, ocular palsy in 3rd week, loss of accommodation and generalized polyneuritis by 3-6 weeks of illness.
  • Renal complications include oliguria and proteinuria.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 214; OP Ghai 10th Edition, Pages 264-265

question_text: A term baby is born via caesarean section to a 30-year-old woman. Immediately after birth he has mild respiratory distress. Chest auscultation in the delivery room reveals clear breath sounds. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
option_c: Observe and administer supplemental oxygen as needed
explanation:
Term baby delivered by Caesarean Section who develops respiratory distress soon after birth, is likely to have Transient Tachypnea of Neonate (TTN).

  • The next step is to observe and administer supplemental oxygen, as needed.
  • Most patients respond to O2 alone & some rare patients may need CPAP for some time.
  • There is no role of antibiotics, steroids, surfactant or ventilation in the management of these patients.
  • Since respiratory rate is often high, these patients are started on IV fluids and gradually shifted to feeds as the distress settles in a few hours.

question_text: A neonate was born at 32 weeks of gestation and developed respiratory distress soon after birth, poorly responsive to warm, humidified oxygen. Which among the following is not true?
option_b: Early use of nasal CPAP is indicated
option_c: Surfactant therapy by INSURE or LISA should precede nasal CPAP
option_d: Prematurity is the most important risk factor
explanation:
Let us evaluate each option

  • Option A is True. Any neonate born <34 weeks with onset of distress soon after birth is likely to have RDS owing to relative surfactant deficiency
  • Option B is True. Early use of CPAP is effective and ensures better oxygenation and stabilization in RDS patients.
  • Option C is False. CPAP is always instituted initially and then, in a severe RDS patient we give SRT= Surfactant replacement therapy using INSURE, LISA or MIST techniques.
  • Option D is True. Prematurity is the most important risk factor for RDS

question_text: A 5-month old baby has intermittent stridor and dysphagia since birth. The symptoms have been present since birth and are exacerbated when child is crying or in prone position and decreased when lying down in supine position and not crying. What is the treatment?
option_d: Get a hemogram and throat swab done.
explanation:
This is a typical presentation of laryngomalacia.

  • Any infant with intermittent stridor and dysphagia since birth should be suspected to have laryngomalacia.
  • The stridor is aggravated by supine position, crying or feeding. It tends to improve in prone position and in a calm, sleeping child.
  • Respiratory distress and retractions are minimal to absent.
  • As per Nelson 21st Ed, expectant observation is suitable for most infants because most symptoms resolve spontaneously as the child and airway grow.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Pages 397, 398; Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 413

question_text: An 8-year-old boy presents to the clinic, for concerns of congestion, rhinorrhea, frequent sneezing, and itchy throat for the last three weeks. On examination, his turbinates are swollen and pale, and there is darkening of the skin below both eyelids. What is the best treatment for his condition?
explanation:
This boy has symptoms and signs of allergic rhinitis.

  • Allergic rhinitis is characterized by upper respiratory congestion, sneezing, and rhinorrhea, along with ocular itching, postnasal drip, and coughing.
  • Physical findings include infraorbital darkening, nasal crease, and crease of the lower eyelids.
  • The first line of treatment for allergic rhinitis is intranasal corticosteroids such as intranasal fluticasone, along with allergen avoidance.
  • Numerous studies show superiority of intranasal corticosteroids over oral antihistamines in the control of nasal symptoms. There are first- and second-generation intranasal corticosteroids, and both are equally effective and work by decreasing the inflammatory response.
  • Common side effects are dryness or burning of the nasal mucosa, and epistaxis.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 386; Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1st SA ed., pg. 1090

question_text: Peak age for Henoch-Schoenlein Purpura?
explanation:
Peak age for Henoch-Schoenlein Purpura, also called IgA Vasculitis is 3-8 years, although the disease can occur at any age, including adults.

Epidemiology of HSP as per Nelson 21st Edition

  • HSP occurs worldwide and affects all ethnic groups but is more common in white and Asian populations.
  • The incidence of HSP is estimated at 14-20 per 100,000 children per year and affects males more than females, with a 1.2-1.8 : 1 male/female ratio.
  • Approximately 90% of HSP cases occur in children, usually between ages 3 and 10 yr.
  • HSP is distinctly less common in adults, who often have severe and chronic complications.
  • HSP is more common in the winter and spring and is unusual in summer months.
  • Many cases of HSP follow a documented upper respiratory infection.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 192.1

question_text: A previously healthy term infant suddenly develops respiratory distress on day 3 of life. An echocardiogram reveals coarctation of the aorta. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for immediate stabilization of this infant?
explanation:
Remember the concept that any neonate who suddenly worsens in the 1st week of life, a possibility of ductus-dependent cardiac lesions should be considered.

  • Ductus dependent lesions like Ebstein's anomaly, tricuspid atresia and isolated TGA present with cyanosis, while those with hypoplastic left heart syndrome and severe coarctation of aorta present with shock, when ductus arteriosus closes.
  • This infant's symptoms started when his ductus arteriosus began to close.
  • A continuous intravenous infusion of prostaglandin PGE1, called Alprostadil will keep the ductus open and allow blood flow to reach past the area of coarctation and perfuse the lower portion of the body.
  • Surgery provides definitive repair of the underlying lesion.

Reference: Park's Pediatric Cardiology, 6th Edition, Page 201; Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 454.6

question_text: A 4-month-old infant is brought to the ED with a respiratory rate of 66/min, along with chest indrawing and nasal flaring. There are no other significant findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

According to the WHO classification of pneumonia in children (2-59 months):

  • Pneumonia is diagnosed when there is fast breathing (RR > 60/min in <2 months; >50/min in 2-12 months) with or without chest indrawing.
  • Severe pneumonia requires additional features such as hypoxemia, inability to feed, lethargy, or convulsions.
  • Since this infant has tachypnea + chest indrawing, but no danger signs, the correct diagnosis is pneumonia.

Explanation of other options:

Severe pneumonia (Option B): Requires danger signs like hypoxia, feeding difficulty, altered sensorium, or convulsions. This infant does not have those features.

Severe asthma (Option C): Rare at 4 months; asthma diagnosis is usually not considered before 1 year. Also, there is no history of wheezing.

Common cold (Option D): Presents with rhinorrhea, cough, and mild fever, but does not cause tachypnea with chest indrawing.

question_text: A 5-year-old child with a known history of asthma was brought to the ER with complaints of sudden onset of breathlessness and wheezing.  On examination, the pulse is 140/min, the respiratory rate 28/min, and the FEV1 is 40% of the predicted value. Which of the following is the best next step in treatment in this case?
option_a: A high concentration of oxygen should be given by a face mask + Salbutamol nebulization
option_b: High doses of SABA to be given by a nebulizer only
option_c: Sedatives should be added to alleviate anxiety
option_d: Nebulized anticholinergics to be added immediately as the mainstay of treatment
explanation:
Explanation:

An FEV1 of 40%, along with tachypnoea and tachycardia, indicates a severe acute asthma exacerbation, which should be managed with oxygen therapy and salbutamol nebulization.

Explanation of other options:

High doses of SABA to be given by a nebulizer only (Option B): Administering SABA alone without oxygen is inadequate in a child with low FEV1 and tachycardia, and may worsen hypoxemia.

Sedatives should be added to alleviate anxiety (Option C): Sedatives are contraindicated in acute asthma exacerbations because they can depress respiratory drive and worsen hypoxia or hypercapnia. Anxiety can be managed with reassurance, not sedatives.

Nebulized anticholinergics to be added immediately as the mainstay of treatment (Option D): Anticholinergics like ipratropium are used as adjunct therapy in severe asthma, not as the main treatment. The primary therapy remains SABA + oxygen. Anticholinergics may be added to improve bronchodilation if the response to SABA is inadequate.

Options B, C, and D are insufficient methods for the treatment of severe acute exacerbation of asthma and are hence incorrect.

question_text: In which of the following conditions is the INSURE technique used?
explanation:
Explanation:

INSURE Technique:

  • INtubation → SURfactant administration → Extubation
  • Used for RDS in preterm infants to administer surfactant while minimizing ventilator time

RDS occurs due to surfactant deficiency. Surfactant, a lipoprotein produced by type II alveolar cells, reduces alveolar surface tension, preventing collapse at end-expiration.

Surfactant production begins around 20 weeks of gestation and peaks at 35 weeks, placing preterm infants (<35 weeks) at higher risk. Without sufficient surfactant, alveoli collapse during expiration, impairing gas exchange, causing hypoxia, increasing pulmonary pressure, and leading to ischemic damage. Protein-rich transudate forms a hyaline membrane in the alveoli.

Clinical Features:
Respiratory distress usually develops within the first 6 hours of life, characterized by:

  • Tachypnoea
  • Retractions
  • Grunting
  • Cyanosis
  • Decreased air entry

Management: Neonates require NICU admission, IV fluids, and appropriate respiratory support (oxygen therapy, CPAP, or mechanical ventilation as needed).

Prevention: Antenatal corticosteroids accelerate fetal lung maturation and reduce the risk of RDS in preterm infants (24–34 weeks gestation).

Betamethasone: 12 mg IM, 2 doses, 24 hours apart

Dexamethasone: 6 mg IM, 4 doses, 12 hours apart

question_text: Which among the following is/are true regarding sweat and pancreatic secretions chloride levels in Cystic Fibrosis?
option_a: Chloride excretion is increased in sweat
option_b: Chloride excretion is decreased in sweat
option_c: Chloride concentration is increased in pancreatic secretions
option_d: Chloride concentration is decreased in pancreatic secretions
explanation:
Explanation of Incorrect Answers:

  • Chloride excretion is increased in sweat:
    • This statement is true. In CF, due to impaired CFTR function, chloride ions are not reabsorbed in the sweat glands, leading to an increase in chloride excretionin sweat. This is one of the hallmarks of the disease and is used in diagnostic tests.
  • Chloride excretion is decreased in sweat:
    • This statement is incorrect. As mentioned above, chloride excretion is increased in the sweat of individuals with CF.
  • Chloride concentration is increased in pancreatic secretions:
    • This statement is incorrect. In CF, the chloride concentration is decreased in pancreatic secretions, which affects the enzyme secretion, leading to pancreatic insufficiency.

Key Takeaway:

  • Cystic Fibrosis is characterized by increased chloride levels in sweat and decreased chloride concentration in pancreatic secretions. This dysfunction in chloride transport leads to various clinical manifestations, such as respiratory issues, digestive problems, and reproductive complications.
  • The sweat chloride test is a key diagnostic tool for CF, where chloride levels greater than 60 mEq/L confirm the diagnosis.

Key takeaways: Cystic fibrosis

Reference: Nelson textbook of paediatrics

question_text: A 2-year-old boy is admitted to the pediatric inpatient service 4 hours after swallowing a small amount of kerosene. On physical examination, the boy has a temperature of 38.0°C, HR of 130 beats/min, BP of 85/50 mm Hg, and RR of 40 breaths/min. He is awake and alert with mild nasal flaring; he has bilateral breath sounds with mild wheezing and mild intercostal retractions. His oxygen saturation on room air as measured by pulse oximetry is 90%. A chest radiograph is obtained. Of the following, the MOST appropriate next step in the management of this boy is administration of.
explanation:
• Hydrocarbon ingestion can manifest in respiratory symptoms or systemic symptoms if gastrointestinal or respiratory absorption occurs.
  • Gastric decontamination (administration of syrup of ipecac or nasogastric lavage) should be avoided in cases of hydrocarbon ingestion because of the risk of aspiration.
  • Management is primarily supportive. Patients often develop bronchospasm and should be treated with a selective agent such as Albuterol, another name for Salbutamol.
  • Antibiotics are indicated only if there are signs of secondary infection (fever or progression of infiltrates on chest radiography after 48 hours).
  • Corticosteroids have not been shown to reduce respiratory symptoms or damage.

question_text: A 1½-year-old child presents with breathlessness, fever, cough, and cold. Examination shows respiratory rate of 46/min and chest retractions, but no general danger signs.What is the most appropriate management?
option_b: Give IV antibiotics and refer to higher centre
option_c: Oral antibiotics, warn of danger signs, and send home
option_d: No need of treatment only home remedies
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical manifestations indicate pneumonia based on WHO IMCI guidelines. The child presents with fast breathing (>40/min for ages 1-5 years) and chest retractions without any general danger signs.

According to standard guidelines, this classification of pneumonia requires oral antibiotic therapy (5-day course of oral amoxicillin) with careful monitoring at home, rather than hospitalization or intravenous antibiotics.

Explanation of Other Options:

Give IV antibiotics and observe (Option A):

  • IV antibiotics are reserved for severe pneumonia or cases with danger signs.
  • This level of intervention is not warranted for a case without danger signs and represents overtreatment.

Give IV antibiotics and refer to higher centre (Option B):

  • Referral to a higher center is indicated only for severe cases with danger signs such as lethargy, inability to drink, or persistent vomiting.
  • The child's current presentation does not warrant this level of care.

No need of treatment only home remedies (Option D):

  • This approach would be appropriate for cases with no fast breathing and no chest retractions.
  • Given the presence of tachypnea and retractions, antibiotics are necessary, making home remedies alone insufficient.

question_text: A 4-year-old child presented with pharyngitis, malaise and fever of 99-100 °F for 3 days, following which the child developed noisy breathing, present only on crying and a peculiar barking cough. The child was otherwise feeding well, SpO2 was 98% on room air and there was no respiratory distress. Which among the following is the first-line management?
explanation:
Since this child has fever, stridor and barking cough, the likely diagnosis is Acute Laryngo-tracheo-bronchitis, also called as Croup. Stridor only on cough or crying is mild croup while stridor at rest indicates moderate to severe croup.

Management Summary For Croup

  • Mild Croup: Manage with humidified air or oxygen and encourage fluid intake, and if needed, oral dexamethasone.
  • Moderate to Severe Croup: Administer nebulized epinephrine,
  • Hospitalization: Consider hospitalization for cases with worsening symptoms, difficulty breathing, dehydration, severe stridor at rest, hypoxia, cyanosis, depressed mental status, poor oral intake, or when reliable observation is necessary.
  • Additional Information: Nonprescription cough and cold medications should not be used in children younger than 4 years of age. Heliox (a helium-oxygen mixture) may be considered in severe croup cases when intubation is being considered, although evidence is inconclusive.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Ed, Table 15.3; Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 20th edition, pg-2034

question_text: A child is brought to the hospital with respiratory distress and biphasic stridor. The radiograph is shown below. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Acute laryngotracheobronchitis (croup) presents with biphasic stridor and a characteristic "steeple sign" on X-ray due to subglottic narrowing.

  • Laryngotracheobronchitis (Croup) is a viral infection of the glottic and subglottic regions of the airway.
  • Causative agents:
    • Most common: Parainfluenza viruses (types 1, 2, and 3) - ~75% of cases.
    • Other viruses:
      • Influenza A and B
      • Adenovirus
      • Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV)
      • Measles virus
  • Common in children aged 3 months to 5 years.
  • Peak incidence: 2nd year of life.
  • Initial Symptoms (last 1-3 days before airway obstruction)
    • Upper respiratory tract infection signs:
      • Rhinorrhea
      • Pharyngitis
      • Mild cough
      • Low-grade fever
    • Progressive symptoms:
      • Barking (seal-like) cough
      • Hoarseness
      • Inspiratory stridor
      • Fever (up to 39-40°C, or may be absent)
      • Child prefers sitting upright
      • Symptoms worse at night, recur over days, and resolve in a week
  • Physical examination findings:
    • Hoarse voice
    • Coryza
    • Mild-to-moderate pharyngeal inflammation
    • Slightly increased respiratory rate
    • Hypoxia/low SpO2 in severe airway obstruction
  • Diagnosis:
    • Clinical diagnosis based on history and exam
    • X-ray (PA neck): Steeple sign (subglottic narrowing)
  • Treatment:
    • Main goals: Airway management and hypoxia control
    • Mild Croup: Single dose of oral dexamethasone (0.6 mg/kg; 0.15 mg/kg may also be effective)
    • Moderate to Severe Croup
      • Nebulized racemic epinephrine + dexamethasone
      • Used in stridor at rest, respiratory distress, or hypoxia
      • May prevent need for intubation
    • Corticosteroids
      • Reduce laryngeal mucosal edema
      • Beneficial even in mild cases
    • Antibiotics: Not indicated (viral etiology)

Explanation of other options:

Acute epiglottitis (Option A): Presents acutely with high fever, drooling, dysphagia, and toxic appearance. The child often sits in a "tripod" position. Radiograph shows the thumb sign due to swollen epiglottis.

Foreign body aspiration (Option C): Sudden onset of cough, gagging, wheeze, or unilateral decreased breath sounds-not typically biphasic stridor. Chest X-ray may show air trapping or radiopaque objects.

Laryngomalacia (Option D): A congenital anomaly with chronic inspiratory stridor starting in early infancy, worsens with crying or feeding. Diagnosis is made by laryngoscopy, showing an omega-shaped epiglottis.

Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK441873/

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK431070/
