question_text: An 8-day-old neonate has TSH >100 mIU/L. Which investigation should be performed next?
explanation:
Explanation:

TSH >100 mIU/L strongly suggests primary congenital hypothyroidism.

  • The best next test is radionuclide scanning (Technetium-99m/Iodine-123).
  • It helps determine thyroid size, location, and function, and differentiates between thyroid dysgenesis, dyshormonogenesis, or ectopic thyroid.

Congenital hypothyroidism:

  • Most common preventable cause of intellectual disability.
  • More common in girls.
  • Thyroid dysgenesis is the leading cause.
  • Aetiology:
    • Primary hypothyroidism: thyroid dysgenesis, dyshormonogenesis, iodine deficiency, transporter defect (MCT8 mutation), maternal antibodies, maternal drugs (iodides, amiodarone, PTU, methimazole, radioiodine).
    • Central hypothyroidism: TSH β mutation, TRH mutation/receptor defect, multiple pituitary hormone deficiencies.
  • Clinical features:
    • Early: prolonged neonatal jaundice, constipation, feeding difficulty.
    • Dysmorphic: coarse facies, macroglossia, wide open fontanelles.
    • Neurological: hypotonia, slow reflexes, developmental delay.
    • Hematological: refractory macrocytic anemia.
  • Diagnosis:
    • Primary: low T4, TSH >100 mIU/L.
    • Central: low T3, T4, TSH.
    • Imaging: Technetium/Iodine scan or USG for thyroid location.
    • X-ray findings: absent femoral/tibial epiphysis, punctate epiphyseal dysgenesis, wide sutures, large fontanelle.
  • Screening:
    • Universal newborn screening using heel prick after 48-72 hrs (not earlier due to TSH surge).
    • Best approach: check both T4 and TSH.
    • ASH strategy: initial TSH screening → if >20 mIU/L → repeat → confirm with venous TSH + T4.
  • Treatment:
    • Levothyroxine is the treatment of choice.
    • Dose: newborns 10-15 μg/kg/day, children 2-4 μg/kg/day.
    • Early treatment prevents irreversible neurocognitive damage.

Explanation of Other Options:

Urine iodine excretion (Option A): used for population iodine deficiency surveys, not diagnosis of CH.

Serum thyroid receptor antibody (Option B): useful in suspected transient CH due to maternal autoimmune hypothyroidism, not first-line.

Perchlorate discharge test (Option D): used to detect organification defects (thyroid peroxidase deficiency), not initial investigation.

Key Takeaways:

  • Technetium scan is the investigation of choice after finding TSH >100 mIU/L.
  • Thyroid dysgenesis is the most common cause.
  • Early levothyroxine therapy is essential to prevent mental retardation.

question_text:
A 10-year-old boy is brought to a pediatric clinic by his parents with pain and weakness in the lower extremities for the past 3 weeks. The patient's mother says that he has been active until the weakness and pain started during his soccer practice sessions.
He says he also experiences muscle cramps, especially at night. His mother adds that, recently, the patient constantly wakes up in the night to urinate and is noticeably thirsty most of the time.
The patient denies any recent history of trauma to his legs. His vaccinations are up to date and his family history is unremarkable. His vital signs are within normal limits.
Physical examination is unremarkable. Laboratory findings are shown below:
Laboratory test Serum potassium 3.3 mEq/L Serum magnesium 1.3 mEq/L pH 7.50 Pco2 - 38 mm Hg HCO3 - 20 mEq/L Po2 - 88 mm Hg
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
explanation:
Gitelman's syndrome is a genetic disorder which results from a mutation in the sodium chloride cotransporter found in the distal convoluted tubule (see image).

This results in an impaired reabsorption of sodium in the distal convoluted tubule which is similar to patients taking thiazide diuretics.

This syndrome is characterized by mild hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, significant hypomagnesemia, and normal blood pressure.

Option A: Fanconi syndrome is a type of proximal renal tubular acidosis. It results in defective reabsorption of amino acids, potassium, phosphates, bicarbonates and glucose. The excretion of bicarbonates results in metabolic acidosis.

Option C: Bartter syndrome is an autosomal recessive condition which results from a mutation in the Na'/K'/CI- cotransporter (NKCC2). It is characterized by hypokalemia, hypochloremia, metabolic alkalosis, and normal blood pressure. These patients also have a raised plasma renin level.

Option D: Liddle syndrome affects the collecting tubules and is caused a mutation that prevents proper degradation of ENaC sodium channels, resulting in an excessive number of these active channels in the tubular epithelial surface. Typical clinical symptoms include hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and hypertension.

Learning objective: Hypokalemia can occur with or without hypertension. If a patient presents with hypokalemia and hypertension as well as metabolic alkalosis, we should think of Liddle's syndrome or Conn's syndrome.

If a patient presents with a hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with a normal to low blood pressure, we should think diuretic therapy (loop or thiazide), Gitelman's syndrome, and Bartter's syndrome. Gitelman's syndrome is a genetic disorder which results from a mutation in the sodium chloride cotransporter found in the distal convoluted tubule.

Clinically, this syndrome is characterized by mild hypokalemia, a metabolic alkalosis, significant hypomagnesemia, and normal blood pressure.

Reference: Guyton & Hall, 14th edition pg no. 575

question_text: In 21-hydroxylase deficiency, which of the following laboratory findings is typically elevated?
explanation:
• 17-Hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP) is a precursor in the cortisol synthesis pathway. In 21-hydroxylase deficiency, the enzyme block prevents 17-OHP from being converted further, leading to its accumulation. Elevated 17-OHP levels are a hallmark laboratory finding and are critical for diagnosing the condition.
  • Serum cortisol is typically low due to the enzymatic block in cortisol synthesis, which disrupts the pathway.
  • Serum aldosterone is usually low or normal, especially in the salt-wasting form, as aldosterone synthesis is impaired.
  • Serum ACTH is elevated as a compensatory response to low cortisol levels but is not the primary diagnostic marker.

Why Not Others:

  • A) Serum cortisol: Cortisol is decreased because 21-hydroxylase is essential for cortisol production.
  • B) Serum aldosterone: Often low or normal due to impaired aldosterone synthesis in this condition, leading to salt-wasting symptoms.
  • D) Serum ACTH: Elevated due to lack of negative feedback from cortisol, but it is not a specific diagnostic marker.

Key Takeaways:

  • Elevated 17-OHP is a diagnostic hallmark of 21-hydroxylase deficiency.
  • Low cortisol and aldosterone with high ACTH are characteristic findings in this enzyme deficiency.
  • CAH commonly presents with virilization in females, salt-wasting in severe cases, and increased androgen levels.

question_text: Which of the following is a common clinical feature of classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency?
explanation:
Explanation:

Ambiguous genitalia in females is a key clinical feature of classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency.

This deficiency causes decreased cortisol and aldosterone production, leading to increased ACTH and excessive androgen production, which can result in virilization of females, manifesting as ambiguous genitalia (e.g., clitoromegaly or labial fusion) at birth.

Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH)

Explanation for the other options:

  • Hypertension: Not typical in 21-hydroxylase deficiency. Hypotension occurs due to aldosterone deficiency and salt wasting.
  • Hypokalemia: Not observed in 21-hydroxylase deficiency; hyperkalemia is common due to aldosterone deficiency.
  • Hyperglycemia: Not associated with 21-hydroxylase deficiency. Reduced cortisol levels may lead to hypoglycemia instead.

Key Takeaways:

21-hydroxylase deficiency in classic CAH leads to ambiguous genitalia in females due to excess androgen production. Salt wasting and hypotension are common in 21-hydroxylase deficiency. CAH is autosomal recessive and is caused by enzyme deficiencies in adrenal steroid synthesis.

  • Congenital adrenal hyperplasia is most commonly caused by 21-hydroxylase deficiency. Severe forms present in infancy with salt-losing crises and females can have ambiguous genitalia.

question_text: A 7-year-old child of short stature presents with skin patches and learning difficulties. Diagnostic workup indicates a defect in DNA repair specifically related to double-strand breaks. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Bloom syndrome, also known as Bloom-Torre-Machacek syndrome or congenital telangiectatic erythema, is a rare autosomal recessive genodermatosis characterized by genomic instability due to mutations in the BLM gene located on chromosome 15q26.1.

The BLM gene encodes a DNA helicase (a RecQ family helicase), which plays a crucial role in DNA replication and repair, particularly in the repair of double-strand DNA breaks. Loss of helicase function leads to increased sister chromatid exchanges and chromosomal breakage, hallmark cytogenetic findings in Bloom syndrome.

Clinical features include:

  • Proportionate short stature (prenatal and postnatal growth retardation)
  • Photosensitive facial rash resembling lupus
  • Café-au-lait spots and telangiectatic skin lesions
  • Immunodeficiency, leading to recurrent infections
  • Endocrine abnormalities such as diabetes mellitus and hypogonadism
  • Intellectual disability and learning difficulties
  • Markedly increased risk of multiple malignancies (especially leukemia, lymphoma, and colorectal carcinoma)

Explanation of other options:

Xeroderma Pigmentosum (Option B): Characterized by defective nucleotide excision repair, causing inability to repair UV-induced thymine dimers, leading to extreme photosensitivity and early-onset skin cancers. The DNA defect involves single-strand damage repair, not double-strand breaks.

Cockayne Syndrome (Option C): Caused by defects in the ERCC6/ERCC8 genes, resulting in impaired transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair. Presents with growth failure, neurodegeneration, photosensitivity, and premature aging, but not associated with chromosomal breakage or malignancy.

Lynch Syndrome (Option D): Results from mutations in DNA mismatch repair genes (e.g., MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2). It predisposes to colorectal and endometrial carcinomas, but the defect is in mismatch repair, not double-strand break repair.

Key takeaways:

  • Bloom Syndrome → Defect in BLM gene, affects DNA helicase, leading to chromosomal instability.
  • Double-strand DNA break repair defect is diagnostic clue.
  • Associated with short stature, sun-sensitive rash, immunodeficiency, and high cancer risk.

References: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK448138/

question_text: A full-term neonate develops the rash seen in the image on the second day of life. The lesions consist of firm, yellow-white papules and pustules surrounded by a blotchy erythematous flare. The infant is otherwise healthy and afebrile, and the rash resolves spontaneously within a week. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

This is a classic presentation of erythema toxicum neonatorum (ETN), a common, benign, and self-limiting rash. The diagnosis is made based on the characteristic morphology (papules/pustules on an erythematous base, often called a "flea-bitten" appearance), the timing of onset (typically day 2-3 of life), its transient nature, and the sparing of palms and soles. A Wright stain of a pustule's contents would classically reveal numerous eosinophils. No treatment is required.

Explanation of Other Options:

Mongolian spots (Option B): These are benign, blue-gray macular lesions most commonly found over the lumbosacral area. They are a form of dermal melanocytosis and do not have papular or pustular components.

Transient neonatal pustular melanosis (Option C): This condition is typically present at birth. It is characterized by superficial pustules that rupture easily, leaving a collarette of fine scale and a hyperpigmented macule. A smear of the pustule contents would show neutrophils, not eosinophils.

Sebaceous hyperplasia (Option D): This appears as tiny, 1-2 mm yellow-white papules without a surrounding erythematous flare. The lesions are located on the nose and cheeks and are caused by maternal androgen stimulation of the infant's sebaceous glands.

question_text: A 5-year-old girl presents with hypertension, hypernatremia and virilization. There is also finding of hypokalemia, what is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Let us go stepwise in this question

  • This is a female infant who presented with a salt retaining crisis. Why? Because there is hypernatremia, hypokalemia and hypertension, suggesting mineralocorticoid excess.
  • Salt-retaining crisis means it is likely to be either 11 beta hydroxylase deficiency or 17 alpha hydroxylase dehydrogenase deficiency, since both present with salt-retaining crisis.
  • It cannot be 3-beta hydroxy steroid dehydrogenase deficiency, since that condition produces salt-wasting crisis.
  • It also cannot be 17 alpha hydroxylase deficiency since it presents with a normal genitalia in females.
  • Now, it is a female child with normal genitalia, so it cannot be 3 beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency, since it always presents with ambiguous genitalia. This means that the likely diagnosis is 11 beta hydroxylase deficiency.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 594; OP Ghai 10th Edition, Table 18.16; Pages 547-548

question_text: A 4-week-old male child is found to have hypoglycemia, hyperpigmented scrotum, hyponatremia and shock-like state. The external genitalia appears to be like that of a female. Which among the following hormone deficiencies can produce such a clinical picture?
explanation:
Types of CAH associated with salt losing crisis(shock, hyponatremia and hyperkalemia) are 21 hydroxylase deficiency, 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency and aldosterone synthase deficiency. And 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency produces ambiguous genitalia in both males and females.

Review of 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency

  • Deficiency of 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (3β-HSD) occurs in fewer than 2% of patients with adrenal hyperplasia. This enzyme is required for conversion of Δ5 steroids (pregnenolone, 17-hydroxypregnenolone, dehydroepiandrosterone [DHEA]) to Δ4 steroids (progesterone, 17-hydroxyprogesterone, and androstenedione).
  • Thus, deficiency of the enzyme results in decreased synthesis of cortisol, aldosterone, and androstenedione but increased secretion of DHEA The 3β-HSD isozyme expressed in the adrenal cortex and gonad is encoded by the HSD3B2 gene located on chromosome 1p13.1.
  • Because cortisol and aldosterone are not synthesized in patients with the classic form of the disease, infants are prone to salt-wasting crises.
  • Because androstenedione and testosterone are not synthesized, boys are incompletely virilized. Varying degrees of hypospadias may occur, with or without bifid scrotum or cryptorchidism. Because DHEA levels are elevated and this hormone is a weak androgen, girls are mildly virilized, with slight to moderate clitoral enlargement.
  • The hallmark of this disorder is the marked elevation of the Δ5 steroids (such as 17-hydroxypregnenolone and DHEA) preceding the enzymatic block.
  • Patients require glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement with hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone, respectively. Hormone therapy may also be needed.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 594; OP Ghai 10th Edition, Table 18.16; Pages 547-548

question_text: A 10-year-old boy presents with sexual maturity rating 5, height for age > chronological age, hyperpigmentation, short stature, and BP 180/110 mmHg. Which enzyme deficiency?
explanation:
Explanation:

In the given clinical scenario, the child is having 11β-hydroxylase deficiency which is evident from his symptoms of :

  • Precocious puberty (sexual maturity rating 5)
  • Hypertension (due to elevated deoxycorticosterone)
  • Hyperpigmentation (ACTH elevation)
  • Virilization from androgen excess

Pathophysiology:

This condition is a form of Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH) caused by a defect in the enzyme 11 β-hydroxylase, which is responsible for converting 11-deoxycortisol to cortisol and 11-deoxycorticosterone (DOC) to corticosterone in the adrenal cortex.

The deficiency leads to a decrease in cortisol synthesis, which removes the negative feedback on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis, resulting in increased ACTH secretion. The elevated ACTH stimulates adrenal hyperplasia and increases the production of steroid precursors proximal to the enzymatic block.

Explanation of Other Options:

21α-hydroxylase deficiency (Option B): Hyperpigmentation and hypertension are present in the given scenario, which are not features of this condition. It typically presents with hypotension and salt wasting due to aldosterone deficiency.

3β-dehydrogenase deficiency (Option C): Hyperpigmentation and hypertension are present in the given scenario which is not a characteristic feature of this disease. Also sexual maturity remains normal here.

Cholesterol side-chain cleavage enzyme deficiency (Option D): This condition causes poorly developed external genitalia, whereas the case described shows well-developed external genitalia (sexual maturity rating 5).

Key Takeaways:

question_text: A 2-month-old infant is presented with failure to thrive, recurrent emesis, hepatosplenomegaly, and adrenal insufficiency. Adrenal calcification is noted radiologically. The most likely diagnosis is?
explanation:
Vomiting, hepatosplenomegaly, adrenal insufficiency and adrenal calcification point to a diagnosis of Wolman Disease.

  • Wolman Disease is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage diseases that results from deficiency of lysosomal acid lipase (LAL) and accumulation of cholesterol esters and triglycerides in histiocytic foam cells of most visceral organs.
  • The LAL gene is on chromosome 10 (10q24-q25).
  • Clinical features become apparent in the 1st weeks of life and include failure to thrive, relentless vomiting, abdominal distention, steatorrhea, and hepatosplenomegaly.
  • There usually is hyperlipidemia. Hepatic dysfunction and fibrosis may occur.
  • Calcification of the adrenal glands occurs in about 50% of patients and is an important clue to the underlying diagnosis, when present.
  • Death usually occurs within the 1st 6 months of life.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 104

question_text: A 4-year child was brought with episodes of icterus and pallor. What is the probable diagnosis and the investigation done for the same?
explanation:
The peripheral smear shows Spherocytes, suggesting Hereditary Spherocytosis (HS). In the osmotic fragility test, HS erythrocytes are incubated in progressive dilutions of sodium chloride causing the cells to swell and lyse, with spherocytes lysing at a lower dilution because of their lower surface area: volume ratio. This test detects the presence of spherocytes in the blood, but it is not specific to HS.

  • Patients with hereditary spherocytosis have severe anaemia with pallor, jaundice, fatigue, and exercise intolerance. Severe cases may be marked by expansion of the diploe of the skull as a result of marrow hyperplasia (frontal bossing), but to a lesser extent than in thalassemia major.
  • The diagnosis of HS can be established from a positive family history and the presence of typical clinical and laboratory features of the disease: splenomegaly, spherocytes on the blood smear, reticulocytosis, and an elevated MCHC.
  • If these are present, no additional testing is necessary to confirm the diagnosis clinically. If the diagnosis is less certain, additional testing can be performed.
  • Binding of fluorescence labelled eosin-5-maleimide (EMA) to band 3 and other membrane proteins is decreased in HS erythrocytes. This flow cytometry-based test is easy to perform and has good diagnostic sensitivity and specificity.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 485

On exam, tonsillar inflammation, palatal petechiae, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly are identified. Which of the following describes the mode of transmission of the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Fever, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, tonsillar enlargement and palatal petechiae, especially at the junction of soft and hard palate suggest a diagnosis of Infectious Mononucleosis, caused by Epstein Barr Virus.

  • Infectious mononucleosis caused by Epstein-Barr virus and occurs most often in adolescents and young adults. Infectious mononucleosis is transmitted by salivary gland secretions, such as by sharing drinks or kissing.
  • The classic symptoms and signs of infectious mononucleosis include pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, fever, fatigue, and splenomegaly.
  • Cervical lymphadenopathy tends to affect the posterior chain more than the anterior chain.
  • Patients presenting with infectious mononucleosis may also have a rash. The rash has various presentations, including petechial, maculopapular, and urticarial variations, and occurs most often after antibiotics were inadvertently administered due to an incorrect diagnosis, such as streptococcal pharyngitis.

Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1st SA edition., pg. 1586

question_text: A 9-month-old child is passing 10 to 12 loose stools per day for last 9 days. There is no blood or mucus in stools. There is no dehydration as well. Which is the therapy of choice in such a child?

question_text: A child presents with a 4-day history of watery stools with increased frequency. On examination, the child is drowsy, unable to feed, and the skin pinch test shows very slow return. Based on the Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness (IMNCI) guidelines, how should this child be classified?
explanation:
Explanation:

The presence of frequent diarrhea for 4 days, associated with drowsiness, inability to drink or feed, and very slow skin recoil are key indicators of severe dehydration under the IMNCI classification system.

Assessment of Dehydration in Children:

  • Clinical Symptoms: Dry oral mucosa, sunken fontanelle (infants), irritability.
  • Skin Turgor: Delayed return of skin pinch indicates dehydration.
  • Capillary Refill Time: Prolonged refill suggests dehydration.
  • Urine Output: Reduced wet diapers or infrequent urination.
  • Vital Signs: Tachycardia, low blood pressure.
  • Mental Status: Lethargy, confusion, or unconsciousness point to severe dehydration.

question_text: While at school, a 6-year-old boy is noted by his teacher to experience 10- to 20-second lapses in consciousness, sometimes with clonic movements of the face. His parents have not noticed this behaviour at home. Electroencephalography shows 3 per second generalized spike and wave discharges. The MOST appropriate therapy for this boy is:
explanation:
The diagnosis is Absence Seizures

  • Absence seizures are one of several kinds of seizures, seen across childhood, adolescence and adulthood.
  • Absence seizures are characterized by a brief loss and return of consciousness, generally not followed by a period of lethargy (i.e., without a notable postictal state)
  • Hallmark is EEG showing 3 Hz (3/Sec) Generalized spikes and slow waves, also called as Spike & Dome pattern of electrical discharges.
  • Treatment of patients with absence seizures only is mainly with valproic acid or ethosuximide, which are of equal efficacy controlling absences in around 75% of patients.

question_text: Which among the following is contraindicated in childhood dysentery?
explanation:

Similarly, antiemetic agents, such as the phenothiazines, are of little value and are associated with potentially serious side effects (lethargy, dystonia, malignant hyperpyrexia).

Incorrect Options:

  • Option B- Ondansetron is safe and a useful adjunct in troublesome vomiting.
  • Option C- Probiotics can be given but are not routinely indicated.
  • Option D- Remember: Ciprofloxacin is the drug of choice in childhood dysentery.

question_text: EEG of which of the following epilepsy syndrome shows centrotemporal spikes?
explanation:
• Rolandic epilepsy now called as Benign childhood epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes.
  • It is characterized by focal seizures, where the child wakes up from sleep with focal seizure and preserved consciousness.
  • As the name suggests it is benign condition and resolves with age (mostly by 12 years). EEG shows spikes in centrotemporal regions.

Option B: Landau-Kleffner syndrome has normal EEG findings or Bitemporal discharge.

Option C: Lennox-gastaut syndrome has 1-2 Hz spike-and-slow waves, polyspike bursts in sleep, and a slow background in wakefulness. Point to note is that it is generalized discharge and not focal.

Option D: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy EEG has generalized 4-5 Hz polyspike and slow wave discharges. Again, a generalized discharge.

KEY TAKEAWAYS: Rolandic Epilepsy is benign condition and resolves with age (mostly by 12 years). EEG shows spikes in centrotemporal regions.

question_text: Regarding childhood UTI, all of the following are true except?
option_a: Most childhood UTI are caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae
option_b: All recurrent UTI need USG Abdomen on follow-up
option_c: MCU may be needed in recurrent UTI
option_d: Bladder and bowel dysfunction increases the risk of UTI in children
explanation:
Let us evaluate each option individually

  • Option A is False. UTIs are caused primarily by colonic bacteria as per Nelson. Escherichia coli causes 54-67% of all UTIs, followed by Klebsiella spp. and Proteus spp., Enterococcus, and Pseudomonas. Other bacteria known to cause UTIs include Staphylococcus saprophyticus, group B streptococcus, and, less commonly, Staphylococcus aureus, Candida spp., and Salmonella spp.
  • Option B is True. All recurrent UTI need USG Abdomen after therapy is over, to rule out any bladder-related anatomic abnormality as a cause of recurrent UTI.
  • Option C is True. AAP Practice Recommendations as well as Nelson suggest that MCU, also called VCUG, is recommended in recurrent UTI as a part of work-up for likely etiology & rule out Vesico-Ureteric Reflux (VUR).
  • Option D is True. In a child with recurrent UTIs, identification of predisposing factors is beneficial. Bowel and bladder dysfunction is a very important contributor to recurrent UTIs and is one of the main reasons for an increase in UTIs around the time of toilet training.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 553

question_text: An 18-month-old child presents with hepatosplenomegaly, a hemoglobin level of 7 g/dL, a white blood cell count of 50,000 cells/cu.mm, and petechiae and purpura. What is the recommended drug treatment for this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

Vincristine + Prednisolone is the standard induction regimen for childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), the most likely diagnosis in this child.

  • The child presents with anemia, thrombocytopenia, leukocytosis, hepatosplenomegaly, and petechiae, which are classic features of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL)-the most common leukemia in children.
  • Initial treatment (induction phase) for ALL aims to achieve complete remission and involves:
    • Vincristine (microtubule inhibitor, halts cell division)
    • Prednisolone (a glucocorticoid, induces apoptosis in lymphoblasts)
  • These agents form the backbone of initial therapy, especially in low-risk or standard-risk ALL.
  • Phases of ALL treatment:
    • Induction therapy: Vincristine + Prednisolone (± L-asparaginase, daunorubicin based on risk stratification)
    • Consolidation: To eliminate residual disease and CNS-directed therapy
    • Maintenance therapy: To prevent relapse using methotrexate, 6-MP, etc.
    • Supportive care: Includes acyclovir for viral prophylaxis and cotrimoxazole for pneumocystis prophylaxis.

Explanation of other options:

IVIG (Option B): Used in immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), not in leukemia. It reduces immune-mediated platelet destruction but doesn't treat leukemic cell proliferation.

L-Asparaginase + Prednisolone (Option C): While this combination is also used in ALL therapy, it typically forms part of expanded induction or consolidation phases. Vincristine + Prednisolone is more appropriate for initial induction.

Daunorubicin + Prednisolone (Option D): This combination is more commonly used in acute myeloid leukemia (AML). In ALL, daunorubicin is reserved for high-risk or poor prognosis subtypes.

question_text: Which of the following malignant tumors, commonly found in children, has a high tendency to spread to the bone marrow?
explanation:
Explanation:

Neuroblastoma is an embryonal tumor of neural crest origin that arises from sympathetic nervous tissue, most commonly from the adrenal medulla or paraspinal sympathetic ganglia.

It is the most common extracranial solid tumor of childhood and the most frequent malignancy in infants.

A hallmark feature of neuroblastoma is its propensity to metastasize to bone marrow, which can lead to:

  • Pancytopenia,
  • Bone pain, and
  • Characteristic "raccoon eyes" (periorbital ecchymosis due to orbital metastasis).

Bone marrow involvement is a major criterion in staging and carries a poor prognosi

Explanation of Other Options:

Wilms tumor (Option A):

A malignant renal tumor in children that primarily metastasizes to the lungs and liver. Bone marrow involvement is rare.

Adrenal gland tumors (Option C):

Usually spread to liver, lungs, and regional lymph nodes, not bone marrow.

Granulosa cell tumor of ovary (Option D):

A sex-cord stromal tumor, uncommon in children. It spreads mainly within the peritoneal cavity and regional lymphatics, with no predilection for bone marrow

question_text: During the surgery for acute appendicitis in a 2-year-old child, the surgeon discovered that the appendix was not inflammed. What is the most probable diagnosis in this case?
explanation:
Explanation:

The description - a 2-inch-long structure located 2 feet from the ileocecal valve - fits the classic "Rule of 2s" of Meckel's diverticulum, the most common congenital anomaly of the gastrointestinal tract.

It results from incomplete obliteration of the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct during the 7th-8th week of gestation.

Explanation of Other Options:

Sarcoma (Option A): Sarcomas are malignant tumors originating from mesenchymal tissues and present as firm, irregular solid masses that may invade surrounding structures and metastasize. They do not appear as diverticular outpouchings or occur 2 feet from the ileocecal junction.

Appendicitis (Option B): Appendicitis refers to inflammation of the appendix, which is located at the base of the cecum-not 2 feet proximal to the ileocecal valve. The appendix, typically measuring 5-10 cm, arises from the cecum at the point where the teniae coli converge.

Zenker's diverticulum (Option D): Zenker's diverticulum is a pulsion diverticulum found in the upper esophagus, specifically between the inferior pharyngeal constrictor and the cricopharyngeus muscles. It usually affects elderly individuals and presents with symptoms such as difficulty swallowing and regurgitation of undigested food.

Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK499960/

question_text:
A 3-year-old child presents with a history of haematuria for 2 days. On examination there is a ballotable abdominal mass. Investigations to be performed are mentioned below.
1. CT abdomen
2. PET
3. FNAC
4. Biopsy
What all investigations should be done?
explanation:
Ballotable abdominal mass with haematuria in a 3-year-old child is highly likely to be of renal origin, likely Wilms tumour.

  • CT abdomen helps to differentiate cystic and solid mass and also helps in the staging of the disease.
  • PET is indicated for suspected malignancy to know the location of metastasis.
  • FNAC and biopsy are generally avoided in a suspected Wilms tumour during initial work-up to avoid seeding and upstaging.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 526; OP Ghai 10th Edition, Pages 636-638

question_text: A 4-year-old child is brought in with a 14 cm firm, tender swelling in the flank that has been progressively enlarging over the past few weeks. On examination, the child looks generally well but has discomfort due to the mass. The lump is non-mobile, non-fluctuant, and firm, with no overlying skin changes or signs of infection. No additional symptoms are reported. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Wilms' tumor (nephroblastoma) is a malignant renal tumor that most commonly occurs in children under 5 years of age. The presentation in this case - a large, firm, non-mobile flank mass - is highly suggestive of Wilms' tumor.

  • It is the most frequent kidney malignancy in the pediatric population, with the majority of diagnoses made before age five.

Explanation of Other Options:

Angiomyolipoma (Option B): These are benign renal tumors usually seen in adults. Although they may present with a palpable renal mass, they are exceedingly uncommon in young children, making this diagnosis unlikely here.

Renal Cell Carcinoma (Option C): This is the predominant kidney cancer in adults. It rarely affects children, and both the age of the patient and the clinical features make it an improbable diagnosis in this scenario.

Neuroblastoma (Option D): The most common extracranial solid tumor of childhood, typically arising from the adrenal gland. Unlike Wilms' tumor, neuroblastomas often cross the midline and are associated with systemic features such as fever, irritability, weight loss, or paraneoplastic syndromes (e.g., opsoclonus-myoclonus).

question_text: Incorrect statement regarding retinoblastoma?

option_b: Optic nerve involvement is considered to be a bad prognostic sign
option_c: Despite good radiosensitivity, mainstay of management is chemotherapy and surgery
option_d: Enucleation is needed in anterior chamber involvement
explanation:
The degree of tumour differentiation in retinoblastoma does not appear to be associated with the prognosis. Hence, option A is incorrect.

About other options:

  • Option B is correct - Poor prognostic indicators in RB include Optic nerve involvement, Orbital involvement and Massive choroidal invasion
  • Option C is correct- Though RB is highly radio-sensitive, the mainstay of therapy is Chemotherapy, with or without surgery. OP Ghai 10th Edition says that for smaller tumours, Argon or diode Laser can be used. For larger lesions, Chemotherapy is used, which enables salvaging the affected eye, avoiding enucleation or external beam radiotherapy and risk of secondary malignancies. Chemotherapy utilizes a combination of Vincristine, Carboplatin and Etoposide.
  • Enucleation (done with a part of optic nerve) is needed if
    • Tumour is involving > ½ of retina
    • Optic nerve is involved
    • Glaucoma develops due to Anterior chamber involvement

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 636; Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 529

question_text: A 6-year-old child was brought to her paediatrician for routine well-childcare. Her physical examination is normal except for a systolic murmur and a widely split-second heart sound that does not vary with respiration. She has no family history of heart disease. Which among the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The systolic murmur and a widely split-second heart sound in an otherwise normal child indicate an atrial septal defect.

Atrial septal defects

Atrial septal defects account for about 5-10% of all congenital heart diseases.

There are of three main types:

  • Ostium primum type
    • Associated with cardiac conduction defects, mitral valve prolapse, and an increased risk of mitral regurgitation.
  • Ostium secundum type
    • The most common form, seen in more than 70% of cases.
  • Sinus venosus type (rare)

Patent foramen ovale (PFO) is not considered ASD, PFO is a benign lesion


Clinical Manifestations:

  • Most children are asymptomatic
  • Failure to Thrive
  • Exercise Intolerance

Physical Examination Findings:

  • Widely Split and Fixed S2
    • The second heart sound is split and fixed due to increased right ventricular diastolic volume.
  • Systolic Ejection Murmur
    • Soft murmur at the left upper sternal border, caused by increased flow across the right ventricular outflow tract.
  • Mid-Diastolic Murmur
    • Rumbling murmur at the lower left sternal border due to increased flow across the tricuspid valve.

Treatment

  • Small ASD usually spontaneously close (Esp. Size <8mm)
    • If not Transcatheter device closure is done
  • Ideal age for device closure is 2-4 years.

Explanation of other options:

Total anomalous pulmonary venous connection (Option A): Children with Total anomalous pulmonary venous connection will not be asymptomatic and often present with cyanosis and congestive cardiac failure with equal saturation levels across all four heart chambers. Examination findings of fixed split S2, systolic ejection murmur, and cyanosis are seen. Ventricular septal defects (Option B): In ventricular septal defect (VSD), a left-to-right shunt occurs, and the clinical presentation depends on the size of the defect. It may range from being asymptomatic with normal pulmonary artery pressure and only a loud, harsh, or blowing holosystolic murmur, to severe cases with pulmonary hypertension and features of congestive heart failure. Pulmonary stenosis (Option D): Pulmonary stenosis is the narrowing of the pathway from the right ventricle to the pulmonary artery, possibly affecting the infundibulum, valve, or main pulmonary artery. It is a component of the Tetralogy of Fallot and often presents with severe cyanosis from birth. The clinical findings include an ejection click heard after S1 (closer to S1 as the severity increases) and a split S2 in moderate to severe cases.

question_text: Which of the following is true regarding paediatric cardiopulmonary resuscitation?
option_a: Chest compression at the rate of 30:2 with 2 rescuers
option_b: Adenosine via intraosseous is preferred over other methods
option_c: In chest compression, depth must be at least 1/3rd of AP diameter of the child's chest
option_d: Adrenaline given in dose 0.01 mg/kg iv/io in 1:1000 concentration
explanation:
Explanation:

In pediatric CPR, the recommended depth for chest compressions is at least one-third the anterior-posterior (AP) diameter of the chest. This translates to approximately 4 cm in infants and 5 cm in children.

Compressions should be performed at a rate of 100-120/min, with proper technique such as the two-thumb encircling method for infants.

Full chest recoil must be allowed between compressions. Adrenaline is indicated if the heart rate remains <60/min despite effective ventilation and compressions, with a dose of 0.01 mg/kg of 1:10,000 solution IV/IO, repeated every 3-5 minutes if needed. The compression-to-breath ratio varies depending on the number of rescuers but is 3:1 in neonates.

question_text: A child is brought to the paediatrician with short stature. On evaluation, growth hormone levels are found to be high and insulin-like growth factor (IGF-1) levels are low. Which among the following could be the likely associated abnormality?
explanation:
Explanation:

The raised levels of growth hormone and low levels of IGF-1 suggest growth hormone insensitivity which is due to GH receptor anomaly.

  • GH stimulates the liver to produce insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), which in turn promotes the growth of bones and tissues.
  • If there is a GH-receptor anomaly in the liver, leads to GH insensitivity.
  • Hene, IGF-1 is not sufficiently produced lowering its concentration in the body.

Growth Hormone Receptor anomalies:

  • Laron syndrome: Mutation of the GH receptor leading to growth hormone insensitivity.
  • The GH receptor has an extracellular, transmembrane, and intracellular domain.
  • Mutation of the extracellular domain
    • Affects the binding of the hormone
    • GH-binding protein activity is low
  • Mutation of the transmembrane domain:
    • Affects the anchoring of the receptor to the plasma membrane
    • Normal or high GH-binding protein
  • Mutation of the intracellular domain:
    • Interferes with JAK/STAT signaling

Explanation of other options:

GH deficiency (Option A): If the child had GH deficiency, both GH and IGF-1 levels would typically be low.

GHRH deficiency (Option B): Growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) deficiency would typically lead to low GH secretion because GHRH stimulates the release of GH.

IGF-1 deficiency (Option D): Low IGF-1 levels can cause short stature, but the presence of high GH levels suggests that the issue lies not in the production of IGF-1 but in the action of GH itself.

Explanation of Incorrect Answers:

question_text: A 4-year-old boy presents following a head injury while running around at nursery and fell over in the playground 3 hours ago. The fall itself was unwitnessed, but the teacher stated that she saw him performing jerking movements on the ground immediately after. He is brought to you while he had vomited twice on the way. He had not vomited at school. On examination, there is no focal neurological deficit, he obeys motor commands, eyes open spontaneously but is confused. He has a laceration measuring 7cm above his Right eye. He has is known case of epilepsy. Which of the following is an indication for a CT head in this case?
explanation:
A GCS of <15 2 hours after the injury, or a GCS of <14 on initial assessment are both indications for a CT head.

  1. Clinical Symptoms:
    • Loss of consciousness (LOC) or altered mental status (e.g., Glasgow Coma Scale ≤15).
    • Persistent headache or vomiting (>2 episodes).
    • Post-traumatic seizures.
    • Amnesia regarding the event.
    • Signs of raised intracranial pressure (e.g., papilledema, unequal pupils).
  2. Physical Examination Findings:
    • Focal neurological deficits (e.g., hemiparesis, cranial nerve palsies).
    • Suspected skull fracture:
      • Open or depressed skull fracture.
      • Battle sign or raccoon eyes (suggestive of basal skull fracture).
    • Scalp hematoma or penetrating head injury (especially in children <2 years).

Option A: He has a diagnosis of epilepsy so is not an automatic indication for CT on its own.

Option B: Vomiting is an indication for further observation, but not an indication for CT head on its own.

It is also worth noting that in adults only 1 episode of unexplained vomiting is required for a CT head, due to vomiting being a common response to pain and trauma in children.

Option C: An unwitnessed fall is common in children, and is not an indication on its own.

KEY TAKEAWAYS: Early imaging ensures prompt diagnosis of life-threatening conditions like intracranial hemorrhage, cerebral edema, or herniation. Avoid unnecessary CT to reduce radiation exposure, particularly in paediatric patients.

question_text: Not useful in the management of hyperkalemia?

Incorrect Options:

  • Salbutamol nebulization:
    • Salbutamol(a beta-2 agonist) helps reduce serum potassium levels by promoting the movement of potassium into cells. This makes salbutamol nebulization an effective treatment in the acute management of hyperkalemia.
  • Calcium gluconate:
    • Calcium gluconate is used in hyperkalemia to stabilize the myocardial membrane and prevent cardiac arrhythmias associated with elevated potassium. It doesn't lower potassium levels but helps protect the heart, especially in severe hyperkalemia.
  • Insulin and Dextrose:
    • Insulin and dextrose are used together in the treatment of hyperkalemia. Insulin helps drive potassium into cells, while dextrose prevents hypoglycemia caused by insulin administration. This is a key treatment strategy for lowering serum potassium levels in hyperkalemia.

Key Takeaway:

  • IV Magnesium Sulphateis not commonly used in the management of hyperkalemia because it doesn't directly lower potassium levels or stabilize cardiac function. The other treatments-salbutamol nebulization, calcium gluconate, and insulin with dextrose-are directly involved in addressing the elevated potassium levels or protecting the heart in cases of hyperkalemia.

question_text: A child with Kawasaki Disease underwent echocardiography and was found to have a giant aneurysm on Right Coronary Artery, for which he was hospitalized and managed. Which among the following is a cut-off to define a giant coronary artery aneurysm in a Kawasaki Disease patient?
explanation:
In KD Patients, large or giant coronary artery aneurysms are responsible for most of the morbidity and mortality.

  • Large or giant aneurysms have been defined by the 2017 American Heart Association (AHA) as having a z score ≥10 or an absolute dimension of ≥8 mm.
  • Japanese Classification of Aneurysms in KD
    • Small: ≤4 mm internal diameter [ID])
    • Medium (>4 to ≤8 mm ID)
    • Giant (>8 mm ID).
  • Specifically, large or giant aneurysms are associated with the greatest risk of thrombosis or stenosis, angina, and myocardial infarction.
  • Rupture of a giant aneurysm is a rare complication that generally occurs in the 1st months after illness onset and may present as hemopericardium with tamponade.
  • Axillary, popliteal, iliac, or other arteries may also become aneurysmal, but always in the setting of giant coronary aneurysms.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 191

question_text: The most common bony finding on a skeletal radiograph in JIA is which of the following?
explanation:
X-ray findings in JIA include:

  • Soft Tissue Swelling: Early in the disease, x-rays may show signs of soft tissue swelling around the affected joints, which is a sign of inflammation.
  • Osteopenia (Bone Density Loss): Decreased bone density, particularly around the inflamed joints, can appear early due to inflammation and reduced use of the joint.
  • Joint Space Narrowing: Chronic inflammation leads to cartilage loss, resulting in reduced space between bones in the joint. This is often seen in more advanced cases.
  • Bony Erosions: In some cases of aggressive JIA, particularly polyarticular and systemic types, inflammation can cause bony erosions or small areas where bone is destroyed near the joint.
  • Growth Disturbances: In children, chronic inflammation in a joint can interfere with normal bone growth, potentially leading to limb-length discrepancies, joint deformities, or growth plate abnormalities.
  • Fusion of Joints (Ankylosis): In severe or untreated cases, the joint can undergo fusion or ankylosis, where the bones grow together, limiting movement. This is particularly noted in the spine or wrist joints in certain types of JIA.

KEY TAKEAWAYS: The most common finding on radiograph is normal bone and joint, followed by periarticular osteopenia. Noting osteopenia on radiograph, however, implies that over 50% of the bone mineral content has been lost due to the inflammation.

Other findings, such as joint space narrowing, periosteal new bone formation, and most ominous, erosions, are late findings in JIA.

question_text: A 2-year-old boy presents with a fever since 2 weeks and loss of appetite. He is miserable, complaining of pain in his neck, and has not been able to walk over the last 3 days. explanation:
Systemic-onset JIA is one of the more serious type of JIA with significant morbidity and mortality.

  • It is associated with fever that rises to 39.5°C for the first 2 days before the diagnosis is made. Fever occurs late in the afternoon or evening and returns to normal, or below normal, in the morning. The child looks ill and miserable, with a salmon-coloured, evanesvent skin rash on the trunk and thighs. The rash may sometimes be itchy.
  • Up to three quarters of patients will have enlarged lymph nodes, spleen and liver.
  • Pericardial and myocardial involvement may also occur in the form of serositis.
  • Pulmonary disease can occur, with infiltrates, pleurisy and pulmonary fibrosis.
  • Arthritis occurs in approximately three-quarters of cases and usually involves the wrists, knees and ankles, but the temporomandibular joints and hands can also be affected.
  • The condition usually lasts between 2 and 5 years before remitting.

question_text: All of the following are consistent with the cardiac complications described in Kawasaki Disease, except?
explanation:
Small pericardial effusions can occur in KD, but they are never big enough to produce cardiac tamponade. Let us review what Nelson 21st Edition Says

  • Cardiac involvement is the most important manifestation of KD.
  • Myocarditis occurs in most patients with acute KD and manifests as tachycardia disproportionate to fever, along with diminished left ventricular systolic function.
  • Occasionally, patients with KD present in cardiogenic shock (KD shock syndrome ), with greatly diminished left ventricular function.
  • Case series of KD shock syndrome indicate that these patients may be at higher risk for coronary artery dilation.
  • Pericarditis with a small pericardial effusion can also occur during the acute illness.
  • Mitral regurgitation of at least mild severity is evident on echocardiography in 10 - 25% of patients at presentation but diminishes over time, except among rare patients with coronary aneurysms and ischemic heart disease.
  • Up to 25% of untreated patients develop CAA in the 2nd to 3rd week of illness; initially these are usually asymptomatic and detected by echocardiography

question_text: A 1-year-old boy, is brought to OPD. He has had a high temperature for the last week. His mother has taken him to the general practitioner on two occasions and he has completed a course of amoxicillin. His eyes are injected and his throat is red. He has marked cervical lymphadenopathy. The skin on his fingers has started to peel. Everyone else in the family is well. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• The child fulfils the major diagnostic criteria for KD
  • Option C: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome has areas of denuded skin as well as fever and malaise.
  • Option D: Scarlet fever has inflammation of the throat but usually a generalized maculopapular rash. This may be followed by peeling of the skin of fingers and toes.
  • Option A: Failure to respond to antibiotics might make you consider tuberculosis but his clinical features, especially peeling of the skin, do not fit this diagnosis.

KEY TAKEAWAYS: Kawasaki disease is a rare, inflammatory condition that primarily affects children under 5 years old. It causes inflammation in the blood vessels, particularly the coronary arteries, which supply blood to the heart. Symptoms include high fever lasting more than five days, rash, swollen lymph nodes, red eyes, red, cracked lips, and a "strawberry" tongue.

question_text: Which of the following is the most common complication associated with Kawasaki disease?
option_c: Congestive cardiac failure due to mitral regurgitation
explanation:
• Most common complication associated with KD is Myocarditis. It might be asymptomatic or present with congestive cardiac failure.
  • Most common cause of death is Thrombosis of Coronary artery aneurysm (CAA).

Other complications include:

  • Kawasaki disease shock syndrome
  • Mitral regurgitation
  • Asymptomatic pericardial effusion

KEY TAKEAWAYS: Myocarditis, or inflammation of the heart muscle, is a recognized complication of Kawasaki disease. It occurs due to the widespread inflammation in blood vessels and heart tissue that characterizes the disease. Myocarditis in Kawasaki disease can lead to symptoms such as rapid or irregular heartbeat, chest pain, fatigue, and in severe cases, heart failure.

question_text: A child is diagnosed with Kawasaki disease and is given a dose of IVIG and aspirin. After 48 hours of dose, the high-grade fever continues. Which of the following is not a treatment option?
explanation:
• IVIG-resistant Kawasaki disease occurs when a patient with Kawasaki disease does not respond to initial treatment with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG).
  • Typically, children with Kawasaki disease are treated with a single dose of IVIG and aspirin, which reduces inflammation and lowers the risk of complications. However, about 10-20% of children do not respond to IVIG treatment, continuing to have fever and signs of inflammation after treatment.
  • IVIG-resistant Kawasaki disease increases the risk of coronary artery complications, as persistent inflammation can damage the heart's blood vessels. In these cases, alternative treatments may be used, including:
    • Corticosteroids (such as methylprednisolone)
    • Infliximab or other tumor necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitors
    • Other immunosuppressive agents, such as cyclosporine or methotrexate, in severe cases

KEY TAKEAWAYS: The child is suffering from IVIG resistant KD which is defined as non-resolution of fever 36 hours after infusion of complete dose of IVIG.

question_text: A 4-year-old boy presents with persistent fever, conjunctival redness, and peeling erythematous skin. A 2D echocardiogram reveals coronary aneurysms. What is the first-line treatment for this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The given presentation-fever, conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue, and erythematous desquamation-together with coronary aneurysms, is characteristic of Kawasaki disease (mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome). The mainstay of treatment is intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) along with aspirin, which reduces vascular inflammation and lowers the risk of coronary complications.

  • Etiology and Pathophysiology
    • More common in children of Asian descent.
    • Vasculitis involving medium-sized vessels, particularly coronary arteries.
  • Pathology
    • Acute Phase (Days 1-10): Neutrophilic vascular inflammation, cellular infiltration, vessel edema.
    • Subacute Phase (Weeks 2-4): Risk of fusiform coronary aneurysm formation.
    • Convalescent Phase (>4 weeks): Healing with risk of arterial wall scarring and stenosis.
  • Clinical Features
    • Fever lasting ≥5 days.
    • Extremities: Redness, swelling, peeling skin of fingers, toes, and nails.
    • Mucocutaneous Signs: Bilateral conjunctivitis, cracked red lips, strawberry tongue, pharyngeal erythema.
    • Rash: Polymorphous (macular, papular, or target-like).
    • Cervical Lymphadenopathy: Usually unilateral and tender.
  • Diagnosis
    • Requires fever ≥5 days plus at least 4 of the 5 "CREAM" features:
      • C: Conjunctivitis (bilateral, non-purulent)
      • R: Rash (predominantly truncal)
      • E: Erythema/Edema of palms and soles ± desquamation
      • A: Adenopathy (cervical, usually unilateral)
      • M: Mucosal changes (strawberry tongue, red lips)
    • Supportive labs: Elevated CRP, ESR, WBC.
    • Echocardiography: Coronary aneurysms.
  • Complications
    • Myocardial infarction.
    • Coronary artery aneurysms.
    • Coronary stenosis.
  • Differential Diagnosis
    • Scarlet fever.
    • Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome.
  • Treatment
    • IVIG: Reduces inflammation and lowers coronary aneurysm risk.
    • Aspirin: High-dose for fever/inflammation, then low-dose for antiplatelet effect.
    • IVIG-Resistant KD: Consider repeat IVIG, corticosteroids, or other immunosuppressants (e.g., infliximab, cyclosporine).

Explanation of other options:

Aspirin (Option A): Important adjunct but not effective as monotherapy; always combined with IVIG.

Clopidogrel (Option C): Used in selected coronary complications, not standard first-line therapy.

LMWH (Option D): Reserved for significant thrombotic complications, not part of initial management.

Key Takeaways:

  • IVIG + aspirin is the first-line treatment for Kawasaki disease.
  • Diagnosis requires fever ≥5 days + ≥4 of the 5-"CREAM" criteria.
  • Coronary aneurysm is the most feared complication.

question_text: Not a feature of Kawasaki disease?
option_d: Peeling of skin of finger tips
explanation:
Kawasaki disease (KD)

  • Formerly known as mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome and infantile polyarteritis nodosa
  • 2nd Most common vasculitis in children after HSP & MC in India, Asia
  • A type of medium vessel vasculitis
  • Diagnosis: KD is essentially a clinical diagnosis and there are no laboratory tests that are pathognomonic of KD. Features include:
  1. Fever persisting at least 5 days
  2. Presence of at least 4 principal features: Changes in extremities:
  • Acute: Erythema of palms, soles; edema of hands, feet
  • Subacute: Periungual peeling of fingers, toes in weeks 2 and 3
  1. Polymorphous exanthem
  2. Bilateral bulbar conjunctival injection without exudate
  3. Changes in lips and oral cavity: erythema, lip cracking, strawberry tongue, diffuse injection of oral and pharyngeal mucosa
  4. Cervical lymphadenopathy (>1.5 cm diameter), usually unilateral

Exclusion of other diseases with similar findings should be made.

  • KD is diagnosed if fever along with 4 criteria is present.
  • KD is called "Incomplete KD" if fever with only 2 or 3 criteria are present
  • KD is called "Atypical KD" if additional CNS or hepatobiliary involvement is prominently seen.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 658, Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 191

question_text: A 4-year-old girl presents with difficulty in going upstairs and leg pains. She is always tired, feels hot and has had some weight loss. The family doctor has seen her on several occasions for erythematous papules on the dorsum of hands. The muscle enzyme is 1500 mmol/l, and ESR is 90, with thrombocytosis. Lactate dehydrogenase is high, as is ANA. Likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Juvenile dermatomyositis is the most common inflammatory myopathy in children. The gene related to HLA-DQA1*0501 is found in 80% of patients with JDM. It can progress slowly with fatiguability, a low-grade fever and loss of weight, all of which are common.

  • The rash usually appears first over exposed areas, followed by proximal weakness. Periorbital violaceous (heliotropic) erythema occurs across the nasal bridge and around the eyelids. It may involve the upper torso, hands and especially the knuckles. Facial oedema is common.
  • Creatinine kinase will be very high, and aldolase, serum aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) will be high, but not specific. An MRI scan is also helpful in diagnosis by using T2-weighted images and fat suppression. This will show the active site of the disease, helping muscle biopsy and EMG testing.
  • Corticosteroids, methotrexate and cyclosporine can be used in management. Long-term complications are calcification and calcified nodules with cardiomyopathies.

Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1st SA edition, pg. 1182

question_text:
A 5 year old child, presents to you as she has been unwell for 2 weeks with lethargy, fever and painful wrists and knees. On examination she has a temperature of 38.5° C and a subtle erythematous rash on her trunk. You identify that several joints are swollen, warm, and painful to move, including the wrists, her right elbow, the knees, her left ankle and left hip. She has some cervical lymphadenopathy and her spleen is palpable. You perform some blood tests and get the following results:

What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• Systemic-onset juvenile idiopathic arthritis is the most likely diagnosis, as she has a systemic illness, polyarthritis (more than four joints) and a salmon-pink rash. The raised neutrophil count and markedly raised ESR are consistent with the diagnosis.

Criteria for the Classification of Juvenile Rheumatoid Arthritis

  • Age at onset: <16 years
  • Arthritis (swelling or effusion, or the presence of ≥2 of the following signs: limitation of range of motion, tenderness or pain on motion, increased heat) in ≥1 joint
  • Duration of disease: ≥6 weeks
  • Onset type defined by type of articular involvement in the 1st 6 months after onset:
    • Polyarthritis: ≥5 inflamed joints
    • Oligoarthritis: ≤4 inflamed joints
    • Systemic-onset disease: arthritis with rash and a characteristic quotidian fever
  • Exclusion of other forms of juvenile arthritis

Option A: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia needs to be considered, but is less likely as the child has numerous joints affected and the blood film is normal.

Option B: Post-streptococcal arthritis is unlikely as the antistreptolysin O titre is normal, although a repeat blood test is required to confirm that the titre remains low.

Option C: SLE may have similar clinical features but is unlikely as the ANA (antinuclear antibody) and double-stranded DNA are negative. SLE is also very uncommon at this age.

KEY TAKEAWAYS: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA) is the most common type of arthritis in children, characterized by persistent joint inflammation lasting more than six weeks in children under 16, with no identifiable cause ("idiopathic"). JIA can cause joint pain, swelling, warmth, and stiffness, particularly in the morning or after inactivity.

question_text: Which among the following is effective in systemic onset JIA (SoJIA)?
explanation:
Systemic onset JIE, also called SoJIA requires is an autoinflammatory disorder.

  • Severe JIA patients may be responsive to Methotrexate.
  • Short course of Oral Corticosteroids, followed by Anakinra/Tocilizumab/Cankinumab is needed in SoJIA.

question_text: Most common cause of death in a child of Kawasaki Disease between 3rd to 6th week of illness?
explanation:
Coronary Artery Aneurysms (CAAs) tend to develop between 2nd to 3rd week of illness and thrombosis of these is considered to be the most common cause of death in KD patients.

  • CAAs tend to form in 20-25% of untreated cases, 15% of IVIG-resistant cases and <5% of adequately treated IVIG-responsive cased of KD.
  • Myocarditis is the most common complication of KD but is usually manageable and causes mortality due to CCF only in the early parts of illness if its severe or in the presence of co-existing complications.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 191, OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 659

question_text: A 3 1/2-year-old child presented with high fever for one-week, cervical lymphadenopathy, red eyes, few erythematous papules on trunk and tongue as shown in the picture. What is the most likely complication you will anticipate in the first 7-10 days of illness?
explanation:
The clinical description along with the image showing Strawberry Tongue is suggestive of Kawasaki Disease.

  • Myocarditis is the most common clinical complication, frequently encountered in the first 1-2 weeks of illness. Usually subclinical, can sometimes produce CCF and very rarely, mortality.
  • The more dreaded complication is Coronary Artery Aneurysm, occurring between 2nd to 3rd weeks of illness. Can cause mortality and is the overall most common cause of death in KD.
  • As per OP Ghai 10th Ed, CAAs can occur in 15-25% of untreated KD and even in 3-5% of treated KD patients.

Reference: OP Ghai Essential Pediatrics, 10th Edition, Page Number-659; Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics, 21st Edition, Chapter 191.

question_text: Peak age for Kawasaki disease?
explanation:
More than 80% cases of KD patients are children below 5 years of age, with peak cases between 18-24 months of age.

  • Also note that KD is the only vasculitis which is never seen in adults. (Old AIIMS MCQ)

question_text: "White strawberry tongue" is seen in a febrile child, as shown in the picture. What can be the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
In both Scarlet fever as well as early Kawasaki disease, tongue initially shows a coated appearance or whitish lingual plaques with underlying hypertrophied papillae, producing the so-called "White Strawberry tongue". These whitish lesions are shed over 2 to 3 days to produce denuded, erythematous patches with prominent papilla, producing the so-called "Red Strawberry Tongue".

question_text: Which of the following statement regarding Kawasaki disease is true?
option_a: Associated with coronary artery aneurysm in up to 25% of untreated cases
option_b: It is the most common cause of vasculitis in children
option_c: IV immunoglobulin are recommended only if coronary artery is involved
option_d: Lymph node biopsy is used for diagnosis
explanation:
Approximately 20-25% of untreated children develop coronary artery abnormalities (CAA) including aneurysms in KD. Also, it is the 2nd MC cause of vasculitis in children after HSP. IVIG is indicated in all cases and the diagnosis is made clinically.

question_text: A 2 year old child was clinically diagnosed as Kawasaki disease and started on IVIG infusion, which was given in a dose of 2 g/kg and completed over 10 hours. He was also give aspirin in a dose of 80 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses. More than 48 hours later, the child continues to have high grade fever. Which among the following is true regarding this child?
option_a: Repeat dose of IVIG followed by steroids will be needed
option_b: Double dose of IVIG and aspirin are indicated
option_c: Cyclophosphamide is the next line of management
option_d: Risk of coronary artery aneurysm is decreased by IVIG even if fever persists
explanation:
If fever persists for > 36 hours after completion of 1st dose of IVIG infusion, it’s called IVIG-resistant KD.

  • Such patients have an especially high risk of developing Coronary Artery Aneurysms
  • Therapeutic options for the child with IVIG resistance include a 2nd dose of IVIG (2 g/kg), a tapering course of corticosteroids, and/or infliximab

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 659, Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 191

question_text: True statement about Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis is?
option_a: Rheumatoid factor is an important diagnostic test to perform in suspected cases
option_d: Methotrexate is the first line drug in therapy
explanation:
Regarding JIA

  • Option A is False. Less than 10% of the cases have positive RF. A more useful antibody to test for is the anti-nuclear factor (ANF), which is seen in most children with pauci-articular JIA.
  • Option B is True. Oligoarticular JIA, where 4 or less joints are involved, is the overall most common type of JIA.
  • Option C is False. Cervical spine involvement is as common as 50% of cases.
  • Option D is False. The first line drugs are NSAIDs, then low-dose methotrexate is considered.

Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1st SA edition, pg. 1179

question_text: A 3 year old child presented with High grade fever, desquamating rash on the body, lymphadenopathy, conjunctivitis and Strawberry tongue in the mouth. Which among the following can be used to clinically distinguish Kawasaki Disease from Scarlet Fever?
explanation:
A common clinical problem is the differentiation of scarlet fever from KD in a child who is a group A streptococcal carrier.

  • Patients with scarlet fever typically have a rapid clinical response of fever to appropriate antibiotic therapy. Such treatment for 24-48 hr with clinical reassessment generally clarifies the diagnosis.
  • Furthermore, ocular findings are quite rare in group A streptococcal pharyngitis and may assist in the diagnosis of KD.
  • Please remember that fever in KD is high-grade, daily, lasting 5 days or longer and is generally unresponsive to beta-lactam antibiotics.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 191

question_text:
A 5/10 year old male was admitted with complaints of fatigue and joint pains. On examination, a rash was found on the hands as shown in the image.

What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The image shows a rash over the knuckles and extensor surfaces of the fingers, which is characteristic of Gottron's papules, a hallmark of Juvenile Dermatomyositis (JDM).

Other options:

(A): Nodules in Juvenile RA: Juvenile Rheumatoid Arthritis can present with joint pain and systemic symptoms

(C): Osteoarthritis: Joint degeneration, stiffness; rare in children, no rash.

(D): Sclerodactyly: Tight, thickened skin on fingers; seen in systemic sclerosis, no Gottron's papules.

Key takeaways:

Juvenile dermatomyositis (JDM) is the most common inflammatory myositis in children, distinguished by proximal muscle weakness and a characteristic rash.


Reference: Nelson textbook of paediatrics

question_text: ACTH is used in the treatment of which of the following?
explanation:
Management guidelines of West syndrome - AOCN 2021 Guidelines

Therapy Of Choice: Hormonal Therapy

  • ACTH is the preferred agent
  • High-Dose Regimen) is used: ACTH 150 U/m2 or 6 U/Kg IM OD x 2 weeks
  • If unavailable, high-dose Prednisolone (4 mg/kg/day) for 2 weeks

Vigabatrin= VGB: Given if ACTH/Steroids fail or are Contraindicated

Incorrect Options:

  • JME (Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy): JME is typically managed with valproate, levetiracetam, or lamotrigine, not with ACTH. ACTH is not a treatment for juvenile myoclonic epilepsy.
  • Rolandic Epilepsy: Rolandic epilepsy, also known as benign epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes, is a self-limiting condition that usually resolves by adolescence. Treatment is typically not required for most cases, though carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine may be prescribed for intractable cases. ACTH is not used.
  • LGS (Lennox-Gastaut Syndrome): Lennox-Gastaut syndrome is a severe epileptic encephalopathy often managed with multiple medications, including valproate, lamotrigine, and topiramate. While ACTH may sometimes be used, it is not considered the first-line treatment. The mainstay treatment for LGS involves polytherapy with antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) rather than ACTH.

Key Takeaway:

  • West Syndrome(infantile spasms) is primarily treated with ACTH or high-dose steroids like prednisolone, with vigabatrin as an alternative when first-line treatments fail or are contraindicated.
  • ACTH is not used for other forms of epilepsy like JME, Rolandic Epilepsy, or LGS.

Reference: Nelson textbook of paediatrics

question_text: Which of the following is not a first line of investigation in a child suspected to be having Acute Myeloid Leukemia?
explanation:
• Bone marrow examination (including aspirate and trephine biopsy) is a definitive investigation to diagnose AML but would not be safe, tolerated or efficient as a first line investigation.
  • The most important initial investigations are a full blood count and blood film. If both are within normal range, acute leukaemia can be ruled out with a relative degree of certainty. Typically, the full blood count will demonstrate pancytopenia (due to bone marrow infiltration by blasts). Although the patient is likely to be neutropenic, many circulating blasts tend to dramatically elevate the overall white cell count, with blasts clearly visible on blood film.
  • In some cases, the white cell count may be only slightly raised and, if blasts remain sequestered within the bone marrow, it may even be lower than normal. Clearly identifiable blasts are not always present on a film. In these cases, the only clue that there is a serious underlying problem may be a few atypical cells in the blood film or the presence of leukoerythroblastic features.

KEY TAKEAWAYS: Bone marrow examination (including aspirate and trephine biopsy) is a definitive investigation to diagnose AML.

question_text:
A 2 yrs. old boy fall from bed. He developed swelling of knee. On examination boy has a hematoma of knee, no history of past surgery, trauma, medications, boy has family history of bleeding.
Following aspiration of hematoma patient develop profuse bleeding
Lab Ix:- platelet: normal, BT: normal, PT: 12s, aPPT: 60 sec, specific factor assay: factor 8 activity <1%
Which of the appropriate mode of the inheritance for the above case?
explanation:
• Coagulation Defect: The laboratory findings indicate a coagulation defect:
    • Normal: Bleeding time and platelet count.
    • Prolonged aPTT indicates an issue with the intrinsic pathway, commonly associated with hemophilia.
    • Decreased Factor VIII activity (< 1%) confirms a diagnosis of Hemophilia A.
  • Family History: The presence of a family history of bleeding suggests a hereditary condition, which aligns with the characteristics of hemophilia.
  • Mode of Inheritance:
    • Hemophilia A is inherited in an X-linked recessive
    • Males (like the patient) are affected if they inherit the mutant gene on the X chromosome, while females are typically carriers unless they inherit two copies of the mutant gene.

Why Not Other Options

  • B (X-linked dominant):
    • Conditions with X-linked dominant inheritance usually affect females more severely than males, leading to more severe manifestations in females who inherit the gene. Hemophilia A is X-linked recessive, primarily affecting males.
  • C (Autosomal recessive):
    • Autosomal recessive conditions require two copies of the mutant gene for the disease to manifest. Hemophilia A does not fit this model since it is X-linked and affects males with a single copy of the mutant gene.
  • D (Autosomal dominant):
    • In autosomal dominant conditions, only one copy of the mutant gene is needed for the phenotype to be expressed, leading to a 50% chance of inheritance from an affected parent. Hemophilia A is not inherited in this manner.

Key Takeaways:

  • Correct Answer: Option A, X-linked recessive.
  • Condition: Hemophilia A, characterized by low Factor VIII and prolonged aPTT, fits the inheritance pattern of X-linked recessive.

Tags: Inicet nov 2020

Tag: Vascular physiology

Level: Must know

Reference: Guyton and Hall the text of Physiology, John E Hall & Michael E Hall, 14th Edition, Page No.485

question_text: A 4-month-old formula-fed infant presents with rectal bleeding without emesis or diarrhea. She was born at term and has not been previously ill. Her weight gain has been appropriate since birth, tracking in the 75th percentile on standardized growth curves. The child is afebrile, with normal vital signs, and appears normal on examination. Of the following which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• The most common causes of rectal bleeding in the infant periodare a milk protein allergy and an anal fissure. The patient in the case presentation has no physical examination finding, so milk protein allergy is more likely.
  • Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is typically seen in premature infants. NEC can rarely occur in term infants with an associated infection. However, with a normal physical examination and no emesis, this diagnosis is unlikely.
  • Patients with UC do not gain weight well
  • Salmonella infection typically results in other symptoms such as fever and emesis.

question_text: Which of the following is the most common cause of shock in paediatric patient?
explanation:
• Dehydration (hypovolemic) shock is the most common type of shock in paediatric population.

Common Causes in Paediatrics

  • Gastrointestinal Losses:
    • Diarrhea (e.g., rotavirus, cholera).
    • Vomiting.
  • Hemorrhage:
    • Trauma (e.g., accidents).
    • Post-surgical bleeding.
  • Burns:
    • Fluid loss through damaged skin.
  • Other Causes:
    • Inadequate fluid intake (e.g., neglect, illness).
    • Third-spacing (e.g., sepsis, nephrotic syndrome).
  • Septic shock is most common in neonates.

question_text: A 3-year-old girl comes to urgent care because since she woke up that morning she has been 'clumsy' and 'has been falling much more than usual.' She has not vomited. On examination, she is afebrile and well appearing. There is horizontal nystagmus on end-gaze bilaterally. When she reaches for a toy, her accuracy is poor bilaterally. Her gait is wide-based and she tends to veer to the side and prefers to walk along the hallway wall to help her balance. Her mother informed that about 10 days earlier she had a febrile illness with itchy vesicular rash which subsided with crusting. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Acute cerebellar ataxia is an infectious or postinfectious process that typically affects preschool aged children.

  • For those in the postinfectious category, there is often a history of a recent febrile or GI illness.
  • It is important to rule out more serious causes of new ataxia in young children, such as a posterior fossa mass or a cerebellar hemorrhage, with brain MRI. However, most children with cerebellar hemorrhage are not well appearing and the onset of ataxia is quite acute.
  • Ataxia from a posterior fossa mass is usually more insidious in onset, unless there has been bleeding into the mass.
  • Hydrocephalus can cause gait disturbance; however, it would not explain the nystagmus or limb ataxia.
  • Young children with Guillain-Barre syndrome are sometimes initially mistaken as being ataxic when they have a lower extremity weakness from ascending paralysis. As a result, in this age group it is important for the clinician to always question whether what they are calling acute-onset ataxia could actually be weakness.

Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1st SA edition, pg. 2886

question_text: Cryoprecipitate will control bleeding due to deficiency of all of the following except?
explanation:
In emergencies when factor IX is unavailable, only FFP is used as cryoprecipitate does not contain factor IX.

  • Cryoprecipitate contains Fibrinogen, VWF, factor VIII, XIII & fibronectin, but no Factor IX.
  • Hence it will not be useful in Factor IX deficiency, i.e., Hemophilia B

question_text: Which of the following is associated with an increased risk of thrombosis?
explanation:
Prothrombin G20210A mutation occurs in approximately 3% of the general population and increases the risk for thrombosis mainly by causing excess prothrombin production.

Regarding other options

  • Factor V deficiency is associated with increased bleeding, not with increased thrombosis. (Factor V Leiden is the most common inherited thrombophilia and the mutation causes a resistance of factor V to inactivation by activated proteins C and S.)
  • Patients with nephrotic syndrome, not nephritic syndrome, are at an increased risk of thrombosis due to loss of clotting factors in the urine.
  • Hyperhomocysteinemia is a risk factor for thrombosis and stroke in children, but not Homocysteine Deficiency.

Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 1st SA edition, pg. 2393
