question_text: A child presents with fatigue, bone pain, and bleeding gums. Examination reveals petechiae on the skin. Which vitamin supplementation will treat this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical picture is suggestive of scurvy, resulting from a deficiency of vitamin C.
This condition arises due to defective collagen synthesis, which leads to fragile blood vessels and connective tissue defects.

Vitamin C plays a crucial role in collagen production, and its deficiency manifests with symptoms such as fatigue, bone pain, gum changes, and easy bruising. Administration of vitamin C usually leads to marked improvement within a few days.

Features of Vitamin C Deficiency (Scurvy):

Differentiation:

Explanation of other options:

Vitamin A (Option A): Deficiency mainly impacts vision and epithelial health, leading to night blindness and xerophthalmia. It is not associated with the bleeding or musculoskeletal symptoms described in this scenario.

Vitamin D (Option B): Deficiency results in rickets among children, characterized by bone deformities and growth retardation. Although it may cause bone pain, it does not produce bleeding tendencies or gum-related issues.

Vitamin E (Option C): Deficiency predominantly leads to neurological problems such as cerebellar ataxia and retinopathy. It is not linked to bleeding disorders or the musculoskeletal manifestations observed in this case.

Key takeaways:

  • Vitamin C deficiency → impaired collagen formation → bleeding and bone pain.
  • Rapid recovery after supplementation.

question_text: Which of the following is the most common type of ectopic tissue found in Meckel's diverticulum?
explanation:
Rule of 2's in Meckel's Diverticulum

  • Seen in 2% population

  • Presents before 2 years of age
  • 2 inches length

Ectopic tissue common in meckel diverticulum:

Gastric tissue(>50% cases)>Pancreatic tissue>jejunum

question_text: A 13-year-old girl had complaints of increased bleeding after dental extraction. Local hemostatic measures failed and she was evaluated. Her PT was normal. Which of the following is correct about the diagnosis in this patient?
explanation:
Let us evaluate the individual options

  • Options B & C are ruled out since they are X-linked recessive and will occur in only boys.
  • Option D will have a prolonged PT and hence ruled put
  • Now option A can present with such a picture. By far, the most common type of VWD is type 1 disease, with a parallel decrease in VWF protein, VWF function, and FVIII levels, accounting for at least 80% of cases. In type 1 VWD, patients have predominantly mucosal bleeding symptoms, although postoperative bleeding can also be seen. Bleeding symptoms are uncommon in infancy and usually manifest later in childhood with excessive bruising and epistaxis. Because these symptoms occur commonly in childhood, the clinician should particularly note bruising at sites unlikely to be traumatized and/or prolonged epistaxis requiring medical attention.
  • As per Harrison 21st Edition, Type 1 VWD may first manifest with dental extractions, particularly wisdom tooth extraction, or tonsillectomy.

question_text: A child presents with bruising, petechiae, and occasional minor epistaxis that does not interfere with daily activities. Workup confirms a mild case of immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP). What is the preferred management approach?
option_c: A single dose of intravenous immunoglobulin
explanation:
Explanation:

In a patient with mild ITP who has bruising, petechiae, and occasional minor epistaxis but minimal interference with daily activities, the preferred approach is watchful expectancy.

  • Indications for Observation:
    • Platelet count >30,000/μL
    • Mild symptoms (bruising, petechiae, minor epistaxis)
    • No interference with daily activities
  • Management Approach:
    • Watchful expectancy: Regular follow-up, monitoring platelet counts and bleeding signs.
    • Education & counseling: Inform parents/patient about bleeding precautions, when to seek care.
    • Avoid unnecessary medications to prevent side effects.
  • Follow-Up:
    • Serial platelet counts (weekly or biweekly initially)
    • Symptom diary for bleeding episodes
  • Natural Course:
    • Most children with acute mild ITP recover within 3-6 months.
    • Chronic cases (>12 months) are less common.

Explanation of Other Options:

Short course corticosteroid therapy (Option A):

  • Reserved for moderate-to-severe ITP or significant bleeding risk.
  • Effective but has side effects (weight gain, hypertension, mood changes, immunosuppression).
  • Not indicated in mild, asymptomatic cases.

Intravenous anti-D administration (Option B):

  • Used in Rh-positive children with moderate/severe ITP requiring rapid platelet increase.
  • Risks: hemolysis, anemia, fever.
  • Not appropriate for mild, minimally symptomatic ITP.

A single dose of intravenous immunoglobulin (Option C):

  • Aggressive and costly therapy reserved for:
    • Severe thrombocytopenia (<5,000/μL)
    • Active or high-risk bleeding
  • Not warranted in mild cases; observation is sufficient.

question_text: A 5-year-old boy presented to ER with acute onset hematemesis and Hb of 6.2 g/dl. Due to hemodynamic instability, he was given fluid boluses for resuscitation & initiation of initial management of upper GIT bleeding was started. All of the following are indicated prior to endoscopy, during management except?
option_a: BT to maintain Hb above 10 g/dl
option_d: Octreotide infusion if variceal bleed suspected
explanation:
In any child presenting with upper GIT bleeding, the principles to be followed in management include, sequentially as below:

  1. Ensuring A, B, C and noting vitals.
  2. If hemodynamically unstable or in shock, obtain IV access and give Fluid boluses for resuscitation
  3. As soon as cross-matched blood is available, start PRBC blood transfusions. However, do not over transfuse, as overtransfusion and targeting Hb>10 g/dl can elevate portal pressure and further worsen bleeds. Target Hb is 7-9 g/dl in children and 8-10 g/dl in adults.
  4. Start Pantoprazole infusion IV in all patients and consider Octrotide OV infusion, especially if variceal bleeding is suspected
  5. Giving 1 dose of IV Erythromycin has prokinetic action and is given prior to Endoscopy
  6. Endoscopy is diagnostic and therapeutic and must be done within 6-12 hr of admission.
  7. Further management depends on endoscopic findings, whether variceal or non-variceal bleeds.
  8. Variceal bleeds usually require Endoscopic Sclerotherapy or Endoscopic Band Ligation.

Reference: AIIMS PICU Protocols 2022; OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 326

question_text: A 3-year-old boy presents with fever, rash, bleeding gums, and a positive tourniquet test. His platelet count is 25,000/mm³. Which of the following is the most important prognostic feature in this clinical scenario?
explanation:
Explanation:

In a suspected case of dengue hemorrhagic fever, platelet count is the most important prognostic indicator, directly correlating with bleeding risk.

  • This clinical presentation; fever, rash, bleeding gums, positive tourniquet test, and thrombocytopenia (25,000); is strongly suggestive of Dengue Hemorrhagic Fever (DHF) or Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura (ITP).
  • In such settings, platelet count is a critical parameter used to monitor the severity of thrombocytopenia and to guide risk of bleeding and decisions like hospitalization or platelet transfusion.
  • Key prognostic roles of platelet count in Dengue:
    • Risk of spontaneous bleeding increases sharply when platelet count falls below 20,000/mm³.
    • Helps classify severity and need for inpatient management.
    • Guides decisions on fluid resuscitation and platelet support.

Explanation

Elevated total leukocyte count (Option B): May indicate secondary infection but is not a key prognostic marker in bleeding complications of dengue or ITP.

Hematocrit (Option C): In dengue shock syndrome, hematocrit helps assess plasma leakage, but bleeding risk is more directly related to platelet count.

Peripheral smear (Option D): Useful for identifying morphological changes or ruling out leukemias or infections, but not prognostic in acute bleeding risk management.

question_text: A 1-week-old presents to your office with bruising and coffee ground emesis. She was a term baby who was born at home and is now exclusively breastfed. Her PT is prolonged >100 seconds, and her aPTT is relatively normal. This patient has?
explanation:
A Neonate delivered at home would not have likely got Vitamin K injection at birth. Now she is presenting with bleeding manifestations.

  • Classical vitamin K deficiency bleeding in newborns presents in the first week of life. Typical symptoms include easy bruising, mucus membrane bleeding, and hematemesis.
  • Risk factors include babies who have not been given vitamin K treatment, are breastfed, or are poor feeders.
  • Such patients will have low levels of vitamin K-dependent factors: II, VII, IX, and X.
  • Prothrombin time will be prolonged
  • Factor V and VIII levels are unaffected.

Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 1st SA edition, pg. 2397

question_text: A 2-week-old with epistaxis, rectal bleeding, umbilical bleeding since birth. Normal PT, aPTT, thrombin time, platelets. Positive urea clot solubility test. Deficient factor?
explanation:
Explanation:

The given clinical feature is characteristic of Factor XIII (FXIII) deficiency, also known as Laki-Lorand factor deficiency.

It is a rare bleeding disorder that manifests with delayed umbilical cord separation, poor wound healing, and severe bleeding episodes, including intracranial hemorrhage.

Factor XIII deficiency presents with:

  • Delayed umbilical separation and bleeding
  • Normal screening tests (PT, aPTT, TT, platelets)
  • Positive urea clot solubility test (diagnostic)
  • Characteristic: Bleeding despite normal coagulation screen

FXIII plays a crucial role in stabilizing fibrin clots by catalyzing the cross-linking of fibrin polymers, thereby strengthening the clot and preventing premature dissolution. The acquired form of FXIII deficiency is more common than the congenital type and may result from hyperconsumption, hemodilution, or decreased synthesis.

question_text: Which among the following is the procedure of choice in aspirated foreign bodies in lower airway in children?
explanation:
Rigid bronchoscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic procedure in children who aspirate foreign body into the lower airway in children.

  • Flexible fiberoptic bronchoscopy is sensitive to visualize but cannot be used to remove stuck FB.
  • As per Nelson 21st Ed, "The treatment of choice for airway foreign bodies is prompt endoscopic removal with rigid instruments by a specialist (otolaryngologist or pulmonologist)."
  • Potential complications of rigid bronchoscopy include bronchospasm, desaturation, bleeding, and airway edema, in addition to the inherent risks of anesthesia.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 414.

question_text: A 4-year-old male patient is admitted with features of raised intracranial pressure & papilledema on fundus examination. His GCS was 9/15 and had Cushing's triad. He was started on IV mannitol & neuroimaging performed. Presence of which among the following would indicate adding dexamethasone to the management?
option_a: Presence of Cushing's triad with papilledema
explanation:
This is a case of raised ICP.

  • Indication to use Corticosteroids, e.g., Dexamethasone in raised ICP include vasogenic edema produced by intracranial space-occupying lesions (ICSOLs) like Cysts, Abscesses and Tumours.
  • Corticosteroids are avoided in raised ICP due to trauma, stroke and active bleeding
  • Also remember that any GCS<8 in raised ICP will need intubation, not steroids.
  • Cushing's Triad includes Bradycardia, Hypertension and Irregular Respiration. It simply indicates raised ICP, along with papilledema and is not used to decide management.

Reference: AIIMS PICU Protocols 2022; Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 85

question_text: A 5-year-old was well till 2 days back when he has profuse bleeding from nose. You suspect him as an ITP initially but then decide against it. Which of the following will indicate that the diagnosis is NOT ITP and something else?
option_a: If patient has >2 episodes of epistaxis in 24 hr
explanation:
Acute ITP is quite common in children and can indeed present with epistaxis and petechiae. However, presence of hepatosplenomegaly, generalized lymphadenopathy and pancytopenia usually indicate an etiology other than ITP.

Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 1st SA edition, pg. 2402

question_text: Reduced levels of which clotting factor can produce Hemophilia C?
explanation:
Factor XI deficiency is an autosomal recessive deficiency associated with mild to moderate bleeding symptoms and is also called as Hemophilia C.

  • The bleeding tendency is not as severe as in factor VIII or factor IX deficiency. The bleeding associated with factor XI deficiency is not correlated with the amount of factor XI.
  • Because factor XI augments thrombin generation and leads to activation of thrombin-activatable fibrinolysis inhibitor, surgical bleeding is more prominent in sites of high fibrinolytic activity such as the oral cavity.
  • Also note that Deficiency of factor V is an autosomal recessive, mild to moderate bleeding disorder that has also been termed parahemophilia . Hemarthroses occur rarely; mucocutaneous bleeding and hematomas are the most common symptoms. Severe menorrhagia is a frequent symptom in women.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapters 503.2 and 503.7

question_text: Which of the following statements about Hemophilia A is incorrect?
option_a: It is an X-linked recessive disorder
option_b: It is caused by deficiency of clotting factor VIII
option_c: It presents as frequent mucosal bleed
explanation:
Hemophilia A is X linked recessive disorder of defective synthesis of clotting factor VIII.

  • As it is an X linked recessive, it will affect mostly males.
  • Any clotting factor defect will present with deep tissue bleeding like joint bleeds, muscle bleeds etc.
  • Any platelet defect will present with superficial bleeds like petechiae and mucosal bleeds.

Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 20th ed., pg. 2385

question_text: A 10-year-old boy presented with complaints of recurrent bleeding. There was also a history of joint pains. There was no mucosal bleeding. Which coagulation factor deficiency can be responsible?
explanation:
Mucosal bleed and cutaneous bleeds are more with Platelet defects. Deep tissue bleeding like joint bleed or muscle bleeds are common with clotting factor deficiencies.

  • Hence, best answer among the options with be Factor 8 & 9 deficiency i.e. Hemophilia A and B.

question_text: A 12-year-old with a history of recurrent infection and bleeding gums. On investigations the patient had pancytopenia and the peripheral smear showed macrocytes. Bone marrow biopsy showed no megakaryocytes and filled with fat globules, your diagnosis?
explanation:
The hallmark of aplastic anemia is peripheral pancytopenia, coupled with hypoplastic or aplastic bone marrow.

Regarding other options

  • ITP has only thrombocytopenia hence ruled out.
  • Myelodysplasia and PNH have pancytopenia but bone marrow is cellular.

This condition is typically caused by a deficiency in certain clotting factors-most commonly Factor VIII in Hemophilia A and Factor IX in Hemophilia B. Because it is X-linked, hemophilia primarily affects males, while females can be carriers.

question_text: A 5 years old boy is troubled by recurrent nose bleeds, the last of which took 1.5 hours to stop. He has no other medical problems. His examination is normal except for pale conjunctivae. Investigation reveals: Hb- 8.6 gm/dL; WBC -10.2x10<sup>9</sup>/L; Platelet count- 350x10<sup>9</sup>/L; Prothrombin time- 16 seconds (control: 12-15 s); Activated partial thromboplastin time -46 seconds (control: 25-35 s); Fibrinogen: 2.5 g/L (normal: 2-4 g/L); Factor VIII: just below the normal range. What is the most likely cause of his bleeding?
explanation:
• On investigation, hemophilia A and von Willebrand disease (vWD) will both have a deranged activated partial thromboplastin time. However, in hemophilia A it is much more pronounced. The clinical features are also less pronounced in vWD, as in this child.

Von Willebrand Disease (VWD) is a common inherited bleeding disorder caused by a deficiency or dysfunction of von Willebrand factor (VWF), a protein that helps blood clot.

  • Cause: Genetic defect affecting von Willebrand factor, impacting blood clotting.
  • Types:
    • Type 1: Partial quantitative deficiency of VWF (most common and mildest).
    • Type 2: Qualitative defects in VWF (subtypes 2A, 2B, 2M, 2N).
    • Type 3: Near-total or complete absence of VWF (most severe and rare).
  • Symptoms:
    • Frequent nosebleeds
    • Easy bruising
    • Heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding
    • Prolonged bleeding after injuries or surgeries
  • Diagnosis: Blood tests measuring VWF levels, activity, and factor VIII levels.
  • Treatment:
    • Desmopressin (DDAVP): Helps release stored VWF in mild cases.
    • VWF concentrates: For severe cases or surgery.
    • Antifibrinolytic agents: Prevents breakdown of clots.

Option B: Spontaneous soft-tissue bleeding, such as large hematomas, does not occur in vWD. A family history is common.

Option D: ITP is ruled out as platelet counts are normal.

Option C: Vitamin K deficiency presents very early, mostly in neonatal or infancy.

KEY TAKEAWAYS: On investigation, hemophilia A and von Willebrand disease (vWD) will both have a deranged activated partial thromboplastin time. However, in hemophilia A it is much more pronounced. The clinical features are also less pronounced in vWD, as in this child.

question_text: You are counseling a father about the treatment options for his child with β-thalassemia major. In addition to the increased risk of infection, splenectomized patients are at an increased risk of which of the following?
explanation:
• Splenomegaly can be a complication of chronic transfusions, which is the mainstay of treatment for thalassemia major.
  • Chronic transfusions can decrease extramedullary hematopoiesis and prolong and improve quality of life. However, patients who develop splenomegaly have an increased transfusion requirement due to the associated hypersplenism and increased RBC clearance. As a result, splenectomy can be recommended.
  • It is well known that asplenic patients are at higher risk of infection from encapsulated organisms, and should be immunized prior to splenectomy. However, these patients are also at higher risk for thrombosis and pulmonary hypertension.

Incorrect Options: There is no known association between splenectomy and renal failure, malignancy, aplastic anemia, or increased bleeding.

question_text: Which of the following conditions can result in dactylitis?
explanation:
Dactylitis is a common manifestation in sickle cell anemia due to vaso-occlusion in the small bones of the hands and feet, which can cause pain and swelling.

Hemophilia: Characterized by bleeding disorders, not dactylitis.

Dactylitis, also known as"sausage digit,"refers to the painful swelling of fingers or toes, often due to inflammation.

question_text: All of the following are true regarding Hemophilia A, Except?
explanation:
• Any clotting factor defect will present with deep tissue bleeding like joint bleeds, muscle bleeds etc.
  • Any platelet defect will present with superficial bleeds like petechiae and mucosal bleeds.

Hemophilia A is an X-linked recessive disorder characterized by defective synthesis of clotting factor VIII. It is a clotting factor defect, which typically presents with deep tissue bleeding like hemarthrosis (bleeding into the joints).

As it is X linked recessive, it will affect mostly males.

Incorrect Options:

  • X-linked recessive inheritance:
    • Hemophilia A is indeed inherited in an X-linked recessive This means the defective gene is located on the X chromosome, and it primarily affects males. Females are generally carriers but can be affected if both X chromosomes have the defect, though this is rare.
  • More common in males:
    • As hemophilia A is an X-linked recessive disorder, it is more common in males because they have only one X chromosome. If that X carries the defective gene, they will manifest the disease. Females, with two X chromosomes, would need both X chromosomes to carry the defective gene to be affected, which is much rarer.
  • Due to Factor VIII deficiency:
    • Hemophilia A is caused by a deficiency of Factor VIII, which is essential for blood clotting. This leads to poor clot formation and difficulty stopping bleeding after injury, especially in deep tissues like joints and muscles.

KEY TAKEAWAYS:


Reference: Nelson textbook of paediatric

question_text: In her second pregnancy, the patient's baby was born with anemia, severe jaundice and edema. The baby showed neurological symptoms of kernicterus. Which of the following is the cause of the features seen in the baby?
option_a: The mother's blood group is A positive. The baby's blood group is A negative.
option_b: The mothers blood group is A negative the babies blood group is A positive
option_c: The mother's blood group is A positive. The baby's blood group is B positive.
option_d: The mother's blood group is B negative. The baby's blood group is A negative.
explanation:
Erythorbalstosis foetalis/Hydrops Fetalis:

  • Definition: A severe condition characterized by an abnormal accumulation of fluid in the fetal compartments.
  • Cause: Often occurs when an Rh-negative mother carries an Rh-positive fetus, leading to the mother's immune response.

Rh Incompatibility Mechanism:

  • Maternal Response: An Rh-negative mother exposed to Rh-positive antigens develops antibodies (agglutinins) against them.
  • Subsequent Pregnancies: In future pregnancies, these antibodies can cross the placenta and attack the fetal red blood cells, causing hemolytic disease of the newborn (erythroblastosis fetalis).

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

Option A: Incorrect because Rh-positive mothers do not produce antibodies against Rh-negative babies.

Option C: Incorrect as A/B antibodies (from blood type incompatibility) do not cross the placenta.

Option D: Incorrect due to the absence of Rh incompatibility in Rh-positive mothers.

Key Takeaways:

Erythroblastosis is seen in a Rh positive baby (2nd pregnancy) in Rh negative mother, who has Rh positive baby in 1st pregnancy. Rh antibodies are IgG type (can cross placenta). ABO antibodies are Ig M type (cannot cross placenta).

Level: Must Know

Tag: Vascular physiology

Reference: Ganong's review of medical physiology, 26th edition, Page 1279-1280

question_text: A child with anemia is found to have the following peripheral smear finding. What is the likely possibility?
explanation:
The peripheral smear is showing hypersegmented neutrophil.

  • In megaloblastic anemias, a complete hemogram with red cell indices shows macrocytosis with MCV>110 fl and cytopenias.
  • Hypersegmented neutrophils, with nucleus >6 lobes as well as macrocytes on peripheral smear may be seen and are clues to underlying megaloblastic anemia.

Reference: OP Ghai 9th Ed/Page 335

question_text: A 3-year-old child presented with trouble walking to paediatrician. He is diagnosed with DMD (Duchenne muscular dystrophy) by polymerase chain reaction. Genetic analysis shows that the patient's gene for the muscle protein dystrophin on X chromosome contains a mutation. Mutation is found in its promoter region. Which would be the most likely defective process in this child?
option_b: Post translational modification in dystrophin protein
option_d: Post transcriptional modification in dystrophin mRNA
explanation:
Option A & Option B: Translation is synthesis of protein from mRNA. Mutation in promoter regions does not lead to any problem during translation or post translational modifications. A deficiency of dystrophin mRNA will result in a deficiency in the production of the dystrophin protein.

Option C: Mutations in the promoter typically prevent formation of the RNA polymerase II transcription complex, resulting in a decrease in the initiation of mRNA synthesis during transcription.

Option D: Post transcriptional modifications like capping, splicing and tailing defects are not a consequence of promoter mutations.

Reference: Harper’s illustrated biochemistry 32nd edition CH 36 PN 379

question_text: A 1-year-old boy is presented with an episode of loss of consciousness followed by jerky movements of his arms and legs for 30 seconds. After this episode, he immediately regained consciousness. The child began crying after his 4-year-old brother snatched a toy from him. The brief shrill cry was followed by a period of expiration; he then turned blue. He had a similar episode 1 week ago when his mother refused to give him ice-cream. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
explanation:
• This patient's episode of cyanosis with loss of consciousness following emotional upset (i.e.,frustration) and vigorous crying is indicative of a breath-holding spell.It typically manifest between the age of 6–18 months.
  • They are typically triggered by emotional distress, as is the case in this patient. The typical sequence includes crying, exhaling, and holding the breath, followed by cyanosis and loss of consciousness. Patients usually resume breathing and regain consciousness in less than 1 minute. Most importantly, parents should be reassured that the condition is benign and their child will outgrow it by the age of 4–8 years.
  • The diagnosis is usually based on the clinical features and a detailed description of the episode; no treatment is required. Parents should be aware of the triggers of breath-holding spells, such as tantrums, minor injuries, and distress. However, they should not avoid reprimands for fear of triggering an episode.
  • Since several studies suggest an association between breath-holding spells and iron-deficiency anemia, confirmatory tests (e.g., CBC, serum ferritin) may be considered. Iron supplements may decrease the frequency of breath-holding spells in these children.

question_text: Which one of the following murmur characteristics supports the diagnosis of an innocent murmur?

question_text: Which among the following is the drug of choice in patients with KD?

question_text: A 3-year-old girl presented with fever since 3 days, vomiting, photophobia, neck stiffness and papilledema. You decide to investigate the child before starting therapy. Which among the following is the investigation of choice in this child?
explanation:
The child has features suggestive of meningitis. Normally, lumbar puncture for CSF analysis is considered the investigation of choice.

  • However, the child is also having papilledema, which suggests a strong possibility of raised ICP.
  • Now, raised ICP is an absolute contraindication for performing LP.
  • Thus, we need to do a non-invasive test, which is sensitive and gives good confirmation of the likelihood of meningitis.
  • Contrast-enhanced CT Scan (CECT) is usually preferred in such cases since it not only delineates meninges inflammation with good sensitivity but can also show dilated ventricles and other sequels associated with raised ICP.
  • Transcranial USG cannot be performed with a good sensitivity in a 3 year old child since the anterior fontanelle will already be closed.
  • MRI Brain is sensitive for picking up inflammation but is time-consuming and can only be done in a stable patient, not in someone with acutely elevated ICP.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 621

question_text: A child is diagnosed with Acute Rheumatic Fever. He also has migratory polyarthritis. Which among the following shall be the preferred drug in the treatment?

  • No carditis, only arthritis or other manifestations: Use Aspirin

Dose of Steroids- Prednisolone 2 mg/kg for 3 weeks, then tapered over 9 weeks; total duration is 12 weeks

question_text: Which of the following is a characteristic of Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis (LCH)?
explanation:
Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis (LCH) is a rare disorder characterized by the proliferation of abnormal Langerhans-like cells. The hallmark feature includes the presence of Birbeck granules, which are tennis racket-shaped organelles seen in the cytoplasm of LCH cells under electron microscopy.

Other Characteristics:

  • Eosinophils (A): Eosinophils are often found in LCH lesions, but they are not specific or diagnostic.
  • Histiocytes (C): While Langerhans cells are a type of histiocyte, their presence alone is not specific for LCH.
  • Granulomas (D): Granulomas may be present but are not a defining feature of LCH.

Key Diagnostic Features of LCH:

  1. Immunohistochemistry:
    • LCH cells express CD1a, CD207 (Langerin), and S100.
  2. Birbeck Granules:
    • Found on electron microscopy and are specific to LCH.

question_text: Question: A 14-year-old boy presents with back pain and pain in both ankles and left knee. When he bends forward, his lower spine remains straight. There is localized tenderness around the left foot. Likely Diagnosis?
explanation:
Ankylosing spondylitis is one of a group of diseases - spondyloarthropathies - which also includes arthritis following inflammatory bowel diseases and chronic reactive arthritis following enteric or genitourinary tract infection.

  • They are characterized by inflammation of the joints and involvement of the axial skeleton.
  • Enthesitis is present and characterized by inflammation at the sites of attachment of ligaments, tendons, fascies and capsules.
  • The diagnosis of a spondyloarthropathy is suggested by onset in an older child with oligoarthritis affecting the hips, knees or ankles and accompanied by enthesitis.
  • Radiographic evidence will help in diagnosing ankylosing spondylitis, and shows evidence of sacroiliitis in the form of extensive sclerosis, erosions of joint margins and apparent widening of the joint space.
  • HLA-B27 occurs in 90% of patients with juvenile ankylosing spondylitis (JAS). The ESR can be high. Iridocyclitis occurs in a quarter of patients with JAS.
  • Controlling pain and minimizing inflammation is the treatment target for these patients.

question_text: Identify this anomaly in a neonate?
explanation:
In classic bladder exstrophy, the bladder protrudes from the abdominal wall and its mucosa is exposed. The umbilicus is displaced downward, the pubic rami are widely separated in the midline, and the rectus muscles are separated.

  • In boys, there are complete epispadias with dorsal chordee, and the overall penile length is approximately half that of unaffected boys. The scrotum typically is separated slightly from the penis and is wide and shallow. Undescended testes and inguinal hernias are common.
  • Girls also have epispadias, with separation of the 2 halves of the clitoris and wide separation of the labia. The anus is displaced anteriorly in both sexes, and there may be rectal prolapse. The pubic rami are widely separated.
  • Persons with exstrophy tend to be shorter than normal.

Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 20th ed, pg. 2575

question_text: A 9-year-old boy complains of sharp shooting pain in right pelvic region for 2 days associated with vomiting. The pain is not relieved with common analgesics. explanation:

Option C: If diagnosis still uncertain, consider low-dose non-contrast CT scan of kidneys, ureters and bladder.

Option B: The CT is more likely to pick up stones smaller than 3mm, but due to radiation, USG remains the first line.

Option D: MRI is used for soft tissue lesions.

KEY TAKEAWAYS: The first line of investigation for Renal stones is Abdominal ultrasound.

question_text: A 4-year-old girl presents with difficulty in going upstairs and leg pains. She is always tired, feels hot and has had some weight loss. The family doctor has seen her on several occasions for eczema that appears on her face and hands. It will disappear and come back within days, even without treatment. The muscle enzyme is 1500 mmol/l, and ESR is 90, with thrombocytosis. Lactate dehydrogenase is high, as is ANA.
explanation:
• Juvenile dermatomyositis is the most common inflammatory myopathy in children. It can progress slowly with fatiguability, a low-grade fever and loss of weight, all of which are common.
  • The rash usually appears first over exposed areas, followed by proximal weakness. Periorbital violaceous (heliotropic) erythema occurs across the nasal bridge and around the eyelids. It may involve the upper torso, hands and especially the knuckles. Facial edema is common.
  • Creatinine kinase will be very high, and aldolase, serum aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) will be high, but not specific. An MRI scan is also helpful in diagnosis by using T2-weighted images and fat suppression. This will show the active site of the disease, helping muscle biopsy and EMG testing.
  • Corticosteroids, methotrexate and cyclosporine can be used in management. Long-term complications are calcification and calcified nodules with cardiomyopathies.

KEY TAKEAWAYS: Dermatomyositis is a rare autoimmune disease marked by muscle weakness and a distinctive skin rash, often purple in color, affecting areas like the eyelids and knuckles. It primarily impacts the shoulders, hips, and thighs, making everyday movements difficult. Treatment includes corticosteroids and immunosuppressive drugs to control inflammation and prevent muscle damage.

question_text: A 5-year-old child developed diphtheria and was managed appropriately. He has a 3-year-old sibling with whom he had close contact. The sibling is immunized with DPT and had got last diphtheria booster about 22 months back. What is to be done with the contact?

explanation:
Exposure of close contacts to Diphtheria Patient. How to manage?

  • Immunized asymptomatic individuals who have not received a diphtheria toxoid booster within 5 years and inadequately immunized individuals all should receive a diphtheroid toxoid vaccine.

Since this child got DPT booster at appropriate time 22 months back, he needs to be given only antimicrobial prophylaxis.

question_text: A 7-year-old girl is taken for a health check-up as her parents feel she is too short. Her height is less than the 3rd centile and she has non-pitting edema of both lower limbs. Her blood pressure is 130/92mmHg in both upper limbs and a radio femoral delay is noted on simultaneous palpation of pulses. What additional finding do you expect on general examination of this girl?
explanation:
The patient in the scenario has short stature, hypertension, non-pitting edema on limbs suggesting lymphedema and examination findings consistent with coarctation of the aorta (HTN + Radio-femoral delay). All these are suggestive of Turner Syndrome.

  • Both bicuspid aortic valves and coarctation of the aorta are common among individuals with Turner syndrome.
  • Bicuspid aortic valves occur in up to 50% of patients with Turner syndrome while coarctation of aorta occurs in up to 20% of cases.
  • Physical findings in patients with Turner syndrome include nonpitting edema of the lower extremities, wide spaced nipples and webbing of neck.

question_text: A 5-year-old girl with a family history of bronchial asthma, presents to emergency with a history of difficulty in breathing. She is sitting, not talking, and looks very anxious. Her saturation in 5 L of oxygen via a facemask is <90%. She is using her accessory muscles, has no audible wheeze and is a known asthmatic. She was playing outside when her mother found her crying and noticed that her breathing was very shallow. She gave her 10 puffs of salbutamol via a spacer and brought her to hospital. What are the plans of action for this patient?
option_c: Intravenous Magnesium Sulphate can be considered
explanation:
As per the details given, the child is having Life-threatening asthma (SpO2 <90% despite oxygen, silent chest without wheeze, anxiety).

  • For life-threatening asthma, previously called as status asthmaticus, all the above-mentioned modalities are started.
  • They should receive Oxygen, Injection of Terbutaline or Adrenaline Subcutaneously, Nebulization with Salbutamol, with or without Ipratropium Bromide.
  • An injection of 5 mg/kg Hydrocortisone is given intravenously and patient is transferred to Pediatric ICU
  • If no improvement or deteriorates, we can consider a slow IV infusion of Magnesium Sulphate (50 mg/Kg). Theophylline can also be considered as an alternative.
  • If there is no improvement in clinical status, intubation and mechanical ventilation is the eventual resort.

question_text: Drug of choice for chest-indrawing pneumonia in a one year old child is?
explanation:
According to latest guidelines, oral amoxicillin at a dose of 80 mg/kg in 2 divided doses is recommended for pneumonia as well as chest-indrawing pneumonia in children aged 2 months to 5 years.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 815

question_text: Most common cause of empyema in a child aged 2 years is?
explanation:
Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of empyema in young children upto 2 to 3 yr of age. In older children Strep pyogenes is more common.

Also note the criteria to define empyema

  • The effusion is an empyema if bacteria are present on Gram staining, the pH is 100,000 neutrophils/µL

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 429

question_text: A 3-year-old boy has complaints of chronic cough, foul-smelling bulky and sticky stools, poor weight gain. On kissing the child, salty taste is felt by the parents. History of sibling death who had similar complaints. CFTR gene mutation was detected. Which ion abnormality should be checked for confirmation of the diagnosis
explanation:
Poor weight gain, steatorrhea, chronic cough & salty kiss are all indicative of Cystic Fibrosis.

  • Cystic Fibrosis is due to CFTR gene mutations, which produce Chloride channel dysfunction or absence, producing the characteristic features.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 432

question_text: Nasal Nitric Oxide measurement is useful to screen for which among the following conditions?
explanation:
Studies showed that nasal nitric oxide concentrations are reduced in subjects with Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia (PCD).

  • Because nasal nitric oxide measurements are relatively easy to perform and non-invasive, this method is a promising screen and potentially a diagnostic test for PCD, provided that cystic fibrosis has been excluded.
  • Currently this is used as a screening test for PCD in children aged 5 years and above.
  • Nasal nitric oxide during plateau <77 nL/min on 2 occasions, >2 months apart (with CF excluded) is suggestive of PCD.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 433

question_text: A child with noisy breathing was found to have stridor on examination. His laryngoscopic finding is as shown below. What is the likely type of stridor in this child?
explanation:
The child is having laryngomalacia since he has stridor & laryngoscopy showing the typical omega-epiglottis.

  • In Laryngomalacia, supraglottic part of the larynx is involved, and thus most patients have episodic or intermittent inspiratory stridor.
  • Remember the concept
    • Supraglottic Obstruction: Inspiratory Stridor is present
    • Infraglottic or Trachel Obstruction: Biphasic Stridor is present

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition

question_text:
Which of the following treatments must be used when a child presents in Status asthmaticus?
1. Chest X ray
2. Salbutamol nebulization
3. Oxygen supplementation
4. Oral prednisolone
explanation:
Management strategy of Status asthmaticus includes:

  • Supplemental oxygen
  • Bronchodilators- Levosalbutamol/Albuterol/Terbutaline
  • Systemic corticosteroids- Prednisolone or Hydrocortisone
  • Anticholinergics- Ipratropium
  • Adrenaline Injection can be considered
  • Refractory Cases: IV MgSO4 or IV Theophylline Infusions
  • Last Resort: Intubation & Mechanical Ventilation
  • There is no immediate role of Chest x ray in an established case of Asthma.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 415; Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1st SA ed., pg. 1106

question_text: All the following PFT findings in a child are suggestive of asthma except?
option_a: Increase in FEV1>12% after salbutamol inhalation
option_d: Day and night variation of FEV1 >15%
explanation:
Lung Function Abnormalities in Asthma

  • Spirometry (in clinic):
    • Airflow limitation:
      • Low FEV1 (relative to percentage of predicted norms)
      • FEV1: FVC ratio <0.80
  • Bronchodilator response (to inhaled β-agonist): Improvement in FEV1 ≥12% and ≥200 mL
  • Exercise challenge: Worsening in FEV1 ≥15%
  • Daily peak flow or FEV1 monitoring: day to day and/or A.M.-to-P.M. variation ≥20%

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 408; Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 20th ed., 1099

question_text: Chloride level is tested in which disease?
explanation:
The sweat test, which involves using pilocarpine iontophoresis to collect sweat and performing chemical analysis of its chloride content, is the standard approach to diagnosis of Cystic Fibrosis.

  1. Cystic fibrosis is an inherited disease caused by mutations in a gene called the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene.

Reference: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics, 20th ed., pg. 2104

question_text: A child has been diagnosed recently as Cystic Fibrosis and his gene analysis report revealed deletion in Phenylalanine residue at position 508. What class of mutation does it belong to?
explanation:
Six Classes of mutations producing Cystic Fibrosis

  • Among these, most common mutations are in Class 2, which includes Delta F508, now known as Del508 Phe mutation.
  • Deletion at 508 position is the most common cause of Cystic Fibrosis overall.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 432

question_text: All of the following new molecular agents are CFTR correctors except?
explanation:
The new molecular agents used in Cystic Fibrosis belong to broadly 2 categories

  1. CFTR Potentiators: Potentiate & facilitate channel opening. These work best in Class 3 mutations like G551D. Example: Ivacaftor
  2. CFTR Correctors: Facilitate proper processing and trafficking of the channel to the cell surface. These work best in Class 2 mutations like Del508Phe. Examples include Tezacaftor, Elexacaftor & Lumacaftor.

Note: Many commercial preparations combine both category of drugs to have a synergistic action.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 432, Cystic Fibrosis Foundation Guidelines

question_text: Kartagener Syndrome is characterized by all of the following except?
explanation:
Kartagener Syndrome is characterized by a triad of

  • Bronchiectasis
  • Situs Inversus
  • Sinusitis

Please note that Kartagener Syndrome occurs in about 50% patients with Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 433

question_text: A 7-year-old child with a strong family history of bronchial asthma has multiple episodes of wheeze and cough whenever he plays or runs. He is diagnosed with exercise-induced bronchoconstriction. What shall be the prophylaxis of choice?
explanation:
Very Controversial. Read carefully. No cut-copy-paste here.

  • As per GINA 2023 guidelines, regular treatment with inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) like Budesonide significantly reduces exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (EIB).
  • Training and sufficient warm-up prior to exercise also reduce the incidence and severity of EIB.
  • Now as per OP Ghai 10th Edition, taking SABA prior to exercise can prevent EIB. However for regular prophylaxis, their use has limitations.
  • According to GINA 2023 guidelines, Use of SABA, LABA and oral chromones like Sodium Cromoglycate prior to exercise can be beneficial, but tolerance develops to their use, restricting long-term efficacy
  • Limited data is there regarding usefulness of Montelukast for EIB.
  • Hence the answer here is Inhaled Budesonide. In future MCQs, if ICS not in options, SABA can be the next best possible answer.

Reference: GINA 2023 Guidelines- Full Report, Page 114; OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 414

question_text: All of the following vaccines are excluded from open vial policy except?
explanation:
Open vial policy allows reuse of previously open multi-dose vials of vaccines upto 4 weeks, provided the vaccines are stored aseptically, the cold chain is maintained and the expiry date has not crossed.

  • Under UIP, its used in OPV, DT, DPT, TT etc.
  • Not applicable in BCG, MR, Rotavirus and JE

Rotavirus vaccine is NOT a part of Open Vial Policy. There is no such update. Vaccines come as a single use vials only, in the NIS now.

Reference: Guidelines on Open Vial Policy for using multi-dose vials in Universal Immunization Program. MoHFW, Immunization Division, New Delhi, India. 2015.

question_text: A baby has received BCG at birth and has been vaccinated at 14 weeks. Which of the following shall be given on the next visit, along with route and site?
option_a: MR Vaccine s.c. on left arm & Oral Vit A, at 9 months completed
option_b: MR Vaccine s.c. on right arm & Oral Vit A, at 9 months completed
option_c: MR Vaccine s.c. on left arm & Oral Vit A, at 8 months completed
option_d: MR Vaccine s.c. on right arm & Oral Vit A, at 8 months completed
explanation:
As per National Immunization Schedule, the child will next require vaccination at 9-12 months, i.e., 9 completed months of age. Vaccines given are

  1. MR Vaccine- Dose of 0.5 ml subcutaneously, given in right upper arm at the insertion of deltoid.
  2. Oral Vitamin A Drops- 1 Lakh IU Given Orally

In addition, JE vaccine is given in endemic areas and since 2023, 3rd dose of fractional IPV has also been introduced at 9-12 months of age.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 198

question_text: Are all the following statements about the vaccine vial monitor are correct except?
option_a: If the inner square is lighter than outer circle, use the vaccine
option_b: If the inner square is changing colour but still lighter than outer circle, use the vaccine
option_c: If the inner square is same as outer circle, use the vaccine
option_d: If the inner square is darker than outer circle, discard the vaccine
explanation: Reference: IAP guidebook on immunization, 3rd ed., pg. 64

question_text: A child reports to you at 1 year of age. He has received DPT at 6 weeks of age but was lost to follow-up. What should be the next vaccination strategy regarding DPT vaccine?
option_a: DPT full course should be repeated
option_b: Only DT needs to be given now
explanation:
If a primary dose of DPT, IPV, Hib, PCV, Hep A, Hep B or MR vaccine is missed, subsequent immunization should be given at the next visit as if the usual interval had elapsed.

  • OP Ghai Textbook says 'A delay or lapse in the administration of a dose does not require the schedule to be repeated; the missed dose is administered and the course resumed at the point it was interrupted. Delaying the dose does not affect adversely the rates of seroconversion or titers.

Reference: Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 188; WHO Update March 2023; IAP guidebook of immunization, 2018, pg. 87

question_text: Which of the following vaccines do you recommend for a 10-year-old school child according to the national immunization schedule?
explanation:
According to NIP, at 10 and 16 years of age, Td vaccine is recommended.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 197

question_text: Dengvaxia is a globally licensed vaccine against Dengue, but is not available in India owing to concerns over a specific adverse effect. What is that adverse effect?
explanation:
Dengvaxia is the only dengue vaccine, which has been licensed for global use.

  • Children aged 9-16 years living in endemic areas and with laboratory confirmation of previous dengue infection are eligible
  • Requires 3 doses at 0,6 and 12 months.
  • Has relatively low protection against Type 2 dengue Infection.
  • Large scale implementation has not been done in India yet owing to safety concerns.
  • One particular concern is the risk of severe dengue infection in those were initially seronegative for any dengue infection.
  • Two more Dengue Vaccines- LATV and DenVax are currently in Phase III Clinical Trials.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 211

question_text: Japanese B Encephalitis Vaccine is recommended in the National Immunization Schedule in endemic areas. Which type of JE Vaccine is currently used in NIS?
option_c: Inactivated Vero cell culture derived Kolar strain
explanation:
The current JE vaccine used is JENVAC.

JENVAC is a single dose inactivated Japanese Encephalitis (JE) Vaccine.

This Vero cell derived vaccine is prepared from an Indian strain (Kolar- 821564XY) of the JE virus.

JENVAC has been developed in collaboration with the National Institute of Virology, India.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Pages 202-203

question_text: A 10-week-old child has come for vaccination. In the previous visit at 6 weeks, post-vaccination, the child had developed fever of 40 C and inconsolable crying for 1 hour. What next should be done?
explanation:
The question is a tricky one. In the previous visit at 6 weeks, following DPT vaccine, the child had fever of 40 Degrees Celsius & inconsolable crying for 1 hour. Please note that none of them is contraindication or precaution to use of DPT in the next visit. Hence, the child should receive DPT Vaccine safely in the next visit at 10 weeks.

  • Contraindications for DPT Vaccine
    1. Anaphylaxis after the previous dose
    2. Encephalopathy within 7 days of the dose
    3. Progressive neurological disease- Relative Contraindication
  • Precautions for DPT Vaccine
    1. Fever >40.5 Degrees Celsius within 48 hours
    2. Hypotonic-Hyporesponsive Episode in <48 hr
    3. Persistent inconsolable crying for >3 hours
    4. Seizures in <72 hours

Kindly note that if there is any contraindication, DPT vaccine should not be used. If any event mentioned in Precautions is seen with the previous vaccine & then in the 2nd vaccine too, then we change DPT to DT vaccine in the 3rd visit.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 196

question_text: An unvaccinated 13-month child comes to your clinic. What vaccines will be given at the 1st visit?
explanation:
Remember the concept that under national immunization schedule, the upper limit for catch-up vaccine in missed doses is 1 year for BCG, Pentavalent & Rotavirus Vaccines. Now since the age of this patient is >1 year, he can not receive BCG, Pentavalent and Rotavirus vaccines. This leaves only option D as the plausible vaccines which can be given in a 13 month old child.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Pages 192, 196 and 201

question_text: All are seen in Henoch-Schoenlein Purpura, except?
explanation:
Palpable purpura in HSP occur in the absence of any platelet abnormalities.

  • Diagnostic criteria for HSP/IgA Vasculitis: Palpable purpura (on buttocks & lower limbs) plus any 2 of the following
  1. Diffuse Abdominal Pain
  2. Tissue biopsy showing IgA deposits
  3. Arthritis or Arthralgia
  4. Renal involvement in the form of glomerulonephritis

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Ed, Box 22.4

question_text: A 6-year-old male was admitted with complaints of fatigue and mild joint pains. On examination, rash was found on the hands as shown in the image. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The diagnosis is Juvenile Dermatomyositis.

  • Fatigue is an early sign of muscle weakness. That along with the characteristic Gottron papules in the image suggest a diagnosis of Juvenile Dermatomyositis.
  • Please note that as per Nelson 21st Ed, 22-58% of JDM patients also have arthralgia and arthritis.

Reference: Nelson 21st Ed, Chapter 184, OP Ghai 10th Ed, Pages 656-657

question_text: Hallmark finding in IgA vasculitis is?
explanation:
Presence of palpable purpuric rash is a hallmark of HSP, seen in 95-100% of all patients.

Diagnostic criteria for HSP/IgA Vasculitis: Palpable purpura (on buttocks & lower limbs) plus any 2 of the following

  • Diffuse Abdominal Pain
  • Tissue biopsy showing IgA deposits
  • Arthritis or Arthralgia
  • Renal involvement in the form of glomerulonephritis
  • the form of glomerulonephritis

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Ed, Box 22.4, Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 192.1

question_text: Risk of chronic renal disease in HSP?
explanation:
Chances of chronic renal disease in HSP

  • As per OP Ghai 10th Edition, risk is 1-5%
  • As per Nelson 21st Edition, Chronic renal disease develops in 1-2% of children with HSP

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Ed, Page 661, Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 192.1

question_text:
A 5-year-old child with multiple hyperpigmented brown macules on the body was also found to have similar findings in axillary region. His IQ was normal but brain MRI revealed basal ganglia hyperintensities on T2-weighed image, without any mass effect, as shown below.

Repeat MRI done in the child 2 years later showed disappearance of these lesions. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Let us go stepwise here

  • A child with multiple hyperpigmented brown macules suggests presence of Café-au-lait macules.
  • Similar hyperpigmented lesions in axilla suggests Axillary Freckling.
  • Likely diagnosis is NF-1
  • Now, MRI shows hyperintensities on T2 in basal ganglia which disappeared after some years.
  • This suggests the finding of UBO- Unidentified bright objects. These Are Abnormal hyperintense signals on T2 in optic tract, globus pallidus, brain stem, cerebellum.
  • As age increases → UBOs Reduce and Disappear
  • Significance is not clear, but is a highly interesting finding seen in children with NF-1

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 614

question_text: Which among the following is not compatible with a diagnosis of Neurofibromatosis-1?
option_a: 6 café-au-lait macules of size 18 mm in post-pubertal male
option_c: 3 Lisch nodules in iris on one side
explanation: Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Table 19.2, Page 576

question_text: A 12-year-old male presents to pediatric OPD with a rough, raised, scaly, yellow-white lesion on the lower back. His mother tells you that the child has some kind of intellectual disability. She also tells you that last night the boy had an attack of abnormal body movements lasting for about 5 minutes. What is the most likely diagnosis in this case?
explanation:
Let us go systematically here and interpret the information provided.

  • Rough, raised, scaly, yellow-white lesion on the lower back is likely to be Shagreen Patch.
  • Intellectual disability and seizure-like episode indicate likely CNS Involvement
  • CNS Involvement + Skin manifestations like Shagreen Patch/Adenoma Sebaceum or Ash-leaf macules indicate Tuberous Sclerosis as the likely Possibility.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 576

question_text: An adolescent girl complains of dropping objects from hands, it gets precipitated during morning. There is no H/O loss of consciousness and her cousin sister has been diagnosed with epilepsy. EEG was s/o epileptic seizures. What's the diagnosis?
explanation:
The patient is suffering from Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy (JME)

Quick Review of Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy

  • Also known as JANZ Syndrome
  • Onset: 12 - 18 years → Adulthood
  • Sex: Female > Male
  • Strong positive family history
  • Many genes eg: CACNB, GABRA-I
    • Morphology
      1. Myoclonic Jerks (100%)
        • Awake state, Increases in morning
        • Precipitated by
          1. Awaking from sleep,
          2. Lack of sleep-in preceding night
        • Frequent fall of objects
      2. GTCS (50 - 90%)
      3. Absence Seizures (25%)
  • No Mental retardation
    • EEG → 4 to 6 Hz Polyspike & Slow wave patterns
  • DOC: Valproate
    • 2nd line - Lamotrigine, Levetiracetam

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 611

question_text: A Pediatric 8 yr old patient presented with GTCS convulsions lasting >45 minutes. What shall be the appropriate management in patient?
explanation:
The child is having Status Epilepticus & the management entails using BZDs like Lorazepam as 1st line therapy, followed by using Antiepileptics like Phenytoin, Valproate & Levetiracetam. Remember that BZDs are always the 1st drug to be given.

As per IAP 2022 Guidelines, the initial management in the first 5 minutes of any child presenting with status epilepticus is as follows:

Reference: IAP Standard Treatment Guidelines 2022- Evaluation and Management of Status Epilepticus in Children, OP Ghai 10th Edition

question_text: Cerebral perfusion pressure equals?
explanation:
A major determinant of brain injury and prognosis in patients with head trauma and raised ICP is cerebral perfusion pressure.

  • Cerebral Perfusion Pressure (CPP) = MAP - ICP or CVP (whichever is highest)
  • Cerebral Blood Flow (CBF) = CPP/CVR [CVR = cerebral vascular resistance]
  • This implies that CPP & CBF depend on both MAP and ICP
  • In hypovolemia, MAP falls and cause reduction in CBF
  • Likewise, in raised ICP, CBF can fall and can cause CNS injury by reduction in CBF

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 85

question_text:
A child presented with multiple small nodular swellings on the body and axillary examination showed hyperpigmentation as shown in the picture. There is a positive family history for these lesions.

Which among the following is the most likely tumour the child will develop?
explanation:
This child is showing axillary freckling in picture. Nodular swellings may be seen due to neurofibromas. Hence the diagnosis is NF-1.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 576

question_text: Which of the following factors are not associated with recurrence of febrile seizure?
explanation:
Risk factors for recurrence of febrile seizures

Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 20th ed., pg. 2829

question_text:
A child aged 6 years has episodes of frequent falls, progressive muscle weakness and his lower limbs are shown below

Which among the following is not true regarding such a child?
option_d: Serum CPK may be normal in late stages
explanation:
This is a child with Pseudohypertrophy of calf muscles with muscular weakness, leading to frequent falls. This is consistent with a diagnosis of Duchenne's muscular dystrophy.

Features include

  • X-linked recessive inheritance; mainly seen in boys
  • Age of onset between 2-6 years; frequent falls are common
  • Cardiomyopathy may be seen
  • Pseudohypertrophy of calf muscles and deltoid may be seen
  • IQ may be normal or low
  • Serum CPK is massively elevated but may return to normal in terminal stages once atrophy kicks in.
  • Muscle biopsy and gene analysis are confirmatory
  • Average life expectancy is 20 years. Treatment is mainly supportive.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Pages 614 - 616

question_text: A 3-month old infant has the following EEG report. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The child is having chaotic EEG, with multifocal high voltage spikes, suggestive of hypsarrhythmia. Classically seen in Infantile spasm (also known as West syndrome), which is a severe myoclonic epilepsy of infancy.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 582

question_text: ACTH is the drug of choice for?
explanation:
West syndrome is best treated with ACTH.

  • High-dose ACTH is preferred over low-dose ACTH
  • Vigabatrin is considered by some as a drug of second choice for infantile spasms and by some even as an alternative to ACTH as a drug of first choice in Tuberous Sclerosis patients.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 582, AOCN 2021 Guidelines On West Syndrome

question_text: A patient has been diagnosed as Guillain-Barre Syndrome. All of the following will be effective in the management of this patient except?
explanation:
Steroids, e.g., Prednisolone do not have any role in the management of GBS.

  • IVIG is the initial drug of choice, in a dose of 2 g/kg given over 3-5 days
  • Plasma exchange, also called as Plasmapheresis is effective in those patients where IVIG is either not available or there is any restriction to its use
  • Chest physiotherapy is recommended in most patients of GBS, especially those who are admitted in ICU and receiving ventilation, to reduce the chances of pulmonary impaction & hypostasis pneumonia.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Page 610; Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 634

question_text: Arnold Chiari malformation is a common association of?
explanation:
Among the options listed, Meningomyelocele is a common association of Chiari-2 malformations, also called as Arnold-Chiari Malformation.

  • Hydrocephalus in association with a type II Chiari malformation develops in at least 80% of patients with myelomeningocele.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 609

question_text: Tongue fasciculations are a characteristic feature of?
explanation:
Tongue fasciculation is typical of LMN nerve dysfunction and indicates progressive denervation.

  • SMA is a LMN disorder that has a floppy child with severe hypotonia, atrophic muscles and tongue fasciculations.
  • Myasthenia is a condition of NM junction
  • DMD is a muscular disorder.
  • GBS is a demyelinating disorder with bilateral symmetrical ascending paraparesis

Reference: Nelson textbook of Pediatrics, 20th ed., pg. 2997

question_text: A 12-year-old boy was playing cricket and got a nasty bouncer, hitting him on head and producing a concussion. Which of the following symptoms after a concussion would warrant further evaluation with neuroimaging?
option_d: Inability to recall his mobile phone
explanation:
In a child with concussion injury to the head

  • Persistent amnesia would warrant further evaluation with imaging.
  • Nausea, fatigue, and difficulty falling asleep are symptoms of concussion that can last several weeks to even months but do not require imaging.

Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1st SA edition, pg. 3350

question_text: A seven-day-old neonate presents with recurrent seizures. Examination reveals tachycardia, S3 gallop, and bruit in anterior fontanelle. Blood investigations are normal. Transcranial USG shows a hypoechoic lesion. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A Neonate with High-Output CCF, bruit in skull in midline and transcranial USG showing a hypoechoic lesion → Vein Of Galen Malformation (VGM).

  • Cause of VGM: Abnormal Persistence of Median Prosencephalic Vein- MPV
  • Treatment: Endoscopic embolization → Surgery

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 609

question_text: SCN1A gene mutations are responsible for which among the following epilepsy syndrome?
explanation:
Dravet syndrome is the most severe of the phenotypic spectrum of febrile seizure-associated epilepsies. Mutations in the SCN1A gene are the most common cause of Dravet syndrome (causing ~ 80% of all cases).

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 611

question_text: Persistent "commando crawl" at one year of age indicates which among the following?
explanation:
Signs in Diplegic Cerebral Palsy

  1. Scissoring of gait
  2. Commando Crawl: Child drags body forward using Upper Limbs.
  3. Fisting of hands- Child usually keeps both the fists tightly closed

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 611

question_text: A 12-year-old healthy boy has noticed some muscle weakness. He has experienced increasing difficulty lifting his backpack and walking long distances. He has no trouble with schoolwork, and he continues to play the piano and video games without tiring. His 38-year-old maternal uncle recently became wheelchair bound for unclear reasons. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This patient does not have muscle weakness that precludes extended use of distal muscles (hands) or limits his manual dexterity.

  • The child's presentation at age 12 years and a 38-year-old wheelchair-bound maternal uncle suggest a diagnosis of Becker muscular dystrophy.
  • Remember that DMD has onset before 5 to 7 years of age!

Reference: Nelson textbook of pediatrics, 1st SA edition, pg. 2977

question_text: Folic acid requirement in pregnancy for prevention of neural tube defects in a lady with previous pregnancy having neural tube defect is?
explanation:
Prevention or prophylaxis of NTDs

  • Done Via Peri-conceptional folate supplementation
  • Ideally started 1 month prior to conception and given daily at least till 12 weeks of gestation
  • Every pregnancy: 0.4 mg/day (400 g/day)
  • In Previous NTD: 4 mg/day (4000 g/day)- Produces 72% risk reduction in NTDs

Reference: AIIMS NICU Protocols 3rd Edition- Additional Protocols, CDC Guidelines

question_text: Identify the incorrect match for the drug used and the underlying condition?
explanation:
Let us evaluate each option individually

  • Option A is incorrect. Eteplirsen, also known as Exondys-51, is a novel exon-skipping gene therapy, useful in patients of Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy. The drug is FDA approved for DMD patients and is considered a type of ASO= Antisense oligonucleotide agent
  • Option B is correct, Nusinersen is used intrathecally in Spinal Muscular Atrophy and acts by partially activating the SMN-2 gene.
  • Option C is correct. High-dose ACTH is the first-line therapy in patients with West Syndrome.
  • Option D is correct. Everolimus is an mTOR inhibitor, useful in Subependymal Giant Cell Astrocytomas (SEGAs) which are not amenable to surgery.

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapters 627 & 630; OP Ghai 10th Edition, Table 20.5, Page 608.

question_text: A neonate was stillborn. His image is as depicted below. Likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Craniorachischisis is characterized by the combination of anencephaly (absence of the brain and cranial vault, without skin covering) with a contiguous bony defect of the cervical spine (also without meninges covering the neural tissue - rachischisis). It is a severe and rare type of neural tube defect and is usually not compatible with life.

Reference: CDC Guidelines- Birth Defects Surveillance Toolkit

question_text: A neonate was born to a mother who did not take folic acid during pregnancy. The baby was absolutely asymptomatic at birth, except for the lesion in the midline back as shown below. Likely possibility?
explanation:
Pregnant mother not taking folic acid is a risk factor for neural tube defects. The image shown is a tuft of hair in the lumbosacral region. This is a cutaneous marker of underlying spina bifida occulta, also known as Occult spinal dysraphism. The patients are asymptomatic and do not require any specific therapy.

Remember- Cutaneous markers for spina bifida occulta include

  • Tuft of hair
  • Lipoma
  • Dermal sinus
  • Hemangioma

Reference: Nelson 21st Edition, Chapter 609

question_text: A 3-year-old child has been diagnosed as a case of pyogenic meningitis on 1st January 2024. He was started on IV Ceftriaxone on the same day at 9 AM after admission and was isolated. From what date onwards, the child can come out of isolation and will be considered non-infectious to others?
explanation:
The question seems tricky, but is not and is a highly-important, applied clinical knowledge kind of question expected for NEXT & INI-CET level.

  • The funda is clear- Any child with pyogenic meningitis, when started on IV 3rd generation cephalosporins, will become non-infectious and CSF will become sterile within 24 hours of the antibiotic therapy initiation.
  • Since here it was started at 9 AM on 1st January, 2024; so the child will not require isolation after 2nd January, 2024, 9 AM onwards.

Reference: Nelson 20th Edition, Page 2941

question_text: In a small child diagnosed with H influenzae associated meningitis, what investigation is needed at follow-up?
explanation:

question_text: A 4-year-old child presented with abdominal pain which was acute in nature, vomiting and progressive lethargy. There was red-currant jelly stools and contrast enema revealed coiled spring sign. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
In typical cases of intussusception, there is sudden onset, in a previously well child, of severe paroxysmal colicky pain that recurs at frequent intervals and is accompanied by straining efforts with legs and knees flexed and loud cries.

  • At times, the lethargy is disproportionate to the abdominal signs. Eventually, a shock-like state, with fever and peritonitis, can develop.
  • Vomiting occurs in most cases and is usually more frequent in the early phase. In the later phase, the vomitus becomes bile stained.
  • 60% of infants pass a stool containing red blood and mucus, the currant jelly stool.
  • The diagnostic findings of intussusception on ultrasound include a tubular mass in longitudinal views and a doughnut or target appearance in transverse images.
  • Contrast enemas demonstrate a filling defect or cupping in the head of the contrast media where its advance is obstructed by the intussusceptum.
  • A central linear column of contrast media may be visible in the compressed lumen of the intussusceptum, and a thin rim of contrast may be seen trapped around the invaginating intestine in the folds of mucosa within the intussuscipiens (coiled-spring sign), especially after evacuation.

Reference: OP Ghai 10th Edition, Pages 304-305

question_text: A 17-year-old girl presents to clinic with fatigue, pallor, and a recent history of easy bruising. She is afebrile. A complete blood count with differential reveals a neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated mean corpuscular volume, and her reticulocyte count is low. She is referred to a pediatric hematologist, and a diagnosis of severe aplastic anemia is confirmed, with a hemoglobin of 9.8 g/dL. What is the first-line therapy for this patient's condition?
explanation:
The only curative as well as 1st-line therapy in Aplastic Anemia is HSCT.

  • An allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the first-line therapy for a patient with severe or very severe aplastic anemia if a human leukocyte antigen-matched sibling donor can be identified. A cause should be identified if possible.
  • Pancytopenia is seen on a complete blood count of a person with aplastic anemia, associated with a low reticulocyte count. A bone marrow biopsy is performed to confirm the diagnosis, which also demonstrates low cellularity of all three cell lines. Severity of disease is based on bone marrow cellularity, absolute neutrophil count, platelet count, and absolute reticulocyte counts.
  • Please note that if HSCT is not possible, Horse Anti-Thymocyte Globulin (ATG) and Cyclosporine have been used. Thrombopoietin Receptor Agonists (TPO-RA) are often added but Granulocyte Colony-Stimulating Factor (G-CSF) is usually ineffective and can cause malignant transformation.

question_text: A child presented with proptosis. You suspect it to be a chloroma. Next investigation to make the diagnosis, among the following, is?

question_text: A 2-month-old male infant is brought to your office for a health supervision visit. When discussing vaccines, his mother reports that her daughter had an intussusception that was reduced by the radiologist. question_text: A 6 year old female presents with recurrent episodes of 'day dreaming'. Parents report during these episodes they are not responsive to any stimuli and then come round and will not be aware of the episode. Similar events are occurring at school. You diagnose the child with absence seizures, which medication would be most appropriate to start?
explanation:
• History is typical of absence seizures characterized by brief staring spells, with no awareness. There is associated poor scholastic performance.

Absence seizures, also known as "petit mal seizures," are brief, sudden lapses in awareness, often lasting only a few seconds. These seizures are most common in children but can also occur in adults. Here are the main characteristics:

Key Characteristics of Absence Seizures:

  • Brief Duration: Usually last between 5-10 seconds, rarely longer than 20 seconds.
  • Sudden Onset: The child or adult may suddenly stop speaking or lose focus, appearing to "stare into space".
  • Lack of Response: During the seizure, the person is unresponsive to external stimuli.
  • Automatic Movements: Some individuals may exhibit slight twitching, blinking, or hand movements.
  • Rapid Recovery: After the seizure, the person usually resumes activities immediately, with no memory of the event.
  • First line of management is Ethosuximide in typical absence seizures and Valproate in Atypical absence seizures.

KEY TAKEAWAYS: Absence seizures are brief episodes of staring or "spacing out," lasting only a few seconds, during which a person is unresponsive. They often occur in children and may involve subtle movements like blinking, with immediate recovery and no memory of the event.

question_text: An infant with repeated attacks of seizures has hypsarrhythmia on EEG. She is a known case of tuberous sclerosis. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
• Hypsarrhythmia in EEG is typical of infantile spasms. It is one of the major features of patients with Tuberous sclerosis.

Infantile spasms (IS), also known as West syndrome, are a rare but severe form of epilepsy that typically begins in infants aged 3-12 months. These spasms appear as sudden, brief jerking movements that often occur in clusters, especially upon waking. Symptoms may include the baby bending forward at the waist, extending their arms and legs, or a "jackknife" movement.

KEY TAKEAWAYS: For infantile spasm DOC is ACTH.

For infantile spasm in Tuberous sclerosis, DOC is Vigabatrin.

question_text: A 4-year-old boy present to clinic with weakness and increased frequency of falls over the past month. His gait is weak, and Gower sign is positive. Purplish swelling of the eyelids is also noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• Dermatomyositis should be suspected in any child with symmetrical proximal muscle weakness and skin changes.
  • Proximal muscle weakness is manifest by difficulty in standing, getting out of bed, climbing stairs, or combing one's hair.
  • Falls may occur with increasing frequency.
  • Affected children may display the Gower sign, where they use their arms to climb up their legs into a standing position because their proximal musculature is too weak to support standing without assistance.


  • Skin manifestations of Dermatomyositis include a classic heliotrope rash and Gottron's papules.
  • Rash is not a manifestation of Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy.

question_text: A 15-year-old male patient presents with abdominal pain. For the past several months, he has had vague complaints of abdominal discomfort. He has felt "bloated" with little appetite. He also states that he is feeling more tired than normal and has been experiencing severe headaches. Although he has had some loose bowel movements, overall, they have been normal, and he that states no blood is apparent in his stool. Prior to this, the patient was healthy. You diagnose the patient with likely celiac disease. What is the first test in work up of the patient?
explanation:
• The screening test for celiac disease is IgA TTG levels.
  • However, If the clinical suspicion for celiac disease is strong and screening test is negative, consider performing an intestinal biopsy as most serologic tests have a sensitivity of 80- 90% and a specificity of 90-96%, with some degree of variation. As a result, it is possible that the tests will be falsely negative and should be followed, if suspicion warrants it, by a biopsy.
  • Delaying diagnosis and treatment is not recommended. If the follow-up test is positive, due to the equivocal nature of one positive and one negative test, it is likely that a biopsy would be performed anyway.
  • Ultrasound and MRI of the abdomen may show signs of inflammation but is not as helpful in the definitive diagnosis of celiac disease.

question_text: Evaluation of a 9-year-old girl with known SCD reveals right-sided weakness and slurring of speech without any associated pain. Her vital signs are within normal limits for her age. Which of the following screening tests might have helped to prevent this complication of SCD?
option_d: Annual neurologic assessments during well-child checks
explanation:
• Transcranial Doppler ultrasound should initially be performed at 2 years of age. If normal, it should be repeated annually until the patient is 16 years old.
  • TCD identifies children with sickle cell anemia who are at high risk for ischemic stroke by detecting elevated blood flow velocities in the cerebral arteries, indicating narrowing or increased resistance.
  • If two ultrasounds are abnormal, transfusion therapy typically is initiated and continued indefinitely to help prevent stroke.

Option A and B: CT and MRI without any signs of stroke are not indicated. A change in hemoglobin level does not indicate potential stroke in a patient with SCD, but may be concerning for infection or aplastic crisis.

Option D: Although neurological examinations are an important part of any physical examination, changes in the examination would indicate an already evolving process, rather than help to predict the potential for future disease.

KEY TAKEAWAYS: Regular TCD screening is a crucial component of stroke prevention in children with sickle cell anemia, allowing for early identification and intervention to reduce the risk of serious neurological complications.

question_text: A 10-year-old patient has a history of arthritis that started in the ankles, moved to the knees, and then shifted to the wrists. On physical examination, there is a fever (40°C) and a friction rub. Echocardiography reveals mitral valve prolapse and left ventricular dysfunction consistent with carditis. The laboratory results show an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate. How long before onset of symptoms does the infection associated with this diagnosis typically occur?
explanation:
• Acute rheumatic fever presents approximately 3 weeks after a group A Streptococcus infection.
  • Diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever (ARF) is based on the Jones criteria, which require evidence of a group A streptococcal infection and either 2 major criteria or 1 major and 2 minor criteria.
  • Major Jones criteria for ARF are
    • Polyarthritis
    • Carditis
    • Sydenham chorea
    • Subcutaneous nodules
    • Erythema marginatum.
  • Minor Jones criteria for ARF are
    • Fever
    • Arthralgia
    • Prolonged PR interval on electrocardiograph
    • Elevated acute-phase reactants

Key takeaways: The process begins with a streptococcal throat infection (pharyngitis) caused by GAS. Certain strains of this bacteria have proteins (like M proteins) that mimic proteins in human tissues, a phenomenon known as molecular mimicry.

question_text: A child presented with proptosis. You suspect it to be a chloroma. Next best investigation to make the diagnosis (among the following) is?
explanation:
Chloroma, also known as granulocytic sarcoma, is a rare extramedullary manifestation of acute myeloid leukemia (AML). It can present as proptosis when the orbit is involved. The best investigation to make the diagnosis of chloroma is a peripheral blood film, which helps identify the presence of myeloblasts. These cells are characteristic of AML and would confirm the diagnosis. In addition, chloromas are often associated with specific cytogenetic abnormalities, such as t(8;21) translocation.

While a bone marrow aspirate and flow cytometry are essential for definitive diagnosis, a peripheral blood smear is a practical, quick test to support the diagnosis. AML patients may also present with unusual symptoms such as "blueberry muffin" lesions, subcutaneous nodules, or infiltration of the gingiva, which can be helpful in diagnosing chloromas.

Incorrect Options:

  • Platelet count: Platelet counts may show thrombocytopenia in AML, but this is nonspecific and does not aid in the diagnosis of chloromas.
  • TLC/WBC Count: Total leukocyte count may show leukocytosis, but it does not provide specific information about the presence of chloromasor myeloblasts, making it insufficient for diagnosis.
  • Hemoglobin: Anemia is common in AML due to bone marrow failure, but hemoglobin levels are not specific for diagnosing chloromas or AML.

Key Takeaway:

  • Peripheral blood film is the best initial test to identify myeloblasts when chloroma is suspected.
  • Definitive diagnosis requires bone marrow aspirate, flow cytometry, and cytogenetic analysis.
  • Chloromas are extramedullary AML manifestationsand can cause symptoms such as proptosis, "blueberry muffin" lesions, and subcutaneous nodules in infants.

Polysaccharide vaccines Internationally marketed meningococcal polysaccharide vaccines are o Bivalent (A and C), Trivalent (A, C and W-135) Tetravalent (A, C, Y and W-135). The vaccines are purified, heat-stable, lyophilized capsular polysaccharides from meningococci of the respective serogroups. A protective antibody response occurs within 10 days of vaccination.
